# Twenty-six times faster line iteration in Python without leaving the Stable ABI

Bypassing Python's redundant buffering layer and scanning newlines in safe Rust speeds up line reads up to twenty-six times while keeping one universal abi3 wheel.

28 November 2026 · 7 min read · [Research result](<#5-where-the-stable-abi-boundary-really-sits>)

When a Rust decoder produces gigabytes per second, the slowest step in Python is often crossing the language boundary. Until recently, mibz2's Python package had optimised whole-file reads. Yet iterating line by line through a compressed log or JSON dump still paid for layers of CPython buffering that repeated work on every call.

We dissected every streaming entry point in mibz2's Python layer. That audit covered raw reader iteration, reading all lines, chunked reads, buffer fills, and whole-stream decompression. Removing extra copies and scanning newlines in safe Rust sped up raw line iteration by 26.1 times. Reading all lines into a list dropped 28%, and line-by-line iteration dropped 13 to 14%. On Wikidata, 64 KiB streaming reads ran 9% faster with 12% less peak memory. Every change stays inside safe Rust and CPython's Stable ABI, keeping one universal wheel across Python 3.10 through 3.15.

The same audit mapped the exact wall that safe Stable ABI code cannot cross on whole-stream reads. There, PyO3's zero-initialisation and glibc's 32 MiB anonymous mapping threshold combine to hold peak memory near twice the decoded output size.

**Takeaways**

- **Raw reader line iteration is 26.1 times faster.** Overriding line iteration directly in Rust eliminates Python's default raw-stream fallback, which previously requested one byte at a time.
- **Skipping Python's redundant buffer removes two copies per read.** mibz2's Rust reader already decodes into block buffers up to 900 KiB. Stacking a 1 MiB CPython buffer on top copied every byte three times instead of once.
- **Direct C-method binding removes Python frame overhead.** Binding Rust line methods directly onto the file object kept full buffered-reader compatibility while turning a 66% wrapper slowdown into a 4% speedup.
- **Safe eight-byte newline scanning avoids per-line GIL churn.** While bytes remain in the current decoded block, Rust scans eight bytes at a time without dropping the Global Interpreter Lock.
- **Whole-stream peak memory hits two external floors.** Safe PyO3 zero-fills a full Stable ABI output buffer before copying into it. Meanwhile, glibc keeps 1 MiB chunks on the process heap unless chunks exceed 32 MiB.

## 1\. Two hidden costs in Python's standard I/O stack

Python's standard I/O module was designed for unbuffered operating-system file descriptors. A minimal raw stream implements one buffer-fill method, and callers wrap it in a buffered reader so small reads hit memory instead of the kernel.

That layering breaks down in two ways when the underlying stream is already a block-parallel Rust decoder.

First, a raw stream that does not override line reading inherits Python's generic fallback. That fallback reads one byte at a time until it sees a newline. On a 1 MiB text slice holding 26,301 lines, raw iteration crossed into Rust over a million times. It spent nearly a full second of CPU time to read a single megabyte.

Second, even callers using mibz2's buffered opener paid for the same buffering twice. mibz2's Rust reader already holds the current decoded bzip2 block in memory (up to 900 KiB) and lends a direct slice of its unread bytes. Stacking a 1 MiB CPython buffered reader on top copied every byte three times. First, bytes moved from the Rust block into a temporary Python bytes object. Next, they moved into the 1 MiB C buffer, and finally into the returned line object.

From three copies to one: streaming lines out of a block-buffered Rust reader

Top: stacking CPython's 1 MiB BufferedReader over mibz2's already block-buffered Rust reader copied every decoded byte three times. Bottom: scanning newlines inside the lent Rust block buffer cuts delivery to one copy while keeping full BufferedReader compatibility.

Even with decoded bytes already in memory, CPython's buffered framing costs twice as much as direct memory iteration. On 28.7 MB of text with 793,778 lines, wrapping a memory buffer in a 1 MiB buffered reader took 227.7 ms of CPU. Iterating the memory buffer alone took 110.4 ms. That gap was pure framing overhead waiting to be removed.

## 2\. Scanning lines in safe Rust without releasing the GIL

Moving line framing into Rust helps only if you do not trade one overhead for another. A naive Rust line reader that drops Python's Global Interpreter Lock on every call would pay 793,778 lock round-trips on our text file. Yet the entire 28.7 MB stream contains only thirty-two bzip2 blocks.

Simple state tracking removes that churn. Inside the Rust reader wrapper, we track how many unread bytes remain in the current decoded block. Whenever bytes remain, line reads and fixed-size reads stay inside the current slice and skip releasing the GIL. The reader drops the GIL only when a block empties, letting parallel workers refill the buffer just thirty-two times across 28.7 MB.

We locate each newline inside the lent block slice with standard integer operations rather than unsafe SIMD intrinsics or external crates. XORing an eight-byte word with repeated newline bytes and applying a zero-byte bitmask checks eight bytes in four instructions. A short scalar loop handles the remaining tail bytes. Exhaustive unit tests check every offset, boundary, and length against byte-by-byte scanning.

Reading all lines into a list goes one step further. Rust scans and allocates every complete line in the current decoded block in one tight loop. It advances the reader cursor once per block instead of once per line, then appends straight to a Python list. When a line crosses a block boundary, only that single line gathers bytes across two blocks before the tight loop resumes.

## 3\. Two surprises caught by benchmarking

Fast Rust methods were only half the story. Two subtle Python-side interactions showed up right away under paired benchmarking and would have erased much of the gain if left unchecked.

**A one-line Python wrapper can cost more than the work it avoids.** Our first prototype subclassed CPython's buffered reader and forwarded line calls through a tiny Python method. Across 793,778 lines, that extra Python call slowed explicit line loops by 66%, jumping from 660 ms to 1,098 ms. CPython had to build and tear down a Python call frame nearly eight hundred thousand times just to pass one argument to C.

Direct C-method binding solves the problem cleanly. When mibz2's file opener creates its buffered reader subclass, it initializes the base buffer to a 1-byte stub, dropping the redundant 1 MiB C buffer. It binds the Rust reader's C methods directly onto the instance for line reading and peeking. It also returns the Rust reader directly as the iterator. Calling detach removes those bindings so a detached stream behaves like stock Python. Standard type checks, raw-stream attributes, and text wrappers keep working unchanged. Explicit line loops flipped from 66% slower to 4% faster.

**Slicing a bytearray silently invokes resizing logic.** During verification, writing decoded bytes into a caller's 1 MiB bytearray via direct slice assignment slowed single-threaded reads by 14.7%. In CPython, bytearray slice assignment runs general sequence-replacement code that checks whether the buffer must grow or shift. Wrapping the target in a byte-cast memory view takes a fixed-size copy path instead, flipping the same workload from 14.7% slower to 2.5% faster.

## 4\. Measured gains across text and Wikidata

We benchmarked the finished safe-Rust code in fresh subprocesses using order-balanced paired trials. The suite covers 28.7 MB of text (793,778 lines) and 210 MB of Wikidata JSON (15,620 long lines). Every workload ran at one and two threads with exact SHA-256 byte parity checks.

Paired CPU time and peak memory change across Python streaming workloads

Order-balanced paired CPU reductions across Python streaming workloads on text and Wikidata, all in safe Rust inside abi3-py310. Peak memory also drops by 6 to 12% on streaming line and 64 KiB reads once the redundant 1 MiB BufferedReader buffer is gone.

Across all twenty-nine workload cells on both corpora, zero cells regressed. Single-threaded peak memory stayed flat or fell by up to 11.8%.

## 5\. Where the Stable ABI boundary really sits

One workload deliberately stayed unchanged. Whole-stream reads and one-shot decompression return the 210 MB Wikidata dump as one bytes object. Peak resident memory sits near 434 MiB, just over twice the decoded output size.

Tracing why uncovered two constraints outside mibz2's own code.

First, PyO3's safe Stable ABI bytes constructor always zero-fills the target buffer before letting safe Rust write into it. For a 210 MB stream, that faults and writes every page twice while the source chunks are still live. Peak memory stays near 2×, and the extra pass adds over a second of work under the GIL. PyO3's newer bytes writer avoids that zero-fill on full CPython builds. Under the Limited API, however, it falls back to an intermediate Rust vector plus a full copy.

Second, glibc's dynamic mapping threshold keeps 1 MiB chunks on the process heap. Copying chunks into a pre-sized buffer and freeing each one right away does not help. Freeing a 1 MiB buffer during startup teaches glibc to raise its dynamic threshold. In a direct allocator probe on 210 MB, 1 MiB chunks stayed on the heap and peaked at 428 MiB. Raising the chunk size past glibc's 32 MiB hard cap put each chunk in its own anonymous mapping. Those mappings returned to the operating system on free, cutting peak resident memory by 41 to 45% down to 251 MiB.

Those two facts draw a clear line between what belongs in a universal wheel and what requires a packaging trade-off. Every streaming and line-oriented gain above ships in safe Rust inside the Python 3.10 Stable ABI, keeping one wheel for Python 3.10 through 3.15. Breaking the 2× peak memory floor on whole-stream reads stays a deliberate choice for later. Doing so means shipping per-version Python wheels for a zero-copy writer, or pairing a small unsafe Limited-API allocation with chunks above 32 MiB.

---

- Full Python delivery bottleneck dissection, PyO3 `PyBytes::new_with` audit, and glibc `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD` probe: [\#1327](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/1327>), [lab notebook](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/60db3337/docs/notebook/2026-11-28-explore-python-abi3-delivery.md>).
- Paired verification across 29 workload cells on text and Wikidata: [delta record](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/60db3337/frontier/deltas/2026-11-28-python-abi3-delivery-build.md>).

# How shrinking one thread's scratch memory sped up a different thread

Shrinking each worker's slab scratch removes almost every extra cache stall on the serial scanner, making the whole eight-worker decode faster.

28 November 2026 · 6 min read · [Research result](<#5-a-sharper-rule-for-multi-core-optimization>)

Shrinking a thread's private scratch buffer usually saves RAM and keeps that same thread warm in cache. You rarely expect it to speed up a completely different thread on another physical core without changing a single line of that thread's code.

Yet that is what just happened on our ten-core Intel Core i9-10900K. Behind an experimental feature flag, our four-lane forward Burrows–Wheeler walk already sped up individual workers by 17% ([walking forward across four lanes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-28-four-lanes-forward/index.md>)). Once the workers outran the serial Huffman scanner at eight threads, hardware counters caught a surprise. Under the experimental walk, the scanner took 6.5% more cycles at eight workers than at four. Under the default decoder, it rose only 2.3%.

We replaced each worker's recycled slab pool with a strictly bounded 80 KiB arena in safe Rust. It writes 4 KiB chunks into the output buffer and permutes them in place. Rerunning the exact same hardware counter test erased 99.1% of the scanner's excess cycles. Eight-worker peak memory dropped below baseline, and pinned-scanner throughput jumped from 4.69 GB/s to 4.96 GB/s.

**Takeaways**

- **Worker scratch memory was stalling a separate core.** Behind an experimental feature flag, our first four-lane walk kept about a megabyte of recycled 32 KiB slabs per worker. Those extra 6.53 MiB at eight workers overflowed the shared 20 MiB L3 cache. They more than doubled L3-miss stalls inside the serial scanner on core zero.
- **An 80 KiB bounded arena uses 4 KiB slabs and in-place reordering.** Each active lane owns one 4 KiB slab, or 16 KiB in total, fitting inside half of L1 data cache. Full chunks flush straight into the output buffer and permute in place with zero extra allocation. A bounded 64 KiB buffer holds only short segment tails.
- **Bounding the arena removed 99.1% of the scanner excess.** At flat clock from four to eight workers, the experimental scanner's cycle rise fell from 6.47% to 2.35%. That matches baseline's 2.31% within four hundredths of a percent.
- **Pinned eight-worker throughput reached 4.96 GB/s in less RAM than baseline.** Clearing 31.5 million extra stall cycles cut Wikidata decode time from 0.1787 s to 0.1691 s. That beats baseline's 0.1910 s by 11.1% while using 1.32 MiB less peak memory.
- **Every megabyte past the L3 cliff taxes the whole pipeline.** Near the shared cache ceiling, each extra megabyte of active eight-worker scratch cost the serial scanner about 4.9 million cycles.

## 1\. The mystery on core zero

Parallel bzip2 decompression in mibz2 splits into two coupled stations. One serial scanner thread parses the bitstream and decodes Huffman symbols. A pool of worker threads then inverts each block's Burrows–Wheeler transform, undoes run-length encoding and checks block checksums.

When we added an experimental four-lane forward walk to the workers, eight-worker Wikidata decoding flipped from worker-bound to scanner-bound. Per-worker busy time dropped cleanly, yet whole-file wall time did not fall as far as an ideal-scanner oracle predicted. Even more puzzling, the serial scanner looked 15% slower at eight workers than at one worker, even though its code had not changed.

First we separated clock scaling from true contention. Our ten-core chip drops its turbo clock from 5.28 GHz at one active core to 4.91 GHz once four cores run. That single step explains roughly 7.5 percentage points of the apparent slowdown between one worker and four. From four workers to eight, however, achieved frequency stays flat at 1.326 cycles per reference cycle.

To isolate what happened at constant clock, we pinned the serial scanner exclusively to core zero and confined the workers to the other nine cores. We attached Linux hardware counters to core zero across twelve interleaved rounds on 839 MB of Wikidata. Every round compared the default build against the experimental walk at one, four and eight workers.

The counters ruled out extra work immediately. Every arm and thread count retired the exact same 1,427.0 million instructions. Four-worker cycles also matched one-worker cycles within 0.03%. Between four workers and eight at constant clock, however, the two builds diverged sharply:

- Under the **default decoder**, scanner cycles rose by 2.30%, adding 17.4 million cycles. Of that increase, 88.4% (15.4 million cycles) came from L3-miss stalls.
- Under the **experimental unbounded-slab walk**, scanner cycles jumped by 6.47%, adding 49.3 million cycles. Scanner IPC fell from 1.872 to 1.759. L3-miss stalls accounted for 76.4% of the rise, or 37.6 million cycles — 2.44 times the baseline increment.

Something the workers were touching on cores one through nine was evicting the scanner's live state from the shared last-level cache on core zero.

## 2\. Why cold slabs still crowd a shared 20 MiB L3

Looking at resident memory pointed straight to the suspect. The first version of the experimental four-lane walk wrote each lane into recycled 32 KiB slabs before stitching them into the output buffer. A full bzip2 block holds up to 900 KiB before final run-length decoding. Each worker therefore built a pool of about thirty 32 KiB slabs — nearly a full megabyte of extra scratch held alongside the output buffer.

At eight workers, that recycled pool added 6.53 MiB of peak resident memory over baseline. Earlier we assumed recycled slabs were mostly harmless because a worker only writes a handful of them at any instant ([walking forward across four lanes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-28-four-lanes-forward/index.md>)). On a processor with a 20 MiB shared L3 cache, that assumption broke down.

Eight workers cycling through a megabyte of slab memory apiece touch roughly 8 MiB of extra dirty cache lines across every wave of blocks. Workers also hold inversion tables, input symbol buffers and queued output blocks. Together, those extra megabytes push active traffic past the 20 MiB L3 ceiling. Cache replacement then evicts core zero's Huffman tables and input streams, forcing the scanner to stall on DRAM.

Core-zero scanner cycle rise and L3-miss stalls from four to eight workers at constant clock

Left: shrinking the experimental worker arena to 80 KiB cuts the scanner's 4W-to-8W cycle jump from +6.47% back to +2.35%, matching baseline's +2.31%. Right: core-zero L3-miss stalls drop from 2.44× baseline down to 1.16×, confirming shared-cache eviction as the cause.

Notice the falsifiable prediction that hypothesis makes. Dividing 31.8 million extra scanner cycles by 6.53 MiB of extra eight-worker memory yields about 4.9 million cycles per megabyte. If worker scratch memory caused those stalls, shrinking the slab pool under 100 KiB should erase the entire 4.17-point gap. The experimental scanner's ratio should fall straight back into the 1.023 to 1.030 band.

## 3\. Bounding the arena to 80 KiB with in-place permutation

How do you keep four independent forward lanes writing out of order without storing a megabyte of temporary slabs? The answer is to use the output buffer that the caller has already allocated.

Inside the safe-Rust experimental forward walk, we replaced the growable slab pool with a strictly bounded per-worker arena of at most 80 KiB:

1. **Four L1-resident lane slabs (16 KiB total).** Each of the four active lanes owns one fixed 4 KiB buffer. Together they fit inside half of a 32 KiB L1 data cache, keeping every lane's write cursor hot without spilling into L2 or L3.
2. **Direct chunk flushing into the output buffer.** Whenever a lane fills its 4 KiB slab, it copies that chunk straight to the end of the output buffer. It then records one byte naming the owning segment and reuses the same 4 KiB slab.
3. **A bounded tail buffer (at most 64 KiB).** When a lane hits the next anchor, it copies any remaining partial bytes into a small contiguous tail buffer. Because a block has at most sixteen segments and each tail is strictly smaller than 4 KiB, the tail buffer can never exceed 64 KiB.
4. **In-place cycle-following permutation.** Once all sixteen segments finish, the output buffer holds every full 4 KiB chunk, interleaved in completion order rather than cycle order. Counting chunks per segment gives each chunk its exact target slot. A cycle-following loop then permutes those chunks in place inside the output buffer. It reuses one 4 KiB lane slab as its temporary slot, with zero extra allocation and zero unsafe code.
5. **One backward pass to insert the tails.** Finally, a single right-to-left shift slides each segment's contiguous chunks into their exact final byte offsets and copies each segment's short tail right behind them.

Because slabs never pile up across a block, retained scratch drops from roughly 1 MiB per worker to at most 80 KiB. That is more than a tenfold reduction.

## 4\. The causal test on physical silicon

Before touching the workstation, we froze three strict verdicts for the excess scanner rise over baseline. **EXPLAINED** required an excess at or below 1.0 percentage point and L3-stall growth within 1.5× of baseline. **PARTIAL** covered 1.0 to 3.0 points, and **NOT EXPLAINED** began at 3.0 points. Then we reran the exact same pinned-scanner hardware-counter benchmark unchanged on our Intel Core i9-10900K.

The verdict came back **EXPLAINED** with room to spare.

| Metric | Base | Pool | **80 KiB** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8W/4W | 1.0231× | 1.0647× | **1.0235×** |
| Excess | control | \+4.17 pp | **\+0.04 pp** |
| L3 stalls | \+15.2M | \+37.6M | **\+17.7M** |
| IPC | 1.841 | 1.759 | **1.840** |
| RSS (MiB) | 104.6 | 111.1 | **103.3** |
| Wall (s) | 0.1910 | 0.1787 | **0.1691** |
| GB/s | 4.39 | 4.69 | **4.96** |

Three numbers stand out side by side:

- **The control reproduced to four decimal places.** Baseline's 8W/4W scanner cycle ratio came in at 1.0231×, matching the earlier run's 1.0230× almost identically. Its 95% confidence interval ran from 1.0199× to 1.0263×.
- **99.1% of the scanner contention vanished.** The bounded experimental walk's 8W/4W scanner ratio dropped from 1.0647× to 1.0235×, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.0202× to 1.0268×. Excess over baseline fell from 4.17 percentage points to 0.04 points. Paired directly at eight workers, the bounded scanner ran at 0.9998× of baseline's cycles. Both arms finished at nearly identical IPC (1.840 vs 1.841) and LLC load misses (1.002×).
- **Peak memory fell below baseline, and eight-worker speed jumped 5.4%.** Peak memory at eight workers dropped by 7.85 MiB compared with the unbounded pool. It finished at 103.3 MiB, which is 1.32 MiB *below* baseline's 104.6 MiB. Clearing 31.5 million extra stall cycles cut pinned eight-worker wall time from 0.1787 s to 0.1691 s. That lifted throughput from 4.69 GB/s to 4.96 GB/s, cutting wall time 11.1% below baseline (12.9% higher throughput).

Eight-worker Wikidata throughput and peak memory: baseline vs unbounded and bounded lanes

Left: bounding worker scratch lifts real pinned-scanner eight-worker throughput from 4.69 GB/s to 4.96 GB/s (nearly matching the earlier 4.99 GB/s ideal-scanner ceiling). Right: eight-worker peak resident memory drops 7.85 MiB and finishes 1.32 MiB below baseline.

The single-worker and four-worker gains stayed completely intact as well. At one worker, the bounded experimental walk decoded Wikidata in 1.0905 s against baseline's 1.3092 s. That is 17.1% faster at identical memory. At four workers, it finished in 0.3010 s against 0.3626 s, running 16.8% faster in 0.7% less memory.

## 5\. A sharper rule for multi-core optimization

This pair of experiments settles a subtle lesson about multi-stage pipelines on shared-cache processors. When you speed up parallel workers until a serial front-end binds, memory footprint on the workers stops being a separate concern from front-end latency. Even temporary scratch buffers that stay private to each worker flow through the same shared L3 cache as the serial stage.

On our ten-core Intel workstation, pushing eight workers a few megabytes past the 20 MiB L3 cliff silently stole 4% of the serial scanner's speed. Each extra megabyte of active working set cost roughly 4.9 million scanner cycles. Keeping the four-lane slabs inside L1 data cache and reordering chunks in place broke that coupling completely.

The bounded four-lane walk remains behind an experimental feature flag today. Its next step is a full unpinned multi-corpus adoption run across Wikidata and six guard corpora. Only after that check passes will we promote it into mibz2's default path.

# Why a brief pause throttled our Intel i9, and how we calibrated memory noise

A brief pause between runs can trap a desktop processor below full boost, while parallel queue jitter dominates peak memory across six server chips.

28 November 2026 · 7 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-changes-for-every-future-benchmark>)

When you tune a parallel bzip2 decoder for 3% speedups, your measuring tape can lie louder than your code. Two recent surprises forced us to test our own benchmarks with the same rigour we apply to the decoder itself.

First, a ten-core Intel Core i9-10900K began showing sudden 18% slowdowns on identical binaries. The culprit was not the decoder, the compiler or the operating system scheduler. It was a 200-millisecond pause we had placed between runs to let the processor settle.

Second, a zero-allocation change tripped a strict peak-memory check on our continuous-integration runners. So we measured 27 zero-change benchmark runs across six server processor families. The results separated deterministic single-thread memory from multi-thread queue jitter by an order of magnitude.

**Takeaways**

- **A 200-millisecond pause triggered 100% of multi-core slow-clock runs.** Across 288 hardware-counter runs on an Intel Core i9-10900K, every multi-core slow-clock event happened after a 0.2 s settle pause. Pausing for 0 s or 2.0 s produced zero slow-clock runs out of 48 each.
- **The slow runs did identical work at 12% lower frequency.** Instructions per byte and cycles per instruction stayed completely flat. Achieved clock rate fell from 1.764 to 1.552 cycles per reference cycle. That shift explained an earlier release check that looked 5.7% to 9.5% faster purely from unequal clock-mode draws.
- **Pinning six workers to six cores cost an extra 17%.** A six-worker parallel decode spawns eight active threads including the reader and serial scanner. Leaving the run unpinned across ten cores ran 17.1% faster with identical executed instructions.
- **Identical binaries fail tight multi-thread memory gates almost every time.** We collected 5,670 paired observations across six AMD and Intel server chips. Every single zero-change run exceeded a 1.005× multi-thread peak-memory bound, and 40.7% exceeded 1.030×.
- **Single-thread peak memory is ten times quieter and catches real heap growth cleanly.** Run-to-run variation at one thread stays below 0.23%, and zero runs crossed 1.005×. Real per-worker heap additions stand out at 17 to 25 standard deviations at one thread and scale linearly with workers.

## 1\. The mystery of the bimodal desktop runs

Our ten-core Intel Core i9-10900K workstation normally repeats an 839 MB Wikidata decode within a fraction of a percent. Yet during release-scaling sweeps, the exact same binary occasionally took much longer than usual. In one check comparing versions 0.5.14 and 0.5.15, the older build landed in the slow cluster eight times out of ten at one thread. The newer build landed there only three times.

Pooled together, those unequal draws made 0.5.15 look 5.7% faster at one thread and 9.5% faster at twelve threads. Yet hardware cycle counts suggested the two builds were within one or two percent of each other. Something inside the benchmark harness was pushing runs into two distinct speed bands.

To isolate the cause without guessing, we ran a full factorial experiment on the workstation with hardware performance counters attached to every single run. We varied three settings at both one thread and six threads:

- **Core pinning:** pinned to physical cores or unpinned across all ten cores.
- **Settle pause:** zero, two tenths or two full seconds of idle sleep before each run.
- **Pair position:** first or second run inside an interleaved pair.

Twelve randomized rounds across all twelve combinations produced 144 runs per thread count, or 288 fully counter-instrumented decodes in total. Before each run launched, the harness also read the processor's current clock frequency straight from the kernel.

## 2\. How 200 milliseconds traps Intel hardware boost

The six-thread table pointed straight at one cell. Out of 144 six-thread runs, 13 crossed the slow-run threshold of 0.338 s. Not a single run did extra work. Zero runs had elevated instructions per byte, and zero had elevated cycles per instruction.

All 13 slow-clock runs landed in the pinned 0.2 s settle condition. Eleven of twelve occurred in the second position of a pair, and two of twelve occurred in the first. Every other cell had zero slow-clock runs. Neither zero-second settle nor two-second settle produced a single slow-clock run in 48 tries each.

| six-thread condition (12 rounds per cell) | median wall | pre-run clock | achieved clock ratio | instructions / byte | cycles / inst | slow-clock runs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Pinned, 0.0 s settle (pos 0 / 1) | 0.298 / 0.297 s | 4.93 / 4.90 GHz | 1.763 / 1.767 | 19.52 / 19.55 | 0.335 / 0.334 | 0 / 0 |
| Pinned, 0.2 s settle, first | 0.303 s | 0.80 GHz | 1.760 | 19.53 | 0.335 | 2 of 12 |
| **Pinned, 0.2 s settle, second** | **0.351 s** | **0.80 GHz** | **1.552** | **19.51** | **0.334** | **11 of 12** |
| Pinned, 2.0 s settle (pos 0 / 1) | 0.299 / 0.299 s | 0.80 / 0.80 GHz | 1.766 / 1.764 | 19.55 / 19.54 | 0.334 / 0.334 | 0 / 0 |
| Unpinned, 0.0 s settle (pos 0 / 1) | 0.247 / 0.246 s | 5.16 / 4.90 GHz | 1.771 / 1.771 | 19.53 / 19.52 | 0.338 / 0.338 | 0 / 0 |
| Unpinned, 0.2 s settle, second | 0.260 s | 0.80 GHz | 1.749 | 19.50 | 0.337 | 0 of 12\* |
| Unpinned, 2.0 s settle (pos 0 / 1) | 0.248 / 0.249 s | 0.80 / 0.80 GHz | 1.761 / 1.749 | 19.53 / 19.53 | 0.337 / 0.338 | 0 / 0 |

*\*Unpinned 0.2 s runs showed the same dip in miniature at pair position 1. Their median slowed by 5.4%, with the slowest round hitting 0.282 s at a 1.531 clock ratio. That stayed below the pooled 0.338 s cutoff only because unpinned runs start 17% faster.*

Why does a 0.2 s pause slow the chip down when neither 0.0 s nor 2.0 s does? The pre-run clock readings explain the physics under Intel Hardware P-States with the powersave governor and balanced energy preference:

- **At 0.0 s settle**, the cores are still warm from the previous burst at 4.90 to 5.16 GHz. The next run starts straight at full turbo.
- **At 0.2 s settle**, 200 milliseconds is just long enough for idle cores to drop to the 800 MHz floor. Yet it catches the package mid-transition inside its short-window boost hysteresis right after the first run of a pair. Average achieved frequency across the decode stalls 12.1% below turbo, turning a 0.298 s decode into 0.351 s.
- **At 2.0 s settle**, the cores also sit at 800 MHz before launch. Two full seconds let the chip's short-window power and boost state reset cleanly. When work arrives, the cores snap straight back to 4.90 GHz.

Six-thread Wikidata decode time by pinning, settle pause and pair position

All 13 slow-clock runs at six threads occurred in the pinned 0.2 s settle cells, with 11 of 12 in pair position 1. Pausing 0.0 s or 2.0 s produced zero slow-clock runs out of 48 each. Leaving six workers unpinned also removes a 17.1% oversubscription tax because the parallel decoder runs eight active threads.

The same pattern held at one thread. Pinned 0.2 s settle explained 4 of 5 slow-clock runs, while pinned 2.0 s had zero in 24 runs. One thread also showed 26 slower runs at full turbo clock with identical instructions per byte. Those runs had 6.9% higher cycles per instruction, concentrated in early rounds, from ordinary fresh-process page and cache placement rather than clock drops.

Two bonus findings fell straight out of the same data. First, pinning a six-worker decode to six physical cores added a 17.1% wall-time tax even in the fast mode. Pinned runs took 0.298 s against 0.247 s unpinned. Because mibz2 pairs six workers with one bitstream scanner and one reader thread, eight active threads were time-sharing six cores.

Second, we re-analysed the earlier 0.5.14 versus 0.5.15 release bundle within each clock mode. Comparing fast runs against fast runs cut the single-thread gap from 5.7% to 1.8%. Within slow runs, the difference was 0.2%. Both figures agree with the frequency-free cycle count.

Hardware clock bins also resolve a subtle cross-thread puzzle on desktop Intel chips. Because all ten cores share one clock domain, single-core turbo sits near 5.28 GHz while four or more active cores run at 4.91 GHz. That 7.5% clock step alone explains most of why the serial scanner appears slower when eight workers run beside it. Only a small worker-coupled residual remains to test next.

## 3\. When identical binaries fail a memory gate

While we were untangling workstation clocks, a second measurement puzzle surfaced in continuous integration. A pull request allocated zero extra heap bytes and even removed an 8 KiB static table. Yet it failed a pre-registered 1.005× peak-memory check on a four-thread runner. Four-thread text showed 1.022× peak resident memory, while four-thread repeating patterns dropped to 0.974×.

Instead of relaxing one threshold by eye, we ran a strict-null calibration. We gathered 27 recent continuous-integration benchmark runs that touched zero Rust source files, meaning the head and baseline binaries were compiled from identical code. Each run executed 10 interleaved paired rounds across 7 corpora and 3 thread counts. Together they gave 5,670 paired observations across six server chips: AMD EPYC Zen 3, Zen 4 and Zen 5, plus Intel Xeon Ice Lake and Granite Rapids.

The false-alarm rates were startling. Across the fourteen multi-threaded cells, identical binaries tripped almost every tight point gate:

| candidate multi-thread peak-RSS gate | 1-thread false-positive runs | 2-thread / 4-thread false-positive runs |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Above 1.005× (+0.5%) | 0 of 27 (0.0%) | **27 of 27 (100.0%)** |
| Above 1.010× (+1.0%) | 0 of 27 (0.0%) | **25 of 27 (92.6%)** |
| Above 1.020× (+2.0%) | 0 of 27 (0.0%) | **17 of 27 (63.0%)** |
| Above 1.030× (+3.0%) | 0 of 27 (0.0%) | **11 of 27 (40.7%)** |
| Above 1.050× (+5.0%) | 0 of 27 (0.0%) | **3 of 27 (11.1%)** |
| Above 1.100× (+10.0%, project hard limit) | 0 of 27 (0.0%) | **0 of 27 (0.0%)** |

Even an uncorrected 95% confidence interval flagged an identical binary as using more memory on 10 of 27 runs (37.0%). Counting either direction, it false-alarmed on 13 of 27 runs (48.1%). Every single server CPU family exhibited the same multi-threaded spread, with the worst zero-change ratio reaching 1.0683×.

## 4\. Two physical regimes of peak memory

The null dataset did not merely show noise; it split cleanly into two distinct physical regimes.

At one thread, peak resident memory is nearly deterministic. Across all seven corpora and 27 runs, the run-to-run standard deviation sits between 0.13% and 0.23%. Not a single one-thread cell ever crossed 1.005×; the highest observed ratio was 1.0047×. Single-block inputs stay just as quiet at every thread count because only one block can be in flight at once.

Add multiple threads over multi-block files, and the run-to-run variation widens 7× to 20×. Run standard deviation jumps to between 0.94% and 2.59%, and single-pair spread reaches 9.1%. Thread scheduling shifts how many decoded output blocks sit queued ahead of the writer and how per-thread allocator arenas expand.

One workload made that queue effect visible to the naked eye. Across 540 four-thread runs on a repeating-pattern input, peak memory split cleanly around a 39 MiB valley. The low mode sat at 35 to 37 MiB, while the high mode sat at 42 to 44 MiB. Those extra 6 to 8 MiB are simply decoded blocks waiting briefly in the output queue when the writer lags. Whenever two identical runs landed on opposite sides of the 39 MiB valley, a single pair swung by 1.139× or 0.881×.

Strict-null peak-memory false alarms across six server processors and two noise regimes

Left: identical binaries trip every uncalibrated multi-thread point bound below 1.10×, while zero one-thread runs ever exceed 1.005×. Right: because single-thread peak memory is quiet to 0.23%, real per-worker heap additions fire at 17 to 25 standard deviations at one thread and scale linearly across 8 and 10 workers.

That two-regime split gives us a sharp diagnostic for real memory regressions. On our ten-core workstation, two earlier slab-allocating prototypes added +524 KiB per worker and +0.89 MiB per worker. At one thread, those modest additions stood out immediately at 17.4 and 24.8 standard deviations against a 0.18% pair spread. Across one, eight and ten workers, the first grew linearly from +0.58 MiB to +4.10 MiB to +5.29 MiB. The second grew from +0.89 MiB at one worker to +6.38 MiB at eight.

Queue jitter never behaves that way. It is silent at one thread and fluctuates unpredictably by two to six percent across multi-thread cells. Checking heap invariance at one thread and verifying linear growth across worker counts separates genuine footprint regressions from allocator weather.

## 5\. What changes for every future benchmark

Both investigations turned directly into permanent rules for how we measure mibz2 going forward:

- **Two-second settle pauses on physical workstations.** We replaced 0.2 s settle pauses with 2.0 s pauses so Intel hardware boost resets cleanly before every timed decode. We also avoid pinning parallel runs to fewer cores than their active thread count when measuring production scaling.
- **Mode-aware counter analysis beside pooled ratios.** Every workstation bundle now records hardware cycle and instruction counters. Those counters separate clock-frequency drops from real executed work and check whether both arms occupied the same clock mode.
- **Two-regime memory gates.** Zero-heap changes are checked tightly at one thread (within 1.010× or 0.5 MiB), where noise is below a quarter of a percent. Multi-thread continuous-integration cells use the calibrated noise bands and the project's 1.10× hard ceiling. Heap-adding designs must state their expected per-worker delta upfront and confirm linear scaling from one thread upward.

Pre-registered stop rules only protect your science if they do not cry wolf on normal hardware physics. Knowing how a 200-millisecond pause moves a desktop clock and how parallel queues move resident memory lets us keep our gates strict without chasing ghosts.

# Walking the Burrows–Wheeler cycle forward across four lanes

Walking the inverse BWT cycle forward across four safe Rust lanes lets workers outrun the serial scanner, alongside three default speedups.

28 November 2026 · 7 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-happens-next>)

Every bzip2 block ends with a pointer chase. Once the decoder builds its inverse Burrows–Wheeler table, it must follow a single cycle through the block to recover the text. The open-returns kernel already shrinks that table to a tenth of the block's rows ([Open Returns](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>)). Even so, a worker still stalls on every cache miss along the chain.

Behind an experimental feature flag, mibz2 now breaks that chain open in pure safe Rust. The decoder samples sixteen anchors along the cycle and walks forward across four parallel lanes at once. Each lane writes into its own recycled 32 KiB slab, keeping four independent memory lookups in flight with zero unsafe code.

On a ten-core Intel Core i9-10900K decoding 839 MB of Wikidata, that experimental four-lane walk cuts single-worker time by 17.2%. At eight workers it pushes real throughput to 4.55 GB/s, and 4.99 GB/s when paired with an ideal scanner. More importantly, it flips the eight-worker bottleneck on Wikidata back from the workers to the serial bitstream scanner.

Alongside that experimental walk, three default-path improvements have merged onto master. They remove an extra buffer copy on Python reads, recalibrate the open kernel's admission bands and fold dense-band cap checks into the first pass.

**Takeaways**

- **Four safe forward lanes cut single-worker time by 17.2%.** Behind an experimental feature, walking forward from sixteen sampled anchors into four private 32 KiB slabs trims single-worker Wikidata decoding on a ten-core workstation from 1.353 s to 1.113 s.
- **Eight-worker Wikidata flips from worker-bound to scanner-bound.** Per-worker busy time falls by 10.6% while contended scanner time rises to 179.4 ms. Real throughput climbs by 5.7% to 4.55 GB/s, and ideal-scanner throughput rises 12.1% to 4.99 GB/s.
- **Hot cache working set matters more than peak memory.** Peak eight-worker resident memory rises by 6.3 MiB for recycled slabs that stay cold between blocks, yet multi-core throughput still climbs cleanly.
- **The walk stays opt-in pending a full-guard adoption check.** Ordinary text ran 0.4% faster at identical peak memory, but fifteen-round jitter nudged its upper confidence bound to 1.017× against a strict 1.010× gate.
- **Three default-path speedups are live now.** Direct-copy Python chunk reads, tighter admission bands and fused dense-band cap checks speed up default decoding across Wikidata, text and Python.

## 1\. Why a compact cycle still stalls the core

mibz2's open-returns kernel already shrinks each compressible block to roughly a tenth of its rows. Every retained row points to its successor and carries a short word of output bytes. To emit the block, the default decoder walks that cycle from both ends at once so two lookups stay in flight together.

Two chains are still far below what a modern out-of-order core can hide. A desktop processor can track ten or more memory misses at once, yet a two-ended walk only ever exposes two dependent loads. Every time a link misses the L2 cache, the core waits tens of nanoseconds before it even knows the next address to fetch.

Earlier experiments ran eight lanes inside the general-purpose kernel. That design hit a wall once eight threads shared the L3 cache ([fast alone, slow in a crowd](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-21-fast-alone-slow-in-a-crowd/index.md>)). In the open-returns kernel, however, the edge table is small enough to stay close to the core. The challenge was splitting one cycle into parallel forward walks without adding unsafe code, extra cache pressure or expensive stitching.

## 2\. Sixteen anchors, four lanes and disjoint slabs

The experimental four-lane forward walk solves that problem in three steps, all inside a module that forbids unsafe code.

First, before the walk begins, the kernel keeps ordinary forward links instead of XOR-paired two-way links. It samples sixteen anchor positions spread across the retained table and marks each one with a stop bit in the high bits of its entry. Those anchors slice the single cycle into up to sixteen independent forward segments, with no search required.

Second, a worker walks up to four active segments in lockstep. On every iteration, all four lanes issue their next table lookup together, exposing four independent misses to the processor at once. Whenever one lane reaches another lane's anchor, it retires and pulls the next waiting anchor from the remaining pool. Each active lane count compiles out of line so the compiler keeps every lane cursor in a register as lanes drain.

Third, each lane writes its decoded bytes into its own private, recycled 32 KiB slab rather than competing over one shared output buffer. Because the four slices are completely disjoint, safe Rust proves they never alias and keeps every write cursor in a register. Long words copy directly into the current slab whenever space remains, avoiding spillovers to a separate side buffer. Once all segments finish, a single linear pass stitches the filled slabs into the block's output buffer in cycle order.

Breaking the pointer-chase chain with four disjoint forward lanes

Top: the shipped two-ended walk keeps at most two dependent loads in flight. Bottom: the experimental four-lane walk splits the cycle at sixteen sampled anchors, overlaps four independent misses in safe Rust and writes into four disjoint 32 KiB slabs before one sequential stitch.

## 3\. Ten-core measurements and the bottleneck flip

We tested the experimental four-lane walk on a ten-core Intel Core i9-10900K against the default 0.5.17 build across fifteen interleaved paired rounds. The main workload was four concatenated copies of the Wikidata dump totalling 839 MB of decoded output, alongside a 52 MB ordinary-text guard corpus. Every single run verified byte-exact SHA-256 parity.

| workload (i9-10900K, 15 paired rounds) | default median | experimental 4-lane median | paired ratio (95% CI) | throughput |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| Wikidata, 1 worker (839 MB) | 1.353 s | 1.113 s | 0.828× (0.816 to 0.834) | 753 MB/s |
| Wikidata, 8 workers, real scanner | 195.9 ms | 184.4 ms | 0.943× (0.938 to 0.948) | 4.55 GB/s |
| Wikidata, 8 workers, ideal scanner | 190.6 ms | 168.3 ms | 0.879× (0.857 to 0.895) | 4.99 GB/s |
| Ordinary text, 1 worker (52 MB) | 135.4 ms | 137.0 ms | 0.996× (0.989 to 1.017) | 379 MB/s |

The single-worker drop of 231 ms (17.2%) comes entirely from the emission walk itself. In the traced single-worker run, walk and induction time fell by 222.7 ms. Move-to-front decoding, table setup and final run-length expansion moved by less than 6 ms combined.

The traced eight-worker cells reveal a deeper system shift. Under the default build on Wikidata, eight workers still set the pace. Each worker stayed busy for 196.5 ms against a 171.8 ms serial scanner, leaving a 24.7 ms worker-bound gap.

Turn on the experimental four-lane walk and those two stations trade places. Per-worker busy time drops 10.6% from 196.5 ms to 169.6 ms. Meanwhile, the serial scanner slows slightly from 171.8 ms to 179.4 ms under the faster eight-worker load. The pipeline flips to scanner-bound by 9.8 ms. Elapsed time settles at 184.8 ms, within 6 ms of the serial scan floor.

Eight-worker station times on 839 MB Wikidata before and after four forward lanes

Traced eight-worker medians on 839 MB Wikidata. Under the default build, workers take 24.7 ms longer than the serial scanner. With the experimental four-lane walk enabled, workers drop inside the scanner's bar and the serial scanner binds by 9.8 ms. Removing scanner cost (ideal scan) shows the full 12.1% worker speedup at 4.99 GB/s.

That flip also answers a puzzle from our previous scaling post ([why compression ratio moves the scaling ceiling](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-27-why-the-scaling-ceiling-moves/index.md>)). Until now, scanner speedups stayed partly hidden on Wikidata at eight threads because workers still bound the pipeline. Once the four-lane walk ships by default, every millisecond shaved off the serial scanner pays directly at eight cores too.

The memory numbers delivered a second lesson. At eight workers, peak resident memory grew from 106.4 MiB to 112.9 MiB. That adds about 0.8 MiB per worker. Earlier, a 4.2 MiB increase from a hot-loop endpoint redesign had slowed eight-worker decoding by 0.7%. Here, most of the extra memory lives in recycled slab pools that stay cold between blocks. Hot per-worker cache footprint governs multi-core scaling, not headline peak RSS.

Why is the experimental walk not the default yet? On the 52 MB ordinary-text guard, both builds route every block to the general-purpose fallback and use identical peak memory (1.000×). The experimental build was faster on nine of fifteen paired rounds, with a median ratio of 0.996×. Normal single-decode jitter on a 135 ms run still lifted the bootstrap upper confidence bound to 1.017×, narrowly missing the pre-registered 1.010× pass mark. Rather than relax a frozen gate, the walk stays behind an experimental feature until a full multi-corpus adoption run confirms it.

## 4\. Three default-path improvements shipped alongside

While the experimental four-lane walk ran on the workstation, three default-path changes landed on master. They build on two companion advances already covered on this blog: [half the memory on compressible files](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-27-bounded-memory-on-highly-compressible-input/index.md>) and [faster decoding for ordinary text](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-27-faster-decoding-for-ordinary-text/index.md>).

**Direct-copy Python chunk delivery.** Reading chunks from Python previously allocated a staging buffer in Rust and copied bytes twice before returning a Python bytes object. mibz2 now writes straight from the decoder's ready buffer into Python bytes. On a virtual machine decoding Wikidata, single-thread reads ran 7.0% faster with 1 MiB chunks and 3.1% faster with 64 KiB chunks. Eight-thread reads sped up by 3.8% and 4.8%.

**Recalibrated open-kernel admission bands.** Earlier changes made the general-purpose segmented fallback markedly faster on dense text blocks. mibz2's default admission rules now reflect that new balance. Sparse blocks under 10% run density enter the open kernel outright with no cap check. Intermediate blocks between 10% and 21% density are capped at 27% retained rows, keeping every full Wikidata block off the fallback's larger scratch arrays. Blocks at 21% density or above skip straight to the fallback without pre-scanning. On a virtual machine, eight-worker Wikidata used 1.9% less processor time and finished 2.6% faster. Single-worker ordinary text ran 4.4% faster at 0.99× peak memory. On continuous-integration runners, Wikidata ran 0.9% faster at one thread and within 0.3% at four threads with zero regressions.

**Fused dense-band cap checking.** For blocks sitting between 10% and 15% run density, the default decoder previously ran a separate scalar pre-scan over the run records before starting construction. That check now happens inside the open kernel's first pass itself, keeping block-by-block routing identical while eliminating a full memory pass over the records. On a virtual machine, this cut Wikidata processor time by 4.1% at one worker. At eight threads it cut processor time by 2.9% and elapsed time by 3.1%. On continuous-integration runners, four-thread Wikidata ran 0.5% faster in 4.2% less peak memory.

## 5\. What happens next

All three default-path improvements are already merged on master and ready for the next release. The four-lane forward walk remains opt-in behind an experimental feature until a full multi-corpus workstation validation clears every guard corpus and thread count.

Once the four-lane walk becomes the default, eight-worker Wikidata throughput will sit right on the serial scanner's heels. Reaching the next tier will take faster serial scanning and lighter worker setup together. Neither station alone can outrun the other by much anymore.

[mibz2 · Research blog](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/index.md>)

# Why compression ratio moves the scaling ceiling

On a ten-core processor, the same parallel bzip2 decoder scales to nine threads on structured dumps yet peaks at five on ordinary source code and text.

27 November 2026 · 8 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-this-means-for-decoding-in-practice>)

Benchmark a parallel bzip2 decoder on a ten-core processor with a 210 MB Wikidata dump. Adding threads keeps paying off all the way to nine workers. Now hand that same binary a compressed archive of Rust source code or JSON. It stops speeding up at four or five workers. Give it eight or ten workers and it actually runs slower.

The reason has nothing to do with thread scheduling or the tool that compressed the file. It is built into bzip2 itself. Every block passes through two stations in sequence ([the decoder as a queueing network](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-25-the-decoder-as-a-queueing-network/index.md>)). One serial front stage decodes Huffman symbols. A pool of parallel workers then inverts the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) to recover the original bytes. The serial stage pays per Huffman symbol. The parallel workers pay per output byte. Compression ratio sets the exchange rate between those two currencies.

Alongside these hardware measurements, three default-path improvements have shipped in mibz2 0.5.15 and 0.5.16. They bring a faster Huffman scanner, wider branchless run decoding and chunked whole-file reads in Python. Together they show why the same speed-up can stay hidden on one benchmark yet pay off cleanly on another.

**Takeaways**

- **The scaling knee moves with the input.** On a ten-core Intel Core i9-10900K, Wikidata keeps scaling to nine workers. Ordinary source code and JSON peak at four or five workers.
- **Symbol density drives the shift.** Scanner time per Huffman symbol barely varies across text corpora (1.41 to 1.48 ns). Ordinary text simply packs three to five times more symbols into each output megabyte than a repetitive dump does.
- **Extra threads hurt past the knee.** Once the serial scanner saturates on Rust source or JSON, adding workers past six slows decoding down. Moving from five workers to ten costs roughly twice as much total processor time.
- **Faster scanning hides until the scanner binds.** The new Huffman scanner in 0.5.15 cut serial scan time on Wikidata by 10.5% and ten-thread time by 4.0%. Four-thread and eight-thread Wikidata timings barely moved because workers still set the pace there.
- **Two more default improvements landed in 0.5.16.** Raising the run-decoding ceiling from 50% to 75% speeds up compressible Markdown, ELF binaries and JSON. Whole-file Python reads now pull 1 MiB chunks directly without changing wheel compatibility.

## 1\. Two stations, two currencies

In a block-parallel bzip2 decoder, one thread must scan the compressed bit stream in order. bzip2 blocks are not byte-aligned and carry no index of their boundaries. That thread reads each block's headers, selector list and Huffman-coded symbols. It then hands the decoded symbols to whichever worker is free. The workers run move-to-front decoding, BWT inversion, run-length expansion and CRC verification in parallel.

Ignore startup and teardown for a moment. Suppose scanning a block takes time \\(S\\) and worker processing takes time \\(W\\). Then \\(k\\) workers keep pace with the scanner when \\(W / k = S\\). That gives a natural balance point:

\\\[ k^\* = \\frac{W}{S} = \\frac{w\_{\\text{byte}}}{s\_{\\text{sym}} \\cdot \\rho} \\\]

Here \\(s\_{\\text{sym}}\\) is the scanner's cost per Huffman symbol and \\(w\_{\\text{byte}}\\) is the worker's cost per output byte. The factor \\(\\rho\\) is the number of Huffman symbols per output byte. Repetitive data compresses tightly because move-to-front and zero-run encoding collapse long runs into very few symbols. That makes \\(\\rho\\) small. Higher-entropy text leaves far more non-zero symbols behind, pushing \\(\\rho\\) up.

We measured \\(S\\) and \\(W\\) directly on one pinned core of an Intel Core i9-10900K. Two controlled runs covered seven corpora in all. The first tested Wikidata beside three repository corpora: Rust source, JSON and Markdown. The second tested Wikidata beside mixed prose and code, random bytes and fixed-width records.

| corpus | compression ratio | symbols / output byte | scanner, ns / sym | worker, ns / byte | balance \\(k^\*\\) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Wikidata dump | 17.7× | 0.119 | 1.41 | 1.60 | 9.55 |
| mixed prose and code | 6.5× | 0.339 | 1.48 | 2.56 | 5.09 |
| JSON | 4.9× | 0.432 | 1.43 | 2.59 | 4.19 |
| Rust source | 5.2× | 0.419 | 1.48 | 2.58 | 4.16 |
| random bytes | 1.1× | 1.000 | 2.00 | 7.79 | 3.90 |
| fixed records | 1.0× | 1.000 | 2.08 | 7.62 | 3.68 |
| Markdown docs | 3.9× | 0.553 | 1.44 | 2.72 | 3.43 |

Look at the fourth column first. Across every text and structured corpus, the scanner spends almost the same time per Huffman symbol: 1.41 to 1.48 ns. On random bytes and uncompressible records, longer average codewords nudge that cost to 2.00 to 2.08 ns.

What changes dramatically is the third column. Wikidata needs only 0.119 symbols per output byte. Rust source and JSON need 0.419 and 0.432 — more than three and a half times as many. Markdown needs 0.553, nearly five times as many. Worker cost per output byte rises too, because less compressible blocks move to the general-purpose kernel ([faster decoding for ordinary text](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-27-faster-decoding-for-ordinary-text/index.md>)). Yet worker cost rises by only 1.6 to 1.7 times on the text panel, far less than symbol density does. The balance point \\(k^\*\\) therefore drops by more than half.

Workers needed to match the serial scanner on ten-core hardware

Single-thread station balance on an Intel Core i9-10900K (median of three rounds, fastest of five passes per block). Wikidata, Rust source, JSON and Markdown come from the text-panel run; mixed prose and code, random bytes and fixed records come from the workstation's default-build balance sweep on the same machine.

A separate eleven-corpus survey on a virtual machine ruled out the encoder as a confound. The Wikidata dump was compressed by lbzip2, while the text corpora were compressed with standard bzip2 at level 9. Re-encoding Wikidata with standard bzip2 left its balance point within 2% of the original dump. The difference comes from the data, not the compressor.

## 2\. Watching the knee move on ten cores

Single-thread station balance predicts demand, not real wall time. Cache contention, thread wakeups and memory traffic can shift the true knee. We therefore ran a pre-registered thread sweep on the same Intel Core i9-10900K. It tested four to ten workers over nine interleaved rounds per thread count. Each text corpus was concatenated into a multi-stream file of roughly 183 to 190 MB of output so startup noise stayed small. Wikidata was tested as four concatenated copies totalling 839 MB.

The frozen criterion defined a corpus's scaling knee as the smallest worker count within 2% of its best nine-round median elapsed time.

| corpus | balance \\(k^\*\\) | 4 workers, ms | 5 workers, ms | 6 workers, ms | 8 workers, ms | 9 workers, ms | 10 workers, ms | median knee | fastest-round knee |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Wikidata (839 MB) | 9.55 | 473.9 | 403.8 | 358.1 | 300.7 | 269.6 | 288.5 | 9 | 9 |
| Rust source (183 MB) | 4.16 | 207.2 | 202.9 | 203.2 | 256.5 | 256.2 | 263.9 | 5 | 5 |
| JSON (190 MB) | 4.19 | 218.5 | 217.5 | 221.5 | 259.4 | 270.1 | 257.4 | 4 | 4 |
| Markdown (184 MB) | 3.43 | 296.6 | 298.8 | 303.8 | 203.9 | 253.8 | 240.3 | 8 | 4 |

The pre-registered hypothesis passed cleanly. The text panel's median scaling knee was five workers, while Wikidata's knee was nine. On Rust source and JSON, adding workers past six did not merely flatten out. It made decoding measurably slower. Moving from five workers to ten pushed median time up 30% on Rust source and 18% on JSON. Total processor time roughly doubled as extra threads contended for shared L3 cache and queue locks.

Markdown looks like an outlier in the median column. It landed at eight workers even though its single-thread balance point is the lowest at 3.43. The per-round timings explain why. The workstation ran under Linux's powersave governor, idling at 800 MHz between runs. Individual 200 ms bursts therefore split cleanly into two speed clusters depending on turbo ramp-up. Full-clock runs at 4.9 GHz took about 190 to 200 ms, while slower-ramp runs took 260 to 305 ms. On Markdown, four of nine rounds stayed fast at four and five workers, versus five of nine at eight workers. That single round flipped which side of the gap the median landed on.

Normalised decode time from four to ten workers on ten-core hardware

Intel Core i9-10900K, nine interleaved rounds per worker count, each corpus normalised to its four-worker time (lower is faster). Left: pre-registered nine-round medians, including the frequency-ramp split on Markdown. Right: fastest of nine rounds, which isolates full-clock runs and shows Markdown already at its floor at four workers while Wikidata drops to 0.52× (183 ms, 4.58 GB/s) at nine workers.

The right-hand panel isolates full-clock runs by taking the fastest of the nine rounds at each worker count. Every single corpus then lines up with its single-thread station balance. Wikidata drops smoothly from 355.5 ms at four workers to 183.2 ms at nine, reaching 4.58 GB/s before ticking up at ten. Rust source hits its floor at five workers (167.4 ms, 1.09 GB/s). JSON sits flat from four to six workers (184.6 ms, 1.03 GB/s) before climbing. Markdown is already at its fastest at four workers (187.5 ms, 0.98 GB/s) and drifts gently upward from there.

## 3\. Why a faster scanner disappears on Wikidata at eight threads

Once you know where the balance point sits, a puzzle from mibz2 0.5.15 makes immediate sense.

Version 0.5.15 shipped a redesigned Huffman scanner in the default decoder. Normally a bzip2 decoder switches Huffman tables every 50 symbols. The new scanner coalesces consecutive groups that reuse the same table into one run. It also packs the primary lookup table into a compact byte-aligned layout and skips redundant zero-initialisation of scratch arrays. Finally, it dispatches BMI2 bit-shift instructions once per block rather than checking inside the hot loop.

On the ten-core workstation, isolated phase timings confirmed a clean 10.5% cut in serial scanning time. Across four copies of Wikidata, scanning fell from 160 ms to 143 ms with non-overlapping ranges over ten paired rounds. In a construction-free test where workers are artificially fast, that scanner win translated directly into 7.8% faster eight-thread decoding and 5.8% faster ten-thread decoding.

Yet in the real decoder on the very same machine, the wall-clock picture was much subtler:

- On four copies of Wikidata, eight-thread decoding sped up by 1.9% and ten-thread decoding by 4.0%. Thirty guard measurements across six other corpora showed zero regressions.
- On the single-copy Wikidata release check comparing 0.5.15 against 0.5.14, single-thread decoding ran 5.7% faster and two-thread decoding 3.4% faster. Elapsed time at four, eight and ten threads stayed flat within 0.4%. At twelve unpinned threads a 9.5% gain re-emerged.

Nothing went wrong with the scanner. On Wikidata, \\(k^\*\\) is about 9.5. At four or eight threads, the workers still take longer than the serial scanner. Shaving 10.5% off the scanner therefore just gives that thread more idle margin while it waits for the admission window. At one and two threads, every saved microsecond comes straight off the active core's total work. At ten threads, workers finally catch up to the scanner and the speed-up shows through again. On ordinary text, where \\(k^\*\\) is four to five, the scanner already limits throughput well before eight cores.

## 4\. Two more shipped improvements in 0.5.16

Two further default-path improvements shipped in mibz2 0.5.16. Both target real workloads that a Wikidata-only benchmark never exercises.

**Wider branchless run decoding.** When a bzip2 block compresses well, its decoded symbol stream consists largely of run-length tokens rather than dense literal bytes. mibz2's branchless run front previously accepted a block only up to 50% of the block length bound. A census across fourteen corpora found forty compressible blocks sitting just above that line, between 50% and 75% of the bound. Those blocks came from Markdown, ELF executables, JSON, prose and Python source, and still held 17% to 49% run symbols.

Version 0.5.16 raises the admission ceiling to 75% of the bound. In the newly widened band, a block must also carry at least 12.5% run symbols. That guard keeps short, small-alphabet random streams (near 3.8% runs) on the column path where they belong. Isolated virtual-machine benchmarks across three compiler profiles measured clear cuts in move-to-front and inverse-BWT processor time. Markdown ran 13.2% to 32.4% faster, ELF binaries 14.5% to 24.7% faster and JSON 9.0% to 9.9% faster. Not a single Wikidata, random, records or pattern block changed route. On the ten-core workstation's 0.5.16 release check, Wikidata elapsed times stayed flat from one to twenty threads, matching the prediction.

**Chunked whole-file reads in Python.** Profiling the Python bindings turned up an unexpected cost on the classic `mibz2.open(path).read()` path. Because `BZ2Reader` inherited `RawIOBase.readall()`, a whole-file read looped through `readinto()` in 8 KiB pieces. Reading one 210 MB file took 25,829 calls across the Python–Rust boundary.

Version 0.5.16 overrides whole-file `readall()` and `read()` in `BZ2Reader` to pull 1 MiB chunks directly from the Rust reader and join them once. On a virtual machine decoding Wikidata, `mibz2.open(...).read()` used 6.3% to 6.8% less processor time and finished 5.7% to 12.5% faster. Direct `BZ2Reader.read()` calls cut processor time by 8.5% and wall time by 20.0%, at 0.99× peak memory. Because the change lives purely in Python above the existing reader, the single stable-ABI wheel for Python 3.10 and newer stays unchanged.

## 5\. What this means for decoding in practice

Two practical rules fall straight out of these measurements.

First, throwing every core on a machine at a parallel bzip2 decoder only helps when the file compresses tightly. Highly repetitive dumps (15× to 20× compression) keep eight to ten workers fed. Ordinary source trees, JSON exports and documentation (4× to 6× compression) saturate the serial Huffman scanner around four to six workers. Beyond that point, extra worker threads burn processor time and cache bandwidth for slower wall-clock throughput.

Second, a single benchmark corpus can hide half the optimisation surface. On Wikidata, worker speed dominates up to eight cores. That masks scanner improvements while leaving ordinary text's run-path threshold untouched. Measuring station balance alongside full-file scaling exposes both sides of the pipeline. All three software changes described here are live by default in mibz2 0.5.16 on crates.io and PyPI.

# Half the memory on bzip2's most compressible files

Workers that pause rather than race far ahead of the reader now let mibz2 unpack a tiny file of runs in half the memory, and sooner as well.

27 November 2026 · 9 min read · [Research synthesis](<#5-what-it-means-for-a-caller>)

mibz2 decodes a bzip2 file the way [lbzip2](<https://github.com/kjn/lbzip2>) does, many blocks at a time. One thread, the scanner, reads each compressed block's [Huffman codes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-05-huffman-bit-buffer/index.md>) in order. A pool of workers rebuilds the blocks' text in parallel, and a reader hands the finished blocks to the caller in sequence ([the decoder, drawn as stations](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-25-the-decoder-as-a-queueing-network/#4-the-decoder-drawn-as-stations>)). Between the scanner and the reader sits an admission window, a fixed number of blocks allowed in flight at once. Beside it sits a cap of 12 MiB on decoded output that the caller has not yet read. Together they are meant to keep the decoder's memory small whatever file it is given.

For ordinary files they do. A block of JSON or text decodes to about a megabyte, so a window of thirty-two blocks holds a few tens of megabytes. But the size of a compressed block says very little about the size of what it decodes to. Two gigabytes of zeros compress to a file of 1,522 bytes. Decoding that file with the library's default settings for eight threads once took 1.27 GB of memory. The cap on unread output was there all along; it was simply checked at a moment when it could not see the danger.

That has now been fixed. Workers consult the cap themselves before they start a block, and the pool of spare output buffers is bounded in bytes rather than in buffers. Take the same file, four workers and a thirty-two-block window: peak memory fell from 1,118 MiB to 545 MiB, a cut of 51%. The decode also finished about 15% sooner. More to the point, memory on such a file no longer grows with the window at all. It is the same 545 MiB with eight, sixteen or thirty-two blocks in flight.

**Takeaways**

- **A tiny file can decode to a vast one.** bzip2's first stage writes a run of up to 259 equal bytes as five. One block of a single repeated byte therefore decodes to about 46.6 MB, from a few dozen compressed bytes.
- **The old cap watched the wrong moment.** It was checked only when the scanner admitted a block. Blocks of runs are scanned in microseconds, so the whole window was admitted before any output existed. The workers then decoded every admitted block in full.
- **Now a worker waits instead.** While the unread output is over the cap, no worker starts a block more than the worker count plus two places ahead of the reader. A bounded pool stops spare 46 MB buffers from piling up behind it.
- **Memory now follows the workers, not the window.** Four workers need a flat 545 MiB for any window from eight to thirty-two blocks. They had needed 589 to 1,118 MiB. Eight workers need 955 MiB, down from 1,528, and ordinary files decode no slower.
- **It is in the default decoder.** The change is on master, in every decoder the library builds by default, and will ship in the next release.

## 1\. How can 1,522 bytes become two gigabytes?

bzip2 compresses in stages, and two of them encode runs. The first is applied to the raw input before anything else. It replaces any run of four to 259 identical bytes by four copies of the byte, followed by a count. A block at the strongest setting holds at most 900,000 bytes *after* this stage. If all of them encode maximal runs, the block holds 180,000 runs of 259 bytes, and it decodes to

\\\[ \\frac{900{,}000}{5} \\times 259 = 46{,}620{,}000 \\text{ bytes} \\approx 46.6 \\text{ MB}. \\\]

The remaining stages then make that block almost free to store. The [Burrows–Wheeler transform](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-bwt-runs-from-mtf-codes/index.md>) of so regular a text is itself a handful of long runs, and move-to-front turns them into zeros. The second run-length stage writes a run of zeros by the binary digits of its length, so the number of symbols grows only with the logarithm of the run. The whole block's coded symbols fit in a few dozen bytes. Two gigabytes of zeros make about 46 such blocks, held in a file of 1,522 bytes: an expansion of well over a million to one.

**Two run-length stages.** bzip2 encodes runs twice. The first stage, on the raw input, exists to protect the block sort from long runs; the second, after move-to-front, compresses the zeros that move-to-front produces. The first stage is what fixes a block's decoded size: at most 900,000 bytes go in, and up to about 52 times as many can come out.

None of this is an attack peculiar to mibz2. Any input dominated by long runs behaves this way: a sparse disk image, a zero-filled log, or a deliberately constructed [decompression bomb](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zip_bomb>). A decoder that holds several blocks at once has to be ready for each of them to be 46 MB rather than one.

## 2\. Why did the queue fill with giant blocks?

The window counts blocks, not bytes. Library callers get four blocks in flight per thread, so thirty-two at eight threads. The byte cap was meant to cover the rest. Once 12 MiB of decoded output was waiting for the reader, the scanner would admit blocks only up to the worker count, plus two, ahead of the reader.

The flaw was in *when* that rule was applied. The scanner checked the cap only at the moment it admitted a block, and only the scanner checked it. On a file of runs the scanner finishes each block in microseconds, long before any worker has finished decoding the first one. When it admitted the second block, and the tenth, and the thirty-second, no output existed yet, so the cap's test passed every time. The window filled entirely with admitted blocks, and the workers then decoded every one of them, each into a buffer of its own of about 46 MB. A pool kept up to one returned buffer per slot for reuse, so that memory stayed held until the decoder was dropped.

A probe on a cloud machine with four virtual CPUs measured the consequence. With four workers, peak memory rose with the window, from 457 MiB with four slots to 943 MiB with thirty-two. At the default window for eight threads it reached 1,273 MiB. At sixteen threads it reached 1,818 MiB, limited only because the file had run out of blocks. Ordinary text, at comparable settings, used between 99 and 148 MiB. The extra memory also cost time, because the kernel zeroes every new page as it is first touched. With four workers, the sixteen- and thirty-two-block windows ran 24% to 28% slower than the eight-block one.

No earlier test had seen this. The most compressible sample in the benchmark set decodes to 20 MB, less than a single block of runs.

Which blocks in the window may be decoded, on a file of runs

Schematic, four workers and a window of thirty-two blocks. Before the fix, nothing stopped any admitted block from being decoded, and each decoded block of runs is about 46 MB. After it, while the unread output is over its 12 MiB cap, only the blocks within six places of the reader may be decoded; the rest wait, holding only their scanned symbols.

## 3\. How does the fix bound the memory?

It has two parts, both in the code that coordinates the scanner, the workers and the reader.

**The workers check the cap.** Before a worker starts decoding a block, it reads the total of decoded bytes still waiting for the reader. That total is kept in an atomic counter beside the shared state. On an ordinary file the total never reaches 12 MiB, so the check is a single memory read and takes no lock. Only at or over the cap does the worker look further. If its block lies more than the worker count plus two places ahead of the block the reader needs next, it sleeps. The reader wakes the sleeping workers each time it takes a block, and each re-checks its own position. Cancelling the decode wakes them too, so none is left waiting on a decode that has ended.

Waiting threads invite deadlock, and this design avoids it by construction. Blocks are handed to workers strictly in order. The block the reader needs next, and the few after it, were therefore handed out before any block far enough ahead to be held back, and they are never made to wait. They finish, the reader takes them, and its progress releases the workers behind.

**The spare-buffer pool is bounded in bytes.** The pool used to keep up to one buffer per slot. It now also stops accepting buffers once their total capacity passes the cap plus 2 MiB for each block that may be in flight: 24 MiB at four workers. Even past that, it keeps up to one buffer per worker. That exception matters. Without it, every block of runs would free its 46 MB buffer and allocate a fresh one, paying the kernel's page faults again each time.

Taken together, the two parts change what the memory on a file of runs is proportional to. Before, it was the window; now it is about two decoded blocks for each worker, whatever the window's size. The change adds no unsafe code. One new test drives a stream of high-expansion blocks through a decoder whose cap is forced to bind, and checks the peak. Another cancels a decode while workers wait behind the cap, and checks that they wake and exit.

## 4\. What did it measure?

The change was measured on its author's development machine, against the master branch it was built on. Each setting decoded the 1,522-byte file of zeros three times, interleaved with the old build, in one session.

| Workers | Window (blocks) | Peak memory before → after | Change | Elapsed time before → after |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 | 8 | 589 → 545 MiB | 7% less | 1.27 → 1.27 s |
| 4 | 16 | 811 → 545 MiB | 33% less | 1.44 → 1.35 s |
| 4 | 32 | 1,118 → 545 MiB | 51% less | 1.38 → 1.18 s |
| 8 | 32 | 1,528 → 955 MiB | 37% less | 2.03 → 1.60 s |

Peak memory decoding 2 GiB of zeros from a 1,522-byte file

Before and after the fix, on the same machine in one session, three interleaved repeats of each setting. With four workers, memory no longer depends on the window. The machine differs from the cloud probe of §2, so the two sets of "before" figures are not directly comparable.

With four workers and thirty-two slots, the decode took half as many page faults as before, about 140,000 instead of 286,000. It also used 23% less processor time. Fewer fresh pages for the kernel to zero is the likely source of most of the 15% saving in elapsed time. At eight workers the elapsed time fell by 21%.

Ordinary input had to decode no slower, a condition fixed before any measurement. Text and a sample of the Wikidata dump were decoded at one and four workers, seven times each, and every 95% interval included no change. The continuous-integration runner, a Xeon with four CPUs, then ran ten paired rounds over the benchmark corpora. At four threads it found the Wikidata sample 2.0% faster, with a 95% interval from 0.3% to 3.7%. The rest were within noise but for one small cell, random data at four threads, which came out 5.2% slower. That file's whole output is 8 MB, under the 12 MiB cap, so neither new check can act on it.

## 5\. What it means for a caller

A caller of the parallel decoder, from Rust or from Python, chooses how many threads to use. That choice also sets how many blocks may be in flight. Until now, it also set the worst-case memory on a highly compressible file. A 1,522-byte input could claim more than a gigabyte at an everyday setting, and more again with more threads. A file of that kind no longer costs memory in proportion to the queue. It costs about two blocks per worker. A wider window can be chosen for throughput without enlarging the worst case, and the decode no longer slows itself by faulting in memory nobody needs.

The bound is not the 12 MiB of the cap itself. A block that is being decoded must have somewhere to go. Each block within the worker count plus two of the reader may still hold a full decoded block of runs, and each worker may keep a spare buffer; 545 MiB at four workers is that floor. A decoder that wanted to go lower would have to decode a block of runs in pieces, which is a different design.

The fix is on the master branch and will ship in the next release. It applies to every decoder the library builds by default: the pool of workers that each take a whole block, and the teams that share one. It changes nothing about their output. The test suite, a fuzzing run and checksums of the decoded files all show the same bytes, and the same errors, as before.

---
