# Posing the inversion problem

The search for a new inversion algorithm became an eight-step programme, from a cost referee and measured ceilings to the model that will say where new mathematics fits.

24 November 2026 · 14 min read · [Research synthesis](<#8-where-things-stand>)

The work began as a search for a new mathematical basis for undoing bzip2's block sort, and it has become a programme in eight steps. The first two are done: a cost referee says what would count as beating the floor ([What else moves together](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-what-else-moves-together/index.md>)), and oracle measurements say where whole-decoder time can be won at all, up to 26% at ten workers, hidden until now behind the serial scanner ([Masked bottlenecks in a two-stage decoder](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-the-scanner-hides-the-emitter/index.md>)). The middle steps treat the decoder as what it is, a closed queueing network, and apply the methods of classical performance analysis to it: operational laws as completeness checks, designed experiments across every worker count, and a model fitted on some counts and judged on the rest. That model's purpose is the seventh step, to say which activities really control throughput at the operating points that matter, and so where a new mathematical device would have to act to move the whole decoder. The mathematics itself, the eighth step, already has a map of the routes ruled out and a conservation law that bounds one class of them. Every figure here comes from [the formulation report](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/reports/2026-11-24-from-search-to-formulated-problem.md>) and the records it cites.

## 1\. The programme

The chain follows [Raj Jain's course](<https://www.cs.wustl.edu/~jain/iucee/index.html>) on computer systems performance analysis, built on his *The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis* (1991): metrics and workloads, then measurement, experimental design, queueing models and simulation ([the programme](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/programme.md>)).

| Step | What it is | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The task and the referee: what counts as success, in which currency | done |
| 2 | The toy problem: a fixed machine, workload and referee, with payoff ceilings by oracle | done; three ceilings unmeasured |
| 3 | The system's structure: activities, buffers, shared resources and the feedback loop | designed |
| 4 | Measurement across 1 to 20 workers | the scanner profile has run; results pending |
| 5 | Experimental design: a baseline at every count, then interventions at chosen counts | being built; the second stage awaits a design review |
| 6 | The model: operational laws, a simulation fitted and held out, a roofline per activity | after step 5's data |
| 7 | Where new mathematics fits: the activities with real control, and what a device must change there | after step 6 |
| 8 | The mathematics, aimed at step 7's targets | continuing |

## 2\. Steps 1 and 2: the referee and the toy problem

The problem statement agreed by three independent answers asks for one uniform program, exact on every column, that builds its structures from the column within fixed budgets and pays at most half the old floor on every block. The currency is real machine cost: unpredictable memory reads (Q), the length of the chain of reads that wait on one another (D), passes over the data (P, at most two) and working memory (S), with the cost of building every structure included ([journal §33](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)). How candidates are found, by changing what moves together and by making existing steps yield more, is the subject of the earlier post; the cost rules referee candidates only once they exist.

Two statements made in earlier summaries, including ours, had to be withdrawn ([journal §42](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)):

- **G1 is not a lower bound on machine cost.** It bounds charges in a calculus of rigid interval moves; carrying it into machine cost needs a bridge theorem that holds for most of the old family but not all of it.
- **The 16% figure was never a ceiling.** It described one intervention, supplying the emitter's codes, at one thread. The four-arm test has since shown that the same intervention is worth nothing measurable at ten workers until the scanner is removed, and then a further 8%.

The referee's rulings close the remaining loopholes. A breakthrough means fewer than one unpredictable read per [width-1 row](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-halving-the-single-row-steps/index.md>), with the target at half of one, within two passes; a large cut in the chain of dependent reads is a real but lesser find. The number of live cursors is limited to about one per letter of the alphabet, so a route that needed some two thousand concurrent cursors to reach its figure was ruled inadmissible ([journal §49](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)).

The toy problem fixes the rest: an i9-10900K with AVX2, ten cores and twenty threads; the six admitted blocks, with synthetic hex beside them; and that referee. Its payoff ceilings come from the four-arm oracle ([journal §44](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)): emission is worth 15 to 17% at one to six workers, and at ten workers the serial scanner is worth up to 19% on its own and 26% together with emission. The decoder's work is divided into six targets, each tied to a stage: emission of the inversion (T1), its construction (T2), move-to-front and run-length decoding (T3), the Huffman scan (T4), riders across stages (T5) and the final run-length expansion and checksum (T6). Only T1, T4 and T5 have ceilings so far ([the targets](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/math-targets/targets.tsv>)).

## 3\. Step 3: the decoder as a closed network

The scanner and its workers are only a coarse picture. The measurement plan, merged from three independent answers to [a brief](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/decomposition.md>), divides the decoder into thirteen activities, from the input feeder through the scanner's table and Huffman decoding to the workers' move-to-front and run formation (one fused activity), the three phases of Open's construction, emission, the fallback route and the final checksum, and adds a serial tail in which a consumer takes finished blocks in order and writes them out ([the plan](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character.md>), §2; [journal §51](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)).

A fixed population of blocks, circulating

Schematic of the measurement plan's structure (§2 of the plan). The admission window holds a fixed number of blocks, so the decoder is a closed network, the case that classical mean-value analysis solves.

The feedback loop in the figure is what makes the network closed. Admission is limited by the blocks issued but not yet taken in order, and by a 12 MiB threshold on finished output, so a block that is queued, running, or finished out of order all hold a slot; one slow early block can stall the scanner through the consumer, and a waiting scanner does not by itself show that the workers are too few ([the outside answer](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/external/chatgpt-decomposition.md>)). Two further corrections from that answer shape every measurement. Requested threads are not actual workers, since a request for ten or more runs seven. And the summation theorem of [metabolic control analysis](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolic_control_analysis>) is no test of completeness: for an activity whose rate is the minimum of two others, the control coefficients sum to two under slowdowns and to zero under speedups.

Completeness comes instead from the operational laws of queueing theory, which hold on any measured trace without assumptions about distributions: Little's law, the utilisation law U = X·S, and the forced-flow law. The plan checks them explicitly for every activity and buffer ([the plan](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character.md>), §7a). Because the window holds W = 4k blocks, the closed-network results apply directly. Each activity's demand Dᵢ, its visits times its service time, gives asymptotic bounds on throughput, X ≤ min(1/D\_max, N/(D + Z)), with a knee at N\* = (D + Z)/D\_max, beyond which queueing is certain; the knee is the analytic counterpart of the worker count at which the scanner takes over. Mean-value analysis, the exact recursion for closed product-form networks, sits beside the simulation as a cheap check on it ([the methods](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/methodology/performance-courses.md>)).

## 4\. Steps 4 and 5: measurement and design

The first stage measures a baseline at every worker count from 1 to 20, in twelve randomised complete rounds, never as a rising sweep: 240 observations, each logging every block's route, stage boundaries, queue transitions and the four kinds of waiting, with separate ledgers for wall states and time on the CPU ([the plan](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character.md>), §3). Because delay depends on the variability of service and not only its mean, the plan reports the second moment of each activity's per-block service time as well. In a single-server queue with random arrivals (M/G/1), the mean wait is λE\[S²\]/(2(1 − ρ)), so in an illustrative case at 80% utilisation and a 10 ms mean service time, it is 20, 40 or 200 ms as the service time's squared coefficient of variation goes from 0 to 1 to 9 ([the outside answer on the courses](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/external/chatgpt-performance-courses.md>); [journal §54](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)). Long-tail blocks are the mechanism behind the admission stalls.

The second stage perturbs the activities one at a time at six worker counts, 1, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 20, slowing each by 20%, with 10% follow-ups to test linearity, using a calibrated busy loop that touches no memory ([the plan](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character.md>), §5). One-factor-at-a-time cannot see interactions, and the four-arm result was itself an interaction. So at 8 and 10 workers, where control is expected to change hands, the plan replaces it with a 2⁹⁻⁴ fractional factorial of resolution IV: 32 runs over nine activities, which estimates every main effect clear of two-factor interactions, at 768 observations against 216 for one-at-a-time ([the plan](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character.md>), §7a). Before that stage is frozen, the design goes to three independent reviewers. They are asked which competing mechanisms it must tell apart, the most informative design for about two to three hours of workstation time, how measurement on the i9 could be biased, whether every input each model needs is logged, and what to cut ([the design review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character-design-review.md>); [journal §55](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)).

## 5\. Step 6: the model

The primary model is a discrete-event simulation of the network above, driven by each block's measured service times in their original order, with a roofline per activity (compute, dependent reads and bytes against what the machine allows at each worker count) to reject infeasible predictions. Mean-value analysis and a fluid approximation of scanner rate against worker demand give closed-form checks. The model is fitted on nine worker counts and judged once on the other eleven, on the 10% follow-ups, on a held-out combined slowdown and on the four-arm arms, against a target fixed in advance: at most 3% median and 5% maximum error on mean runtime, with the waiting fractions within five points. A model that fits throughput but gets the queues wrong fails ([the plan](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character.md>), §7).

## 6\. Step 7: where new mathematics fits

The model's purpose is to price a mathematical idea before anyone builds it. Modification analysis, from [Mor Harchol-Balter's course](<https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~harchol/Perfclass/class.html>) on performance modelling, asks what happens to a closed system when one device's demand changes; a candidate device is then a change to one Dᵢ, and the bounds and mean-value analysis say what it would buy the whole decoder ([the methods](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/methodology/performance-courses.md>); [the plan](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/briefs/character.md>), §7b). A recitation in that course shows why this matters: raising an LRU cache's hit ratio can lower throughput, by intensifying contention on the hit path, so that measurement, simulation and a bound together trace a rise, a plateau and a decline. It is a classroom version of the masked bottleneck, in which speeding up one stage did nothing until another was cleared ([the outside answer on the courses](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/external/chatgpt-performance-courses.md>)).

Engineering leads wait for the same answer. Stream compaction, the `copy_if` that does not autovectorise because each output position depends on every earlier predicate, can be done branchlessly by compressing the selected lanes of a vector and advancing by the popcount of the mask ([the post that measured it](<https://loonatick-src.github.io/posts/vectorized-copy-if-analysis/>)). The workstation has AVX2 but not AVX-512, so the decoder would use a shuffle table indexed by an 8-bit mask, or BMI2's `pext`, in the workers' filter steps: run-record extraction, the thin and thick partition of Open's construction, and the appends of emission. It lowers the unit price of those steps without changing what the algorithm does, and it is held until the decomposition shows that one of them controls throughput ([the lead](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/leads/vectorised-compaction.md>)).

## 7\. Step 8: the mathematics

Every route so far wins one cost by paying another

Schematic, with figures from the reviews ([the six senses](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/reviews/neon-movement-critique.md>), [the fourth cycle](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/reviews/neon-movement-cycle4-critique.md>)) and journal §§39 and 41. Routes that need few unpredictable reads take far more than two passes; routes that shorten the chain of waiting reads leave the reads where they were; routes that share reads need repeated text, which novel random IDs lack. With every charge counted, no route reaches the middle.

Twelve candidate senses of moving together were built, measured on the six real blocks and reviewed, and none brought the reads below one per width-1 row once every charge was counted. The best composed routes cost 1.3 to 2.8 reads per width-1 row all in, against 4.3 to 6.9 for [Open](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>)'s own walk measured the same way ([the fourth cycle's review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/reviews/neon-movement-cycle4-critique.md>)). Pointer doubling and independent-set contraction reported zero unpredictable reads, but at 117 to about 600 passes, and building their inputs costs reads after all; both are known list-ranking algorithms for external memory ([the review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/reviews/neon-movement-critique.md>)). Landmark induction, recounted, brought the chain of waiting reads to 0.07–0.22% of the block, a record that has been reproduced, but left the reads at about one per row ([journal §41](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)). Four further objects, boundary chords, radix-fibre cones, quotient slabs and unitigs, were ruled out, two of them repeating an investigation from four days earlier ([the review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/reviews/carbon-cycle1-critique.md>)), and lazily contracting the thin runs was closed by a rule registered in advance, because removing interior rows fragmented the order of reads 4 to 9 times over ([journal §49](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)).

Of the sweep that keeps its form and loses its compactness

One result explains why so many routes fail in the same way. [Record 119](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/8cf099eb24d9943417cfccdf3763b54fbcd9c26b/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-closure-problem.md>) shows that a sweep over the block is itself an induction, and that composing steps preserves the *form* of the access schedule but not its *compactness* on high-entropy rows. On the first block, the shipped decoder's next-row addresses fall into 2,148 orderly segments, 0.061 per width-1 row; one round of composition shatters them into 44,814–52,319, some 21 to 24 times as many ([journal §42](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)). The law accounts for that figure, and settles the closure problem negatively within its class: no cleverer sweep of this kind can compose without fragmenting. Smaller results stand beside it ([the review of records 118–125](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/reviews/monodromy-118-125.md>)):

- a lower bound on failing steps for every interleaving of monotone cursors ([record 118](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ad169f87d657edca999d503b3637da1b6ca0a597/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-interleaved-orders.md>));
- the block length, the run count, the number of width-1 rows and the run-width histogram are free by-products of the Huffman scan, and parsing blocks in parallel is exact, as [lbzip2](<https://github.com/kjn/lbzip2>) already does ([record 122](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/c348f8f5135959cf6d3dbf318001797673ec7201/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-scanner-corrected.md>));
- an exact composable summary of each chunk for move-to-front, run-length decoding and the run records ([record 121](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a3facefcb7d927e8284381a299c6a80f0b58409f/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-scanner-summary.md>));
- building the structures by interval-exchange acquisition costs 0.10–0.34 reads per width-1 row, which puts construction back at its true scale ([journal §49](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a4bef380a2585687d773064617d5713f8cdc66b5/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)).

Five threads remain open. Acquisition is the binding cost on real blocks, and a search-free strip contraction projects about 0.6 reads per width-1 row but is unmeasured ([record 120](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/5d0795c81f073c44cf1b2f9d62f0ac190ca07dd3/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-thin-strip-acquisition.md>)). A representation outside record 119's class could compose without fragmenting, which by the law no cleverer sweep can. The relation that pairs the same offset in repeated JSON records is open again, since the obstruction claimed against it proved invariance only. Riders across stages are not excluded by the theorems against them, which rule out final values before the block ends but not deferred ones. And at the scanner there is engineering to do: a parallel scan gated by worker count, which the four-arm test prices at up to 19%.

## 8\. Where things stand

The first two steps are done, and the structure is designed. The profile of the scanner across all twenty worker counts, recording memory, scheduling and waiting for each decode, has run on the workstation, and its results have not yet been read. The first stage of the characterisation, the baseline at every count, is being built. The second stage waits on the design review, whose three answers will be merged into the plan before it is frozen. Nothing in the model, and so nothing in the ranking of where mathematics fits, has been measured yet; the mathematics continues meanwhile against the targets as they stand.

The ceilings came from oracles run before any candidate was built, and the routes' figures from reviews made independently of the work they judged; most of the headlines shrank under that review. What remains is a referee for any candidate, a price for each stage, a record of the routes already closed, and a plan to find out which stage the next idea must change.

# Masked bottlenecks in a two-stage decoder

Supplying both the serial scanner's output and the emission codes cuts whole-decoder time by 26% at ten workers, more than either stage supplied alone.

24 November 2026 · 7 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-it-changes>)

Our first supplied test, handing mibz2's emitter its decoding order for free made the whole decoder 16% faster on one thread and barely faster on ten ([the supplied test](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-7132792060>)), which suggested that at ten workers there was little to gain from cheaper emission. A four-arm test now shows that suggestion was wrong. At ten workers the decoder waits on its serial scanner, the single thread that reads the compressed bits ahead of the workers, and the scanner hid the emitter's gain. Supplying the scanner's output alone cuts whole-decoder time by 19%; supplying it together with the emission codes cuts it by 26%, and the codes, which bought 2% on their own, then buy a further 8%. These are oracle bounds, measured with the supplied work done outside the clock, so they say how much time a better algorithm could free, not that we have one.

**Takeaways**

- At 1 and 6 workers the workers are the bottleneck: supplied codes save 15 to 17%, and a supplied scanner saves 2% at most.
- At 10 workers the scanner is the bottleneck: a supplied scanner saves 19%, and supplied codes alone save nothing distinguishable from zero.
- Together they save 26% at 10 workers, 8% more than the scanner alone, which by the rule fixed before the data is an interaction.
- The gain is there to be had only by an algorithm that changes both stages at once, and the scanner's serial cost comes first.

## 1\. The decoder as a small factory

mibz2 decodes a bzip2 file in two kinds of work. One thread, the scanner, reads the compressed file in order and decodes each block's Huffman codes into symbols ([the Huffman stage](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-05-huffman-bit-buffer/index.md>)). The workers, running in parallel, take one block each: they undo the move-to-front and run-length coding, invert the Burrows–Wheeler transform and emit the text ([why the scanner is serial](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/index.md>)). The scanner is the factory's doorman, unpacking each parcel at the door, and the workers are its assemblers.

One doorman, many assemblers: where the decoder waits

Schematic. With one worker, blocks queue for the worker, so making the worker's job cheaper (arm B) saves time and making the scanner's cheaper (arm C) does not. With ten workers, the workers wait for the scanner, so only a cheaper scanner helps until the door is cleared, and then a cheaper worker job helps again.

## 2\. The test: four arms, two stages supplied

The question was whether removing two costs together frees time that removing either alone does not. The two costs are the scanner's Huffman decoding and the code ordering in [Open](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>)'s emission, the stage the earlier supplied test had halved. One binary carries four arms ([the registration](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/5731db1908d58fa4a51d22baf473d2f61ccd670e/docs/journal/2026-11-24-four-arm-registration.md>)):

| Arm | Scanner | Emission |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | as shipped | as shipped |
| **B** | as shipped | its codes supplied, in output order |
| **C** | its output supplied: each block's recorded symbols, replayed through the production job queue | as shipped |
| **D** | supplied | supplied |

In arms C and D the scanner thread reads no bit and decodes no Huffman code; it copies each block's recorded symbols into the same buffer the scanner would have filled and sends the block on, so everything downstream runs as in production and stays on the clock. The run decoded our Wikidata benchmark four times over, at 1, 6 and 10 workers, for 20 rounds with the arms in a balanced order, on one i9-10900K. Every round's output matched the reference: 838,800,784 bytes, with no mismatch.

The verdict was fixed before any data. At 10 workers the result is an **interaction** if D's upper 95% bound is at most 0.90 of A, D sits more than 0.03 below the better single arm, and D beats that arm outright; it is additive if only the first holds, and there is no potential if D's lower bound is above 0.95. The run is also invalid unless arm B reproduces the earlier supplied test, which it does: 0.976 against 0.988, with overlapping intervals.

## 3\. Results

Which supplied stage frees time, by worker count

Measured. Whole-decoder wall time against arm A, with 95% intervals, on Wikidata ×4 on one i9-10900K, 20 rounds. At 1 and 6 workers supplied codes (B) carry the whole gain and a supplied scanner (C) adds almost nothing; at 10 workers the order reverses, and both together (D) beat either alone.

| Workers | B: codes supplied | C: scanner supplied | D: both | D against the better single arm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.830 \[0.825, 0.834\] | 0.996 \[0.991, 1.001\] | 0.825 \[0.820, 0.831\] | 0.994 against B |
| 6 | 0.850 \[0.844, 0.855\] | 0.982 \[0.979, 0.986\] | 0.830 \[0.827, 0.834\] | 0.977 against B |
| **10** | **0.976 \[0.936, 1.017\]** | **0.806 \[0.782, 0.831\]** | **0.741 \[0.717, 0.766\]** | **0.920 \[0.901, 0.939\] against C** |

At 10 workers all three conditions of the rule hold: D's upper bound is 0.766, D is 0.065 below C, and D against C is 0.920 with its interval below 1. The verdict is interaction ([the verdict](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-7144221012>)). Peak memory was 3 to 5% lower in the arms that replay the scanner's output.

## 4\. Why ten workers reverses the picture

With one worker, the worker is the slow stage, so the scanner always has the next block ready and removing its work changes nothing, while making emission cheaper shortens the slow stage directly. With ten workers, the ten together consume blocks faster than one scanner can produce them, so the workers stand idle at the door. Making their work cheaper then only lengthens their wait, which is why the supplied codes bought nothing in the first test and nothing distinguishable from zero in arm B. Once the scanner's work is removed in arm C, the workers become the slow stage again, and the same supplied codes buy 8% more in arm D.

The earlier null at ten workers was therefore masked rather than absent: the emission gain was there, hidden behind the scanner. Together the two stages put up to about a quarter of whole-decoder time on the table at ten workers.

## 5\. What it changes

The gain is an oracle bound. Both supplied stages were computed outside the clock, and removing the scanner also removed serial bit-decoding that any real decoder must still do somewhere, in parallel or more cheaply. What the test establishes is where the time is and how much of it there is, and that the two stages must be changed together.

It changes the order of the search ([what else moves together](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-what-else-moves-together/index.md>)). At ten workers the first target is the scanner's serial cost, and only behind it does cheaper emission pay. The question it puts to the mathematics is a case of enrichment: what does the scanner already see while it decodes each block that the workers later have to work out again, and could it pass that along cheaply? Earlier attempts to split the scanner's work across threads failed on scheduling and memory rather than on the size of the prize, which this test has now measured ([journal §44](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2f03450661a08ebd7f42e8d0d7050fb96ac25418/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>)).

---

**Sources:**

- [The registration](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/5731db1908d58fa4a51d22baf473d2f61ccd670e/docs/journal/2026-11-24-four-arm-registration.md>), frozen before the data, with the arms, the rule and the harness.
- [The verdict](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-7144221012>), and the run's bundle, `four-arm/run-20261124T204154Z`, on the [evidence branch](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/c930253967e56d1b9eef955adbd3c68fb354eb0f/four-arm>).
- [Journal §44](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2f03450661a08ebd7f42e8d0d7050fb96ac25418/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md>), with the interpretation and the caveats.
- [The earlier supplied test](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-7132792060>), which arm B reproduces.

# What else moves together: the search for a decoder below the proved floor

The next decoder for bzip2's block sort will come from rows that move together in a new sense, or from inversion steps that yield more information.

24 November 2026 · 11 min read · [Meta](<#9-what-comes-next>)

[Our last post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-halving-the-single-row-steps/index.md>) set a target that no decoder in our current family can meet: at most half an event per width-1 row. This post is about where a decoder that meets it will come from. Rauzy–Veech induction, the step that took us beyond the walk, was found by noticing that a whole stretch of rows takes the same step, so that the step can be composed once and shared. Our proved floor says only that width-1 rows have nothing to move together with *in that sense*. The search is therefore for other senses in which they do, pursued all at once, and, beside it, for ways to make the steps we already take yield more information than they do now.

From one step per row, to one step per run, to the open question

Schematic, on a column of nine rows. The walk follows the block's cycle one dependent step at a time. Rauzy–Veech induction lets each run of equal letters share one step, but a width-1 row (b, x) has no neighbour to share with, and every current decoder pays at least one step for each: the proved floor. The search is for a sense in which those rows do move together, and for steps that yield more than where their own row goes.

How a candidate is judged is a separate matter, and this post settles it too. The target as first written turned out to be decided by a bookkeeping convention rather than by the data, so we have restated it in real machine cost on a declared model, where the floor has to be transferred by a proof of its own. Those rules referee a candidate once it exists; they do not produce one. The first candidate has already been through them: it shortened the chain of memory reads that wait on one another by 50 to 75 times on our real blocks, a real find, but it did not reduce the number of unpredictable reads, which is where the floor lies.

## 1\. Where the last post left us

The last post's terms are used here without being explained again:

- **The target:** at most h₁/2 events in all, in two passes over the block, with no more memory than Open, and faster than Open on whole decoding time ([§7](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-halving-the-single-row-steps/#7-where-the-search-stands>)).
- **The floor:** G1 proves that every decoder in the current family pays at least one event per width-1 row, so anything meeting the target is new by theorem ([§3](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-halving-the-single-row-steps/#3-three-routes-back-from-the-bwt>)).
- **The way out it left:** a rule applied to a whole scattered set of rows, short to describe and cheap to apply, in the form Build, Advance, Emit ([§6](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-halving-the-single-row-steps/#6-what-a-new-route-would-have-to-be>)).
- **The method:** the [Mario](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/aff4172ec770b24fecb934d8eee7b18f30cbb047/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md#2-the-ssl-coq-material>) move, which supplies the payoff first and looks for the mechanism second, and the supplied test that came of it ([§2](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-halving-the-single-row-steps/#2-four-reframings-of-the-search>)).

## 2\. What moves together

Rauzy–Veech induction came from an observation about the data, not from an accounting of cost: a stretch of rows holding the same byte takes the same step. Comparing the two algorithms, the walk and the induction, and asking what the two have in common, which is the question the last post took from [Hilbert's 24th problem](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_twenty-fourth_problem>), gives an answer in two parts, which together we call *contraction along composition*:

1. **a notion of "these move together",** which for Rauzy–Veech is adjacent rows holding the same byte;
2. **a rule for composing what moves together,** and then recursing on what is left.

G1 says that width-1 rows have nothing to move together with in that first sense. It does not say that they have nothing to move together with in any sense, and the distinction decides where to look.

Of the arches, and of walks in disguise

Contracting harder in the same sense is the failure to avoid, and our most recent rounds of candidates show what it looks like. The best of them, "arches" cut at the low points of the map and swept twice, reached 0.366 of an event per width-1 row, but only on synthetic random hex and only with a third pass. On our six real blocks the same construction cost 3.18 to 9.03 per width-1 row, and a single sweep we already had gave 0.412 on the same hex. Other builds that looked free walked the map row by row inside them, one read the true decoded text, and the arches themselves turned out to be a known suffix-array technique, SA-IS ([the review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/aff4172ec770b24fecb934d8eee7b18f30cbb047/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/neon-cycle5-critique.md>)). Each squeezed the same notion of moving together further, and paid for it with an extra pass or a hidden walk. Contracting the left-over cycle again does not escape either: that recursion is list ranking by contraction, a known technique for linked lists, and each row it removes still costs that row's own event, so the depth falls but the count does not ([the record](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/299a0624baadacfa079d1bf4d64939b326293b1a/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-supported-rows.md>); see also [our synthesis](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/cdeef65aba3b5ebad758cf4f5d169f0534bf80ab/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-synthesis.md>)).

The way forward is to change what moving together means. The phrase is deliberately loaded with several meanings at once: no one of them leads, all are pursued side by side, and finding further ones is part of the work ([the principle](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/efac4a340723e2b26ba66a91105ab6b4c14e1e22/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/ESSENCE.md>)). Three are named so far:

- **Contract along the text, not along the rows.** A repeated stretch of text is a run in the other direction, and copy plans are the start of it.
- **Move together up to a consistent relabelling,** rather than by exact equality.
- **Find a recurrence among the induction's own steps,** as the Pell rule in the last post ([§2](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-24-halving-the-single-row-steps/#2-four-reframings-of-the-search>)) generates new triangles where an oracle could only hand them over.

## 3\. Making each step yield more

The second principle, *enrichment along composition*, comes from another of Louis's projects, [page-dewarp](<https://github.com/lmmx/page-dewarp>). Its large speedups came from rewriting its projection so that automatic differentiation could supply gradients, which let it switch from a derivative-free optimiser to a better algorithm. Forward-mode differentiation lifts a computation into a richer algebra of pairs, with (a, a′)(b, b′) = (ab, a′b + ab′), so that extra information rides along with the ordinary result ([the account](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/efac4a340723e2b26ba66a91105ab6b4c14e1e22/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level.md#37-enrichment-along-composition-the-second-principle>)).

Where contraction does less work by recognising that computations are the same, enrichment makes work already done yield more, so that later work becomes unnecessary. Here it asks what one LF step, or one step over a run, reveals for free beyond where its own row goes, and whether something computed in an earlier stage, the Huffman or move-to-front decoding, could give the later ones what they need. One test keeps it honest: the extra quantity must be cheap to acquire and must not restate the inversion. Each row's position in the text is the answer itself, and a fingerprint of the column can separate every pair of inputs and still decode nothing.

## 4\. The first candidate, measured

The first worked notes already sharpen the search ([record 113](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/806aa0123c9a24ad7a1e9ef15da015e1408022f0/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-moving-together.md>), [record 114](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/bfdbc245fce475fbb7d017501a1e7423dd20eaf5/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-more-senses.md>)). Every sense of moving together puts the rows in some order, and it helps exactly as far as that order agrees with the order of the text, so the search becomes one for a cheap ordering of rows that correlates with text position.

The first candidate worked up in full, *landmark induction*, starts a chain at every row holding a chosen common byte. Those rows sit together in one known block and cost nothing to find. It advances all the chains at once to the next landmark, and repeats on what remains. It leaves the number of unpredictable reads where it was, but makes those reads independent of one another, so the chain of reads that must each wait for the last was estimated to fall from about one per byte to a few hundred on hex-dense content.

Measured on our six real blocks, that chain fell to 1.3–1.9% of the block's length, some 10,000 to 17,000 dependent steps: a cut of roughly 50 to 75 times, but far short of the estimate. On JSON the most frequent landmark strings stay frequent as they lengthen (`"`, then `,"`, then `","`), so the final walk dominates. The unpredictable reads rose by 5 to 20%, and width-1 rows turned out to be under-represented among the landmark rows ([the measurement](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/1799a29e7fcc2a63e06f8849bf939b318624fef4/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/m21/m21-results.md>)). Under the referee's ruling (§6), a breakthrough is a cut in the unpredictable reads, and a large cut in the waiting chain is a real find that is measured rather than claimed ([the ruling](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/3c19c9a2fb4e7831d1bf7a1d0e554c1bc6f8c6f2/channel/coordinator-to-neon.md>)). Landmark induction is therefore a real but modest find, and a reminder that estimates which assume random text can be badly wrong on real data.

## 5\. Why the target had to be restated

The rest of this post is the referee. Its first task was to repair the target, whose decisive gaps were in its accounting. Every known route that beats the floor does so with a *build pass*: a sweep over all the block's [run records](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) that composes facts in bulk, as squaring the map or batching the frontier does. The target never said whether such a pass is charged, and [our record of the question](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/8e9b962c5fc94da61e1d47a0868897b7e96ccf0c/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-charge-convention.md>) found that each reading settles it without looking at a single block:

- **If every record a pass reads is charged,** every exact decoder pays for nearly every width-1 row, since each such row's byte is recorded nowhere else. The answer is no, by definition, and it tells us nothing.
- **If a sweep is free and only row-by-row steps are charged,** the number of passes decides it. With passes unlimited, repeated doubling of the map brings the count below h₁/2 with nothing new in it. With the two passes the target allows, the best known decoder, squaring the map on Open's retained rows, still pays at least 0.60 of h₁, and misses.

The frozen target's verdict was therefore fixed by two conventions, the charge on a pass and the pass budget, and not by any fact about the column. A target that a choice of convention can satisfy or defeat cannot tell a new algorithm from a relabelled old one, which was the whole reason for setting it.

## 6\. Two yardsticks, kept apart

An [outside review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/a12492459dc8e9fb26a8ca4fc0dd36a3392b4769/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/council/chatgpt.md>) of the problem, one of three [compared side by side](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/18c74a670b70304c501078b0cef6ed9be706c4f6/docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/council/COMPARISON.md>), made the decisive distinction. G1 is proved in bookkeeping units: it counts charges in a calculus of facts, not instructions, memory traffic or time. Two yardsticks are therefore in play, and they must not be allowed to blur into one:

|  | Bookkeeping (version 1) | Real machine cost (version 2) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it counts** | events: charges per row in the calculus of rigid facts | unpredictable memory reads, the longest chain of them, passes, and peak memory |
| **What is proved in it** | G1: at least h₁ for the current family | the bridge, for most of the family (§7) |
| **The target** | at most h₁/2 events, as frozen | fewer unpredictable reads than one per width-1 row, within a fixed budget |

The original target stays exactly as frozen, as version 1. The machine-cost target is a new version and is labelled as one, because changing the yardstick without saying so can look like solving the problem. It judges a candidate by what it makes the hardware do ([the decision](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/9fb7b227063fe0439aac13b06cbf841bad99b066/channel/coordinator-to-neon.md>)).

The model separates the two kinds of memory access that matter. A *streamed* access moves a cursor one step along memory, which the hardware can anticipate. An *addressed* access goes to an address computed from data, which it cannot. Every run reports four figures, all of them, always ([the formal statement](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/303b48c8ff010ba3fd6576d89d6fec2987409f09/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-council-formulation.md>)):

- **Q**, the number of addressed accesses, in which the floor is to be beaten;
- **D**, the longest chain of addressed accesses in which each address depends on what the one before it returned, which is what makes the walk slow;
- **P**, the passes: bytes streamed, divided by the block's length;
- **S**, the peak working memory.

The budget fixes the passes at two and the number of live cursors at one per letter of the alphabet, plus a constant, which is enough to distribute rows by their letter. Holding the budget fixed is what makes relocation visible: a fall in Q bought with an extra pass, or with more memory, shows up in the other coordinates instead of disappearing from the count.

**Counting bytes** would have been the obvious yardstick, and the wrong one, for a decoder must write every byte of its output; whence a target stated in bytes written is impossible for a reason of no interest whatever: the output alone costs n, and n is never less than h₁. The review pointed out the trap, and the adopted yardstick counts accesses instead.

## 7\. The bridge

G1 alone proves no floor of h₁ in the machine yardstick. It bounds a sum of charges in the calculus, so it says nothing directly about Q. To claim that a candidate goes below the old family's floor in machine cost, we need a second theorem: that every decoder in the old family, executed on the declared machine, pays at least a fixed multiple of its bookkeeping charge in Q. Without it, "below the floor" would compare a machine count with a calculus bound, which is not a theorem at all. The yardstick also has to be fixed before any candidate is judged, or a convenient one can be chosen after the fact.

The bridge has now been attempted ([record 112](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ed6a3e9668587b993ab6a7f4732b043da03937e5/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-24-spec-pi-and-bridge.md>)). It holds with a constant of 1 for the walk, for Open and for lanes, and with one half for a single doubling sweep. It fails as a universal constant for one family, in-place sweep composition, where the floor becomes an input-defined count rather than a fixed multiple of the bookkeeping charge. That failure is not a counterexample to G1; it names the first candidate escape. The family is built entirely from old objects, though, so it would escape by how its work is laid out rather than by a new sense of moving together.

Two more terms needed the same treatment:

- **A pass** had no definition. There was no rule for a partial scan, for two scans merged into one, or for a scan that reads values it updated earlier in the same scan. The cursor model now supplies one: P counts bytes streamed through cursors, whatever the program calls its loops.
- **New** had been defined by what an object is not ("not rows, not intervals"), which renaming can satisfy. It now means new *relative to the method being escaped*, with a measurable gap in cost. Rauzy–Veech induction shows why the relativity matters. Against the walk it was a genuinely new basis: its cost scales with the number of runs, not of rows, and its records come from one pass. Against today's floor it is no escape at all, because G1's family already contains it. A definition that asked our own historical step to beat h₁ would be testing the wrong floor.

## 8\. The question in full

With the rules fixed (the machine model, the yardstick, the inputs and the budget), the question becomes one of existence. Is there a decoder with a new kind of object, a way to build that object from the column without the old pointer-following, and a cost law, such that:

1. it is exactly correct on every input, deterministically;
2. it builds its object only from what it is given, within the budget;
3. its cost, Q above all, is low enough on the random-looking content where the width-1 rows live;
4. and under a model of time fitted to our machine, it beats the current decoder on whole decoding time, judged at one thread and at the default ten separately?

The last condition reflects the [supplied test](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-7132792060>): handed a free decoding order, the whole decoder took 0.838 of its time on one thread and 0.988 on ten, two results that differ in kind and cannot be averaged into one.

A negative answer is harder than it sounds. It must rule out every allowed decoder, not the ones we have tried, and it must fix the budget, because with unlimited passes sorting alone brings Q to zero. No lower bound of that kind is known for inverting a permutation presented as a BWT; the only negative result on record is the scoped one, G1, in the bookkeeping yardstick.

**The Mario proof,** on a closer reading, is narrower than our last post allowed, and it is not where the payoff-first move came from. That move belongs to a separate effort on the Shifting Sand Land level. The [Rocq repository](<https://github.com/tra38/sm64-wmotr-abc-proof>) proves, for the Wing Mario over the Rainbow level, that a run with no A press never makes Mario fly, and even that theorem still rests on named residual hypotheses; its theorem that the level needs an A press is not yet started. What we borrow from both is the method, a large claim split into premises that are proved one by one, and not the standing of a finished impossibility proof.

## 9\. What comes next

The order of work follows from the two halves of this post. The search is for new senses of moving together and for steps that yield more, all pursued at once, and a candidate is first an idea of that kind, an object with its own rule of composition, before it is a cost. Once one exists, the referee applies: the specification of the machine, the bridge, and the four figures (Q, D, P, S) with building the object included. In the Mario manner, the supplied test then measures what the candidate's object would buy before anyone pays to build it.

Nothing is ruled out for having been tried before. An earlier idea may be taken up again when there is reason to think something in it was missed, but it may not be presented as new. Every proposal therefore starts by searching our records, and says either that it is new or which earlier attempt it revisits, and what that attempt missed.

The review that clarified the yardstick also found errors in our own records, and they are part of the work ahead. It listed 21 places where records contradict one another, have been superseded, or differ in scope. Among them, the draft negative theorem's list of excluded mechanisms omitted one that its own text calls open, and one measurement note compared about forty edges against the number of width-1 rows in an example with two runs, which cannot be right, since a block never has more width-1 rows than runs.
