# Sixteen at a stroke: fixed-width writes that stop the processor guessing

Writing sixteen at a stroke and keeping only what it needs spares the processor a guess per run, so mibz2 0.5.8 decodes Wikidata 5% faster on ten cores.

21 November 2026 · 11 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-did-it-buy-on-ten-cores>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.5.8](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-5-8>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#058---2026-11-21>))

mibz2 0.5.8 changes how its decoder writes short, variable-length sequences into memory. It used to write a run of row numbers one at a time, stopping when the run ended. Now it always writes sixteen consecutive numbers in one fixed copy, then moves its write position on by the run's true length. Whatever was written past that point is spare, and the next write covers it. The same technique applies to the decoded text. Each word of up to 16 bytes is copied as a whole 16-byte block, and the output position moves on by the word's real length. What is decoded does not change. The bytes are identical; only the shape of the writes is new.

This helps because a loop that runs a different number of times on every call makes the processor guess, each time, where it will stop. A modern processor works ahead of the instruction it is finishing, so it must decide early whether the loop goes round again. When run lengths vary at random between 1 and 16, it often decides wrongly. It then discards the work it did past the real end and starts again. A fixed-width write has no such decision to make. That is our explanation of the gain, reasoned from how processors work and supported by a controlled test in a C harness. It has not been measured separately with the processor's own counters ([section 2](<#2-why-would-writing-more-be-faster>)).

The change is inside Open, the decoder's newest way of undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), which [Open Returns](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>) introduced. bzip2 stores each block of up to 900,000 bytes as the last column of the sorted rotations of its text. Equal bytes on neighbouring rows form *runs*. Open keeps the rows of narrow runs, those at most 16 rows wide, which make up about a tenth of a Wikidata block. The rest travel through the decoding in groups and come for free. It files each kept row into one of 256 queues, one per byte value. Later passes wire those queues into a table that says where each kept row leads. A final walk follows the table and writes out each step's word. Filing the kept rows and building that table take half or more of Open's time, as [Research by obligation](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-research-by-obligation/index.md>) recorded. Open runs only when the decoder has many parallel workers. That means 8 workers or more on most machines, and 6 threads or 8 and up on the ten-core i9 we test releases on.

The change made Open itself about a fifth faster. Over the whole Wikidata benchmark file on one thread, its time fell from 433–441 ms to 347–359 ms. Those are four runs of each build on a cloud container. The decoder as a whole got 5% faster at ten threads, mibz2's default on the i9-10900K. Its wall time was 0.947 of the old, with a 95% interval of 0.939 to 0.955, and it used 5% less processor time. The ratio was 0.922 at 6 threads and 0.974 at 8. Peak memory stayed within 3.4%, and every output byte was identical.

That result covers one machine and one corpus, a pinned Wikidata sample. Below 8 workers on other machines nothing changes, because Open doesn't run there. The worker counts the decoder picks per machine are being re-checked for 0.5.8.

The decoder on the ten-core i9: new wall time over old, with 95% intervals

Measured on the i9-10900K, 16 paired rounds at each thread count, decoding four copies of the Wikidata sample end to end (839 MB out). Green is wall time, blue is processor time. Every interval lies below 1, so the new build is faster beyond noise at all three counts. Ten threads, production's default, was the count the registered rule judged.

The idea came from our research line, which works through candidate ideas under the [research charter](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-research-by-obligation/index.md>). It found the cost while explaining why a different idea had failed. It measured the fix in a C harness, but a first port to Rust then showed nothing on CI's benchmark. That null turned out to be expected, because the benchmark never runs Open. Native timing showed the kernel gain was real, and a registered test on the i9 adopted it. [Section 4](<#4-where-did-the-idea-come-from>) tells the story in order.

[Section 1](<#1-what-does-open-do-with-a-narrow-run>) works the queue fill on a toy column, the old way and the new. [Section 2](<#2-why-would-writing-more-be-faster>) explains why writing more can cost less, and [section 3](<#3-the-other-two-parts-a-counter-and-a-16-byte-copy>) the change's other two parts. [Section 4](<#4-where-did-the-idea-come-from>) traces the idea to the release, [section 5](<#5-what-did-it-buy-on-ten-cores>) gives the i9 result in full, and [section 6](<#6-what-comes-next>) says what comes next.

## 1\. What does Open do with a narrow run?

The toy block here has a last column of ten rows, `aabaaacabb`. Its byte `a` has three runs, of widths 2, 3 and 1. On real blocks Open keeps every run of at most 16 rows. Every run here is that narrow, so every row is kept, and a row's number among the kept rows is simply its row number.

Open reads the block's runs in order, and each kept row joins the queue for its byte. Reading the queues back in byte order gives the kept rows sorted by byte, with ties in row order. That sorted order is what tells each kept row where the decoding goes next ([Cutting the loop open](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open/index.md>) works it through). So the queue for `a` must end up holding the rows of its three runs, in order.

The old fill wrote each run's rows with a loop, one row per turn. After each row it asked whether the run had another:

The toy column, and the old fill of a's queue

Conceptual: the toy column and the old fill, one row per turn of the loop. Each run ends with a "no", and the "no" comes after a different number of rows each time. In code this was one line, `queue.extend(m..m + w)`, a loop whose trip count is the run's width w.

The new fill makes no per-row decision. A narrow run has at most 16 rows. So the fill writes 16 consecutive numbers, starting from the run's first row, all at once at the queue's current end. Then it moves the end on by the run's real width. The numbers written past the new end are spare, and the next run starts writing exactly there, so it covers them:

The same queue, filled sixteen at a stroke

Conceptual: the new fill on the same three runs. The first run writes 0 to 15 into slots 0 to 15 and keeps two; the second writes 3 to 18 from slot 2 and keeps three; the third writes 7 to 22 from slot 5 and keeps one. The queue's contents up to its end, 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, are what the old fill gave. The stamp analogy holds for the shape of the work; it stops holding on cost, since the spare numbers are real writes to the cache, 64 bytes per run where the old loop wrote 6 to 9 on average.

Two details make this safe. The queue's buffer is grown before the write whenever fewer than 16 slots remain past its end, so the fixed write never runs off the buffer. And the spare numbers are never read, because everything downstream reads a queue only up to its end. In Rust the fill is a few lines ([`push_rows`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/70b18ca4411fa10c9f29b80821c835358dde2f9e/src/open.rs#L233>)):

```rust
let iota: [u32; 16] = std::array::from_fn(|i| m.wrapping_add(i as u32));
queue[at..at + 16].copy_from_slice(&iota);
// the caller then moves the end on: thin[a] += w
```

The 16 numbers are 4 bytes each, so each run is a fixed 64-byte copy with no loop over the width. It is safe Rust, with every index checked.

## 2\. Why would writing more be faster?

The new fill writes seven to ten times as many numbers as it keeps. That it is faster says the old fill's cost was never the writing.

A processor doesn't run one instruction at a time: it fetches and starts instructions well ahead of the one it is finishing. To get past a decision such as "go round the loop again?", it guesses the answer and carries on. A component called the branch predictor makes those guesses from the pattern of past answers. When a guess is right, the work done ahead counts. When it is wrong, the processor throws away everything it started past the decision and begins again from the right place. That restart costs many cycles, far more than writing a few numbers.

The old fill's loop ended at a point set by the run's width, and the widths of consecutive narrow runs follow no pattern. The research line studied six Wikidata blocks. Each had 48,000 to 126,000 narrow runs, averaging 1.6 to 2.2 rows. Most loops therefore ran once, twice or three times, in no predictable order:

Why the loop's end is hard to guess, and why the fixed write has nothing to guess

Conceptual, with made-up widths in the real range. The upper lane is the old fill: every amber "?" is a run's end, which the processor must guess before it knows. The lower lane is the new fill: one fixed write per run, whatever its width. The clerk analogy stops holding in one respect: the processor's guesses are often right, and the cost is only in the wrong ones.

The new fill moves the width out of the decisions and into arithmetic. The width still sets where the queue's end goes, but that is an addition, and nothing branches on it. So the processor can run ahead through run after run with nothing to mispredict.

**How we know, and what is not yet known.** The research line tested this in its C harness before anything was ported. It built the same queues two ways on three of the six blocks. With a plain loop over each run's rows, a rival design tied the shipped one. Giving each the fixed 16-number write cut its construction time by 23–28%. The rows written were the same, so the cost was not the queues' memory traffic; the loop is what changed. It is still an inference, because no one has yet counted the mispredicted branches before and after with the processor's performance counters. So the mechanism above is our reasoned account, not a measurement, although the speed-up itself is measured.

## 3\. The other two parts: a counter and a 16-byte copy

The release changes two more things in Open, both following from the same idea of keeping decisions and bookkeeping off the per-run path.

**The queue's end kept in a counter.** A growable array in Rust, a `Vec`, records its own length in memory. Every append reads that length, checks the buffer has room, writes, and stores the new length back. The first port did that twice per run, once to append the 16 numbers and once to cut the queue back to its true width. Open already counts each byte's kept rows as it goes, for its own bookkeeping. So the new queues use that count as their end, and the buffer itself is kept at its full length. A run is then one bounds check and the 64-byte copy, and no length is written back. The rewrite also spelled out the per-run step so that its two common cases compile inline, without a function call.

**The 16-byte emit.** Open's last pass walks the table of kept rows and appends each step's word. A word is either a single byte or a longer piece from a dictionary. The old walk asked at every step which kind it had, then copied that many bytes. The new walk keeps every word as a 16-byte slot, padded with blanks, beside its true length. A step copies the whole slot to the write position and moves the position on by the length, so the next copy covers the blanks. On the six blocks, 92.5–94.4% of steps had words of 16 bytes or fewer. The rest, longer words, take a separate path that copies them in full. The figure shows the emit on the four words from Open Returns' toy, whose walk spelled `ana`, `d`, `nabana` and `nab`:

The walk's output, copied in 16-byte slots

Conceptual: the 16-byte emit on the toy from Open Returns. Each copy writes all 16 bytes of a slot; only the first "length" of them are kept, and the next copy starts at the amber line. The buffer is 16 bytes longer than the block so that the last copy fits, and it is cut back to the block's length at the end ([`emit`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/70b18ca4411fa10c9f29b80821c835358dde2f9e/src/open.rs#L653>)).

**Which part did the work.** The two rounds of porting let us split the gain. The fixed fill and the 16-byte emit came first, and the counter queues second. On one thread, over the whole corpus, the kernel's time moved like this:

Open's time over the whole Wikidata corpus, one thread

Measured on a shared 4-CPU cloud container (Xeon, 2.10 GHz), one pinned thread, each block's best of 5 summed over the corpus's 431 blocks, four interleaved runs per build. Indicative: CI and the i9, not this container, are where decisions are made.

The emit is the smallest of the three. In the C harness, the 16-byte copy on its own barely changed the walk's time, at 0.96–1.0 of the old. So in the harness, most of the first round's gain came from the fill. The native timings don't separate the fill from the emit, because the two were ported together.

## 4\. Where did the idea come from?

It came from a failure. [Research by obligation](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-research-by-obligation/index.md>) described how we now judge ideas by the work they remove. It listed "building the map of retained rows" as half or more of Open's time. One attempt on it, building the map backwards ([\#659](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/659>)), had lost natively: it took 1.10–1.15 times as long. The research line's second cycle asked why.

Its answer was the ablation in section 2. On that account, the rival design and the shipped queues had both been paying for the same mispredicted loop exits. A fixed 16-number write removed them from either. The research line then built that write and a 16-byte copy for the walk into a test arm. It was the single-walk control for a larger candidate that ran eight walks at once. On its own, that arm took 0.84–0.86 of Open's time to build and walk each of the six blocks, over 25 interleaved rounds ([the research journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/8b54b0243c2448b647e53c81e95b6e999ae54ef0/docs/journal/2026-11-20-carbon-cycle2-bvsmc.md>)). The records call that arm U16Q, and the counter queues added later Vec16.

The road from there to the release had a dead end in the middle:

From research idea to release, 20–21 November 2026

The chain of evidence. Amber marks the step that showed nothing; it was explained two steps later, not overruled. Each figure is from the step's own record: the research journal, CI's paired bench on \#664, the calibration and stage-attribution journals, \#666's stage table and the i9 evidence bundle.

Wherein the first port showed nothing, and the harness was wrongly suspected

**The first port showed nothing.** The safe Rust port ([\#664](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/664>)) passed every test, including 200,000 random walks checked byte for byte against the old emit. CI's paired benchmark then found no change: −0.1% (−0.4%, +0.1%) at one thread, and nothing beyond noise at two or four. The first reading was that the C harness had flattered the idea.

**The harness was fair.** A calibration timed the C harness's copy of Open against the real Rust kernel on the same six blocks. They agreed within a few percent on five blocks. The ported kernel ran at 0.86–0.91 of the old Rust kernel's time, a 9–14% gain ([the calibration](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/70b18ca4411fa10c9f29b80821c835358dde2f9e/docs/journal/2026-11-20-open-u16q.md>)). So the gain was real in the kernel, and the question became why it didn't reach the benchmark.

**The benchmark was blind to it.** A stage-by-stage timing of the decoder answered that ([stage attribution](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/70b18ca4411fa10c9f29b80821c835358dde2f9e/docs/journal/2026-11-20-open-stage-attribution.md>)). CI's benchmark runs 1, 2 and 4 threads. Below 8 workers the decoder uses not Open but Cells, the kernel that is faster for one worker. Open's smaller memory footprint pays only when many workers share the processor's cache. So CI had timed code the change never touched, and its null was the expected result. Over the whole corpus, the same timing found the first port cut Open by 11%, with every other stage level.

**The second round.** A later cycle of the research line proposed the counter queues. With them came a fused front end, feeding runs straight into the queue fill without the list of runs in between. Ported natively ([\#666](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/666>)), the counter queues paid and the fusion didn't. The fused route took 408–433 ms, against 384–398 ms for the two stages done separately. So the fusion was dropped, and the release carries the fill, the counter queues and the emit ([\#668](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/668>)).

## 5\. What did it buy on ten cores?

Because CI can't see Open, the decision went to the maintainer's i9-10900K, a ten-core desktop processor with twenty hardware threads. The test ([\#669](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/669>)) compared the release candidate against master, changing `src/open.rs` and its tests alone, on the whole Wikidata sample decoded four times end to end. It ran 16 rounds at each of 6, 8 and 10 threads, alternating the two builds. At those counts the i9 runs Open, with 6 workers at 6 threads and 8 at 8. From 10 threads the decoder trims its workers to 7, to fit the cache.

The rule was fixed before any data. To be adopted, the change had to make the 10-thread wall time faster beyond noise, with 6 and 8 threads not slower. Median peak memory could grow by at most 10% at each count. The outcome, beside that rule:

| threads | role | wall time, old → new (median, s) | wall ratio \[95%\] | processor time ratio \[95%\] | peak memory ratio |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 6 | must not be slower | 0.327 → 0.301 | 0.922 \[0.915, 0.929\] | 0.935 \[0.932, 0.938\] | 1.034 |
| 8 | must not be slower | 0.294 → 0.285 | 0.974 \[0.961, 0.986\] | 0.966 \[0.954, 0.978\] | 1.002 |
| 10 | must be faster | 0.299 → 0.284 | 0.947 \[0.939, 0.955\] | 0.952 \[0.943, 0.961\] | 1.015 |

All three counts were faster beyond noise, memory stayed within 3.4%, and the output was byte-identical in every round. The verdict was adopt ([evidence bundle](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/2d6e5503c2c49db8e79d889e084da7569291ef5d/open-vec16>)). The intervals describe variation across the 16 rounds, on one machine and one corpus.

**Why a fifth off the kernel is 5% off the decode.** Open is about three quarters of a worker's computing on its route. But a decode at ten threads also waits on the single thread that reads the compressed stream ahead of the workers, and this change doesn't touch it. A simple model in the stage attribution puts the balance between that reader and the workers near seven workers. That is where the i9 runs from ten threads, so at ten threads only part of the kernel's gain can show in wall time. The model assumes the container's stage ratios hold on the i9. At 6 threads, with fewer workers sharing the work, more of it shows: 7.8%. The records don't explain why 8 threads gained least, at 2.6%.

**What it costs.** Peak memory rose by at most 3.4%, at 6 threads. The queue buffers stay at full length between blocks, and each carries 16 spare slots, so a little more memory stays allocated. No part of the change adds unsafe code.

## 6\. What comes next

mibz2 0.5.8 ships the change. Its worker-count recalibration, the check of how many workers each machine should run, and its release-on-release scaling run are queued on the i9.

In short, Open spent much of its time filing narrow runs into queues, and the filing loop's end was unpredictable. Writing a fixed sixteen and moving on by the true width removed the guess. The same shape was applied to the queue's length and to the walk's output. A benchmark that never ran Open nearly hid the gain, until a stage timing showed where to look. The step not yet taken is measuring the mispredictions themselves, with the processor's counters, so that the explanation in section 2 stands on its own data.

The general lesson is about short loops whose length the data decides. Where such a loop has a small known maximum, it can often become one fixed-width operation and a variable advance. The buffer needs room for the overrun, and nothing may read past the true end. The decoder has other loops whose length the data decides, and we have not yet studied them this way. One candidate is the last stage, which expands bzip2's run-length codes into 4 to 255 copies of a byte. Its maximum is larger, so a fixed write there would need a different width, or a split into short and long runs.

# Research by obligation: modelling the work, not the algorithms

We now track the work any decoder must pay for rather than the algorithms that pay it, and a claimed Riemann proof has sharpened how we hunt.

20 November 2026 · 15 min read · [Meta](<#7-where-this-leaves-us>)

**What changed.** mibz2's biggest speed-ups did not come from tuning code. They came from changing what the decoder computes: walking a block's rows one by one gave way to [rearranging whole intervals of rows at once](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>), and that gave way to [keeping a tenth of the rows and letting the rest travel in groups](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>). This week we set out to find the next change of that size, and spent much of it learning how *not* to search for one. The result is a written research method, the [research charter](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/932ff82c5/docs/team/research-charter/METHOD.md>), whose central idea is simple: keep a register of the **obligations**, the kinds of work every decoder we have built must pay for, and judge every new idea by which obligation it removes and what it pays instead.

**Why obligations, not algorithms.** An algorithm is a bundle: it pays for several obligations at once, so when it loses, it is hard to say what lost. An obligation is the part that decomposes: "follow the retained rows one at a time", "build the map that says where each retained row goes next". Candidates come and go; an obligation stays open until something removes it or a proof bounds it. Six candidate improvements to the current kernel lost this week, and every one of them left the register knowing more than before.

**What happened today.** Two developments sharpened the method after it was written. A measurement traced the expensive work back to the text it produces, and [found it sitting in random identifiers](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-where-the-decoding-work-goes/index.md>). And a mathematician announced a claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, found with an AI system, whose account of *how* it was found gave us a better way to look for new ideas. [Section 1](<#1-the-obligation-register>) explains the register and [section 2](<#2-generate-from-structure-judge-against-obligations>) the cycle that uses it. [Section 3](<#3-five-research-cycles-read-through-the-register>) reads this week's five research cycles through the register, [section 4](<#4-where-ideas-come-from-the-leads>) describes where new ideas come from, and [section 5](<#5-working-backwards-from-the-text>) what working backwards from the text showed. [Section 6](<#6-adapting-the-method-toy-missing-effect-native-surrogate>) is the adaptation we made today, with a worked toy and a measurement of how to break it.

## 1\. The obligation register

A short recap of the setting. bzip2 stores each block of text as the last column of a sorted table of the block's rotations. Rebuilding the text means following a path through the table's rows, one byte per step. Equal bytes on neighbouring rows form a **run**, and rows in a wide run move together. mibz2's current kernel, Open, treats wide runs as single units, keeps the rows of narrow runs (about a tenth of all rows), and walks those one at a time.

Profiling Open splits its time into a handful of jobs, and each job is an obligation: something this family of decoders cannot avoid paying for. The register lists them with their measured cost, and beside each, the candidates that tried to remove it:

The obligations, and the candidates they outlived

The obligations are from the [register](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/932ff82c5/docs/team/research-charter/FRONTIER.md>); the shares of Open's time are measured (\#653). Each grey box is a candidate rejected on native timing or by a decisive count, except for overlaps, where it is the known, costly route.

Reading across a row says what was learned about that obligation. Three candidates attacked the walk over retained rows: a software-pipelined walk (the processor already issues the next load early), a compact rank structure in place of the stored edges (two to three times slower, because one load became four dependent ones), and several walks at once (no gain in our test harness). Three attacked the build: fusing passes, compressing queues, and building the map backwards. The backward build was the most instructive. It removed the queues it targeted, but its second pass over the run records cost about as much as the queues had.

The register also keeps an object apart from the route to it. One cycle found that the structure of where runs overlap is small: about 1.3 transitions per run on our blocks. The only known way to obtain it costs about 1.8 steps per run, which loses. Those are two findings, and rejecting the route must not erase the object: a cheaper way to the same small structure would still be worth having.

When a failure exposes a real obstruction, the register records three things: the concrete **witness**, the exact **scope** (which algorithms and cost model it binds), and the **escape condition**, the assumption a different formulation would have to drop. An obstruction without a stated scope does not count. That rule matters, because after six losses it is tempting to conclude that the walk is a law of nature. It is only a law of the representations tried so far.

## 2\. Generate from structure, judge against obligations

The register is for judging, not for generating. Early in the week it was used for both, and the ideas it produced were rephrasings of the costs in its own rows: "make the queue smaller", "make the walk shorter". So the method now separates the two, inside a cycle of five phases:

The research cycle

Conceptual. Ideas come from mathematics; the register decides which survive.

**Explore** generates from mathematical structure. The charter names four routes, as tools rather than quotas. *Representation import* asks what richer object this is an instance of: both earlier breakthroughs came this way, from seeing the row map as an interval exchange. *Obstruction inversion* takes a failure's narrowest witness and asks which assumption another primitive could escape. *Primitive ablation* forbids a dominant operation and checks the cost doesn't reappear elsewhere. *Small-instance discovery* finds the best exact construction on tiny inputs and looks for the law behind it.

**Triage, Deepen, Confront and Learn** judge. Every candidate must say which paid work disappears, what replaces it, and how the information it needs is obtained: we call this *acquisition first*, because several elegant ideas died on the cost of getting their inputs rather than using them. Every cost model is treated as a diagnostic, and with reason. A cache model ranked two of Open's variants the wrong way round, predicting a win for the one that runs 10–16% slower natively. None of the six candidates that passed a model passed native timing.

The cycle asks two separate questions of every candidate. Has the primitive changed, or only how the same operations run? We call the first *reorientation* and the second *traction*: Rauzy–Veech induction was reorientation, replacing single steps with operations on whole intervals, while the backward build was traction on Open's existing return map. And has the complete cost fallen? A new representation is not automatically a cheaper computation. The compact rank structure did change the primitive, removing the stored edges entirely, and lost because each step became several dependent lookups.

Two smaller rules hold the process together. A research session pushes its work at every handoff and at least every half hour. The rule has already paid for itself: one session was cut off mid-cycle by a usage limit, and its earlier cycles survived only because they were already published. And new mathematical leads go into an inbox that the researcher reads at a cycle boundary, so a good idea from outside never derails an experiment halfway through.

## 3\. Five research cycles, read through the register

The register earns its place when a cycle fails, because a failure read against it says which obligation resisted and why. A research model worked through five cycles this week under the charter, after a run of earlier candidates that prompted it. The table lists them all, with the obligation each attacked and what the attempt left behind.

| Attempt | Obligation it attacked | Outcome | What it left in the register |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Precomputed jumps per run record (\#652) | following retained rows | lost | building the jumps costs about one whole Open |
| Fused passes; compressed queues (\#654) | building the map | lost | the expansion to one entry per retained row is needed, and cheapest done in one sequential fill |
| Pipelined emit (\#656) | following retained rows | not adopted | the processor already issues the next load early |
| Tuning the thin/thick limit (\#657) | both | not adopted | 16 rows is best; choosing per block gains at most 1%, even with hindsight |
| Cycle 1: contracting the exchange from both ends | metadata; overlaps | lost on cost | the overlap structure is small (1.25–1.37 transitions per run); grammar machines pay 40–100 bytes per run |
| Cycle 2: building Open's map backwards (\#659) | building the map | 1.10–1.15× slower natively | the second pass over run records costs about what the queues did |
| Cycle 3: bucketed streaming exchange | building the map | lost (reported) | a claimed limit on keeping the exchange in the last-level cache; not yet audited |
| Cycle 4: contracting an unsplit forest | both | lost (reported) | claimed structure theorems about the run graph; not yet audited |
| Cycle 5: implicit rank in place of stored edges | following retained rows | 1.7–2.8× slower | one dependent load became four; memory fell to 0.36–0.49× |

*Measured where a PR is cited or a ratio is given; cycles 3 and 4 are as the research model reported them, and are still to be checked.*

Two patterns run through the table. Representations that are expensive to build lose on construction; representations that are compact lose on consumption, because recovering each next step takes several dependent operations instead of one load. The fifth cycle shows both sides at once: it cut peak memory to under half and modelled memory traffic by a quarter or more, and still ran two to three times slower, because a smaller description is not a cheaper computation. Neither pattern is a lower bound for the problem. Both are evidence about the families tried, recorded with their scope so the next idea can aim at the assumption that bound them.

The table also shows what the cost models were worth. Every candidate that reached native timing had first passed a model, and every one lost. The register now records each model's track record beside the candidate it scored, in a *fidelity ledger*, so a model that has mis-ranked before is read with that history in view.

## 4\. Where ideas come from: the leads

If the register judges, something else has to generate. The charter keeps an inbox of mathematical leads: directions from outside the cycle, which the researcher reads at a cycle boundary and is free to follow or set aside. Three came out of this week, each from asking what richer object a block's runs might be.

**A square-tiled surface.** Pairing the row map with the plain step to the next row turns the block into a surface glued from unit squares, a branched cover of a torus. Its singular points sit exactly where runs begin and end, and on our six blocks there are only one to eight of them. That is a striking amount of structure, but it forgets the runs' lengths, so it cannot decode a block by itself. The open question is whether directions on the surface, and how points move along them, recover what it forgets ([journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/932ff82c5/docs/journal/2026-11-20-origami-lift.md>)).

**A train track.** The runs can be drawn as a graph, with an arc wherever LF carries one run's rows into another. The arcs number exactly \\(2r - 1 - C\\), and 88–89% of runs simply pass their rows on to one other run, leaving a branching core of about a tenth of the runs. With the order of strands kept at each junction, this is a measured train track, the object Thurston used to carry tangles of curves on a few weighted branches, and whose basic move is the same as the induction behind our earlier kernel ([the train-tracks post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-train-tracks/index.md>)). A census found no small separators in the core, and as a set of retained rows it does worse than Open's.

**Interval pairings.** Agol, Hass and Thurston gave an algorithm that works on huge implicit families of strands through intervals paired by translation, without walking the strands. A block's runs have exactly that shape. Their algorithm counts components, not order; the lead asks whether a version that carries words could recover the text more cheaply.

None of these is a decoder yet, and the charter does not ask them to be. They are where a change of primitive might come from, and the register is what will say whether one does.

## 5\. Working backwards from the text

The register describes costs in the decoder's terms: rows, runs, passes. Today we asked the same question in the text's terms, prompted by a contrast with the Hutter Prize, which rewards the smallest self-extracting description of Wikipedia and lets decompression take tens of hours. mibz2 sits at the other end: its description is fixed by bzip2, and the goal is the least computation to recover the text. One Hutter winner, STARLIT, won by reordering Wikipedia's articles so similar ones sat together. bzip2 has already done a reordering of its own, sorting every byte by what follows it, and we asked what that exposes.

Tracing every expensive row back to the byte it spells answered it. The repetitive JSON skeleton is already nearly free: keys are about a third of the text and about 1% of the rows that stand alone. Unique random statement IDs, about 5% of the text, hold about 62% of them. Hashes that are reused form small runs, one row per copy. So the obligation "follow retained rows one by one" is, in large part, the obligation to spell random strings ([the post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-where-the-decoding-work-goes/index.md>)).

That reshaped an idea we had been circling: a zoo. Rather than one universal decoder, a repertoire of exact methods, each very good on one kind of structure, with the decoder recognising which applies. Repeated random strings might be copied once one copy is decoded; unique ones might be a true floor for any method that relies on repetition. Recognition has to be cheap, read from what the compressed block already gives us, and the first number to know is how much a perfect choice of method could save. An earlier attempt to tune Open per block found under 1% to gain, which is why that number comes first.

## 6\. Adapting the method: toy, missing effect, native surrogate

Today Levent Alpöge [announced](<https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf>) that he believes he has proved the Riemann Hypothesis, and its generalisation, working with Claude, with the argument formalised in Lean. Nothing here depends on it being right. What interested us is his account of how the argument was found, because it describes a way of searching that our method lacked.

**Since then** (a note of 21 November): the same day as the announcement, members of the Lean community reported that three independent proof checkers, nanoda, con-leche in its verified mode and pestka, each accepted the Lean development, about 17 million lines, as proving the Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. We have not checked it ourselves, and mathematicians are still digesting the argument.

As he tells it, he started from a *toy* setting where the theorem was already known (the Riemann Hypothesis over function fields) and re-proved it in a new way chosen so the proof might travel. He then named the ingredient that the hard setting lacks: Stepanov's classical argument uses *multiplicity*, a polynomial vanishing to high order, which over the integers would be "something like differentiating whole numbers". The decisive step was to find a different mechanism, native to the hard setting, with the same effect: chains of theta lifts, each standing in for one order of multiplicity. The human held the analogy; the AI system supplied the technical mastery to build it.

We have a toy setting of our own. When a block's last column has exactly one run per letter, its text is the coding of an especially simple interval exchange; Ferenczi and Zamboni proved that these "perfectly clustering" words are exactly the codings of symmetric interval exchanges, the structure our earlier kernels rest on. With two letters they are the Christoffel and Sturmian words, and their text needs no walk at all.

For the slope \\(3/8\\), letter \\(k\\) of the word is \\(b\\) when \\(\\lfloor 3(k+1)/8 \\rfloor - \\lfloor 3k/8 \\rfloor = 1\\) and \\(a\\) otherwise, which for \\(k = 0, \\dots, 7\\) gives `aabaabab`. Sorting its eight rotations and reading the last column gives `bbbaaaaa`, two runs, the smallest a column can have. A decoder that knew the slope would not need the column at all. It could write any letter of the text directly from its position, in any order, with no step depending on the one before. For an irrational slope \\(\\alpha\\) the same holds with \\(\\lfloor (k+1)\\alpha \\rfloor - \\lfloor k\\alpha \\rfloor\\): every output position is computed, not reached.

Toy, damaged toy, real block

Conceptual. The middle panel's measurements are in the table below.

How a surrogate was tried the same evening, and answered the wrong question

The first version of our transfer went wrong in an instructive way. We named the missing ingredient as run width, since the toy has two enormous runs and the random IDs have none, and tested an obvious surrogate the same evening: walking many independent stretches of the path at once, as mibz2's plain decoder already does. It gave no gain on Open's walk, and more to the point, it was the wrong test. Running walks side by side still follows the same edges; it is a speed-up of the old operation, not a new one.

The correction, which came out of the discussion, is that the toy's real power is not width but **cheap global coordinates**: a compact number (\\(k\\alpha\\) modulo 1) from which any position's letter follows. In the toy the two coincide, which is why they were easy to confuse.

They come apart if the toy is damaged on purpose. The damage keeps the rotation by \\(\\alpha\\) and both letters but cuts the circle into \\(p\\) pieces, each lettered \\(a\\) or \\(b\\) at random. The coordinate survives untouched: letter \\(k\\) is the letter of the piece holding \\(x + k\\alpha\\) modulo 1, found by one binary search over the cut points, for any \\(k\\), in any order. What changes is the column, which we measured on texts of 5,000 letters with the golden-ratio slope:

| Pieces \\(p\\) | Runs in the last column | Mean run width (rows) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 | 26 | 192 |
| 8 | 44 | 114 |
| 64 | 218 | 23 |
| 256 | 802 | 6.2 |
| 1,024 | 2,018 | 2.5 |

*Measured ([`toy2.py`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-11-20-toy-transfer/toy2.py>), two letters throughout).*

*Correction, 20 November 2026:* the first version of this table gave each piece its own letter, so at 1,024 pieces it had a 1,024-letter alphabet and its run count mostly counted letters. The research line caught it. With two letters the effect is stronger, not weaker.

With a few pieces the column stays wide, so a small cut barely damages the toy. With a thousand pieces the runs average two and a half rows, narrower than the random strings in our real blocks, and the coordinate still answers any position in one search. So a block can be almost all narrow runs and still have a global coordinate that makes the walk unnecessary. Width-based methods, ours included, would find almost nothing to exploit in it.

There is a limit, which the research line also proved. Every text coded from a rotation has zero entropy: a handful of numbers describe it completely. Real blocks are not like that. A block with about 760 random statement IDs holds about 90,000 random bits, and no global coordinate can be smaller than the information it determines. So on real data the coordinate we are looking for cannot be a single number like \\(k\\alpha\\). At best it describes the structured part, and the random strings must be paid for some other way.

That is the precise form of the question for the research line: what object, native to real blocks and cheap to read off the compressed input, gives coordinates the way \\(k\\alpha\\) does, or lets long stretches of the path be composed without walking them? Part of the answer may already exist in outline. For a rotation, the digits of a position in the Ostrowski numeration, built from the continued fraction of \\(\\alpha\\), say where it sits at every scale. For a general interval exchange, the induction that our earlier kernel performs builds a comparable hierarchy, and a position's path down that hierarchy is its coordinate. Our kernels pay to build the whole hierarchy and then write the text from it. Whether a position's coordinate can be read off without paying for the whole build is open, and it is exactly the kind of question the register exists to price.

**Ostrowski numeration** sets forth a whole number as a sum of the denominators of \\(\\alpha\\)'s continued-fraction approximations, each taken at most as many times as the next partial quotient allows, as decimal writes it as a sum of powers of ten.

## 7\. Where this leaves us

Three pieces now fit together. The obligation register tells us what our present algorithms pay for. Importing mathematical structure tells us what other operations might exist. Toy-to-hard transfer tells us which missing effects those operations should try to reproduce.

The method in one chain: model the obligations, because they decompose and algorithms don't; generate ideas from mathematical structure; judge them against the obligations, with acquisition counted and models treated as diagnostics; and when a phenomenon makes the problem easy somewhere, find what makes it easy, break it on purpose, and look for a different mechanism that recreates the effect where it is missing.

The method has not yet been shown to produce breakthroughs: five research cycles under it found real structure and no faster decoder. What it has shown is narrower: failed approaches are cheaper to reject, their hidden costs are easier to see, and the mathematics they leave behind is harder to lose.

A new research line is running now, independently, with the geometric leads (square-tiled surfaces, train tracks, interval pairings) as starting points and the toy-transfer lead waiting at its next cycle boundary. Its results come back for independent verification before anything reaches the decoder.

# Where the decoding work goes: random IDs in repetitive JSON

Tracing each costly row back to the text it spells shows that JSON keys cost almost nothing, while random statement IDs claim two thirds of the hardest rows.

20 November 2026 · 9 min read · [Open question](<#5-what-comes-next>)

**What we measured.** Undoing bzip2's Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) means rebuilding a block's text one byte at a time from a sorted table of its rows. Each byte of the text comes from exactly one row. Some rows are cheap, because they belong to a large group of rows that the decoder moves together. Others are expensive, because they stand alone and the decoder has to visit each of them in turn, waiting on memory every time. Until now we have counted the expensive rows but never asked *which text they spell*. So we decoded six blocks of the Wikidata dump, followed every row back to the byte it produces, and sorted those bytes by kind: JSON keys, numbers, words, and the long random identifiers that Wikidata attaches to its records.

**What we found.** The repetitive part of the JSON, which looks like the obvious target, is already nearly free: keys such as `"mainsnak"` are about a third of the text but about 1% of the rows that stand alone. Those rows belong overwhelmingly to random strings. The 36-character IDs that Wikidata gives each statement are about 5% of the text and about 62% of the lone rows. The 40-character hashes that identify a reference are a different case: each one is used several times, so its rows come in small groups, one row per use.

**Why it matters.** It says where a better decoder must win, since collapsing repeated structure is what the current decoder already does well. What remains splits into random strings that repeat, which could be copied once one copy is decoded, and random strings that don't, which no amount of recognising structure can help with. This post builds the measurement up from one example ([section 1](<#1-one-snippet-character-by-character>)), gives the totals over six blocks ([section 2](<#2-the-totals-over-six-blocks>)), explains why random strings behave this way ([section 3](<#3-why-random-strings-stand-alone>)), says why we went looking ([section 4](<#4-why-look-at-the-text-at-all>)), and ends with the questions it opens ([section 5](<#5-what-comes-next>)).

## 1\. One snippet, character by character

A quick recap of the setting, which [Open Returns](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>) works through in full. bzip2 sorts all the rotations of a block of text and stores the last column of the sorted table. The decoder rebuilds the text by walking that column backwards: from each row, a step called LF finds the row holding the previous byte. Equal bytes on neighbouring rows form a **run**. Because a run's rows move together under LF, mibz2's current kernel, Open, treats a wide run as one unit. The rows of narrow runs it keeps individually and walks one by one. They are about a tenth of a block's rows, and walking them is most of the decode's cost. Below we call a run of fewer than 16 rows **thin**, which is close to, though not exactly, the set of rows Open keeps.

The figure shows how that looks on real text, in three snippets of block 0. Each character is shaded by the width of the run that holds it, so a wide cell is cheap and a dark cell costs a step of its own.

Three snippets of block 0, each character shaded by the width of its run

Measured on block 0 of the admitted Wikidata blocks. The JSON keys sit in runs of hundreds to tens of thousands of rows. Every byte of a hash used six times sits in a run of six or seven. A statement ID's characters sit in runs of one or two from its first digit.

The three snippets behave in three different ways:

- **The JSON skeleton** (`"mainsnak":{"snaktype":"value","property":"P`) sits mostly in runs of 763 to 26,407 rows. The same bytes, followed by the same text, appear thousands of times in the block, so their rows lie side by side in the sorted table and travel as one group.
- **A reference hash used six times** sits in runs of six (twice seven). Each of its 40 hex digits is followed by the same rest-of-hash in all six places, so the six rows sort together. They form a thin run: six rows, not one, but far from the thousands of the skeleton.
- **A statement ID** sits in runs of one or two from its first digit. Its 32 hex digits are random, and no other text in the block continues the same way, so almost every row is alone.

## 2\. The totals over six blocks

The snippet is one example, whereas the measurement covers every byte of the six blocks, about 5.4 million bytes. A short script ([`costmap.py`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2b2499d89/docs/journal/2026-11-20-working-backwards/costmap.py>)) classifies each byte by a pattern: statement IDs, 40-digit hashes, entity IDs such as `Q42`, other numbers, JSON keys, other letters, and the remaining punctuation. The chart compares each kind's share of the text with its share of the thin-run rows and of the one-row runs.

Share of the text against share of the expensive rows, by kind of text

Measured; each bar is the mean over the six blocks. The classes are pattern matches, and "thin" means a run of fewer than 16 rows, an approximation to the rows Open keeps. The per-block figures are in the [research journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2b2499d89/docs/journal/2026-11-20-working-backwards.md>).

The per-block ranges tell the same story as the means. Statement IDs are 3–8.5% of the text in each block but 54–67% of the one-row runs. JSON keys are 33–38% of the text but 1–4% of the thin-run rows. IDs and hashes together hold 32–53% of the thin-run rows. The other kinds, numbers, words and entity IDs, cost at most about twice their share of the text. By contrast, a statement ID's share of the one-row runs is about thirteen times its share of the text.

## 3\. Why random strings stand alone

The table's rows are sorted by the text that follows each byte. Two rows therefore sit next to each other when their following text agrees for a long stretch. A run of width 6 therefore means six places in the block where the same byte is followed by the same text; a run of width 1 means that combination happens once.

Repeated structure gives wide runs: a key that appears 3,000 times, followed by the same punctuation and the same next key, puts 3,000 rows in one run. That is why the skeleton is cheap, and also why bzip2 compresses this kind of text well: a few wide runs describe many bytes.

A random string does the opposite. A statement ID is 32 random hexadecimal digits. The row of a byte inside it is sorted by the text that follows that byte, which is the rest of the ID. Even four random hex digits allow 65,536 continuations, and the block holds only about 760 IDs, so that following text is almost always unique and the row stands alone. The same is true of a hash the first time it is used. But a hash used six times has six rows for each digit, all followed by identical text, so it forms runs of six. Its cost is in the thin runs, not the one-row runs, which is exactly where the chart puts it: in block 0, 841 hash fields hold only 137 distinct hashes.

Three kinds of text, three kinds of cost

Conceptual. The three kinds need three different treatments, which is why one decoder that treats every thin row alike leaves something on the table.

None of this is special to Wikidata. JSON from logs, APIs and database dumps has the same shape: a repetitive skeleton with random identifiers and hashes threaded through it. The measurement uses Wikidata's text, but the conclusion is about that shape.

## 4\. Why look at the text at all?

The question came from a contrast with the [Hutter Prize](<http://prize.hutter1.net/>), which rewards the smallest self-extracting description of a gigabyte of English Wikipedia. Its rules allow decompression to take tens of hours on one core. mibz2 is the opposite case: the description is fixed by bzip2, and the goal is the least computation to recover the text. A short description is not the same as a cheap one to use. Our own research has met that gap directly: an earlier experiment shrank the decoder's lookup table to a compact form and found the decode 1.7 to 2.8 times slower, because each step took several dependent lookups instead of one.

**A short description**, a compact table even, buys naught at decode time: shrunk to a compact form, the decoder's lookup table made each step several dependent lookups instead of one, and the decode ran 1.7 to 2.8 times slower. A fact about one table, not a verdict on every compact form.

One Hutter winner in particular suggested the question. STARLIT ([Margaritov, 2021](<https://github.com/amargaritov/starlit>)) did not improve the compressor at all. It reordered Wikipedia's articles so that similar articles sat together, and the unchanged compressor then did better. bzip2's encoder has already done a reordering of its own, sorting every byte by the text that follows it. We asked what that reordering exposes about the text, working backwards from the structure we know the text has to what it costs to decode. The first answer is the one above: the structure we expected to exploit is already exploited, and the cost sits in the parts of the text that have no structure.

## 5\. What comes next

The measurement turns a vague idea, a "zoo" of decoding methods each suited to a different kind of text, into three concrete questions for the research line:

1. **Repeated random strings.** A hash's six copies spell the same 40 bytes. If the decoder could find out cheaply that a thin run's rows are copies of one another, it could decode one copy and write the others. Finding that out from what the decoder already holds, before the text exists, is the hard part, and its cost must be counted.
2. **Unique random strings.** Statement IDs have nothing to share, so their one-row runs may be a true floor for any method that works by recognising repetition. Is there an operation on them that is not a step-by-step walk, or can we prove there isn't one, for a stated class of methods?
3. **A method per kind.** Before any classifier is built, the first measurement is the best case: if each block, or each part of a block, could use whichever method suits it best, how much would that save? An earlier attempt to tune Open per block found less than 1% to gain even with hindsight, so this is the number to know first.

These are now recorded as a lead for the research line. The measurement script is in the [research journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2b2499d89/docs/journal/2026-11-20-working-backwards.md>), and anyone can rerun it on the six blocks.

---

- [Working backwards from the text](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2b2499d89/docs/journal/2026-11-20-working-backwards.md>): the discussion, the per-block table and `costmap.py`.
- [The run network](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2b2499d89/docs/journal/2026-11-20-run-network.md>): the runs as a graph, and the longest chains of thin runs.
- [Open Returns](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>): the current kernel, and which rows it keeps.
- [The Hutter Prize](<http://prize.hutter1.net/>) and [STARLIT](<https://github.com/amargaritov/starlit>).

# Train tracks: carrying a tangle of paths on a few weighted branches

Thurston's train tracks squeeze a tangle of curves onto a few weighted branches that can be edited directly, and a compressed block's runs form something very like one.

20 November 2026 · 9 min read · [Open question](<#6-what-is-known-and-what-is-open>)

**What a train track is.** A curve drawn on a surface, such as a sphere with a few holes or a doughnut, may be long and looping. Many stretches of it then run side by side before they part. A **train track** replaces all those side-by-side strands with a single branch, and writes on the branch how many strands it stands for. Where strands part or meet, the branches join at a **switch**, smoothly, like railway points, and the numbers must add up there. William Thurston introduced train tracks in the late 1970s to study curves and the maps that move them on surfaces. With a track, a few branches and a few numbers stand for a curve that might wind around thousands of times. Lee Mosher's three-page note[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-train-tracks/#mosher] is the gentlest way in.

**Why it matters to mibz2.** Undoing bzip2's Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) means following one long path through the rows of a block until it has visited every row; each step reads one byte. That walk is most of the cost. mibz2's kernels save work by treating whole groups of rows that move together as one unit ([A new way back from the BWT](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>), [Open Returns](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-19-open-returns/index.md>)). That is the train-track idea, applied to rows. The central operation of train tracks, *splitting*, is the same operation as the Rauzy–Veech induction behind our Cells kernels. Dunfield and Thurston say so in as many words, and we show their figure in [section 3](<#3-interval-exchanges-are-train-tracks-and-splitting-is-rauzy-induction>).

**What this post does.** It explains train tracks from the beginning using figures from the papers that define them ([sections 1–3](<#1-from-curves-to-branches>)). It then lays a small compressed block over the picture: its runs become branches, and the places where groups of rows merge or part become switches ([section 4](<#4-a-compressed-block-as-a-weighted-track>)). It shows the next layer of the theory, maps that write words ([section 5](<#5-maps-that-write-words>)), and ends with what the theory gives us already and what is still open ([section 6](<#6-what-is-known-and-what-is-open>)). No new decoder comes out of it yet; this is a map of the territory.

## 1\. From curves to branches

The name comes from Thurston's own drawings. In his lecture notes[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-train-tracks/#thurston] he asks us to picture a curve on a surface as "many parallel strands in thin, branching corridors". Then: "Imagine squeezing the nearly parallel strands of γ in each corridor to a single strand. One obtains a train track τ (with switches) which approximates γ. Each leaf of γ may be imagined as the path of a train running around along τ."

Thurston's corridors, and the track they squeeze down to

Top: the strands of a curve running side by side in branching corridors. Bottom: each corridor squeezed to one line, a train track, with a train running on it. Reproduced from Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of 3-Manifolds*, §8.9 (p. 204 of the notes), for commentary.

The figure below, from Dunfield and Thurston's 2006 paper[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-train-tracks/#dt], shows two train tracks: one on a sphere with four holes (drawn as a disc with three holes plus the outside), and one on a torus. Each thick line is a branch. Where two branches meet a third, they arrive from the same side and merge smoothly; that junction is a switch.

Two train tracks

Train tracks on a four-punctured sphere and on a torus. Reproduced from Dunfield and Thurston (2006), Figure 16, for commentary.

A track becomes useful once it has numbers. Each branch gets a non-negative **weight**, the number of strands it carries, and at every switch the weights must balance. In Masur, Mosher and Schleimer's words, a transverse measure "satisfies the *switch conditions*: for every switch \\(x \\in \\tau\\) we have \\(w(a) + w(b) = w(c)\\)" (2010, p. 4)[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-train-tracks/#mms]. Here \\(a\\) and \\(b\\) are the two branches on the narrow side of the switch and \\(c\\) is the branch on the wide side. So if 5 strands come in on one branch and 3 on the other, the shared branch carries 8.

A weighted track like this stands for a whole curve, or a whole family of curves, without drawing any of them. That is the first idea: **many paths that travel together are stored once, with a count.**

## 2\. Editing the track instead of the curves

The second idea is what makes train tracks a tool rather than a notation. The track can be changed by a local move, and the change can be computed on the weights alone, while the curve it stands for stays the same.

The basic move is a **split**, which acts on a branch that is the wide side of a switch at both ends (a *large* branch). Two pairs of strands enter it, one pair at each end, and run side by side through it. Splitting pulls the branch apart in one of three ways, depending on which strands end up next to which.

The three splits of a large branch, and a slide

"Top: A large branch admits a right, central, and left splitting. Bottom: a mixed branch admits a slide." Reproduced from Masur, Mosher and Schleimer (2010), Figure 1, for commentary. The inverse of a split is called a fold.

The weights decide which split to make. Two groups of strands enter the large branch on the same side, one from each end. If one group is heavier, the right or left split keeps every strand on the track, according to which; if they weigh the same, the central split does. The branch that now joins them carries the difference of the two weights. Applied again and again, the move shrinks the weights by repeated subtraction, the way Euclid's algorithm shrinks two numbers to their greatest common divisor. On a torus, a sequence of left and right splits spells out the continued fraction of a curve's slope ([Mosher 2003](<https://www.ams.org/notices/200303/what-is.pdf>)).

So a split costs a comparison and a subtraction, however many strands the branch carries, which is the property we care about.

## 3\. Interval exchanges are train tracks, and splitting is Rauzy induction

mibz2 does not start from curves. It starts from an **interval exchange**: a line cut into pieces, with the pieces put back in a different order. The BWT's LF map is one ([A new way back from the BWT](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) builds it in full): the rows are the line, and each run of equal letters in the BWT's last column is a piece that LF moves as one block, keeping its rows in order.

Dunfield and Thurston show that an interval exchange is a train track with a single switch. In their Figure 17, the left picture is a track on a sphere with five holes whose branches all meet at one point. The right picture thickens it: the shaded bar is the line being cut up, and each loop is a band that carries one piece of the bar's top edge to a piece of its bottom edge.

An interval exchange drawn as a train track

"At left is an interval exchange τ on a 5–punctured S². At right is a regular neighborhood of τ." Reproduced from Dunfield and Thurston (2006), Figure 17, for commentary. The shaded bar is the interval; the bands are the pieces that get exchanged.

**How to read these band pictures.** The black lines are not paths. The gap between each pair of neighbouring black lines is a band: a strip carrying a whole interval of points side by side. The shaded horizontal bar is the interval itself. A band leaves the bar from one stretch of its edge and comes back to another stretch, and every point carried along the band arrives in the same order it left. The loops that leave and return on the same side of the bar, and look like a pair of rabbit ears, are bands that reverse direction; Dunfield and Thurston allow them. The interval exchanges in mibz2 never have them: every band of LF goes from the top edge to the bottom edge. There is one band per run of the BWT's last column, with the run's width as its weight.

Then they split it. In the next figure, \\(t\\) and \\(b\\) are the rightmost bands on the top and the bottom of the bar. Band \\(t\\) is wider than band \\(b\\), so \\(b\\) is cut out of \\(t\\)'s end and glued on: the new track \\((\\tau', w')\\) has a band \\(t'\\) of weight \\(w\_t - w\_b\\) and a band \\(b'\\) of weight \\(w\_b\\), and nothing else changes. If \\(t\\) carries 7 points and \\(b\\) carries 3, after the split \\(t'\\) carries 4 and \\(b'\\) carries 3. No point was dropped; the same points are carried by differently drawn bands.

Splitting an interval exchange

"Splitting an interval exchange." Reproduced from Dunfield and Thurston (2006), Figure 18, for commentary. Their text continues: "The basic operation is called Rauzy induction in the context of interval exchanges, and splitting or sliding in the context of train tracks."

That sentence is the bridge. Rauzy–Veech induction, the operation behind our Cells kernels, *is* train-track splitting: it compares the two rightmost pieces, subtracts the shorter from the longer, and records which piece followed which. Dunfield and Thurston use the same move to count how many separate closed curves a weighted track carries, without ever drawing one. That is close to our problem, but not the same: they need the number of curves, and a decoder needs the exact order of every byte along one of them.

## 4\. A compressed block as a weighted track

Here is what the picture looks like for a real (tiny) block. bzip2 turns the text `banana$` into the last column `annb$aa`, with the original text starting at row 4. Grouped into runs, the column reads `a`, `nn`, `b`, `$`, `aa`, five runs over seven rows. LF moves each run as a block. Where the image of one run lands in another, we draw an arc between them and give it the number of rows it carries. That gives the **run network**:

| Arc | Rows it carries | What happens there |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| `a` → `nn` | 1 | row 0 goes to row 1 |
| `nn` → `aa` | 2 | rows 1 and 2 travel together to rows 5 and 6 |
| `b` → `$` | 1 | row 3 goes to row 4 |
| `$` → `a` | 1 | row 4 goes to row 0 |
| `aa` → `nn` | 1 | row 5 goes to row 2 |
| `aa` → `b` | 1 | row 6 goes to row 3 |

Read as a track, the runs are branches and the weights are the row counts. Two switches stand out. At `nn`, two single strands, from `a` and from `aa`, merge into a branch of weight 2, and the order is fixed: the strand from `a` is on top (row 1), the one from `aa` below it (row 2). At `aa`, that bundle of 2 parts again, one strand to `nn` and one to `b`. Every switch condition holds: \\(1 + 1 = 2\\) at `nn`, and \\(2 = 1 + 1\\) at `aa`. Following the strands from row 4 visits rows 4, 0, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3 and spells `$ananab`, which is `banana$` read backwards.

On real blocks the same network is cheap to build: one pass over the runs, with no row-level work. We measured it on six blocks of Wikidata JSON, each about 900,000 rows ([the census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/915ba45647f0d8a4bd1f3f8bf03bca2a8cc0d51b/docs/journal/2026-11-20-run-network.md>)). It has 1.21 to 1.25 arcs per run. Between 88 and 89 percent of runs are plain stretches of track, with one arc in and one arc out, and merging those leaves a branching core of about a ninth of the runs. So a block's paths really do travel in bundles along a few branches and part at a modest number of switches.

One piece is still missing before this is a train track in Thurston's sense: a track lives on a surface, and the order of strands at each switch comes from that surface. For a BWT block we have one. Pairing LF with the move to the next row glues the rows, as unit squares, into a closed surface whose corners all sit at run boundaries ([the origami lift](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/915ba45647f0d8a4bd1f3f8bf03bca2a8cc0d51b/docs/journal/2026-11-20-origami-lift.md>)). The run network is drawn on it.

## 5\. Maps that write words

A second kind of train track, from Bestvina and Handel's work[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-train-tracks/#bh] on maps of graphs, is closer to what a decoder does. Here the track is a graph, and a map sends each edge not to one edge but to a whole path of edges. Rafiqi and Zeytin's survey (2026)[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-20-train-tracks/#rz] gives an example on a surface of genus 2, a doughnut with two holes: a track with four edges \\(e\_1, \\dots, e\_4\\) meeting at one vertex \\(v\\), and a map that sends, for instance, \\(e\_1 \\mapsto e\_1 e\_2 e\_3 e\_1 e\_3\\) and \\(e\_4 \\mapsto e\_1 e\_2 e\_4 e\_3\\).

A track on a genus-2 surface, mapped into itself

"A genus 2 surface with a train track invariant under a pseudo-Anosov map." Reproduced from Rafiqi and Zeytin (2026), Figure 1, for commentary. The map sends each coloured edge to a word in the edges, such as *e*<sub>1</sub> ↦ *e*<sub>1</sub>*e*<sub>2</sub>*e*<sub>3</sub>*e*<sub>1</sub>*e*<sub>3</sub>.

**A pseudo-Anosov map**, as the reader may meet it in Thurston's classification, stretches a surface by a fixed factor along one family of curves and shrinks it along another, everywhere save at finitely many singular points. Thurston's classification makes it the typical kind of map of a surface to itself, beside periodic and reducible ones.

Such a map holds two kinds of information. Counting how often each edge appears in each image gives a matrix of non-negative integers, and its largest eigenvalue says how fast paths grow when the map is applied again and again. The words themselves give the order. For a decoder only the second kind is enough: knowing that a stretch of text holds three `a`s and two `n`s does not say which comes first.

mibz2 already builds such words. Each step of the Rauzy–Veech induction in Cells records which piece followed which, and the result is a grammar whose rules spell the block. In the language of this section, that grammar is the sequence of edge-to-path maps the splits produce.

## 6\. What is known, and what is open

The table below sets the parts of the theory against what mibz2 already does.

| Train-track idea | In mibz2 | Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Strands that travel together stored once, with a weight | Runs, and Open's convoys of rows that move together | in use |
| Splitting a weighted track | Rauzy–Veech induction in Cells | in use; the same move |
| Maps that send edges to words | Cells' grammar of return words | in use |
| Weights and their matrix | Counts of each letter | known; cannot give the order |
| The run network as a track on a surface | Built cheaply from the runs; surface from the origami lift | measured; the census is above |
| Folds, and the "illegal turns" of Bestvina and Handel | none | open |
| Choosing a different track for the same paths | none | open |

The open rows are where something new could come from. Bestvina and Handel simplify a map of graphs by *folding* (gluing together two edges that leave a vertex in the same direction) and by tracking which pairs of directions are eventually glued, the **illegal turns**. Folding is cheap and works on edges, not on the paths they carry. If the run network can be turned into such a map without walking the rows, its illegal turns might single out the few branchings where the order of the text is really decided. That is a question, not a result. Two easy uses of the network have already failed: its branching core has no small cuts to split it at, and walking the rows of the core costs more than Open does ([the census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/915ba45647f0d8a4bd1f3f8bf03bca2a8cc0d51b/docs/journal/2026-11-20-run-network.md>)).

These leads now sit in the project's list of open mathematical directions, for the research agent working on new decoders to take up. The general point holds whatever comes of them: a decoder gets faster when it stops following paths one at a time and starts editing a small object that carries many of them. Rauzy–Veech induction was the first such operation we found, and train tracks are the theory it belongs to.

---

**Research records:** [the run network and its census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/915ba45647f0d8a4bd1f3f8bf03bca2a8cc0d51b/docs/journal/2026-11-20-run-network.md>); [the origami lift](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/915ba45647f0d8a4bd1f3f8bf03bca2a8cc0d51b/docs/journal/2026-11-20-origami-lift.md>).

Figures from the papers above are reproduced at reduced size for commentary and criticism, each credited in its caption.
