# Open Returns: decoding a block from a tenth of its rows

mibz2 0.5.7 decodes Wikidata up to 11% faster on ten cores by keeping a tenth of each block's rows and letting the rest travel together in convoys.

19 November 2026 · 10 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-did-it-buy>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.5.7](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-5-7>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#057---2026-11-19>))

**The setting.** bzip2 compresses text in blocks of up to 900,000 bytes. For each block it sorts every rotation of the text and stores only the last column of the sorted rows, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), plus the row that holds the original text. Decoding means walking a map called **LF**, which sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier. Each step reads one byte, so the walk spells the block backwards, but each step also needs the row the previous step found. That chain of dependent memory reads is most of the cost of decoding. Repeated letters sit together in the last column as *runs*, and mibz2's kernels so far, eager Cells and LazyCells, save work by reasoning about runs instead of single rows ([A new way back from the BWT](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>), [Lazy letters](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-lazy-letters/index.md>)).

**What Open does.** mibz2 0.5.7 adds a third kernel, Open. It keeps only the rows that sit in *short* runs, about a tenth of a Wikidata block, and for each kept row works out its **return**: the next kept row the walk will reach, and the bytes it spells on the way. Decoding then jumps from kept row to kept row, writing whole words at a time. The rows it drops are the ones in long runs, whose neighbouring rows move together under LF like a convoy. Open therefore traces one member of each convoy and the rest of it comes for free: on Wikidata, one traced letter spells about sixteen bytes.

**What it bought.** 0.5.7 decodes Wikidata 7–11% faster than 0.5.6 from 8 to 20 threads on a ten-core i9, with 23% less peak memory, and Open alone is the cause. The release's only other decoder change affects 6 threads, which this comparison doesn't run, and a test of Open alone against 0.5.6 found the same gain. Below 8 threads nothing changes, because Open runs only on the parallel workers' route.

The gain depends on using Open only where it pays. Open has fixed setup costs, and on text, where runs are short, it is up to 5× slower. Each block is therefore checked first: Open runs only if its run records are between 1/64 and 15% of its rows, the range the existing LazyCells kernel already used. The check is two integer comparisons and adds no new tuned constant.

The result comes from one machine (an i9-10900K) and one workload (a pinned Wikidata sample), and it did not come at the first attempt. The first registered test of Open failed on a badly designed guard rule, and that verdict stands; a second test, with its rule fixed in advance, passed.

**The guard rule** of the first test compared single estimates with a 2% bound across 39 noisy cells, wherein a change with no effect at all would fail about 97% of the time. Its verdict stands; the second test, registered separately, is the one that adopted Open.

Measured on the i9-10900K: 0.5.7 against 0.5.6 on the Wikidata sample, the median of 10 paired rounds at each thread count (release-scaling/run-20261119T203443Z). The two releases are level up to 4 threads, where Open is not on the route. From 8 threads up, the shaded gap is Open: 2,557 MB/s against 2,356 at 10 threads.

[Section 1](<#1-how-can-a-decoder-skip-nine-rows-in-ten>) works a small example by hand. [Section 2](<#2-why-do-long-runs-travel-together>) explains the convoys and what they look like in real blocks, and [section 3](<#3-how-are-the-returns-found-without-walking>) how the returns are computed without walking. [Section 4](<#4-why-not-use-open-everywhere>) covers the gate, and [section 5](<#5-what-did-it-buy>) the road from a research idea to the release.

## 1\. How can a decoder skip nine rows in ten?

The 13 bytes `bananabandana` make a small example. Sorting their rotations and reading down the last column gives `nndnbbaanaaaa`, with the text itself at row 6. Its runs are `nn`, `d`, `n`, `bb`, `aa`, `n` and `aaaa`.

On real blocks Open keeps every run of at most 16 rows. In a block this small, that would keep everything, so the toy keeps runs of one row only, plus the start row 6. That keeps rows 2, 3, 6 and 8 and drops the other nine.

The worked example. Kept rows are blue; the runs Open drops are grey. The amber arrows are LF on the long run of four a's: rows 9 to 12 go to rows 2 to 5, still side by side, as LF does to any run (section 2).

Following LF from each kept row until it reaches another kept row reads one letter per step. That trip and its word are the row's **return**:

| kept row | its letter | LF goes through | returns to | word |
| ---: | :---: | :--- | ---: | :--- |
| 6 | a | 0 (n), 9 (a) | 2 | `ana` |
| 2 | d | – | 8 | `d` |
| 8 | n | 12 (a), 5 (b), 7 (a), 1 (n), 10 (a) | 3 | `nabana` |
| 3 | n | 11 (a), 4 (b) | 6 | `nab` |

Decoding is now four jumps instead of thirteen steps:

The four returns, chained from the start row. Joined, the words read the block backwards, exactly as a row-by-row walk would. Every byte is still written; what shrinks is the number of dependent jumps and the rows the decoder has to keep.

The words still have to come from somewhere, and in this toy they were found by walking. The point of Open is that on real blocks the words can be built far more cheaply than by walking, because the dropped rows travel in convoys.

## 2\. Why do long runs travel together?

Within one run, every row holds the same letter, and LF sends consecutive rows with the same letter to consecutive rows. LF therefore moves a run as a block: its rows stay side by side until the convoy reaches a place where the runs around it change, and splits. In the toy, the four a-rows 9–12 arrive together at rows 2–5. The earlier post called these groups *bundles*; a convoy of width *b* that travels *h* steps spells *b·h* bytes, but finding its route means tracing only one member, *h* steps.

Long runs make long convoys, and keeping the short runs removes most of the places where convoys would split, so everything else travels through intact. Medians over the 233 large Wikidata blocks in the sample ([counts](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/0ebbe09f75cdc7c1b26c26972c237a92d07ecec5/docs/journal/2026-11-18-astra-investigation-2.md>)):

Counted, at Open's threshold of 16 rows: medians over 233 large Wikidata blocks and six prose blocks. Wikidata keeps 11.3% of its rows; 88.7% ride in convoys, of which Open traces 5.5% of the block itself. Each traced letter spells about 16 bytes (median 15.9). In prose the convoys are about as wide, but they cover only a third of the block.

That is the whole source of the saving, and also of its limit: a block whose runs are short has little to drop.

## 3\. How are the returns found without walking?

The returns split cleanly into two independent pieces, a result proved in [Cutting the loop open](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open/index.md>):

- **The kept rows among themselves.** The order in which kept rows hand over to each other depends only on their own letters, a stable sort of the kept part of the column. Open builds it as the run records stream in: each kept row joins a queue for its letter.
- **The convoys' routes.** Where each convoy enters and leaves the dropped region, and the word it spells, are found by a small auxiliary computation on the long runs alone. It needs at most about three records per long run, however the kept rows are wired. The words are stored as a dictionary of shared pieces, not spelled out per row.

On one test block of 899,931 rows, that meant 89,874 kept rows, an auxiliary problem of 7,786 records solved in 11,215 steps, and 7,334 dictionary rules. The decoder then walks the kept rows' returns and copies words forwards.

Less to hold means less memory traffic. On that block, a full decode asked for 6.3 MB of extra heap against 10.4 MB for eager Cells and 15.4 MB for LazyCells, and in a cache simulation it executed 11% fewer instructions with 27% fewer first-level data-cache misses ([measurements](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/0ebbe09f75cdc7c1b26c26972c237a92d07ecec5/docs/journal/2026-11-18-open-return/evidence/>)).

## 4\. Why not use Open everywhere?

Because its setup has to pay for itself. Every block was timed both ways, on one thread ([census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/0ebbe09f75cdc7c1b26c26972c237a92d07ecec5/docs/journal/2026-11-19-open-admission.md>)):

| corpus | blocks | Open's time ÷ the existing kernel's |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Wikidata, admitted | 228 | **0.972** |
| Wikidata, too many runs (small blocks, 2% of the rows) | 155 | 1.005 |
| text | 48 | 5.11 |
| pattern (very few runs) | 88 | 1.55 |
| one byte repeated | 2 | 1.87 |

Open won exactly where LazyCells already admitted blocks, and nowhere else. LazyCells decides with two tests on a block's **record density**, its run records *R* divided by its rows *n*. A record holds a run of up to 127 rows, so *R* is close to the number of runs, and the decoder already has it. Open's admission reuses those two lines unchanged: 1/64 ≤ *R*/*n* \< 0.15, that is, 64·*R* ≥ *n* and 20·*R* \< 3·*n*.

The admission test, on a log axis of record density. Below 1/64 the block is nearly all one letter and LazyCells handles it well; at 15% and above, runs are too short for convoys to pay. The dots are examples: 50,000 records in a 900,000-row block is 5.6%, admitted; 300,000 records is 33%, not.

The test is a cheap predictor, not a guarantee: two blocks with the same density can differ in how their convoys split. The 228 admitted Wikidata blocks hold 98% of the sample's rows, so Open does almost all of Wikidata's work while every other block keeps the kernel it had.

## 5\. What did it buy?

Getting from the idea to a release took seven steps over two days:

From research to release, 18–19 November 2026. The research decoder used unsafe code; the production version has none, and passed Miri, fuzzing and an exhaustive audit of every return on small columns before any timing counted. The first registered test's guard rule compared single estimates with a 2% bound across 39 noisy cells, a rule a change with no effect would fail about 97% of the time. Its verdict stands; the second test, registered separately with its rule fixed in advance, is the one that adopted Open.

The release-on-release run that every mibz2 release gets, on the same i9, agrees with the adoption test:

Measured on the i9-10900K, 10 paired rounds (release-scaling/run-20261119T203443Z): 0.5.6's wall time over 0.5.7's on Wikidata, with 95% intervals. At 1–4 threads the intervals span 1. From 8 threads up, 0.5.7 is 7–11% faster. The release's attribution ledger credits the step to Open's merge alone.

**What comes next.** Open still builds and walks a table of every kept row's return, and that is now where its time goes. A research variant, scalar-cap, measured 2–5% faster than Open at 7–10 workers in the research harness on the same i9. It will need the same block-by-block checks before it can follow Open into a release.

[mibz2 · Research blog](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/index.md>)

# What decoding pays for: how long run boundaries persist

Three ways of undoing bzip2's block sort spend about two operations per run, and how long run boundaries persist explains much of why Cells and the forest vary.

18 November 2026 · 16 min read · [Research result](<#6-where-things-stand>)

Over the past two days we built three new ways to undo the Burrows–Wheeler transform, and studied a fourth that describes the text by copies. The aim was a method that does less work than the kernel mibz2 ships. That kernel, Cells, was introduced in [A new way back from the BWT](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>). [Cutting the loop open](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open/index.md>) then reported one of the new constructions, open return, which cuts LF's loop at chosen rows and decodes along the open paths left. This post sets all of them side by side. It asks what work each one cannot avoid, and why that work is so similar from one construction to the next.

bzip2 stores each block of text as the last column \\(L\\) of the block's sorted rotations, which is the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). A map called **LF** sends each row of the sorted table to the row of the rotation one byte earlier, so following LF reads the text backwards, one byte a step. A **run** is a stretch of equal bytes in \\(L\\), and LF moves all the rows of a run by the same amount, so the whole map is a list of shifted runs ([One shift per run](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/index.md>)). We write \\(n\\) for a block's rows and \\(r\\) for its runs. A Wikidata block has about 900,000 rows and 50,000 runs. Cells works on runs, not rows. It shrinks the map one comparison at a time until a single row is left, recording how to spell the text as it goes. [The mathematical dictionary](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-mathematical-dictionary/index.md>) names the objects it keeps.

The **structural work** of a construction is the number of basic operations it performs on the runs before it writes any output. Every construction must also write the 900,000 output bytes, so the structural work is where they differ by design.

We counted the structural work on all 233 large blocks of mibz2's Wikidata benchmark. Cells and two of the new constructions, adjacent-rank induction and forest-section elimination ("the forest"), do about the same work: 1.78 to 1.93 operations per run at the median. Their counts also rise and fall together from block to block, yet they do not perform the same operations, as a small example shows.

Much of the shared part is explained by one property of the block. We call the place between two neighbouring rows of a run a *gap*. Followed through LF, a gap's two rows read the same bytes until one of them crosses a run boundary. How long these pairs stay together, counted over the whole block, is the block's *boundary-orbit profile*. The persistence of boundary-orbit chains explains much of the variation in the structural work done by Cells and the forest. Yet it explains adjacent-rank induction's count poorly.

The obvious ways to lower that work did not lower it where we tried them. Refining the description of the block raised the forest's count on one block, and Wikidata has almost no repeated steps to accelerate. Splitting one block across cores was only modelled, and the model does far more total work. A description by copies of earlier text is far more compact, about 11,000 copies for a 900,000-byte block, but it is written in text positions. The copy routes we tested had to get those positions by walking LF, the walk the other constructions avoid.

Cells is therefore the best-performing formulation tested, although nobody has shown that it is optimal. The open question is whether a gap's separation depth, the number of bytes its two rows read together, can be found without walking its path.

Each figure is labelled as measured or proved, and each reading of it as interpretation. Sections 1 and 2 count the work and compare it, and section 3 builds the profile on a seven-row example. Sections 4 and 5 cover the routes that failed to do less, and section 6 says where things stand.

## 1\. How much work does each construction do?

Each construction counts a different kind of operation, so the fair comparison divides each count by the block's runs.

- **Cells** counts its *steps*. Each step compares the last stretch of rows in the runs' order with the last stretch in the order after LF, and trims the longer by the shorter. [The earlier post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/#1-rebuilding-aab-in-two-steps>) works two steps by hand. Our *test block* is one block of the benchmark, with 899,931 rows and 51,184 runs; Cells takes 92,570 steps on it.
- **Adjacent-rank induction** cuts LF's loop at the rows that are smaller than both of their neighbours along the loop, joins the paths between them, and repeats on the shorter loop. Stretches of neighbouring rows that move together are its *atoms*. It counts its *atom visits*: 102,233 on the test block, over 12 rounds ([the first investigation](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/1eb99cf48d5b5d8b62f70262ddf8cded98c38ca7/docs/journal/2026-11-18-astra-investigation-1.md#7-astras-final-result-adjacent-rank-gap-induction-draft-pr-553-head-79688e06>)).
- **Forest-section elimination** draws each run as a site. Each slice of a run that LF sends into a single run is an *arc*, and the test block has 62,138. It keeps a forest of arcs whose inside is fixed by their boundary, and computes the returns through the arcs left over. Then it repeats on that smaller system until one row is left. It counts the *arcs summed over its levels*: 90,945 ([the third investigation](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/1eb99cf48d5b5d8b62f70262ddf8cded98c38ca7/docs/journal/2026-11-18-astra-investigation-3.md>)).

Over all 233 blocks, the three counts per run look like this:

Three constructions, about two operations per run

Measured: the structural counts of 233 large Wikidata blocks, each divided by the block's runs. The box is the middle half of the blocks, the whiskers the full range, and the triangle the test block. Population coefficients of variation: 4.27% (Cells), 2.66% (adjacent-rank induction) and 3.45% (forest). The units differ (steps, visits, arcs), so the near-equality is a finding, not a definition.

The medians are 1.837, 1.929 and 1.778 per run, and each count varies by only 3–4% across blocks ([the synthesis](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/d256502657463014f64820865093fb419e89b7a3/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-synthesis.md#2-the-shared-count>)). An [independent verification](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6983166783>) reproduced every figure from the three census files.

**Why the alternatives are slower anyway.** Equal counts do not mean equal time. Dividing each construction's time on the test block by its count gives about 17–28 ns per Cells step, 270 ns per adjacent-rank visit and 430 ns per forest arc. Cells is a tight loop over flat arrays; the other two use balanced trees, matching and stored recipes. Decoding the whole Wikidata stream on the calling thread of a four-CPU cloud virtual machine, against eager Cells (the form that lays out all its records before it starts):

| Construction | Full Wikidata stream, calling thread, against eager Cells |
| --- | ---: |
| Open return ([Cutting the loop open](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open/index.md>)) | 17.1% slower |
| Adjacent-rank induction ([its study](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/79688e06/docs/journal/2026-11-18-adjacent-rank-gaps.md#what-the-frozen-and-full-workloads-cost>)) | 11.5× slower (8.370 s against 0.729 s) |
| Forest-section elimination | 15.23× slower (median of paired rounds) |

With a pool of worker threads the gaps change. Open return is 21.1% slower with two workers and 9.1% slower with four. Adjacent-rank induction is 7.8× slower with four (2.682 s against 0.345 s). The per-operation figures are quotients of times by counts in different units. They say where the time went, not that cost per operation is the only difference. The forest, for one, also makes 48,647 slab matches on its first level that its arc count omits.

## 2\. Is it the same work?

The three medians are close. The stronger finding is that the counts move together from block to block: a block that is expensive for Cells is expensive for the forest too.

Cells and the forest rise and fall together, and the profile explains much of what they share

Measured, on 233 large Wikidata blocks. Top: Cells' steps per run against the forest's arcs per run. Bottom: the correlation between the two counts' fitted residuals, after removing, by linear regression, the quantities named on each bar. The second bar's term is the historical proxy for the excess (one less than the first historical depth count, per run), and the third bar's is the historical profile's tail, counted with row 0; both are explained in section 3. The per-block points were joined from the Cells census and the forest census; the third and fourth bars come from [the profile test](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2157acad18598e9aa555b4f5e5576c0f875779de/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-q-profile.md#2-does-the-profile-explain-the-three-counts-for-cells-and-the-forest-yes-c>), whose per-block profile values are not published.

The Cells–forest Pearson correlation is 0.906. Part of it could be run density, \\(r/n\\), which differs from block to block. Removing \\(r/n\\) by regression leaves 0.859, so most of the agreement is about something else in the block. The agreement is weaker for adjacent-rank induction: 0.74 with the forest and 0.68 with Cells.

Of a tempting reading, undone by thirteen bytes

**Not the same events.** A tempting reading is that the constructions perform the same operations in different clothes. An independent verification refuted that on a 13-byte column, `1111000011100`. The forest has a free choice when two arcs have equal width. Reversing only those ties leaves the input, the starting network and the first level's output the same, yet the forest's total goes from 12 arcs to 15. Cells has no such choice, and its count is unchanged. So the shared count is not an event-by-event match but a shared dependence on something in the block, which the next section names.

## 3\. What the profile measures

The worked example is the seven rotations of `banana$`, sorted, with their last bytes. Its last column `annb$aa` has five runs: `a`, `nn`, `b`, `$` and `aa`.

Two neighbouring rows read the same bytes until a run boundary separates them

Conceptual, on the worked example. Rows 1 and 2 are neighbours inside the run `nn`. LF keeps neighbours in one run as neighbours, so the pair moves together until it straddles a run boundary. Read the chain the other way, from the boundary between rows 2 and 3: it pulls back to the gap between rows 5 and 6, then to the gap between rows 1 and 2, and stops there, because the rows LF sends to 1 and 2 (rows 0 and 5) are not neighbours. The profile counts four gaps at depth 0 and one each at depths 1 and 2.

The two rows stay together because, inside a run, LF sends neighbouring rows to neighbouring rows: both end in the same byte, and LF ranks rows with equal last bytes in their original order. So the pair reads the same byte, moves one step, and, if it is still inside a run, does so again. It parts only when it lands on a **run boundary**. The number of bytes the pair reads together is its gap's **separation depth**. In `banana$`, the gap between rows 1 and 2 has depth 2 and the gap between rows 5 and 6 has depth 1. The four gaps that are run boundaries have depth 0.

**The boundary-orbit profile** counts the gaps by depth. Let \\(q\_k\\) be the number of gaps between neighbouring rows whose rows read exactly \\(k\\) bytes together. For `banana$`, \\(q\_0 = 4\\), \\(q\_1 = 1\\) and \\(q\_2 = 1\\).

**Why it counts chains.** Read backwards, as in the figure, each run boundary starts a chain of gaps. In `banana$`, the boundary between rows 2 and 3 leads to the gap between rows 5 and 6, and then to the gap between rows 1 and 2. A chain that lasts \\(\\ell\\) steps has exactly one gap at each depth \\(0, 1, \\dots, \\ell\\). So \\(q\_k\\) is also the number of chains that last at least \\(k\\) steps. In `banana$` one chain reaches depth 2 and the other three stop at once, which is why \\(q\_1 = q\_2 = 1\\). The profile records how long the run boundaries persist when pulled back through LF. This is **proved**, and checked on all 233 blocks ([the chain record](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2e31341f46e5c44d7398ebfa2dd7babb3bc35af7/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-q-lcp.md#1-the-exact-correspondence>)).

**Why the short tail is the part that matters.** Added over every depth from 1 up, the profile is the total length of the chains, and that is always \\(n - r\\): in `banana$`, \\(q\_1 + q\_2 = 2 = 7 - 5\\). This holds for any block that is not one word repeated, which covers all 233. (In a repeated word such as `abab`, some gaps lie on loops and belong to no chain.) So the total alone cannot tell apart two blocks with the same rows and runs, though the whole profile can. What separates them is how early their chains die. The **short tail**, \\(\\sum\_{k=2}^{8} q\_k\\), counts one gap for each chain still alive at each depth from 2 to 8. In `banana$` it is 1: the single chain that outlives its first step.

**How the profile meets the forest.** The start of the profile is already part of the forest's network. Overlay two ways of cutting the rows into pieces: at the run boundaries, and at the boundaries of the runs' images under LF. Each has \\(r - 1\\) internal cuts. If \\(C\\) of the cuts coincide, the overlay has

\\\[E\_0 = 2r - 1 - C\\\]

pieces, and those pieces are exactly the forest's arcs. This is **proved**, and it holds on all 233 blocks. The forest's *excess* is \\(E\_0 - V\_0\\), its arcs minus its sites (\\(V\_0 = r\\)). A gap has depth 1 when LF carries it onto a run boundary, and the run boundaries reached that way are the \\(r - 1 - C\\) that are not also image cuts. So

\\\[q\_1 = r - 1 - C = E\_0 - r,\\\]

the excess. The forest's leftover arcs, its *chords*, number one more, \\(E\_0 - r + 1\\). In `banana$`, \\(C = 3\\) and \\(E\_0 = 6\\), so \\(q\_1 = 1\\) and the forest has 2 chords.

**The profile test's convention.** The profile test that the fits below come from counted one point more. Row 0 starts a run but sits at no gap, and the test added it at the depth \\(d\_0\\) where row 0's own path first lands on a run boundary. We write that *historical* profile as \\(\\tilde q\_k = q\_k + \[k = d\_0\]\\). On 229 blocks \\(d\_0 = 1\\), so \\(\\tilde q\_1\\) equals the chord count: 10,955 on the test block, against \\(q\_1 = 10{,}954\\). On the other four, \\(d\_0 = 2\\) and the extra point falls in the tail. The three-byte column `100` shows the same case: there \\(\\tilde q\_1 = q\_1 = 1\\), while the forest has 2 chords. So the historical \\(\\tilde q\_1\\) matches the chords only when \\(d\_0 = 1\\), not by a rule ([the check](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2e31341f46e5c44d7398ebfa2dd7babb3bc35af7/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-q-lcp.md#1-the-exact-correspondence>)). On the test block, \\(\\tilde q\_2\\) to \\(\\tilde q\_5\\) equal exactly the excesses of the refined networks in section 4.

On the real blocks the profile decays slowly. The median of \\(\\tilde q\_k/r\\) over the 233 blocks falls only from 0.223 at \\(k = 1\\) to 0.101 at \\(k = 8\\) ([the profile test](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/2157acad18598e9aa555b4f5e5576c0f875779de/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-q-profile.md#1-the-identification-verified-p-c>)). After eight steps, there is still about one chain running for every ten runs.

**The test.** It compared the short-tail sum with the depths fitted one by one. Each count per run was fitted by least squares, with leave-one-out error, using the historical profile:

| Model | Cells \\(R^2\\) | Forest \\(R^2\\) | Adj.-rank \\(R^2\\) | Residual correlation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| \\(r/n\\) and the excess proxy \\((\\tilde q\_1 - 1)/r\\) | 0.825 | 0.887 | 0.529 | 0.393 |
| the same, plus \\(\\sum\_{k=2}^{8} \\tilde q\_k/r\\) | 0.925 | 0.923 | 0.557 | −0.061 |
| \\(r/n\\) and \\(\\tilde q\_1, \\dots, \\tilde q\_8\\) separately | 0.946 | 0.959 | 0.570 | 0.307 |

**From one chain to the fit.** The first model already holds run density and the historical proxy for the excess, \\((\\tilde q\_1 - 1)/r\\). The exact excess \\(q\_1\\) counts the chains reaching at least one step. On the 229 blocks with \\(d\_0 = 1\\) the proxy equals the exact excess per run, \\(q\_1/r\\), and on the other four it is lower by \\(1/r\\). The first-depth count includes longer chains, but it cannot tell how long they last. What it cannot see is chains like the one in `banana$` that outlive that step, and that is where Cells and the forest still agree. The last column is the correlation between the two counts' fitted residuals, the part of each that the model leaves unexplained. It is 0.393 under the first model. Adding the tail, the chains that persist, takes it to −0.061: about zero. As a separate check, the leave-one-out error falls by 34% for Cells and 17% for the forest. Fitting all eight depths separately fits each count more closely, but leaves 0.307 in common, so the single tail sum accounts for more of what the two share. Adjacent-rank induction stays poorly explained under every model, at \\(R^2 \\le 0.570\\). Its rounds are chosen by local minima of the rows' order rather than by run boundaries, which may be why some other property drives it.

These fits use the historical profile as recorded. On the four blocks with \\(d\_0 = 2\\) its tail holds row 0's extra point, and the fit's excess term, taken as \\((\\tilde q\_1 - 1)/r\\), is one gap low. A fit on the internal-gap profile alone has not been run.

So, **measured:** the persistence of boundary-orbit chains explains much of the variation in the structural work done by Cells and the forest. **Our interpretation**, not a proof: both pay roughly once for each point on a boundary chain until the chains collide. Cells meets those points in order, and the forest by levels. The profile is fixed by the column \\(L\\) before any construction runs. It is not an exact accounting of either count, and it gives no lower bound on the work of other constructions.

## 4\. Why not do less of it?

If the work follows the boundary chains, there are three obvious ways to try to reduce it. None lowered it where we tried it, on evidence of three kinds: a count on the test block, a measurement on Wikidata, and a model.

**Refining the presentation.** The forest pays for its excess, so the first route describes the block with smaller pieces that have less excess. At depth \\(k\\), a piece is a stretch of neighbouring rows that pass through the same runs in their first \\(k\\) steps of LF; at depth 1 the pieces are the runs themselves. The excess does fall, from \\(0.21\\,r\\) to \\(0.07\\,r\\), yet the total work rises:

Smaller pieces lower the excess, and raise the work

Measured on the test block, from the first refinement record: the forest's arcs summed over all its levels (amber), and its first-level excess (steel, dashed), both in units of the block's runs, at depths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 16 and 32. The horizontal axis is logarithmic.

The arcs summed over levels go from 90,945 at depth 1 to 208,766 at depth 32. Part of the reason is **proved**. Refining by one more step turns every arc of the old network into a site of the new one, \\(V\_0(k+1) = E\_0(k)\\). So the sites grow by the old excess, and the first level's arcs by the new one. That the later levels shrink by less is **counted** at the nine depths tried, not proved ([record of the refinement test](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/049464756c76addb72cbfaed42d421d006126eab/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-o3-o5.md#1-o3-a-smaller-excess-presentation-decisive-and-negative>)). Coarser pieces fail the other way, with an excess of about \\(r\\). So among the presentations tried, runs are best. That is a finding about this block, not a theorem: on the three-byte column `100`, refining lowers the total from 5 arcs to 3.

**Accelerating repeated steps.** When a stretch of the map repeats, one division can stand in for many identical steps, and adjacent-rank induction does exactly this. On an artificial text, \\(abcd\\) repeated with an end marker, whose column has five runs, it decodes 875,001 bytes about 9.5 times faster than mibz2's shipped route: 0.161 ms against 1.526 ms, over five runs. That route sends so sparse a column to its Segmented decoder, not to Cells. Wikidata, however, has almost nothing to accelerate. Division compresses only repeated passes through one atom, and Cells' census on the test block finds no repeated steps. On the full benchmark adjacent-rank induction is the slower of the two (section 1).

**Splitting a block across cores.** Cells is one sequential chain of 92,570 steps on the test block: each step reads the state the previous one left. Adjacent-rank induction is more parallel, in a model. A row-by-row model reproduces its 12 rounds exactly, and their combined longest path is 87 row steps: the classical parallel route of contracting a list at an independent set of its points. But the model executes 1,337,701 row steps, \\(1.49\\,n\\), against Cells' 92,570 steps, about \\(0.1\\,n\\). The real decoder routes atoms, not rows; how long that routing runs in sequence was not measured, and no threaded version was built. Meanwhile, one block per thread already fills a ten-core Intel desktop (an i9-10900K), which is limited by memory contention and power at seven to ten busy cores. So the model trades much more work for a shorter path, with no speed-up shown on the test machine. Our reading is that giving another core another block remains the better use of it.

**Contracting a list** at an independent set is the classical parallel way to shorten a chain. Herein adjacent-rank induction cuts the loop at the rows smaller than both their neighbours, joins the paths between them, and repeats: in the model, a longest path of 87 row steps, bought with 1,337,701 row steps in all, against Cells' 92,570.

## 5\. Why not copy earlier text?

The fourth route leaves the run network behind. Much of a block repeats earlier text, so the text can be described as literal bytes plus *copies*, each a pointer back to an earlier stretch of output and a length. This is the idea behind LZ77-style compressors, and decoding a copy is a plain memory copy.

**It is compact.** Seeded with the 51,184 run-head bytes in text order, a greedy parse covers the rest of the test block with 11,145 copies and 33 single literal bytes. Replaying them is estimated, not timed, at 0.1–0.3 ms a block. The inverse BWT it is set against, the control in that assessment, took about 2.4 ms on the same block in the original investigation; it was not timed again.

**It needs text positions.** The short parse needs its seed bytes in *text* order, and the BWT gives its rows in *sorted* order. With the same seed bytes in sorted order, the parse needs 18,132 copies. The BWT does carry a copy description of its own: neighbouring rows of a run read the same bytes (section 3), so each one can copy from its neighbour. Grouped into phrases, this is a known scheme (Navarro, Ochoa and Prezza, Theorem 7). On the test block it has 51,184 literal bytes and 10,954 copies. But 5,611 of its copies have sources that overlap them or come later in the text. An evaluator that sweeps front to back needs 12,406 sweeps; one that follows the dependencies could order them differently, but was not tried. Putting the copies in text order needs each row's place in the text, and the routes we tested got those places by walking LF. Whether list ranking or another method could recover them more cheaply is open. The obstacle here is a different one from the run network's ([the copy-route assessment](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6982429070>); [its independent reproduction](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6982850361>)).

All four routes, side by side:

What each route avoids, and what it still pays

A summary of sections 1, 4 and 5. Counts are medians per run over 233 blocks; times are full-stream slowdowns against eager Cells on a four-CPU cloud virtual machine, on the calling thread unless a worker count is named; the copy route's replay is an estimate. Open return, reported in its own post, avoids induction on the narrow runs and is 17.1% slower than eager Cells on the calling thread, 9–21% across the calling thread and two or four workers.

## 6\. Where things stand

**Measured and proved.** Three unlike constructions do about 1.8 operations per run on Wikidata, their counts correlate strongly, and they do not process the same events. The identity \\(E\_0 = 2r - 1 - C\\) is proved and holds on every block, and the depth-one count \\(q\_1 = E\_0 - r\\) is the forest's excess, one less than its chords. The short tail of the profile, as historically counted, explains much of the variation Cells and the forest share. Refinement raised the work on the test block, acceleration has nothing to act on in Wikidata, and in a model, splitting a block costs far more total work; no threaded version was tested. The copy route is compact, but the routes tested had to walk LF for its text positions.

**Not shown.** No one has shown that Cells is optimal. The shared count is not a lower bound, and the only proved bounds are the trivial ones: reading the \\(r\\) runs and writing the \\(n\\) bytes. Cells is the best-performing formulation tested.

**The open question.** On our reading, Cells and the forest pay for each boundary chain step by step. Some shortcuts exist: division compresses repeated passes through one atom, and a one-bit test tells when two neighbouring paths spell the same word. But among the methods we measured or costed, learning how long an *aperiodic* chain runs meant walking it, or pointer jumping after preprocessing of order \\(n \\log n\\). What remains open is whether a gap's separation depth can be found without walking its path. A method that could would attack the work Cells and the forest share.

**Next.** Two studies are under way: a bounded study of whether steps of different kinds in Cells can be fused into one, and a literature study of these gap chains.

In short: three constructions count about the same work, and much of what they share is how long the run boundaries persist. The ways tried to shorten that work raised it, found nothing to act on, or, in a model, multiplied it. When unlike methods agree on a count, the reason is worth looking for in the input before tuning the methods.

# Cutting the loop open: decoding a block along shared paths

Snip the decoder's one long loop open and most of each Wikidata block falls into bundled paths, where one traced letter spells about sixteen.

18 November 2026 · 13 min read · [Research result](<#7-what-comes-next>)

Much of mibz2's research is about one stage of bzip2 decoding: turning each block's Burrows–Wheeler transform back into text. [A new way back from the BWT](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) showed how the kernel mibz2 ships, Cells, does it by shrinking a map instead of walking it. [The mathematical dictionary](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-mathematical-dictionary/index.md>) then named the objects that kernel works with. This post takes the same map apart another way, by cutting its one long loop open, solving the pieces separately and joining them back.

bzip2 stores a block as the last column \\(L\\) of its sorted rotations, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). Alongside it is the *primary row*, the row that holds the original text. A map called **LF** sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier. Following it from the primary row therefore reads the block backwards, one byte a step, until it comes back to the primary row. That trip, the *marked loop*, is the decoder's loop. When LF is a single loop, as in the example below, the trip visits every row once, but it need not. The periodic text `abab` has the column `bbaa`, and its LF makes two loops, 0 → 2 → 0 and 1 → 3 → 1. The marked loop covers only half the rows, yet the decoder still writes the whole block. One lap reads `ba` backwards, which is `ab` forwards, and the decoder repeats that spelling up to the block's known length of four bytes, giving `abab`. A **run** is a stretch of equal bytes in \\(L\\). Because LF shifts all of a run's rows equally, the map is a list of shifted blocks of rows ([One shift per run](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/index.md>)).

The loop is slow because each step needs the row that the step before it found. A plain decoder therefore makes up to 900,000 memory reads per block, each waiting on the last. Cells avoids most of them by working on runs rather than rows. It comes in two forms. Eager Cells lays out all its records before it starts. Lazy Cells, by contrast, makes them as it goes, which suits many threads at once ([Lazy letters](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-lazy-letters/index.md>)).

The idea of this post is to choose some rows to keep, the primary row among them, and cut the arrow leaving each one. The marked loop then falls into open paths. Each path starts at an *entrance*, a row whose incoming arrow was cut, and ends at a kept row. Where each path ends, and what it reads on the way, can be found from the uncut arrows alone. What the cut loses is which kept row's arrow went to which entrance, and a stable sort of the kept rows' letters rebuilds that separately. Joining the two gives back the loop, and with it the text.

The first finding is that the loop factorises. The trip from one kept row to the next is the open-path map applied after the stable sort of the kept letters, and neither needs the other's input. This is proved, and the proof has been verified twice, independently. Nor is the operation new. In Markov-chain theory it is the *stochastic complement* (Meyer, 1989), the chain watched only on the kept states. Here the chain is one permutation with a letter on each arrow, so the complement's infinite sum stops.

The pieces are also few, because the open paths travel in *bundles* of neighbouring rows. If the rows left on the open paths form \\(H\\) wide strips (stretches of long runs), there are at most \\(3H + \\sigma\\) bundles, where \\(\\sigma\\) counts the distinct bytes. Few bundles does not by itself mean little work, however.

The choice of rows to keep matters. On Wikidata the cut keeps every run of 16 rows or fewer. On a test block those are 93% of the runs but hold 10% of the rows. Keeping them therefore removes most of the places where neighbouring paths would split, while 90% of the rows stay on open paths.

On Wikidata, one traced letter spells about sixteen. Over the large Wikidata blocks, bundles cover a median 88.7% of each block, and tracing one path per bundle reads 5.5% of it. Yet two blocks of nearly equal run density differ by 66% in that cost. Sixteen is the saving in finding the paths, not in decoding, because the decoder still writes every output byte. It also still builds and walks a table of the kept rows' returns, one entry per kept row.

The decoder built on it, in one decode of the test block, asked for about 40% less additional heap than eager Cells. Over the whole Wikidata benchmark, on one four-CPU cloud virtual machine without SMT siblings, it is 9–21% slower than eager Cells and 7–8% faster than lazy Cells. The test with many blocks competing for cache is still to come.

Each claim below says whether it is **proved**, **counted** on the blocks, **measured** on a machine, or an **interpretation** that relates it to other work.

Sections [1](<#1-what-happens-when-the-loop-is-cut>) to [3](<#3-stitching-the-loop-back-together>) cut, rebuild and join a seven-byte example by hand; section 2 is the key step. [Section 4](<#4-the-same-move-in-markov-chain-theory>) relates the result to the stochastic complement and to Cells. Sections [5](<#5-how-many-pieces>) and [6](<#6-what-do-real-blocks-look-like-after-the-cut>) count the bundles, in theory and on Wikidata, and [section 7](<#7-what-comes-next>) reports the decoder, its table and its costs. The [technical notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open-notes/index.md>) hold the longer proofs.

## 1\. What happens when the loop is cut?

The worked example is the seven bytes `banana$`, where `$` sorts before every letter and appears once. (It keeps the example small; bzip2 blocks don't need one.) Sorting its seven rotations gives the table below. The last column, read down, is \\(L\\) = `annb$aa`, and the text itself is row 4.

The sorted rotations of `banana$`, with each row's last byte and its LF arrow:

| Row | Rotation | \\(L\\) | LF |
| ---: | :--- | :---: | ---: |
| 0 | `$banana` | `a` | 1 |
| 1 | `a$banan` | `n` | 5 |
| 2 | `ana$ban` | `n` | 6 |
| 3 | `anana$b` | `b` | 4 |
| 4 | `banana$` | `$` | 0 |
| 5 | `na$bana` | `a` | 2 |
| 6 | `nana$ba` | `a` | 3 |

LF comes from \\(L\\) alone: \\(\\mathrm{LF}(i) = C\[L\[i\]\] + \\mathrm{rank}\\). Here \\(C\[c\]\\) counts the block's bytes smaller than \\(c\\), and the rank counts the earlier rows that also end in \\(L\[i\]\\). Row 5 ends in `a`; one byte is smaller, and one earlier row ends in `a`, so \\(\\mathrm{LF}(5) = 2\\). From row 4 the arrows make one loop through all seven rows, and read `$ananab`: `banana$` backwards. Row numbers are places in the sorted table, not in the text, which is why each step must wait for the last.

The stepper below keeps rows 0, 4 and 5 and cuts the arrows leaving them. Only paths are left, because every row has exactly one incoming arrow and a row on a loop already uses it to stay there. An entrance has lost its incoming arrow, so a path that starts there can never join a loop. It must run until the arrows stop, at a kept row. Each press of Next makes one change and says why.

Step through it: cut the arrows leaving the kept rows, then follow each open path

← BackPlayNext →

1. **The loop:** the arrows go 4 → 0 → 1 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 3 → 4 and read `$ananab`, `banana$` backwards.
2. **Keep rows 0, 4 and 5.** In row order they are exit indices 0, 1 and 2.
3. **Cut the arrows leaving them:** 4 → 0, 0 → 1 and 5 → 2. Rows 0, 1 and 2 lose their incoming arrows and become entrances 0, 1 and 2.
4. **Entrance 0** is row 0, a kept row: no steps, exit index 0, no letters.
5. **Entrance 1:** row 1 → row 5, reading `n`. Exit row 5 is exit index 2.
6. **Entrance 2:** row 2 → 6 → 3 → 4, reading `nab`. Exit row 4 is exit index 1.
7. **So** P = \[0, 2, 1\], with the words: none, `n` and `nab`. No path joined a loop: each row of a loop already uses its one incoming arrow.

Use Next and Back, or Play. Circles are rows, with their last-column letters; arrows are LF. An amber ring is a kept row, where open paths end; a green dot is an entrance, where an open path starts. Think of the loop as a circular railway with a station at every row: keeping a row makes it a terminus, the track out of it is lifted, and each lifted track's far end becomes the first station of a line. The analogy stops at order: a railway's stations have no ranking, and here the rows' sorted order is what rebuilds the lifted track (section 2).

**What exactly is \\(P\\)?** The kept rows are numbered in increasing order, \\(s\_0, s\_1, s\_2\\) = rows 0, 4, 5, and the entrances likewise, \\(e\_0, e\_1, e\_2\\) = rows 0, 1, 2. Then \\(P(k) = i\\) when the path from entrance \\(e\_k\\) ends at kept row \\(s\_i\\). So \\(P\\) maps entrance indices to exit indices. It is neither a map of text positions nor LF; it records how the open paths connect, in the entrances' and exits' own numbering. Here an entrance's row and its index happen to agree, whereas an exit's need not: exit row 5 is exit index 2.

The three open paths of `banana$`, with rows and indices kept apart:

| Entrance row | Entrance index \\(k\\) | Path | Exit row | Exit index \\(P(k)\\) | Word \\(w\_k\\), in LF order |
| ---: | ---: | :--- | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | none |
| 1 | 1 | 1 → 5 | 5 | 2 | `n` |
| 2 | 2 | 2 → 6 → 3 → 4 | 4 | 1 | `nab` |

**Why each kept row ends exactly one path.** A kept row has no outgoing arrow, and every other row on a path has one of each. The stepper's argument, run backwards from a kept row, therefore reaches exactly one entrance. Any loops left over never meet a cut, and play no part in the text read from the primary row.

## 2\. Where do the cut arrows go?

The paths needed only the arrows that were left. Putting the loop back together also needs the cut arrows: from each kept row, which entrance does its arrow reach? Looking that up row by row would bring back the walk, so the answer comes instead from how LF is built.

LF is a **stable sort**. It lists the rows by their last letter, keeping equal letters in row order, and each row's arrow points to its place in that list. If every row that is not kept is struck out, what remains is still sorted by letter, ties still in row order. It is therefore the stable sort of the kept letters alone. Let \\(v = L\[s\_0\]\\,L\[s\_1\]\\cdots\\) be the short column of kept letters. Then kept row \\(s\_j\\)'s arrow reaches entrance \\(e\_k\\) with

\\\[k = \\mathrm{LF}\_v(j),\\\]

where \\(\\mathrm{LF}\_v\\) is the LF rule applied to \\(v\\). This is the **restriction lemma**, the key step, because it gives the cut arrows from the kept letters without reading any other row.

For `banana$`, the kept rows hold `a`, `$` and `a`, so \\(v\\) = `a$a`. Its stable sort puts `$` first, then the two `a`s in order, so \\(\\mathrm{LF}\_v = \[1, 0, 2\]\\). The table agrees. Row 0's arrow reaches row 1, which is entrance 1. Row 4's reaches entrance 0, and row 5's entrance 2. Here an entrance's rank and its row agree, by accident; the figure's lower half shows a kept set where they don't.

Restricting a stable sort to some rows gives those rows' own stable sort

Conceptual, on the worked example. Left: the column in row order, with each kept row's index *j*. Middle: the same rows sorted stably by letter; a row's arrow (LF) points to its place here. Right: the kept letters, sorted on their own. The green entries appear in the same order in both sorted lists, so the short column's LF gives each kept row's entrance. Below: with rows 0, 4 and 6 kept, the entrances are rows 0, 1 and 3. The short column is again `a$a`, so *k* is again \[1, 0, 2\], but *k* = 2 now means row 3: *k* is a rank among the entrances, and the rank is all the sort can give.

On its own, \\(\\mathrm{LF}\_v\\) has two loops here, 0 → 1 → 0 and 2 → 2. The short column is not a smaller BWT of the text; the open paths are what join its loops. Its stable sort is a counting sort, one pass over the kept letters. On the test block of section 5 it sorts 89,874 letters, against the block's 899,931 rows.

## 3\. Stitching the loop back together

Each kept row now has a whole trip to the next kept row: the cut arrow, then an open path. In indices, the cut arrow takes kept index \\(j\\) to entrance \\(\\mathrm{LF}\_v(j)\\), and the path then takes that entrance to exit \\(P(\\mathrm{LF}\_v(j))\\). So the **first return** to the kept rows is

\\\[g(j) = P\\big(\\mathrm{LF}\_v(j)\\big).\\\]

On the way, the trip reads the kept row's own letter \\(v\[j\]\\), then the path's word.

The three trips of `banana$`. Each kept index \\(j\\) reaches entrance \\(k = \\mathrm{LF}\_v(j)\\) and then the next kept index \\(g(j)\\); the trip reads \\(v\[j\]\\) then the word \\(w\_k\\), in LF order, and the decoder writes it reversed:

| \\(j\\) | Kept row | \\(v\[j\]\\) | \\(k\\) | Word \\(w\_k\\) | \\(g(j)\\) | Written, \\(\\mathrm{rev}(w\_k)\\,v\[j\]\\) |
| ---: | ---: | :---: | ---: | :--- | ---: | :--- |
| 0 | 0 | `a` | 1 | `n` | 2 | `na` |
| 1 | 4 | `$` | 0 | none | 0 | `$` |
| 2 | 5 | `a` | 2 | `nab` | 1 | `bana` |

So \\(g = \[2, 0, 1\]\\): one loop through the three kept rows. LF reads the text backwards, so to write it forwards the decoder starts at the primary row's index, 1, and follows \\(g\\) backwards. Each step writes its trip in reverse, as in the table's last column: \\(\\mathrm{rev}(w\_k)\\), then \\(v\[j\]\\). Going back from 1 to 2 writes `bana`, from 2 to 0 `na`, and from 0 to 1 `$`. Together that is `banana$`. When the marked loop is shorter than the block, as for `abab`, the decoder writes this spelling and repeats it until it has written all \\(n\\) bytes.

Two jobs that never read each other's input, joined at the end

Conceptual, with the worked example's values in green. Job 1 needs only the rows that are not kept (here, the arrows left after the cut) and which rows are kept or entrances. Job 2 needs only the kept letters. After the spelling, the decoder finishes the block as usual: bzip2's final run-length decoding (RLE1) and the CRC check.

The same result, stated formally, with each line read on the example:

The open-return factorisation, stated formally and read on banana$

**1\. The cut.** Rows \\(0, \\dots, n-1\\), last column \\(L\\), and \\(f = \\mathrm{LF}\\). Choose a set \\(S\\) of kept rows containing the primary \\(p\\), and put \\(E = f(S)\\), the entrances. Number both in increasing order, \\(s\_0 \< \\dots \< s\_{m-1}\\) and \\(e\_0 \< \\dots \< e\_{m-1}\\), and let \\(v = L\[s\_0\] \\cdots L\[s\_{m-1}\]\\).

On banana$ \\(S = \\{0, 4, 5\\}\\), \\(E = \\{0, 1, 2\\}\\), \\(v\\) = `a$a`.

**2\. Two maps.** If \\(f(s\_j) = e\_k\\), then \\(k = \\mathrm{LF}\_v(j)\\) (the restriction lemma). With the arrows out of \\(S\\) deleted, each \\(e\_k\\) reaches a unique \\(s\_{P(k)}\\), reading the word \\(w\_k\\).

Sections 1 and 2 \\(\\mathrm{LF}\_v = \[1, 0, 2\]\\); \\(P = \[0, 2, 1\]\\), with words none, `n`, `nab`.

**3\. Factorisation.** The first return to \\(S\\) is \\(g(j) = P(\\mathrm{LF}\_v(j))\\), reading \\(v\[j\]\\,w\_k\\); its inverse writes \\(\\mathrm{rev}(w\_k)\\,v\[j\]\\). \\(P\\) and \\(w\\) depend only on the arrows outside \\(S\\) and on \\(S\\) and \\(E\\); \\(v\\) only on the kept letters.

Section 3 \\(g = \[2, 0, 1\]\\), writing `bana` · `na` · `$`.

Black: the statements and proof outline of the project's [proof](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/f9bbd135e8e5512e9b1335e18468e1f3fd5a1d71/docs/journal/2026-11-18-open-return/proof.md#restricting-a-stable-match>). Colour: the worked example. The proof holds for any column with a valid primary row, including columns whose LF has several loops, and for any kept set containing the primary.

**Proved, and checked twice.** The proof holds for any kept set containing the primary row, including columns whose LF has several loops. Two independent verifications rebuilt the construction from the proof alone, and compared it with a plain LF walk on thousands of small columns ([first](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/7747fddd11684e7959cb75f8de19a5b26138aef1/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-open-return-verification.md>), [second](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6978935386>); the [notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open-notes/#what-the-two-verifications-checked>) list what each checked).

## 4\. The same move in Markov-chain theory

Keeping only some states and recording the returns between them is an old operation. A Markov chain moves between states at random, and \\(M\_{xy}\\) is the probability of a step from \\(x\\) to \\(y\\). With the states split into the kept set \\(S\\) and the rest, \\(C\\), and the kept states ordered first, the matrix is

\\\[M = \\begin{pmatrix} M\_{SS} &amp; M\_{SC} \\\\ M\_{CS} &amp; M\_{CC} \\end{pmatrix}.\\\]

Suppose the chain is watched only while it is in \\(S\\). From one kept state to the next, it either steps straight within \\(S\\), or it leaves, spends some number \\(a\\) of steps in \\(C\\), and comes back. Adding up every such excursion gives the watched chain's matrix:

\\\[M\_{SS} + M\_{SC}\\Big(\\sum\_{a \\ge 0} M\_{CC}^{\\,a}\\Big) M\_{CS}.\\\]

The term with \\(M\_{CC}^{\\,a}\\) covers returns that take \\(a\\) steps from \\(C\\) to \\(C\\) before coming back. Carl Meyer named this matrix the **stochastic complement** ([Meyer, 1989](<https://doi.org/10.1137/1031050>)); it is also called the trace chain. In general the sum is infinite. When the chain cannot stay in \\(C\\) for ever (every state of \\(C\\) is transient), it converges to \\((I - M\_{CC})^{-1}\\).

LF is a far simpler chain because it is a permutation. Each row of its matrix holds a single 1: every row has one next row, with certainty. Once any loops lying wholly inside \\(C\\) are deleted, as section 1 did, what remains of \\(M\_{CC}\\) is a set of disjoint paths. A power of it is therefore zero, and the sum stops. Each arrow's letter is then written in place of its 1, and multiplication becomes joining words. The sum then gives each kept row its one return and that return's word. So the factorisation of section 3 is the stochastic complement of LF, with letters on the arrows (**proved**, and confirmed by both verifications).

The stochastic complement on banana$: each return is one term of the sum

Conceptual, on the worked example. Left: LF as a matrix, each 1 drawn as the letter its arrow reads, with the kept rows first. Right: the three returns, each picked out by one term of the complement. The block from C to C holds two arrows, 2 → 6 and 6 → 3. Its square is the two-step excursion 2 → 3, and its cube is zero. Railway reading: the complement is the timetable printed only for the termini, with each journey's intermediate stations folded into its word.

The formula says what the kept system is, not how to compute it fast: a dense matrix over 900,000 rows would be hopeless. The Markov view says what must result, and LF's strips say how to remove rows cheaply, many at a time (section 5). The restriction lemma says how to reconnect them.

**How this relates to Cells** (an **interpretation** from the [first verification](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/7747fddd11684e7959cb75f8de19a5b26138aef1/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-18-open-return-verification.md>), not a theorem). Cells also computes first returns. It shrinks LF's interval exchange from the right-hand end (Rauzy–Veech induction), and each surviving interval stands for a longer word. One of the two ways we compute \\(P\\) (section 7) takes the same right-end steps, but only over the wide strips and the entrances and exits around them. On the frozen block of section 5 that is 7,786 intervals to begin with, where Cells begins with all 51,184 runs. The narrow runs never enter the induction, because the stable sort wires them. Read this way, cutting open splits the interval exchange by run width.

The two approaches side by side, as we read them:

|  | Cells | Cutting open |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Where returns are taken | a shrinking interval, step by step | a chosen set of rows: here, the narrow runs |
| How returns are built | composed during the induction | open paths, solved apart from the kept rows' wiring |
| What is left at the end | one interval holding the text's word | \\(P\\), its words, and the short column \\(v\\) |
| What it relies on | interval lengths and joining words | stable sorting, open paths, rows moving together |

## 5\. How many pieces?

The construction is worth having only if the open paths can be solved many rows at a time, and the runs make that possible. Suppose the cut keeps the *narrow* runs, those of at most \\(t\\) rows (section 6 uses \\(t = 16\\)), and the primary row. The other rows then form \\(H\\) **wide strips**. A strip is a stretch of consecutive rows that LF shifts by one amount, each row reading the same byte. (It is a wide run, or half of one if the primary row splits it.)

**Why keep the short runs?** The project keeps one 899,931-row Wikidata block as a fixed test case, *the frozen block*. Of its 51,184 runs, 68.6% are a single row long, yet they hold only 3.9% of the rows. At the other end, runs longer than 256 rows are about 1.0% of the runs, yet hold 73.9% of the rows. These shares come from the cut at \\(t = 256\\), which leaves 496 wide strips. One of them may be half of a run that the primary row splits, and runs of exactly 256 rows fall on the kept side. So the short runs make most of the boundaries, and the long runs hold most of the text. Left on the open paths, every short run would add edges where the paths split apart. Kept, they go to the stable sort, which wires them in one pass. The open paths are left a few wide strips, which hold most of the rows.

Most runs are narrow, but most rows are in wide runs

Counted on the frozen block, at threshold 16: 89,874 kept rows (narrow runs, plus the primary row) and 3,448 wide strips out of 51,184 runs. The shares are derived from those counts; a strip split by the primary row counts twice, so the wide share of runs is at most 6.7%.

Two neighbouring entrances in the same strip are still neighbours after the step, since the strip shifts both by the same amount. They stay together, strip after strip, until a strip's edge falls between them, or they reach kept rows. A maximal set of neighbouring entrances that pass through the same strips and end at neighbouring exits is a **bundle**. The records call it a band. A bundle has a **width** \\(b\\), its number of rows, and a **height** \\(h\\), its number of steps. Tracing one of its paths costs \\(h\\) steps, and spells all \\(b \\times h\\) of its letters.

A bundle is traced once for all its rows, but a strip that moves a little makes bundles one row wide

Conceptual. Top: a bundle of width 4 and height 2 passing through two strips; in railway terms, a convoy on parallel tracks, surveyed by one train. Bottom: the proof's one-strip example, with *w* = 6 rows. When a strip moves by *d* rows with 0 \< |*d*| ≤ *w*, its paths have heights ⌊*w*/|*d*|⌋ and ⌈*w*/|*d*|⌉; when |*d*| ≥ *w*, each has height one. A shift by one row gives one tall path, a bundle one row wide with nothing to share, and a move clear of itself gives one short, wide bundle. The analogy fails at the edges: a bundle splits wherever a strip's edge or a kept row's falls between its rows.

Two totals describe a cut. The **bundled area** \\(A = \\sum\_i b\_i h\_i\\) is the number of letters the bundles spell. For a block whose LF is one loop, it is every row not kept, \\(n - m\\). The **traced letters** \\(U = \\sum\_i h\_i\\) are what tracing one path per bundle costs. The ratio \\(A/U\\) is how many rows travel together, on average, for each letter traced.

**The bound (proved).** There are at most \\(3H + \\sigma\\) bundles. The proof follows the gap between two neighbouring entrances as it moves with them through each strip. The two sides part only where the gap meets a strip's edge or the edge of a run of kept rows, and no two gaps meet the same edge first. The bound is attained on small columns ([notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open-notes/#the-bundle-bound>)). Real blocks sit far below it: the frozen block has 3,204 bundles, against a bound of 10,433.

**Few bundles is not little work.** The bound counts bundles, not their heights. In the figure's lower half, one strip shifted by one row is a single bundle, yet tracing it costs a step for every letter. So \\(U\\) can scale with the block rather than with \\(H\\), as can the endpoint steps of section 7. Those are the figures to watch on real data.

## 6\. What do real blocks look like after the cut?

**The threshold sets the balance.** Raising \\(t\\), the widest run kept, keeps more rows for the sort to wire, and leaves fewer, wider strips. On the frozen block that leaves less to trace at every threshold swept, but that is not a rule. Raising \\(t\\) can cut open a loop the marked one never met, and so add paths to trace; the [notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open-notes/#one-strips-heights>) give a six-row case. The frozen block's counts, recomputed independently from the proof:

| \\(t\\) (rows) | Kept rows \\(m\\) | Wide strips \\(H\\) | Bundled area \\(A\\) | Traced letters \\(U\\) | Bundles (nonempty) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 35,116 | 16,068 | 864,815 | 555,357 | 12,526 (5,862) |
| 16 | 89,874 | 3,448 | 810,057 | 50,709 | 3,204 (1,326) |
| 256 | 235,281 | 496 | 664,650 | 4,658 | 738 (294) |

At \\(t = 16\\), \\(A/U\\) is 15.97: each traced letter spells about sixteen. On this block's sweep, up to \\(t = 16\\), the ratio rises roughly in step with \\(t\\). The median over many blocks at \\(t = 16\\) is 15.92, yet section 6 shows two blocks of equal run density that differ widely.

Kept rows rise with the threshold while traced letters fall

Counted on the frozen block, at eleven thresholds. *m* is the rows the stable sort wires; *U* the letters traced, one path per bundle; *K* the endpoint constructor's steps (section 7). Their sum, dashed, is least at *t* = 16, at 151,798. The sum is our reading of the decoder's cost, not a measured time: it weights a sorted row, a traced letter and an endpoint step equally. Threshold 16 was chosen from timed trials on this block.

**All 233 large blocks.** Over the Wikidata blocks of at least 65,536 rows, at \\(t = 16\\), the median bundled area is 88.7% of the block and the median traced letters 5.5% (**counted**, and re-derived by a verification). Prose differs. Over its six blocks the wide strips cover a median of 32.3% of each block, from 27.6% to 49.0%. Most of a prose block is therefore kept rows.

Run density says little about how much tracing a block needs

Counted, at *t* = 16, from the per-block records ([blocks.csv](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/f9bbd135e8e5512e9b1335e18468e1f3fd5a1d71/docs/journal/2026-11-18-open-return/evidence/blocks.csv>)). Each dot is one of the 233 Wikidata blocks of at least 65,536 rows; hover for its numbers. The rank correlation between the two axes is −0.36: denser blocks trace slightly less, not more. Blocks are numbered from zero in the benchmark file.

**Run density misses it.** Blocks 118 and 176 both have 900,000 rows, and run densities of 0.06348 and 0.06342. Yet block 118 needs 57,626 traced letters and block 176 needs 34,775: 66% more. Their bundled areas are nearly equal, and so are their numbers of wide strips. The difference is in how the bundles break up (**counted**). Block 118 has 53% more nonempty bundles, while their mean height is only 8% greater. One verification reads this as the narrow runs cutting across the wide strips' paths more often in block 118 (an **interpretation**). A run count can't see that, whereas how the runs' images overlap can.

## 7\. What comes next?

**Two ways to compute the open paths.** The *tracer* follows one path per bundle and measures each bundle's width as it goes. The *endpoint constructor* never follows a path. Instead it puts \\(m\\) terminal points before a copy of the rows, and joins them to the entrances and exits by arrows with empty words. It then removes rows from the right-hand end. Removing a row joins the arrow into it and the arrow out of it into one arrow, with their words joined. The terminals are never removed, so when only they are left, each terminal's arrow is a whole path, with its word. That is \\(P\\).

The endpoint constructor removes rows from the right until only the paths' ends are left

Conceptual, on banana$, with every row not kept treated as wide. The decoder removes a common stretch of rows from the end of two strips in one step, where the figure removes one row; the joining is the same. Removing rows 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 in turn leaves terminal 2's arrow reading `nab` to terminal 1, terminal 1's reading `n` to terminal 2, and terminal 0's empty arrow to itself: *P* = \[0, 2, 1\].

The two constructors gave the same bundle counts and traced-letter counts on all 431 Wikidata blocks and the six prose blocks ([notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open-notes/#the-two-constructors-of-the-open-paths>)). The decoder below uses the endpoint constructor, and does the stable sort as it reads the runs, by queueing each kept row under its byte.

**The decoder so far (measured).** Its output has the same length and SHA-256 as libbz2's on the frozen block, the whole Wikidata benchmark and the prose. It rejects a damaged block CRC and a damaged stream CRC. The timings come from a four-CPU cloud virtual machine without SMT siblings. Each round decodes the Wikidata benchmark, 209,700,196 bytes of output, with eager Cells, lazy Cells (both as in mibz2 0.5.5) and the open decoder in turn. The times are medians in seconds, and the open decoder cuts at \\(t = 16\\). A ratio is the median over the rounds of that round's ratio, and no interval was computed.

| Workers (rounds) | Eager (s) | Lazy (s) | Open (s) | Open ÷ eager | Open ÷ lazy |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| calling thread (11) | 0.751 | 0.972 | 0.896 | 1.171 | 0.918 |
| 2 (9) | 0.459 | 0.583 | 0.543 | 1.211 | 0.931 |
| 4 (11) | 0.336 | 0.399 | 0.383 | 1.091 | 0.928 |

The open decoder beat lazy Cells at every worker count and lost to eager Cells at every one; on prose, on one thread, it took 1.455 times eager Cells' time. The figure below puts the wall times beside the two smaller measurements, each on its own scale: they have different units and cover different amounts of work.

Slower than eager Cells, faster than lazy, lighter on memory: three measurements, three scales

Measured on one four-CPU cloud virtual machine. Top: the paired wall-time ratios of the table above. Middle: the peak additional heap requested during one fresh decode of the frozen block. Bottom: the inverse transform alone, repeated on the frozen block, split into building the kept rows' table and writing the output; the switch cut is the harder cut described below. The three panels are not comparable with each other.

A cache simulation of the frozen block's decode counted 11% fewer instructions and 27% fewer first-level data-cache misses than eager Cells; those are simulated counts, not times. How much of the wall-time gap comes from building and walking the kept rows' table is not yet measured over the whole decode. Our reading, an **interpretation**, is that this table is the main cost eager Cells does not pay. The phase measurement shows its size on one block.

Of the switch cut, that kept fewer rows and paid more to find them

**A smaller kept system is not always cheaper to build.** A harder cut, the *switch cut*, keeps only the rows where a path switches between narrow and wide runs. On the frozen block its output phase took half as long as the decoder's above. But its build took 3.6 times as long, because finding the narrow side's words meant tracing 58,581 more letters. The smaller system was real, and this way of reaching it was slower.

**What comes next.** The open decoder holds less per block, and on many cores mibz2's speed has been limited by blocks competing for the shared cache ([Modelling the cache](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers/index.md>)). The test that matters is therefore on a ten-core Intel desktop (an i9-10900K), at the worker counts where that competition starts, against the release that ships. A run that settles how the test machine's clock behaves under sustained load comes first. Whether the kept system could itself be cut open again is an open question.

The ten-core comparison is queued behind the sustained-load run; this post will be updated with what it finds.

**The chain, in three steps.** Cutting the arrows that leave the kept rows turns the marked loop into open paths, which the rest of the block determines alone. A stable sort of the kept letters rebuilds the cut arrows, and joining the two gives the exact return to the kept rows. On Wikidata the open paths travel in wide bundles, so tracing 5.5% of each block spells nearly 90% of it.

The general lesson is about where to cut. A chain of dependent steps can be split into paths and a reconnection when the reconnection has a cheap rule of its own, as the stable sort is here. The split is worth making when many starting points share the paths.

- The second independent verification: [its review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6978935386>) and [its report](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/432a6ce03857b21e57b03ff8d97094d0f96eff97/state/reports/open-return-6978698021>).
