# Technical notes: cutting the loop open

These notes hold the detail that [the main post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-18-cutting-the-loop-open/index.md>) leaves out to keep its argument moving. They use its notation. \\(L\\) is the block's last column, of \\(n\\) rows, and \\(f\\) is LF. \\(S\\) is the set of kept rows, with \\(m = |S|\\) and the primary row \\(p\\) among them, and \\(E = f(S)\\) is the set of entrances. After the cut, the rows not kept form \\(H\\) wide strips, and \\(\\sigma\\) counts the distinct bytes in the block. Every statement here is from the project's [proof](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/f9bbd135e8e5512e9b1335e18468e1f3fd5a1d71/docs/journal/2026-11-18-open-return/proof.md>), checked by the two verifications cited at the end.

## The bundle bound

Partition the row line into the \\(H\\) wide strips and the \\(s\\) intervals of consecutive kept rows. That makes \\(H + s\\) pieces, with \\(H + s - 1\\) internal boundaries. Let \\(e\\) be the number of intervals of consecutive entrances. The entrance intervals can also be cut wherever the first-column byte changes. Then every entrance in a bundle is reached from a kept row with the same letter, so a bundle has one kept letter as well as one word.

**Bound.** There are at most \\(e + H + s - 1\\) bundles. With the byte cuts, there are at most \\(3H + \\sigma\\).

**Proof.** Represent a gap between two neighbouring entrances by the row on its right. Inside one strip, a gap moves to the gap between the two rows' images, since the strip shifts both by the same amount. This map of gaps is injective, because LF is. Its image lies inside a strip's image, so it never produces a gap inside \\(E\\), and two distinct entrance gaps start disjoint gap paths. A gap between two different bundles must meet one of the \\(H + s - 1\\) internal boundaries before both sides reach the same interval of kept rows. Charge it to the first boundary it meets. Since the gap paths are disjoint, each boundary takes at most one charge. Add one bundle for the left end of each entrance interval. Finally, \\(E\\) is the complement of the strips' images, so it has at most \\(H + 1\\) intervals, and the byte cuts add at most \\(\\sigma - 1\\); so \\(e \\le H + \\sigma\\). Likewise \\(s \\le H + 1\\). Together, \\(e + H + s - 1 \\le 3H + \\sigma\\). ∎

**Tight cases.** Both verifications found columns with one wide strip that attain the bound. The column `110020000011` at threshold 2, with primary 9, has \\(H = 1\\) and \\(\\sigma = 3\\), and six bundles: \\(3 \\times 1 + 3\\). It attains the finer bound too, with \\(e = 4\\) and \\(s = 2\\), since \\(4 + 1 + 2 - 1 = 6\\). The column `abbbbdddaaaaaaaacccddddaabbbcccc` at threshold 4, with primary 21, has \\(H = 1\\) and \\(\\sigma = 4\\), and seven bundles: \\(3 \\times 1 + 4\\). One verification checked the bound on 19,717 run-structured cases, with no violation. On the frozen block, at \\(t = 16\\), there are 3,204 bundles against \\(3 \\times 3{,}448 + 89 = 10{,}433\\).

## One strip's heights

The bound limits the number of bundles, not their heights. Take a single wide strip of \\(w\\) rows that LF moves by \\(d \\ne 0\\). There are \\(\\min(w, |d|)\\) rows entering it. When \\(0 \< |d| \\le w\\), each entering path advances by \\(d\\) a step until it leaves the strip, so the paths' heights are \\(\\lfloor w/|d| \\rfloor\\) and \\(\\lceil w/|d| \\rceil\\). These are the quotients of a Euclidean division of \\(w\\) by \\(|d|\\).

The two extremes are a shift by one row and an image disjoint from the strip. A shift by one gives one path of height \\(w\\): a bundle of width 1, so the traced letters \\(U\\) equal the area \\(A\\). A disjoint image gives one bundle of width \\(w\\) and height 1, so \\(U = 1\\) for \\(A = w\\). Two twelve-row columns with the same run widths and byte counts, `220021021110` and `110010202221`, show both behaviours at threshold 2. In the first the strip's displacement is \\(-3\\), and three rows cross in parallel for one traced letter. In the second it is \\(+1\\), and one row takes three steps along the strip.

This is why neither the bundle count nor a small \\(H\\) bounds \\(U\\) by a multiple of \\(H\\). The same holds for the endpoint constructor's step count \\(K\\) below. It removes a common suffix one step at a time, without dividing, so a thick strip with a small displacement costs about \\(w/|d|\\) steps.

**More kept rows can mean more to trace.** On the frozen block, \\(U\\) falls at every threshold swept, but that is not a rule. The column `110000` with primary 2 has \\(f = \[4, 5, 0, 1, 2, 3\]\\) and two loops, 2 → 0 → 4 → 2 and 1 → 5 → 3 → 1. At \\(t = 1\\) only the primary is kept. Its one open path, 0 → 4 → 2, traces two letters, and the other loop is never cut. At \\(t = 2\\) rows 0, 1 and 2 are kept. That cuts the second loop open. The nonempty paths, 4 → 2 and 5 → 3 → 1, are one and two steps long and lie in separate bundles, so \\(U\\) rises from 2 to 3.

## The two constructors of the open paths

**The tracer.** Start at the leftmost entrance not yet covered, and follow its path through the wide strips. At each strip, and at the final interval of kept rows, note the distance from the path's row to that piece's right-hand edge. Count the starting entrance interval's edge as well. The smallest of these distances is the width of the bundle: every row in it follows the same strips to consecutive exits. Advance by that width and repeat. The tracer needs only the wide strips and the intervals between them.

**The endpoint constructor.** Build an auxiliary interval exchange on \\(m + n\\) points: a prefix of \\(m\\) terminal points, followed by a shifted copy of the \\(n\\) rows. Its arrows are:

1. terminal \\(k \\to m + e\_k\\), with the empty word;
2. \\(m + x \\to m + f(x)\\) on the \\(H\\) wide strips, with their bytes;
3. \\(m + s\_i \\to i\\), with the empty word.

The terminals of each kind join up into intervals, so at most \\(3H + 2\\) intervals start the exchange. Its first return to the prefix is exactly \\(P\\), with the words \\(w\_k\\), because the two empty arrows delimit each path. Now remove rows from the right-hand end until only the prefix is left. If the last domain strip is \\(X\\) and the last image strip is \\(Y\\), remove the common suffix of their widths. The shorter strip's record keeps the joined word, the reverse word of \\(X\\) then that of \\(Y\\). The prefix boundary can never be crossed, and the number of live strips never increases. On the frozen block, at \\(t = 16\\), the exchange starts from 7,786 intervals and takes 11,215 steps, making 7,334 rules that each join two words. The word dictionary is then expanded by copying the rules already expanded.

**Agreement.** The two constructors gave identical bundle and word-length counts at \\(t = 16\\) on all 431 Wikidata blocks and the six prose blocks.

**The queued decoder.** As the run records arrive, each narrow row appends its kept index to a queue for its byte. Consecutive entries of a queue are then wired to consecutive exits of a bundle. That is the stable sort of the main post's section 2, done during the pass that reads the runs. A packed table, of four bytes per kept row when the row and the word's code fit in one word and eight otherwise, holds each kept row's inverse return and its word. On the frozen block it is 359,496 bytes. Output follows the marked loop, copying each word's bytes forwards.

## The narrow–wide switch cut

Colour each arrow narrow or wide, by the run it leaves. A *switch row* is a row whose incoming and outgoing arrows have different colours. Narrow-to-wide switches are the rows of \\(E \\setminus S\\), and wide-to-narrow switches the rows of \\(S \\setminus E\\). Since \\(|E| = |S|\\), the two counts are equal:

\\\[h = |E \\setminus S| = |S \\setminus E| = m - |E \\cap S|.\\\]

The count can be taken before any word is known, by intersecting two tilings of the row line into runs. On the frozen block at \\(t = 16\\), \\(h\\) = 15,278 in both directions, as one verification recomputed. Keeping only the \\(2h = 30{,}556\\) switch rows, plus the primary if needed, gives a smaller kept system than the 89,874 narrow rows. But its construction traverses those 30,556 arrows one at a time, and traces 58,581 more letters to find the narrow side's words. In the repeated inverse-only measurement, its emitter took 0.511 ms against the queued decoder's 1.018 ms, and its constructor 6.771 ms against 1.857 ms. One verification corrected a detail of the convention. The program reclassifies a wide primary row as narrow before counting, so on `111000` at threshold 2 with primary 0 it finds switch rows \\(\\{0, 3\\}\\), not \\(\\{0\\}\\).

## What the two verifications checked

Both verifications rebuilt the construction from the proof, not from the project's code.

| Claim | First verification | Second verification |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Restriction lemma | proved | proved |
| Factorisation, spelling, independence | proved; 6,000 random cases against a plain LF walk | proved; 30,557 small column and kept-set pairs, at every kept mark |
| Stochastic complement | proved, with the closed loops in \\(C\\) deleted | proved, with the closed loops in \\(C\\) deleted |
| Bundle bound | proved; tight; 0 violations in 19,717 cases | proved; tight |
| Endpoint constructor | proved; step count not recomputed | proved |
| Switch identity | proved; 15,278 both ways on the frozen block | proved; marking convention corrected |
| Frozen-block counts | recomputed exactly at \\(t\\) = 1, 16, 256 | checked as recorded at \\(t = 16\\) |
| Medians over 233 blocks | taken from the records | re-derived: 88.6689% and 5.4943% |
| Timings | not re-run | paired ratios recomputed from the raw rounds |

The project's own checks, separately, compare each constructor with a plain decoder on 198,790 column, primary and threshold combinations. They also check the destination and word of every kept row's arrow on 26,135 more, and compare complete streams with libbz2.

# Raising the knee: scaling throughput to the limit of physical cores

mibz2 0.5.4 now speeds up until all ten physical cores of its test processor are busy, then holds level on the whole machine up to twenty threads.

17 November 2026 · 13 min read · [Research result](<#6-what-comes-next-for-the-knee>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.5.4](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-5-4>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#054---2026-11-17>))

[Ten days ago](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/index.md>), mibz2's problem was that giving its bzip2 decoder more work at once could make it slower. The decoder processes a compressed file in independent blocks, so it can decode several simultaneously. But each block has its own data structures, and those structures compete for the processor's shared cache. More blocks promise more parallelism while making each block more expensive. Past a certain point the extra cost wins. The throughput curve bends over: the *scaling knee*.

The default decoder once dealt with that risk by stopping at a fixed number of decoding teams. It could avoid a fall, but only by declining to use the extra threads. Since then, mibz2 has changed both how it reconstructs a block and how many workers it starts. Version 0.5.4 puts the result in view. Our test machine is a ten-core Intel desktop (an i9-10900K, with 20 logical CPUs and a 20 MiB level-3 cache that all ten cores share). On it, ten requested threads decode a 210 MB Wikidata sample in **0.102 seconds**, the fastest median in the release sweep. The knee is still there, but it has been raised and softened. It is raised because the best point has moved from eight threads to ten, the machine's physical-core count. It is softened because asking for more now costs little or nothing. In 0.4.0 and 0.5.0, 12 to 20 threads took 11–18% longer than the best point. In 0.5.4's release sweep they take 4–5% longer by the medians, but that sweep pins ten threads and gives twelve or more the whole machine. With placement held constant, 10, 12 and 20 threads decode in the same time, to within half a per cent. It is not straightened: the extra hardware threads add nothing yet. At 12 to 20 requested threads 0.5.4 runs seven active workers, not twelve or twenty. Memory bandwidth is close to binding there: the plateau moves 75% of the memory traffic the machine can sustain, but that is not yet a hard ceiling.

Throughput against threads, five releases on the test machine

Measured on the test machine: the median of 10 paired rounds per point, decoding an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump to 209.7 MB of output. Each release is taken from its own [release-scaling run](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/745a7381ab72ca07675ddfcb000c4156f926c0eb/bench/release-scaling/>) (0.2.4 from 6 November; 0.5.0, 0.5.1 from 16 November; 0.5.3, 0.5.4 from 17 November). The runs pin 10 threads or fewer to one CPU a core, and give 12 threads or more the whole machine.

**The result is a flatter *default* curve, not the disappearance of the knee or of contention.** The decoder now starts fewer workers than threads in the measured configurations where extra workers made decoding slower. In effect, 0.5.4 caps its workers at the number that pays off: seven, from ten requested threads. The cost of competing for the cache remains; it is now part of the plan rather than a surprise in the benchmark. Here is how we reached that result, what the release run establishes, and what the plateau still leaves open.

## 1\. What was the knee?

A bzip2 file is made of blocks that can be decoded independently. mibz2 has two ways to spend its threads. In a *team*, several threads share the work of one block. With *workers*, each thread decodes a block of its own. The second arrangement can keep more cores busy, but it also puts more blocks' working data in the shared last-level cache (the L3 on the test machine).

The first scaling investigation measured the trade-off directly. On the test machine, each additional block in progress slowed the others. Three teams of three decoded faster than four teams of two. Version 0.2.5 adopted that smaller number of teams and gained about 9% at ten threads against 0.2.4, in two registered runs.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Levelling off is not the same as falling**
>
> The old **shipped** curve mostly *levelled off*: version 0.2.4 ran four teams of two from eight requested threads upwards, instead of allowing concurrency to keep growing. The falling side of the knee was visible when experiments forced too many blocks to run at once. The policy avoided that fall by leaving extra threads unused. It had contained the problem, not made more concurrency productive.

The kernel changed next. [Cells](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) reconstructed the text from compact rules rather than the old row-by-row navigation table. [Lazy letters](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-lazy-letters/index.md>) then kept working state for only the letters that needed it, reducing the amount each worker touched. Those gains reached the workers, which ran below ten threads, but not the teams, which still ran from ten. So by 0.5.0 the shipped curve really did fall: eight threads ran eight workers, ten or more ran three teams of three, and 12 to 20 threads took 16–18% longer than 8. In 0.5.1, workers with lazy letters displaced teams at ten threads and above. What was now faster than teams could still become slower if too many workers ran together. That was the next knee to control.

What mibz2 runs at each thread count, release by release

From the decoder's thread names, recorded in each release's release-scaling run, and the release notes. A team (amber) shares one block between several threads; a worker (green) decodes a whole block on its own. A thick border marks a cell that changed from the release before. Where a cell has two counts, the first is the plan when the process is pinned one CPU a core, which is how the release-scaling runs measure 10 threads or fewer, and the second the plan on the whole machine.

## 2\. What does the new curve look like?

The [release-scaling benchmark](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/index.md>) decodes the same Wikidata sample on the test machine at each requested thread count. It reports the time to produce about 210 MB of output. Lower is better. These are the medians from the 0.5.3 and 0.5.4 release runs:

| threads requested | 0.5.3, seconds | 0.5.4, seconds |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.387 | 0.385 |
| 2 | 0.244 | 0.241 |
| 4 | 0.148 | 0.144 |
| 8 | 0.110 | 0.105 |
| **10** | **0.115** | **0.102** |
| 12 | 0.107 | 0.106 |
| 16 | 0.107 | 0.106 |
| 20 | 0.106 | 0.108 |

The runs of ten threads or fewer are pinned one logical CPU per physical core; the higher counts use the whole machine. The paired version comparisons preserve placement within each count.

The shape matters more than the last decimal place. In 0.5.3, asking for ten threads made the decoder slower than asking for eight. At twelve and above it recovered. In 0.5.4, **ten threads are the fastest point**, while twelve to twenty sit between 0.106 and 0.108 seconds. Across eight to twenty threads that is **1.95–2.06 GB/s of decoded output**. Twenty is still about 5% slower than ten by these medians. As the box below explains, most or all of that is a change of placement, not of thread count.

The paired comparison is stronger evidence for the version change than the medians alone. Across ten paired rounds, 0.5.3 took **1.123 times** 0.5.4's wall time at ten threads (95% interval 1.094–1.152), or about 11% less elapsed time in 0.5.4. At eight threads the ratio was **1.045** (1.038–1.053). The new version also used less processor time and peak memory at those counts. At one, two and twelve to twenty threads, the release comparison detected no change. The apparent improvement at four threads was too small to resolve from the run's variation.

These comparisons show a real improvement at eight and ten threads. They do not by themselves establish that ten is statistically faster than every other count within 0.5.4; the table shows the median ordering, not paired confidence intervals between different thread counts. The figure below gives those within-release comparisons against eight threads, for selected releases since 0.2.4. It leaves out 0.2.5 to 0.3.3. The history between was not one continuous fall. In 0.2.5, ten threads took 0.918 of eight threads' wall time (95% interval 0.910–0.927).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The decline past ten is a change of placement**
>
> Paired round by round within 0.5.4's run, the higher counts took longer than ten threads:
>
> | threads | wall time against ten threads (95% interval) |
> | ---: | ---: |
> | 12 | 1.049 (1.022–1.076) |
> | 16 | 1.044 (1.025–1.064) |
> | 20 | 1.074 (1.031–1.117) |
>
> Past ten, extra threads would land on the cores' second hardware threads. But the run also changes placement at that point. Ten threads ran pinned to one logical CPU a core. Twelve to twenty ran on the whole machine, with the same seven workers. So the decline can't be put down to hyperthreading.
>
> The knee diagnostic did hold placement constant: it ran every count on the whole machine, in one session. Its medians, in seconds, with the interquartile range for four copies:
>
> | threads | four copies of the sample | one copy |
> | ---: | ---: | ---: |
> | 10 | 0.3661 (0.365–0.368) | 0.1013 |
> | 12 | 0.3657 (0.365–0.369) | 0.1009 |
> | 20 | 0.3664 (0.364–0.370) | 0.1010 |

Its build falls between 0.5.3 and 0.5.4, which run the same plan on the whole machine. A release-build sweep from eight to twenty threads, all on the whole machine, would confirm it for 0.5.4 itself.

Each mark is a release's wall time at 10, 12, 16 or 20 threads divided by its own wall time at 8 threads, as the geometric mean of 10 rounds, paired by round, with its 95% interval across those rounds (one run, one machine, one file). Selected releases: 0.2.5 to 0.3.3 are not shown. Sources: the [release-scaling runs](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/745a7381ab72ca07675ddfcb000c4156f926c0eb/bench/release-scaling/>).

## 3\. Why did ten threads dip, and what fixed it?

The ten-thread regression in 0.5.3 was a placement mistake in the planner. Version 0.5.3 tried to recognise the test machine from the CPUs the *process was allowed to use*. With the process pinned to ten CPUs, it no longer recognised the full machine and declined to apply its seven-worker limit. It started **ten workers**, with forty blocks allowed in flight.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **How the release runs place their threads**
>
> The release harness pins runs of ten threads or fewer to one logical CPU per physical core. At ten requested threads, the process may use CPUs 0–9: one logical CPU from each physical core. Its workers, scanner and reader share that set. Runs of twelve threads or more may use all 20 logical CPUs. Pinning is how mibz2 runs under `taskset` or in a container limited to some CPUs; the whole machine is how it usually runs.

Unpinned, 0.5.3 did apply the limit: a later check of production on the whole machine found it building seven workers in all six runs. That check, run after 0.5.3 shipped, also timed seven workers against ten directly, with the counts set explicitly, and seven took 0.873 of ten workers' time (95% interval 0.866–0.880). The release benchmark's ten-thread dip was therefore not evidence that the seven-worker idea failed. It was evidence that the intended plan had not run.

Version 0.5.4 [separates the two questions](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/537>). It identifies the machine from all present and online CPUs, but still reads the process's affinity to decide which measured plan applies. Pinned to ten cores, it now starts **seven lazy-letters workers**, with 28 blocks in flight. Pinned to eight, it starts six, and pinned to six and four it trims one worker as well. Those three pinned trims did not carry over to the whole machine: in the same check, six workers at eight threads took 1.000 of eight workers' time, the six-thread trim was no faster, and the four-thread trim took 1.21 times as long. Competition for CPUs with the decoder's scanner and reader, which share the workers' cores when the process is pinned, is implicated, so 0.5.4 applies those trims only when pinned. The ten-thread trim holds in both modes; why exactly it pays is not settled.

The machine-wide check is cached once per process. An early release check caught repeated hardware discovery adding overhead to short decodes; that was fixed before 0.5.4 shipped. The result is a narrower policy than a universal formula: it applies to the test machine and its tested placement modes, not automatically to every ten-core processor.

## 4\. Does the plateau mean memory bandwidth is full?

Nearly, but not yet. The plateau uses 75% of the memory bandwidth the machine can sustain, and every worker past seven adds traffic faster than it adds output.

With ten workers reduced to seven, the [worker-count study](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers/index.md>) found about **half as many last-level-cache misses per decoded byte** and **25% fewer cycles per byte**. Instructions and clock frequency stayed approximately level.

At ten workers, each was busy about 76% of the time; at seven, each was busy about 92%. The smaller group offered less aggregate worker time, yet it decoded each byte much more cheaply. That is why removing workers can make a parallel program finish sooner. The utilisation arithmetic alone does not establish the cause; the cache counters supply the evidence for interference.

A diagnostic run on the plateau itself rules out the simplest alternatives. Decoding four copies of the sample on the whole machine, the workers compute 93–95% of the time at every thread count, so no serial stage, such as the scanner that reads the file or the reader that hands bytes back in order, is starving them. What rises with the workers is memory traffic. Counted at the memory controller, reads and writes come to 7.5 bytes for every byte of output at four workers, 11.0 at seven and 12.4 at eight.

More workers, more memory traffic for every byte decoded

Measured on the test machine at the memory controller, reads and writes per byte of output. Green: the current decoder, decoding four copies of the Wikidata extract, in the [knee repeat with the memory-controller counters](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/evidence/knee/run-20261117T230729Z.tar.gz>) of 17 November (the whole machine, except the hollow point, pinned). Amber: an older decoder that held a slot for every letter of a block, over 15 repeated decodes of the single Wikidata sample a reading ([memory-controller run](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/evidence/cells-imc/run-20261114T180428Z.tar.gz>), 14 November). The two runs used different decoders and workloads, so they are drawn side by side, not joined. The first knee diagnostic counted only reads that missed the L3, 6.9, 11.0 and 12.7 bytes at 4, 7 and 8 workers, close to the green totals. The analogy stops where caches differ from kitchens: data is not used up, it is copied in 64-byte lines.

It is tempting to read the two-gigabyte-per-second plateau as a DRAM bandwidth limit, so we measured it. A repeat of the diagnostic with the memory controller's own counters found the seven-worker plateau moving 24.8 GB/s of DRAM traffic: 11.0 bytes per output byte, of which 7.0 are reads and 4.0 writes. A separate test that streams memory as fast as it can reaches 33.1 GB/s on the same counters, so the plateau runs at 75% of the measured ceiling. On an older version of the Cells kernel, on 14 November, the same counters measured 22.7 and 24.2 bytes per output byte at eight and ten workers. The decoder has roughly halved its DRAM bytes per output byte since.

More workers push the traffic up faster than the output. Eight workers reach 83% of the ceiling at 12.4 bytes per output byte, and ten pinned workers 85% at 13.9, and both decode more slowly than seven. So bandwidth is close to binding, and every worker past seven spends it on traffic rather than output. It is not the hard ceiling at seven: the registered rule called bandwidth the limit only at 80% of the ceiling or more, and 75% leaves the question open.

At the plateau: how close is memory traffic to its ceiling?

Measured on the test machine, decoding four copies of the Wikidata extract ([knee repeat with the memory-controller counters](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/evidence/knee/run-20261117T230729Z.tar.gz>), 17 November). Each bar is DRAM reads plus writes counted at the memory controller, the median of 10 rounds, with idle traffic subtracted. The ceiling is measured too: the best median of a separate test that streams memory as fast as it can (`ab stream`, its scale kernel), read on the same counters. At 7 workers the decoder writes 2.27 GB of output a second; at 8 and at 10 pinned workers it is slower than at 7, while moving more memory traffic.

There is another reason to be precise about the word *plateau*. At twelve to twenty **requested** threads on this machine, 0.5.4 still runs **seven decoding workers**. The decoder is not starting twelve, sixteen or twenty competing workers; the plan has capped the number of blocks being decoded simultaneously. A nearly flat result there means the planner has kept the most expensive part of the curve out of the default path. It does not prove that the hardware would scale if twenty independent decoding workers were set loose.

## 5\. How would we straighten the knee?

Straightening the knee means a curve that keeps rising past the ten physical cores. The second hardware thread on each core (simultaneous multithreading, which Intel calls hyperthreading) would then add speed. Today it adds none. Three routes could change that. Each is a hypothesis with a measurement that tests it; none is a result yet.

**Cheaper bytes per worker.** At seven workers, the reads that miss the L3 come to 11 bytes for every byte of output. A smaller hot set per worker would cut that: the store and the tables the kernel keeps for a block. So would less traffic on the output side. One piece of the output side is folding the block's checksum into the final pass. That is an open research arm ([\#535](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/535>)), and its measured 1.5–3% gain is not yet settled. Fewer bytes moved per output byte raise the number of workers that pays, so more workers, and eventually the second hardware threads, can contribute. With bandwidth close to binding, this is the route that raises the ceiling. The test: bytes per output byte and wall time by worker count, before and after each cut.

**Latency hiding with the second hardware threads.** The counters run at ten threads measured about 2.2 reads that missed the L3 in flight at once, whenever any were. That is little memory-level parallelism. If the plateau is bound by latency rather than bandwidth, two workers sharing a core can overlap each other's misses: one computes while the other waits. That is the classic case where hyperthreading helps code that waits on memory. The test: the same number of workers placed as pairs on shared cores, against one worker a core.

**Helpers on the second hardware threads.** The decoder's other threads already gain from spare CPUs. Decoding four copies of the sample with four threads took 0.405 seconds on the whole machine, against 0.535 seconds pinned. Pinned, the scanner, reader and main thread share the workers' cores. The second hardware threads could host prefetch or helper threads that bring the next block's data into cache ahead of the workers. The test: a helper arm against none, at the same worker count, with the misses per output byte counted.

**Which first.** The memory-controller run in §4 puts the plateau at 75% of the measured bandwidth ceiling, with traffic per byte rising faster than output past seven workers. That makes cheaper bytes per worker the main route: every byte saved per output byte is room for more workers before the ceiling. Latency hiding with the second hardware threads stays open, since a quarter of the bandwidth is still unused at seven workers.

## 6\. What comes next for the knee?

The other task is to make the planner portable. The measured seven-worker choice is not a general law. The cache model under test correctly recovered some counts on this machine, then predicted the wrong optimum for smaller bzip2 blocks. Other processors have different core counts, cache sizes, cache-sharing domains and memory systems. The right worker count needs to follow those facts, with tests that can prove a proposed rule wrong.

For now the release result is a good one, with a precise boundary. **mibz2 no longer punishes a request for more threads with a large fall in throughput on this measured workload and machine.** In the release sweep the penalty past the best point is 4–5%, down from 11–18%. With placement held constant, no decline is seen. It gets there by doing *less work in parallel*, more efficiently. The old knee exposed a bad trade-off between concurrency and interference. Version 0.5.4 runs on the better side of it.

What remains is a flat stretch past the cores to turn into a rising curve, a ceiling to raise, and a policy to generalise. That is a more useful problem than a curve that falls whenever we give it another core.

# Modelling the cache to rightsize workers

mibz2 now runs fewer workers than threads on a ten-core desktop and finishes sooner, while a cache model is tested to pick the count on any machine.

17 November 2026 · 14 min read · [Research in progress](<#5-what-shipped-and-what-the-model-still-needs>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.5.4](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-5-4>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#054---2026-11-17>))

mibz2 decodes a bzip2 file by handing its blocks to *workers*: threads that each decode a whole block at a time. How many workers to start is a choice mibz2 makes once, at startup, and the obvious answer, one per thread the caller asks for, is wrong. On our 10-core test machine, running fewer workers than threads first took 11.5% less wall time in pinned runs, or about 13% more throughput, and 12.7% less in a later unpinned run. We found that by measurement alone, sweeping selected worker counts at each thread count. A sweep like that has two faults. A change to the algorithm can change how much memory a worker uses, or how much processor time it needs, and with them the best count, so the sweep has to be redone. And it describes one machine: a policy measured on one processor's 20 MiB cache is "works on my machine" for everyone else.

So we are working to replace the measured policy with a model of what the workers share: the shared cache, the processor time left over after the decoder's other threads, and the processors themselves. When the algorithm changes, we would update the model's inputs instead of re-running the sweep; on another machine, the model would read that machine's caches and processors. The model is a proposal under test, not the decoder's policy. Its predictions are frozen before each new experiment (pre-registered: fixed before the data, and tested out of sample), so it can be shown wrong in public, and it has been. It reproduced the counts it was fitted to and, under pinning, the lower thread counts it was asked about next. At a smaller block size it named the wrong count.

**The simplest correct picture.** Fewer workers give up some parallelism, but each one gets more of the shared cache, so each byte it decodes costs fewer processor cycles. On this machine the cheaper bytes win, up to a point, and the point is roughly where the workers' data would fill most of the cache. Why exactly the bytes get cheaper is only partly known.

**What the sweep found.** The test machine is a ten-core Intel desktop (an i9-10900K), with 20 logical CPUs and a 20 MiB level-3 (L3) cache that all the cores share. On this chip the L3 is the last-level cache (LLC); the post says LLC in general statements and L3 for this machine. The test file is four copies of an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump, decoded in 10 paired rounds. Every worker in these runs uses the [lazy letters](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-lazy-letters/index.md>) kernel. Below, *threads* means the number the caller asks for, *workers* the number mibz2 runs, and *cores* the physical cores. Each run is compared with a *reference plan* at the same thread count: the plan mibz2 0.5.2 used, one worker a thread up to 10 threads, and nine workers beyond the physical-core count (12 to 20 threads, the SMT regime, where a core runs two threads). Runs of up to 10 threads were limited to one hardware thread a core.

Fewer workers, less time: the test machine at 10 and 8 threads

Measured on an Intel i9-10900K, decoding four copies of an 11.9 MB Wikidata extract, 10 paired rounds a point, with the process limited to one hardware thread a core. Each point is the wall time against the plan of one worker a thread at the same thread count (10 workers at 10 threads, 8 at 8); the bars are 95% intervals over the rounds, on one machine. The hollow point (6 workers at 10 threads) was run as context and not judged. 5 workers at 8 threads, run later in the low-thread sweep, took 0.997 of 8's time: no gain.

At 10 threads, seven workers, with 28 blocks in flight, take 0.885 of the reference plan's time, with a quarter less peak memory. At 8 threads, six workers take 0.929. Past the cores, seven take 0.921, 0.930 and 0.923 of nine workers' time at 12, 16 and 20 threads. A second run tested these choices directly, beside two files that played no part in choosing them, binary records and text compressed with 100 kB blocks, and confirmed all three: 0.881 at 10 threads, 0.933 at 8, and 0.921 to 0.930 past the cores. No cell on either held-out file was judged slower, though on the small-block text every cell was inconclusive, which is not the same as no difference. All these runs of 10 threads or fewer were pinned, and below 10 threads that turned out to matter (section 5).

## What was found

- **From 10 threads up, fewer workers than threads take less time on the test machine, pinned or not.** 7 workers take 0.885 of the time at 10 threads pinned and 0.873 unpinned, and about 0.92 past the cores; confirmed on held-out files. Below 10 threads the pinned gains (0.929 at 8 threads) did not transfer to the full machine: unpinned they vanish, and competition for the CPU with the decoder's other threads is implicated ([section 1](<#1-what-does-a-worker-do-and-what-do-the-workers-share>)).
- **The counters point to the shared cache, not to the clock or idle cores.** From 10 workers to 7, the cycles per byte fall 25% and the LLC misses per byte 48%, while the instructions and the clock stay put. What exactly the remaining cost is made of is not settled ([section 2](<#2-why-are-fewer-workers-faster>)).
- **The model takes the smallest of a few bounds,** a heuristic fitted to these runs. It names 7 at 10 threads and 6 at 8 only with a tie-break fitted to those two counts: on its own cost curve, 8 workers are 0.7% cheaper than 7. The 8-thread case, measured pinned, implicates CPU competition, so it can't calibrate cache contention alone ([section 3](<#3-a-model-of-what-the-workers-share>)).
- **Its frozen prediction for smaller blocks failed.** At `bzip2 -3` it predicted the best count would rise to 9 or 10; it stayed at 7. Contention did shrink roughly with the footprint, but not as a function of how full the cache is alone ([section 4](<#4-the-test-that-failed-smaller-blocks>)).
- **What shipped is narrower than the model.** mibz2 0.5.4 trims on the test machine only, in two configurations: pinned to exactly one CPU on each of as many cores as threads, at 4, 6, 8 and 10 threads; or with the whole machine available, from 10 threads. Any other affinity mask keeps the old plan. No general selector has shipped ([section 5](<#5-what-shipped-and-what-the-model-still-needs>)).

The scoring of every frozen prediction, the contention hypotheses and the derivations are in the [technical notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers-notes/index.md>).

## 1\. What does a worker do, and what do the workers share?

Who does what in mibz2's parallel decoder

Conceptual. The thread names are the code's (src/parallel.rs); the kitchen labels are an analogy. In the kitchen, each cook prepares a whole dish at a station, and all of them spread their ingredients on one worktop; more cooks crowd it. The analogy stops at eviction: a cook's ingredients never vanish from a worktop, but a worker's data does leave the cache and has to be fetched again from main memory.

mibz2's parallel decoder ([`src/parallel.rs`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/33e7225ba6147fb480168dc54fe30727f0b93aea/src/parallel.rs#L1-L22>)) has three kinds of thread. The *scanner* reads the compressed stream in order; a block's end is only known once its Huffman-coded symbols have been read, so this scanner reads them one block after another. Each *worker* then finishes one block on its own: the move-to-front step, the inverse Burrows–Wheeler transform, a run-length step and the block's checksum. The *reader* takes the finished blocks back in order and hands out their bytes. The decoder lets up to four blocks a worker be in flight at once, in one window shared by all of them: 28 blocks for seven workers.

Blocks decode independently, so more workers means more blocks at once. But the workers are not independent: they run on cores that share one L3.

The test machine's caches: private L2s, one shared L3

The test machine. The L1 caches, per core and smaller still, are left out. A worker's footprint is about eight times its core's L2, so it lives in the shared L3.

Each core has its own 256 KiB level-2 (L2) cache. Behind them sits the 20 MiB L3, shared by all ten. A lazy-letters worker rebuilding a 900 kB block has a *footprint* of about 2.1 MB: the size of what the kernel stores for the block, an estimate of the memory it reuses while it decodes. It is a proxy for the worker's working set, not a measurement of what it occupies in the LLC. That is far more than the L2, so the footprints meet in the L3.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Working set, footprint and occupancy**
>
> A *working set* is the data a program reuses over some window of time. A *footprint* is an estimate of its size. *Occupancy* is how much of a shared cache a worker actually holds at a moment, which depends on the other workers. The standard tools for the first are reuse (stack) distances, introduced by [Mattson et al. (1970)](<https://doi.org/10.1147/sj.92.0078>), and the miss-ratio curves built from them; [Qureshi and Patt (2006)](<https://doi.org/10.1109/MICRO.2006.49>) use such curves to divide a shared LLC between programs. A curve from one trace is an approximation for a given replacement policy, not the exact miss count of every cache and schedule. mibz2 hasn't measured one yet.

Workers filling the shared L3

Workers: 7

Drag the slider to change the number of workers; the text below the bar says what the measurements show at that count. Each green block is one worker's footprint, about 2.1 MB for a lazy-letters worker on a 900 kB block, in the test machine's 20 MiB (21.0 MB) L3. This is capacity accounting, not a model of the misses: footprints overlap and change while a block decodes, and the cost rises smoothly as they grow, with no cliff at 100%. The dashed lines are the teams policy's 0.7 of the L3 and the fitted optimum's 0.8.

## 2\. Why are fewer workers faster?

Three explanations suggest themselves. The clock: fewer busy cores may each run faster. Idle time: with more workers than the processors can keep busy, some wait. The cache: each worker slows the others by evicting their data. The hardware counters at 10 threads tell these apart. They count per byte of output, against 10 workers.

Fewer workers, cheaper bytes: the work is the same, the shared-cache misses fall

Measured on the test machine at 10 threads, one copy of the Wikidata extract, 10 repetitions under perf stat, pinned one thread a core. L3 misses are the last-level cache's load misses. The clock (cycles over reference cycles) was 1.326 at every count, so the cycles are not falling because the cores slowed or sped up.

The clock is ruled out first: cycles over reference cycles, which measures the clock against its base rate, is 1.326 at every worker count. The work is the same: instructions per byte fall by under 2% from 10 workers to 7. The private L2 caches see about the same traffic, with L2 misses up about 3%. What changes is the shared cache. From 10 workers to 7, LLC misses per byte fall 48%, and cycles per byte fall 25%. The fall is smooth: an earlier prediction of a cliff, once the footprints fit, was refuted by exactly this shape.

**Lost parallelism against cheaper bytes.** The wall time is the cycles each byte costs, divided by how many processors are working on the bytes. At 10 workers each worker's CPU utilisation is 0.763, so 7.63 processors' worth are working; at 7 workers it is 0.925, 6.48 processors' worth. That is 15% less processing power. The cycles per byte fell 25%. So the wall time is \\(0.752 / 0.849 \\approx 0.886\\) of what it was, against 0.885 measured.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Why this bookkeeping proves nothing by itself**
>
> When the clock is flat, cycles per byte divided by the CPUs at work equals the wall time almost by definition, so any cause would balance this sum. The evidence for the cache comes from the counters' pattern instead.

The evidence comes in three tiers. **Observed:** with fewer workers, the LLC misses per byte and the cycles per byte both fall, while the instructions, the clock and the private-cache traffic stay about the same. **Supported:** interference for the LLC's capacity contributes materially to the cost. **Under investigation:** what the rest is made of. A counters run has since measured the latency of loads that hit in the L3 falling from about 91 cycles to 65 as workers go from 10 to 7, which fits queueing in the L3 and the ring that links it to the cores; but it missed that hypothesis's predicted size, and traffic to main memory was not measured, so main memory isn't ruled out ([notes, section 2](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers-notes/#2-what-the-contention-associated-overhead-is-made-of>)).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Interference, not (as far as we can tell) coherence**
>
> The workers decode independent blocks and don't write to each other's block data, so the main effect is interference in a shared cache's capacity and the paths to it. They do share a queue, hand-offs and allocator state, so some coherence traffic exists. Nothing in the counters points to it as the explanation, but they don't rule it out either.

## 3\. A model of what the workers share

The model takes the smallest of a few bounds, each counted in workers:

\\\[m = \\min(N,\\ W\_{L3},\\ 0.80\\,N,\\ W\_{\\mathrm{ser}}).\\\]

\\(N\\) is the logical CPUs the process may use; SMT enters through each worker's cost, not through this cap. \\(W\_{L3}\\) is a cache bound, summed over LLC-sharing domains \\(d\\) (one on this machine) as \\(\\sum\_d \\min(N\_d,\\ 0.8 \\times L\_d / F)\\), with \\(N\_d\\) a domain's logical CPUs, \\(L\_d\\) its LLC size and \\(F\\) the footprint: about 7.9 on this machine. \\(0.80\\,N\\) is a CPU bound, and \\(W\_{\\mathrm{ser}}\\) a serial bound, how many workers the scanner can keep fed, added after the small-block test of section 4. This is a resource-constrained heuristic: each bound is estimated separately and the smallest taken, and the resources interact. Predicting performance from shared-cache contention has a literature of its own; [Xu, Chen, Dick and Mao (2010)](<https://doi.org/10.1109/ISPASS.2010.5452065>) is the closest to this approach.

**The cache bound.** At 10 threads, the cycles per byte with \\(W\\) workers fit \\(c(W) = a + b\\,W^2\\) with \\(a \\approx 0.42\\) and \\(b \\approx 0.0068\\). These are normalised costs: the measured cycles per byte at 10 workers, about 23, count as 1. The fit is not forced through that point, and gives \\(c(10) = 0.422 + 0.0068 \\times 100 = 1.102\\). A refined form, \\(c(W) = a + b\\,W\\,W\_{\\mathrm{run}}\\) with \\(W\_{\\mathrm{run}}\\) the workers running at once, removes most of that residual (it gives 0.983); the quadratic is the simpler illustration. \\(a\\) is an extrapolated intercept, and the square is a fit: exponents from 1.5 to 2.5 fit these points about as well. If every worker is kept busy, the wall time goes as \\(a/W + b\\,W\\), smallest at \\(\\sqrt{a/b} \\approx 7.9\\), where the footprints fill about 0.8 of the L3. The 0.8 is a fitted constant, and the bound is a modelled throughput optimum, not a hard ceiling.

**The CPU bound.** A worker with a processor to itself has a CPU utilisation of 0.93; the rest of the time it waits on the pipeline. The scanner and reader use about \\(0.16\\,W\\) processors, and a fully subscribed set of processors leaves about \\(0.125\\,N\\) idle, a residual idle capacity whose cause isn't established. Solving \\(0.93\\,W = N - 0.16\\,W - 0.125\\,N\\) gives \\(0.80\\,N\\).

**One worked example, and the tie-break.** At 8 threads, the bounds give \\(m = \\min(8,\\ 7.9,\\ 6.4) = 6.4\\), so the candidates are 6 and 7. At 10 threads, \\(m = \\min(10,\\ 7.9,\\ 8.0) = 7.9\\), with candidates 7 and 8. The rule chooses between them on the fitted cost, and within 1% it takes the smaller. That tie-break was fitted to these two counts, not predicted: on the cost curve below, 8 workers cost \\(0.10715\\) against 7's \\(0.10789\\), 0.7% cheaper, and at 8 threads the model puts 6 and 7 level. The measured bests are 7 (8 was 1.9% slower) and 6 (7 was 5% slower). A separate, more conservative rule, sizing the footprints to 0.7 of the L3 as mibz2's teams policy does for its tables, also gives 7 at 10 threads; it is a different rule, not the fit rounded.

The fitted cost prefers 8 workers; the measured wall time prefers 7

Dashed: the fitted cost, *a*/*W* + *bW* (modelled), which assumes every worker is kept busy, against its value at 10 workers. Solid: the measured wall time at 10 threads against 10 workers (figure 1). The two needn't agree point by point, since the measured wall also includes the workers' CPU utilisation; the point is that the fit's cheapest whole count is 8, while the run's is 7.

The rule at two thread counts: bounds, the rule's pick and the measured best

Modelled, from measured inputs. The bars are the continuous bounds, in workers; the solid bar is the smallest, and the dashed line marks it. The rule then chooses between the whole numbers either side on the fitted cost, taking the smaller within 1%, a tie-break fitted to these two counts. The measured bests are from figure 1.

The same rule gives 5 workers at 6 threads and 3 at 4, and pinned runs found 5 and 3 best there, on the older (eager) kernel. The 8-thread result was already known when the CPU bound was written. All these points below 10 threads were pinned, which section 5 shows matters more than the model allowed.

**The contention–parallelism trade-off.** At the fit's optimum, the contention-associated overhead \\(b\\,W^2\\) equals the base cost \\(a\\), so it is half the total; for a general exponent \\(p\\) it is \\(1/p\\) of the total. At 7 workers the fit puts it at about 44% of the cost. That is a modelled cost share, not a measurement: it doesn't say how much time any other change could recover, and with other exponents it ranges from about 34% to 60%. The derivation, its sensitivity and what is known about the overhead's make-up are in the [notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers-notes/#1-the-trade-off-at-the-optimum>).

## 4\. The test that failed: smaller blocks

The test that could fail was the same file compressed with `bzip2 -3`, whose blocks are a third the size. Each worker's footprint shrinks with its block, to about 0.38 of its size at `-9`, so the cache bound moves from about 8 to about 22. Frozen beforehand: the trim disappears, and the best count at 10 threads is 9 or 10, with 7 workers no better than 0.98 of 10 workers' time. The three-bound model of the time agreed, predicting 9 workers, with 7 slower than 10.

Smaller blocks, a smaller gain, the same best count

Measured on the test machine at 10 threads, the process limited to one hardware thread a core, 10 paired rounds a point; bars are 95% intervals over the rounds, on one machine. The `-9` curve is the first 10-thread run (figure 1); the `-3` curve is the same Wikidata extract recompressed with 300 kB blocks. Each point is against 10 workers on the same file.

The best count stayed at 7, so the prediction failed. At 10 threads, 9, 8, 7 and 6 workers took 0.992, 0.987, 0.978 and 0.987 of 10 workers' time, and 4 workers took 1.343. The gain fell from about 12% to 2%, and 7 workers at 0.978 (0.973, 0.983) leave "no better than 0.98" borderline. Part of the model held up. Contention did shrink with the footprint: comparing slopes over the same worker counts at both block sizes, the contention term's exponent in the footprint comes out between 1.85 and 2.23, near the 2 it has in \\(W\\). But a sharper test, whether misses depend only on how full the cache is, failed at 3 workers: they were 34% below its prediction. That suggests contention depends on how many workers run at once as well as on their footprints.

What sets 7 at `-3` is a hypothesis: the scanner. Part of its work, and the reader's, is paid once a block, and a `-3` file has three times as many blocks a byte. An occupancy trace showed the workers idle waiting on the scanner 28% of the time at `-3` against 5% at `-9`, and throughput in the timed runs stayed near 2.5 GB/s from 6 workers to 10. But that trace came from a run that failed its own memory-ledger check and was not pinned like the timed runs, so it suggests the serial bound \\(W\_{\\mathrm{ser}}\\) without establishing it. The bound was added after the data, so it needs its own frozen test.

Every other frozen prediction, met and failed, is scored in the [notes' ledger](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers-notes/#3-the-ledger-of-frozen-predictions>). Selected:

| frozen prediction | measured | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| at 10 threads, 7 workers at 0.93 (0.90, 0.98) of 10's time | 7, at 0.885 | count right, gain outside the interval |
| at 6 and 4 threads: 5 and 4 workers, with flat CPU utilisation | pinned: 5, then 3 eager workers at 4 (0.959); utilisation flat near 0.74 | right at 6; overtaken at 4; pinned only |
| 0.7 of the threads, rounded or floored | fails at 6 and 4 threads (rounded) and at all three counts (floored) | refuted |
| at `bzip2 -3`: the best count rises to 9 or 10 | 7 | refuted |
| at `bzip2 -3`: misses depend only on how full the cache is | 34% below at 3 workers | refuted |

## 5\. What shipped, and what the model still needs

**Status on 17 November 2026.** mibz2 0.5.4, released today, trims its workers on the test machine in two modes. Pinned to one logical CPU on each of exactly as many cores as threads, it runs 7 lazy-letters workers at 10 threads, 6 at 8, and 5 and 3 eager workers at 6 and 4 threads. Unpinned, it runs 7 lazy-letters workers from 10 threads, at 0.873 of 10 workers' time, and changes nothing below. It recognises the machine from its present and online CPUs. It is not the model: no general selector has shipped.

The two modes differ because the pinned gains below 10 threads did not transfer to the full machine. Every sweep of 10 threads or fewer ran pinned, so the workers shared their cores with the scanner, the reader and the main thread, and a worker fewer freed a core for them. Unpinned, those threads have CPUs of their own: at 8 threads 6 workers took 1.000 of 8's time, and at 4 threads 3 took 1.214 of 4's. That implicates competition for the CPU, the effect the CPU bound is meant to capture, but it doesn't rule a cache benefit in or out. A net ratio can hide both: a cache saving to 0.96 of the cycles and a parallelism loss of 1.0417 multiply to 1.000. So the pinned 6- and 8-thread points can't calibrate cache contention alone, and they come out of the contention fit. At 10 threads the gain survives unpinned, at 0.873, and the counters support interference in a shared resource, with the exact mechanism unresolved. (0.5.3 had read the machine through the process's affinity set, which a pinned 10-thread run limits to 10 logical CPUs, so its trim fired only unpinned; 0.5.4 fires in both.) Beyond the cores, 0.5.3's release run measured about 6.5% less wall time than 0.5.2 at 12 to 20 threads, with about 25% less processor time and 22% lower peak memory. 0.5.4 admits only the two configurations above: a 10-CPU mask spread over five cores' hardware threads, say, gets the old plan. Whether a general model should read topology machine-wide or through the affinity set is still open.

Two LLC-sharing domains: the limit is summed per domain

Conceptual: a processor with two LLC-sharing domains, as on many AMD chips (one per core complex, or CCX) or a two-socket server. F is a worker's footprint. The cache bound is the sum of each domain's bound, each capped by its logical CPUs, provided the workers are spread across the domains.

The same question arises on processors with several LLC-sharing domains: many AMD chips have one per core complex (CCX), and a two-socket server at least one per socket. Workers compete for an LLC only within their domain, though they still share main memory, so the cache bound sums over the domains the process may use, each capped by its own logical CPUs \\(N\_d\\). The current [`l3_bytes()`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/33e7225ba6147fb480168dc54fe30727f0b93aea/src/parallel.rs#L2831-L2846>) reads one file, the first processor's `cache/index3/size`. The planned fix finds the cache whose level is 3, groups the CPUs in the affinity set by the LLC they share (`shared_cpu_list`), and gives each worker a soft affinity to a domain. On a free GitHub runner with 2 cores, 4 logical CPUs and one 32 MiB L3, the rule gives 3.2 and so 3 or 4 workers; those runs are pending, and the [notes](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers-notes/#5-topology-and-transfer>) list the three results that would refute the model there.

The design is to detect once, decide once and then decode: read the logical CPUs, the LLC-sharing domains and the block size at startup, pick the count, and keep it, without tuning mid-stream, since streams are often short, timings noisy, and output timing should stay repeatable.

The chain, in short: a sweep found that fewer workers decode faster on the test machine; the counters pointed to the shared cache; a model of the cache, the processors and the scanner reproduces the counts it was fitted to, with a fitted tie-break; its first test at a new block size refuted its best count while its contention term roughly held; and an unpinned run showed that the gains below 10 threads don't transfer beyond pinning, where CPU competition is implicated, while the 10-thread gain survives, with its exact mechanism unresolved. A measured count describes the machine and the affinity it was measured with. A modelled count can be checked anywhere, and has to be.

# Technical notes: modelling the cache to rightsize workers

These notes hold the detail that [the main post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-17-modelling-the-cache-to-rightsize-workers/index.md>) leaves out to keep its argument moving. They use its notation: \\(W\\) workers, \\(N\\) logical CPUs in the process's affinity set, the normalised cost per byte \\(c(W) = a + b\\,W^2\\) with \\(a \\approx 0.422\\) and \\(b \\approx 0.0068\\), and the footprint \\(F\\). Measured figures are on the test machine, a ten-core Intel i9-10900K desktop, decoding four copies of an 11.9 MB Wikidata extract with the lazy-letters kernel, unless a row says otherwise. Its sections can be read in any order.

## 1\. The trade-off at the optimum

With every worker kept busy, the wall time goes as \\(c(W)/W = a/W + b\\,W^{p-1}\\) for a cost \\(c(W) = a + b\\,W^p\\). Setting the derivative to zero gives \\(a = (p-1)\\,b\\,W^p\\), so at the continuous optimum the contention-associated overhead \\(b\\,W^p\\) is \\(1/p\\) of the total: half at \\(p = 2\\), two thirds at 1.5, 40% at 2.5. It is a fitted term, not counted stall cycles.

The fits over 6 to 9 workers at 10 threads, and what each says at 7 workers:

| exponent *p* | *a* | *b* | continuous optimum | overhead share at 7 | cost ratio *c*(7)/*a* |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1.5 | 0.300 | 0.0248 | 8.37 | 60.5% | 2.53 |
| 1.75 | 0.370 | 0.0129 | 8.02 | 51.2% | 2.05 |
| 2 | 0.422 | 0.0068 | 7.88 | 44.1% | 1.79 |
| 2.5 | 0.494 | 0.0020 | 7.70 | 34.4% | 1.52 |

The range is sensitivity to the model's form, not a confidence interval. The cost ratio is what the model would charge with the overhead removed and nothing else changed. It is not a speedup anyone has measured or can expect: removing contention by any other means would change other costs too. At 7 workers the share is under half because 7 is below the quadratic's optimum of 7.9; under that fit alone, 8 workers would cost \\(0.10715\\) against 7's \\(0.10789\\).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A familiar curve, a different cause**
>
> Throughput proportional to \\(W / (a + b\\,W^2)\\) has the shape of [Gunther's Universal Scalability Law](<https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.1431>): a rational function that rises, peaks and then falls (retrograde scaling). The resemblance is in the shape only. In the USL the quadratic term models coherency between processors; here it is fitted to interference in a shared cache.

## 2\. What the contention-associated overhead is made of

**A smaller footprint at 7 workers.** A variant of the lazy-letters kernel that stores its rules in 12 bytes instead of 16 shrinks each worker's footprint. With 9 workers past the cores it took 0.98 to 0.99 of the wall time. With 7 it cut LLC misses per byte to 0.926 at 12 threads, with 1.6% more instructions, and no change in wall time was detected: 1.012 (0.998, 1.028), 0.996 (0.987, 1.005) and 1.002 (0.985, 1.018) of the 16-byte kernel's at 12, 16 and 20 threads. That is consistent with the saved misses overlapping other work and being offset by the extra instructions. It doesn't identify what the overhead is.

**The cycles per miss avoided.** Across the 10-thread arms, the cycles saved per LLC miss avoided come to about 589 from 10 workers to 7. That is a slope across arms, not a cost per miss: it moves with the cost of the misses that remain, with overlap, and with every other cost that changes with the count. A conditional calculation is all it supports: *if* each removed miss carried 390 to 490 unhidden cycles, the cost of an uncontended trip to memory at an assumed 80 to 100 ns, *and* nothing else changed, fewer misses would account for 66% to 83% of the saving. Neither assumption is established. The counters run below measured a loaded miss latency of about 595 cycles, already outside that range, with about 2.2 misses in flight at once; dividing one by the other doesn't give the exposed critical-path cost either. The remainder can't be assigned to anything by subtraction. Misses serviced in parallel cost less than isolated ones, so a cut in misses need not cut stall cycles in proportion, as [Qureshi, Lynch, Mutlu and Patt (2006, §1.1)](<https://doi.org/10.1109/ISCA.2006.5>) show, and stall counters overlap, as [Yasin (2014)](<https://doi.org/10.1109/ISPASS.2014.6844459>) warns.

**The two hypotheses, scored.** Before the counters run, the model's [record 47](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/0e7c6888bcba2ce8dd3056c587a23be958d6de4f/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-17-contention-counters.md>) froze predictions for two readings: queueing in the L3 and the ring that links it to the cores (Q), and main-memory latency rising with load (D). [Record 51](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/c7ea4a5c5e8447fbdfd407c6f0ae07b6669bd87e/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-17-miss-cost-scoring.md>) scored them, from 10 workers to 7 at 10 threads:

| frozen prediction | measured | status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Q: L3-hit latency falls 10% to 25% | derived from demand-read occupancy: 91.0 → 65.2 cycles, −28% | direction right, size outside the range |
| Q: L3-miss latency falls 5% to 15% | 594 → 552 cycles, −7% | met |
| D: L3-miss latency falls 25% or more | −7% | not met |
| main-memory traffic at 10 workers: 4 to 9 GB/s under Q, 60% of peak or more under D | not measured; demand L3-miss reads alone are 1.8 GB/s, not total traffic | untested |
| Q: stalls on L3 misses at most 45% of the cycle cut | 43% | met |
| Q: stalls on L2 misses at least 70% of the cut | 46% | not met |
| L3-hit loads per byte flat within 5% | 0.908 | not met |
| L3-miss loads per byte, 7 against 10, about 0.52 | 0.390 | not met |

Q is not refuted, and D is unsupported but not formally refuted, since its traffic half wasn't measured. Neither is identified as the mechanism. The record fits the derived L3-hit latency as about 44.8 cycles plus a term proportional to the L3-miss reads per byte, which would mean each miss also slows the hits around it; that is a model on four points, not a measurement of cause.

## 3\. The ledger of frozen predictions

Each prediction below was frozen before its run. Where a later record corrected a model, both versions are kept.

| record | frozen prediction | measured | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 41 | a capacity cliff: misses flatten from 7 workers to 6 | fell a further 28% | refuted |
| 42 | ring or bandwidth contention with flat misses | misses fell 41% from 8 workers to 6 | refuted (this rival only) |
| 43 | 10 threads: 7 workers, at 0.93 (0.90, 0.98) of 10's time | 7, at 0.885 | count right, gain outside the interval |
| 44 | counts at 8, 6 and 4 threads, with 11 ratio intervals | counts right; 5 of 11 values outside their intervals (record 49's heading says four; its own table shows five); its near-saturated utilisation refuted | mixed |
| 45 | `-3`, 10 threads: the best count is 9 or 10 | 7 | refuted |
| 45 | `-3`: 7 workers no better than 0.98 of 10's time | 0.978 (0.973, 0.983) | borderline |
| 45 | `-3`, if bandwidth-bound: 7 at about 0.885 | 0.978 | refuted |
| 45 | CI runner: 4 workers, and the reference plan stays | not yet run | pending |
| 46 | 8, 6 and 4 threads: 6, 5 and 4 workers; utilisation flat near 0.76 | pinned: 6, 5 and the reference 4; 0.742, 0.725, 0.740; later, eager 3 beat 4 (0.959) | right at 8 and 6, overtaken at 4; pinned only, confounded |
| 46 | rival idle term: 3 workers at 4 threads; utilisation 0.56, 0.67, 0.74 | the reference 4; flat | refuted |
| 46 | `-3`, 10 threads: 9 workers, 7 at about 1.18 of 10's time | 7 best, at 0.978 | refuted |
| LOG | 0.7 of the threads, rounded: 6, 4 and 3 | penalties of 12% at 6 threads and about 11% at 4 | refuted |
| LOG | 0.7 of the threads, floored: 5, 4 and 2 | fails at all three counts | refuted |
| 47 | Q and D, the counters run | see section 2 | mixed |
| 48 | `-9` misses at 4 workers match `-3`'s at equal fullness | 0.00368 against 0.0045 (0.0035, 0.0058) | met |
| 48 | the same at 3 workers | 0.00225 against 0.0034 (0.0027, 0.0042), 34% low | refuted |
| 49 | eager kernel at the trimmed counts: 5 workers at 6 threads at 0.90 (0.86, 0.95), 3 at 4 threads at 0.99 (0.95, 1.03), against the reference plan | pinned: 0.938 and 0.959 | both inside their bands; pinned only |
| 49 | eager 7 workers over lazy 7 at 10 threads: 0.98 (0.95, 1.02) | 1.0906 (1.0821, 1.0992) | refuted |

The 8-thread count was observed before record 46's CPU bound was written; the low-thread sweep re-measured it and tested 6 and 4 threads afresh. All of it ran pinned. An [unpinned run](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6949008682>) later found no gain at 8 threads (1.000) and losses at 6 and 4. So these gains did not transfer to the full machine, and competition for the CPU with the decoder's other threads is implicated. Net ratios don't separate the parts: a cache saving to 0.96 and a parallelism loss of 1.0417 also net to 1.000. The 6- and 8-thread points can't calibrate cache contention alone, so they come out of the contention fit.

**The low-thread sweep in full.** Each arm against the reference plan at its count, 10 paired rounds, pinned one CPU a core:

Below 8 threads, pinned: 5 lazy workers win at 6 threads, and no lazy count beats the reference 4 at 4

Measured on the test machine, decoding four copies of the Wikidata extract, 10 paired rounds a point, the process limited to one hardware thread a core; the bar is the 95% interval over the rounds. At 6 and 4 threads the reference plan runs the older (eager) kernel, one worker a thread, so the 6-worker point at 6 threads and the 4-worker point at 4 threads measure the lazy-letters kernel alone. The 2-worker point at 4 threads, 1.533, is off the chart.

| threads | reference plan | arm | wall |
| ---: | --- | --- | ---: |
| 8 | lazy 8 workers, window 32 | lazy 6/24 | 0.925 (0.918, 0.933) |
| 8 |  | lazy 5/20 | 0.997 (0.984, 1.010) |
| 6 | eager 6 workers, window 24 | lazy 6/24 (kernel control) | 1.040 |
| 6 |  | lazy 5/20 | 0.963 (0.948, 0.977) |
| 6 |  | lazy 4/16 | 1.077 |
| 4 | eager 4 workers, window 16 | lazy 4/16 (kernel control) | 1.098 |
| 4 |  | lazy 3/12 | 1.113 |
| 4 |  | lazy 2/8 | 1.533 |

At 6 threads the 0.963 includes a change of kernel; the lazy kernel alone costs 4% there, so the count's own share is about \\(0.963 / 1.040 \\approx 0.93\\), a descriptive ratio, not a paired result.

**The `-3` hot-set ratio.** The 0.355 first used was the ratio of the workers' total buffers at the end of a block (5.97 MB against 16.81 MB). Counting the kernel's per-letter store directly gives a hot-set ratio of 0.377, and the exponent of the footprint in the contention term then comes out at 2.03, 2.23, 1.85 and 2.05 from the four slope ratios (cycles and misses, over 6–9 and 7–10 workers). The cache bound at `-3` is about 22.

## 4\. The CPU bound and the tie-break

**Per-worker CPU utilisation.** A worker with a CPU to spare is busy 0.93 of the time. With \\(\\nu\\) the non-worker threads' CPU use and \\(\\iota\\) a residual idle capacity, the workers get \\(\\min(0.93\\,W,\\ N - \\nu - \\iota)\\) CPUs. At 10 threads, with \\(\\nu\\) counted and \\(\\iota = 0.125\\,N\\), that reproduces the measured utilisation: 0.767, 0.851, 0.930, 0.930 and 0.930 for 10 down to 6 workers, against 0.763, 0.857, 0.931, 0.925 and 0.931.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A correction to this term**
>
> An earlier version of the busy term was derived from the wall times and the cycles, and the review of the runs pointed out that with a flat clock it is close to an identity, so its match was not independent evidence. The term is now built from each thread's counted processor time: a separate measurement, but still calibrated to these runs.

**The rule's history.** Record 46 wrote the CPU bound as \\((N - \\nu - \\iota)/0.93\\): 8.2 at 10 threads and 6.6 at 8. Record 49 replaced the counted \\(\\nu\\) with \\(\\nu \\approx 0.16\\,W\\), which gives \\(0.80\\,N\\); it also replaced the physical-core caps with logical CPUs, since counting SMT siblings as fractional cores would cap a 2-core, 4-thread runner at 2. Its first tie-break, the larger of two candidates within 1%, gave 7 at 8 threads and 8 at 10 against the measured 6 and 7, so it was reversed to the smaller, a choice fitted to those two counts. [Record 50](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/c7ea4a5c5e8447fbdfd407c6f0ae07b6669bd87e/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-17-rule-scope.md>) found that with its own \\(\\nu\\) the rule gives 3 at 4 threads, against the reference plan's measured 4, hence the exception at 4 threads or fewer. Against the fitted model's own joint optimum, composing the bounds costs at most 0.7% at the measured counts; the model itself is the larger error.

## 5\. Topology and transfer

The cache bound sums over LLC-sharing domains: \\(\\sum\_d \\min(N\_d,\\ 0.8 \\times L\_d / F)\\), with \\(N\_d\\) the logical CPUs of the affinity set in domain \\(d\\). The sum holds only if workers are spread across domains, which soft affinity per domain would arrange. The CPU bound stays process-wide. SMT enters through each worker's cost \\(c(W)\\), not through the caps.

On the free GitHub x86 runners sampled so far (AMD EPYC 7763, 9V74 and 9V45: 2 cores, 4 logical CPUs, one 32 MiB L3) the cache bound is about 12.8 and never binds, and the rule gives \\(m = 3.2\\). "Within one worker" can only fail there on an outcome the existing data already rule out, so the runners are judged on three frozen refuters instead: 3 workers beating 4 by more than 2%; 2 workers coming within 3% of 4; or any lazy-letters plan beating the reference plan by more than 2%.

0.5.3 read the machine through the process's affinity set, so a 10-thread run pinned to CPUs 0 to 9 saw 10 logical CPUs and no trim. 0.5.4 recognises the test machine from its present and online CPUs and trims in both modes, and the unpinned 10-thread trim measured 0.873. For a general model, whether to read topology machine-wide or through the affinity set is still open.
