# Stop and walk: cutting a BWT inversion short and walking the rest

Halting each block's rebuild early spares mibz2 a third of the text pieces it stores, but on ten cores the slower walk outweighs the memory saved.

16 November 2026 · 17 min read · [Research result](<#6-what-did-the-timing-show>)

*Stop and walk* is a new way for mibz2 to finish rebuilding a block of text. It stops the rebuild partway, walks once round the small loop that is left, and writes the text out as it goes. The rebuild never makes the pieces of text its last steps would have built: a third of them, for about 2% more instructions. It did not ship. On our 10-core test machine it ran slightly slower, because the walk waits on one memory load after another, and those waits cost more time than the smaller memory saved.

**How it works, step by step.** mibz2's Cells kernel rebuilds a block by shrinking a map of it, one step at a time. Each step builds a longer piece of the text, a *word*. The full rebuild can't put any word in the output until near its end. So it keeps every word until then. Stop and walk stops partway instead, after 1.5 steps for every run of equal bytes in the block. That leaves one small loop of points. One point on it has a known place in the output. Walking round the loop from that point puts each point's word next to the one before. So the words the last steps would have built never get made.

**Why that could make mibz2 faster.** Fewer words mean less memory per block. That matters where many threads share one cache. Our test machine is an Intel i9 with 10 cores. Since mibz2 0.5.1, it decodes one block per thread at every thread count. From 8 threads up, mibz2 switches to the [lazy-letters](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-lazy-letters/index.md>) version of Cells. Before 0.5.1, the highest thread counts ran [teams](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/index.md>) of threads sharing one block, and memory cuts to Cells never reached them. Now a cut to the lazy kernel reaches every count from 8 to 20 ([section 5](<#5-why-test-it-now>)).

**Where it stands.** We built stop and walk, and it gives the same bytes as the shipped kernel. We counted its instructions and timed it on the i9. It did not meet the rule we set before the timing, so mibz2 keeps the shipped kernel ([section 6](<#6-what-did-the-timing-show>)).

The rest of the opening gives the background the idea rests on.

**The BWT, in brief.** mibz2 is our bzip2 decoder, written in Rust. bzip2 compresses text in blocks of up to 900 kB. It stores each block as the last column of the block's sorted rotations: the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). To undo it, a decoder follows a map, LF, from row to row of the sorted block, one byte per row. Within a *run*, a stretch of equal bytes in that column, LF moves every row by the same amount. So the map is one shifted interval per run, not one entry per row ([the post of 8 November](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/index.md>)).

**Cells.** [Cells](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) shrinks that map step by step, and records each step as a word. Each step deletes rows that the path through the block can only pass through, and gives an interval a longer word to stand for the bytes it skipped. The code calls an interval a *letter* and each step a *cell*. When one letter is left, its word is the whole block, and a final pass, the *writer*, expands it into bytes. The technique is Rauzy–Veech induction ([the technical companion](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-12-rauzy-technical-companion/index.md>)), and [section 1](<#1-how-does-cells-rebuild-a-block>) runs it by hand on a three-byte block.

**What the kernel keeps.** It keeps two things while it works. The first is the letters' bookkeeping: their lengths, links and places. [Hand-me-down slots](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-slot-recycling/index.md>) and [smaller second-order slots](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-bottom-slots/index.md>) trimmed it, and lazy letters then cut its slots from 20 bytes a letter to 6.4. The second is the words. The kernel stores a word of up to 16 bytes as its bytes, and a longer one as a 16-byte rule naming its two halves. Those *word bytes* average 15.6 a letter on mibz2's Wikidata benchmark, an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump that decompresses to 210 MB. The lazy kernel touches 29.5 bytes a letter besides its output, so the words make up about half ([the ring's record](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/docs/journal/2026-11-16-lazy-ring.md>)). No change so far has cut them.

**The numbers.** On Wikidata a block's rebuild takes about 1.8 steps a run in all, so stopping at 1.5 leaves out about the last fifth. At the stop, the loop has about one point for every 22 rows of the block.

## What was found

The takeaways, each shown in a section below:

- **The kernel never makes a third of the word bytes.** Stopping at 1.5 cells a run leaves 33% of the word bytes unmade. That is 5.0 bytes a letter, counted by a prototype on all 233 large Wikidata blocks. The saving comes to about a sixth of everything the lazy kernel touches. The timing showed the relief indirectly, as less extra processor time at 10 threads ([section 2](<#2-why-does-the-rebuild-hold-its-words-to-the-end>), [section 4](<#4-where-should-it-stop-and-what-does-it-cost>), [section 6](<#6-what-did-the-timing-show>)).
- **The walk writes each word once and copies it after.** It goes once round the loop, one point at a time. The walk expands a long word where it first meets its letter, and every later point copies it from there. The built kernel gives the same bytes as the shipped one on all 431 blocks of the Wikidata extract ([section 3](<#3-how-can-a-walk-place-the-words>)).
- **It costs 10 to 12 instructions a letter.** Over the whole decode, that adds about 2% to the shipped decoder's instructions. The build had to stay under +20 a letter, and it does. On one thread its kernel runs about 10% slower, because the walk waits on one memory load after another. A cloud machine took that timing, so it hints at speed and proves nothing ([section 4](<#4-where-should-it-stop-and-what-does-it-cost>)).
- **It did not ship.** On the 10-core i9 it ran 1% to 1.5% slower at 8, 9 and 20 threads, and we detected no difference at 10 and 12. The memory relief was real, but with one worker a core the walk's waits outweighed it. It could only have replaced the lazy kernel everywhere that kernel runs, and never had a thread range of its own ([section 6](<#6-what-did-the-timing-show>)).

Run to the end, or stop at 1.5 cells a run and walk

Above and middle: conceptual bars, with counted figures. Wikidata's blocks need about 1.8 cells a run in all; stopping at 1.5 leaves 33% of the word bytes unmade (a prototype's count over 233 blocks). Below: the analogy. Each bead is a point of the map left at the stop, its colour is the letter it belongs to, and the letter's word is the bead's piece of text. The real loop has about one point for every 22 rows. The analogy stops holding for the induction itself: it does not thread beads one at a time, but deletes whole intervals of points at each step, under one rule per letter.

**Where things stand.** We built stop and walk as test variants of the lazy kernel and timed them on the i9 from 8 threads to 20 ([\#493](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/493>)). Under the rule we set before the run, stop and walk is [not adopted](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6922810916>), and mibz2's default stays as it was. [Section 6](<#6-what-did-the-timing-show>) has the figures. The test variants stay on their branch.

## 1\. How does Cells rebuild a block?

This post uses these terms, each worked through on an example below:

| Term | What it is in mibz2 |
| --- | --- |
| run | a stretch of equal bytes in the BWT's last column |
| letter | an interval of rows that the map moves as one; at first, one run |
| word | the bytes a letter's interval stands for; one byte at first, longer as the rebuild goes on |
| cell | the overlap of an interval in one order with an interval in the other; each step makes one |
| induction | replacing the map by a smaller one that skips some rows, while recording their bytes in words |
| rule | a long word kept as its two halves, such as X = AB, each an existing word |

Take the three-byte block `aab`. Its rotations, sorted, are `aab`, `aba` and `baa`, so its last column reads `baa`. That column has two runs: `b` in row 0 and `aa` in rows 1 and 2. Call them B and A. LF sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier. It sends B's row to row 2. It sends A's two rows to rows 0 and 1, shifting both by the same amount. Followed from row 0, LF visits row 2, then row 1, then row 0 again. That is one cycle through every row, and it reads the block's bytes backwards.

The block aab as two intervals and one cycle

Worked by hand. On the left, the sorted rotations and their last bytes. On the right, the two runs as intervals, in the last column's order and in the order LF lands them. Moving the intervals around without reversing any of them is what makes this an interval exchange. Section 1 of [the Cells post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) runs the same block.

**One step of the induction.** Look at the right-hand end of both orders. In the last column, the last interval is A, two rows long. Among the places LF lands, the last is row 2, where B lands. B is the shorter, and it lands inside A, at A's end. Nothing else reaches row 2, and from row 2 the path always goes on to row 1. So the step can delete row 2, as long as it keeps its byte. B's word grows from `b` to `ab`: A's `a` followed by B's own `b`, in the order the rebuild records them. Both intervals are now one row long, and the map is 0 → 1 → 0.

One step: row 2 goes, its byte stays in B's word

Worked by hand, on the block aab. The smaller map skips row 2, and loses nothing: B's word now holds its byte. Each move of the smaller map stands for the run of moves of the old one that it skips, which is what a first-return map means.

On a real block each step does the same at the right-hand end. It deletes a whole interval's worth of rows at once and records the new word. The kernel records a long word as a rule naming its two halves, so it costs 16 bytes whatever its length. When only one letter is left, its word is the whole block. On `aab` one more step would finish it. A and B now have the same length, so they join into one letter whose word is `aab`.

**The rule that makes the walk possible.** Moving along the smaller map moves through the text by exactly the length of the word that move stands for. If \\(p(x)\\) is the place in the block of the text at point \\(x\\), \\(T\\) is the smaller map, and \\(w\_\\alpha\\) is the word of the letter \\(\\alpha\\) that holds \\(x\\), then

\\\[ p(T(x)) \\equiv p(x) - |w\_\\alpha| \\pmod n , \\\]

where \\(n\\) is the block's length. The word \\(w\_\\alpha\\) lies just below \\(p(x)\\) in the text, and \\(T(x)\\) starts where it ends. On `aab` after one step, point 0 holds the two bytes `ab` and point 1 holds `a`. Going round the loop once moves through 2 + 1 = 3 bytes, the whole block. The design's [record](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-16-stop-and-walk.md>) proves this as its invariant I. It holds at every stage of the induction, not only at its end.

## 2\. Why does the rebuild hold its words to the end?

To put a word in the output, the writer needs its place: the offset in the block where its bytes begin. Cells learns places from one row only. bzip2 records which row of the sorted block holds the original text's first rotation. Cells keeps that row marked, as a letter of its own. The kernel can fix a word's place only once the word has become part of the word around that row. In Cells' order of steps, that word grows only in the last steps, so until then it knows almost no word's place.

That has a direct consequence for memory. [A census of every word](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-16-words.md>) followed each word from when the kernel made it until nothing needed it. It covered Wikidata's 233 blocks of at least 65,536 rows. It found that the writer still needs 72% of the word bytes when the induction ends. The other 28% die earlier. A short word that every longer word built from it has copied is dead once its letter no longer holds it.

The kernel can't give those 28% back cheaply. A dead word almost never sits at the top of the store. Its letter kept it for a long time, while the kernel added other words above it. A store that only frees from the top, the cheapest kind, reclaims none of them on any block. Reclaiming them needs a free list or a compaction pass, which is bookkeeping for every letter, in a loop that is already short of registers. Writing words out early doesn't help either. The writer can't write a word before it knows the word's place, and it learns places only at the very end.

So the census closed with a lower bound. **While places come only from that one row, the kernel has to keep every word not yet inside the word around it.** In Cells' order that is the writer's whole set of words until the last step, which is exactly what the kernel holds. The words weren't too big; the kernel just didn't know their places yet. The one way out the census named was to learn places some other way: by walking.

## 3\. How can a walk place the words?

Stop the induction early, and it leaves a smaller map of the same kind. It has a set of points, each belonging to a letter, and a rule for moving from a point to the next. Because LF passes through every row of a block in one cycle, the smaller map also forms one loop through all its points. The rule of [section 1](<#1-how-does-cells-rebuild-a-block>) says each move round the loop passes over exactly one letter's word. So once the walk knows one point's place, the word lengths give every other place.

The walk does know one point's place. [The design's record](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-16-stop-and-walk.md>) proves that the mark on bzip2's starting row always stays on an interval one row long. So at the stop the mark sits on a single point. Its place follows from the row's offset within its word, which the writer already finds. The stopped map still holds everything the rebuild needs. It records where each letter's intervals lie in both orders, each letter's word and its length, and the mark. The induction has discarded nothing; it has only changed how it describes the text.

**Two ways to finish.** On `aab`, after one step, ordinary Cells would take the second step and then expand `aab`. Stop and walk instead stops there and walks the two points.

Two ways to finish aab

Worked by hand. The places follow the rule of section 1: each point's word ends at its place, and the next point's place is this one's less the word's length. Here the walk starts at point 0 for the illustration; in the kernel it starts at the marked point.

**The walk in the kernel.** The built kernel, in [\#493](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/493>), walks the loop once. It follows the map forwards from the marked point and moves down the output. It writes each point's word so that the word ends at the point's place. After as many points as the loop has, it is back at the marked point, one block lower, and it has written the whole block. If the loop closes too early, or the bytes don't add up to the block, the kernel decodes the block again the shipped way.

**Expand once, then copy.** A letter's interval may hold many points, and each has the same word. Expanding a long word from its rules at every point would repeat the same work. An earlier version did just that, and its writing pass cost about twice the shipped writer's instructions. The walk expands a long word the first time it meets its letter, and notes where it wrote it. Every later point of that letter copies the bytes from there, so the output itself serves as a store of words already expanded. The walk copies a short word, kept as bytes, straight from where the induction stored it. The copy is a fixed 32 bytes, then 16 at a time for a longer word, so the walk doesn't branch on a word's length.

Writing abracadabra from a loop of four points

Conceptual: a made-up loop, not a real block's. The walk moves down the output, so it writes the first X (places 7 to 10) before, and above, the copy at 0 to 3. In a real block the loop has about one point for every 22 rows.

**Why the wide stores are safe.** A 32-byte copy of a 4-byte word writes 28 bytes too many. They land below the word, at places the walk hasn't reached yet, because places only fall as it goes. The walk writes each of those bytes again, correctly, when it gets there. A copy's source is always the first occurrence, which lies wholly above, so the walk finished it before reading it. Two places break that rule: place 0, where the walk wraps round the block, and the walk's last 32 bytes, just above where it began. There the walk writes each word exactly.

The only new table the walk needs is one 4-byte first place for each letter alive at the stop, about a tenth of the letters. As we first built it, we sized its tables to every letter, and they added about 20% to the peak memory of a [worker](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-01-block-dispatch/index.md>), the thread that decodes a block. Before any timing, we cut them to the live letters. Locally the peak now matches the shipped kernel's: 37 against 37 MB on one thread, 83 against 85 on four ([the revised rule](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6920355683>)).

**Why one lane.** An earlier design split the walk into eight lanes, so that their waits on memory overlapped. That needed an extra pass to measure each lane's stretch of the output first. And one lane's wide stores could overwrite bytes that a neighbouring lane had already written. A single ordered walk needs neither the extra pass nor any guard at the boundaries. It pays with a single chain of dependent loads, which [section 4](<#4-where-should-it-stop-and-what-does-it-cost>) comes back to.

## 4\. Where should it stop, and what does it cost?

The stop needs a test, and the induction's inner loop has no room for one. That loop already uses more values than the processor has registers. An earlier version tested the map's remaining size on every cell. That test alone cost about 10 instructions a cell, whether the block stopped or not, and cancelled what the stop saved. So this design puts the stop on a count the kernel already keeps. The kernel refuses any block that would take more cells than a budget allows, so it counts every cell down already. Stopping after ⌈β r⌉ cells, where r is the block's number of letters at the start, needs only a different starting count. The design priced that at nothing. In the build, the cleanest form of it spilled the counter to memory and cost 16 to 38 instructions on every cell. So the build compares the counter with a stored bound instead. That costs about 2 instructions a cell.

We set the stop as β r cells, not as a size of the map. The kernel knows r before the induction starts, but not the total number of cells. On Wikidata a block takes 1.29 to 2.08 cells a run in all. Early in the induction most of the map disappears cheaply. Late in it few rows are left, but each step still makes a long word. Stopping earlier saves more words and leaves more points to walk, so β = 1.5 is a compromise read off the counts, not an optimum. Our prototype counted three settings over the 233 large blocks:

| β (cells a run at the stop) | blocks that stop | map left, as a share of the rows (median) | points walked a letter | word bytes never made |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1.4 | 232 of 233 | 0.082 | 1.23 | 43% (6.5 B a letter) |
| 1.5 | 232 of 233 | 0.046 | 0.66 | 33% (5.0 B) |
| 1.6 | 232 of 233 | 0.022 | 0.34 | 23% (3.4 B) |

A block that takes fewer cells than β r never stops, and the kernel rebuilds it as before. The table shows the striking thing. By the stop at 1.5, the map has shrunk to under a twentieth of the rows. Yet a third of the word bytes are still to come. The count measured word storage, the rules and the stored bytes. It is not the process's memory, and we have not measured any drop in memory traffic or cache misses.

**What it costs.** The prototype predicted that stopping at 1.5 would save about 20 instructions a letter against the shipped kernel. [The kernel's count](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6920005870>), over the whole decode of the Wikidata extract with callgrind, an instruction counter, came out the other way. A letter here is one run of the 11,090,867 in the blocks Cells takes, and the whole decode costs about 550 instructions a letter. Before any timing, the team set a limit of +20 instructions a letter, under 4% of the decode.

| β | whole decode, first passing build | a letter, against the shipped lazy kernel | a letter, on the build the i9 run uses |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| shipped | 6.076 G instructions |  |  |
| 1.4 | 6.360 G | \+25.6 | \+27.3 |
| **1.5** | **6.196 G** | **\+10.8** | **\+12.3** |
| 1.6 | 6.154 G | \+7.0 | \+8.1 |

β = 1.5 stays under the limit. The counter itself varies by about 10 a letter between builds of the same source. So the count shows that β = 1.5 stays under the limit, not that it costs exactly 11 or 12 instructions. The two builds' figures agree within that noise.

The trade: word bytes never made, against instructions added

Counted and modelled, not timed. The heights, the share of word bytes never made, are a prototype's counts over the 233 large Wikidata blocks. The filled points are the built kernel's whole-decode instruction counts on the build the i9 run uses (the first passing build counted +25.6, +10.8 and +7.0); the hollow ones are what the design's model predicted, including the cost of reading the stopped map.

The count also shows where the prediction went wrong. At β = 1.5, on the first passing build, three costs differ. The cells never made were the cheap ones. The tail of the induction reads no new runs, so each of its cells costs about 38 instructions, not 71. Skipping them saves 13.2 a letter, not 21.5. The walk costs 52.1 instructions a letter, against the shipped writer's 49.5. The prototype's standalone walk cost 38.3. Each point takes about 31 instructions of fixed work: a rank lookup, a bit count and a read of the letter's record. Expanding each letter's first occurrence adds 14.6 a letter. And reading the stopped map into the walk's tables costs 18.9, not the 10 the model allowed. About 6,000 letters are alive in a block at the stop, and the kernel reads each twice.

**Time on one thread.** On a cloud machine, with the kernel's phases timed, β = 1.5 was about 10% slower than the shipped kernel. The walk runs about the writer's instructions in about twice the writer's time. Its step from one point to the next is a load, a bit count, a second load and an add. That takes about 20 cycles, and each step needs the one before it. That machine's timings prove nothing about speed; the i9 later measured 6.4% ([section 6](<#6-what-did-the-timing-show>)). They did say what the decisive run had to show: that when many threads share the cache, the bytes saved buy back more than the walk costs. A second lane, walking the other way round the loop, would halve the chain, but needs more tables, so it waits on the result.

**Why the design is this way.** An earlier version of stop and walk made the two mistakes this design avoids. It tested the map's size on every cell, which cost about as much as the stop saved. And it expanded each long word from its rules every time it appeared. Together they made it about 97 instructions a letter dearer than the shipped kernel, far over the limit. The figure sets its costs against this design's, item by item. The team now asks every failed build for that item-by-item list and sends it back to the design's author ([§11a of its protocol](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/docs/team/PROTOCOL.md#11a-a-failed-gate-goes-back-to-its-author-term-by-term>)).

Why the design is this way: an earlier version against this one, in instructions a letter

Counted with callgrind over the whole decode of the Wikidata extract, in instructions per run of the blocks Cells takes, against the shipped lazy kernel; this design's figures are from its first passing build. The two builds stop at different points, a 32nd of the rows and 1.5 cells a run, so the rows compare designs, not one stop. “The rest” is each total less its listed terms, worked out here, not counted. The earlier version's two largest avoidable costs, the stop test and writing the text, are the two this design removes.

**Why stop only once.** [A follow-up record](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/806979d4402945685da22a334bde4a63db83b470/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-16-tower.md>), in review as [\#492](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/492>), tried stopping again, on the walk's own tail. It gives the right bytes, but describing each extra level of the map costs about as much as the words it saves. The best two-stop version saves 1.3 bytes a letter more, for about 16 to 26 more instructions a letter. The single stop at 1.5 stays the design.

**What is known, and how.** The records label each statement as proved, counted or modelled:

| Status | What the records support |
| --- | --- |
| Proved | the stopped map keeps every path and its words; one loop with one known place gives every place; an ordered walk with first-place copies never overwrites a byte still needed |
| Counted or tested | a third of the word bytes never made at β = 1.5 (prototype, 233 blocks); +10.8 and +12.3 instructions a letter (kernel, callgrind); the same bytes as the shipped kernel on all 431 Wikidata blocks, the test files and 4,000 random columns |
| Measured on the i9 | slower at 8, 9 and 20 threads, level at 10 and 12; 5% less extra processor time from 1 thread to 10; 6.4% slower on one thread; faster with two workers forced onto each core |
| Modelled | whether the cache's size, its misses or the bandwidth to memory limit it; what a second lane would save |
| Not done yet | the Miri and fuzz runs, the mutation pass and the review of the new unsafe code, which the records list as owed before any adoption |

## 5\. Why test it now?

The kernel's bytes matter only where threads compete for the cache. On one thread, instructions decide the time. That is why lazy letters lost at 4 and 6 threads and won from 8. So the question is which thread counts run the lazy kernel, and until recently the answer was few of them. [Why mibz2 stops scaling](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/index.md>) found the *knee*: past about 8 threads, each block decoded at once slowed the others. mibz2 answered with [teams](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/#1-how-does-mibz2-decode-with-several-threads>) of threads that share one block: three teams of three at 10 threads. Those teams were [later pipelined](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-pipelined-teams/index.md>), and later still given a [pit crew of two service threads](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-09-pit-crew-service-threads/index.md>) for each block's serial steps. Those teams ran their own kernel, so Cells' memory cuts reached only 8 threads and below.

That changed in 0.5.1. [\#462](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/462>) gave each of 10 threads a block of its own, decoded with lazy letters. [\#468](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/468>) covered machines with 8 to 10 physical cores asked for more threads than that. They run one lazy worker a core, and leave the second hardware threads idle. The thread plan in the code, [`plan_with`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/src/parallel.rs#L2680-L2706>), now runs on the 10-core i9 as follows:

| Threads asked for | What runs |
| --- | --- |
| 1 to 7 | a worker a thread, eager Cells |
| 8 to 10 | a worker a thread, lazy letters |
| 11 to 20 | 10 workers, one a core, lazy letters |

Teams now run only on other machines. A machine with 6 or 7 physical cores gets teams of two when asked for more threads than it has cores. So does a machine with 11 cores or more, asked for 11 threads or more. Where the machine's topology can't be read, which includes every system other than Linux, mibz2 runs a worker a thread at every count.

[The release ledger](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/docs/journal/release-attribution.md>) shows why that matters. It lists, for each release, which merge moved which thread count on the i9 by 3% or more. From 0.2.4 on, 10 to 20 threads moved in only three ways. Two changed how mibz2 grouped its threads: the teams, then pipelining them. One was an existing kernel ported to the teams. The third was 0.5.1's move onto Cells, which sped up 10 threads by 7.3%. Each of Cells' memory cuts, from the 20-byte slot to lazy letters, sped up only 8 threads or fewer, because teams ran above that. Now a cut to the lazy kernel's working set reaches every count from 8 to 20. Stop and walk trades instructions for memory, the trade lazy letters won and [a ring of shared buffers](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ea393f96dcfaed63581db6548e63795869c47a12/docs/journal/2026-11-16-lazy-ring.md>) lost. The ring cut the lazy kernel's bytes by 15% for 13% more decoder instructions. It ran slower at 8 threads and level at 9 and 10. By the prototype's count, stop and walk would cut 5.0 of those 29.5 bytes a letter, about a sixth, for about 2% more instructions.

## 6\. What did the timing show?

We timed it on the i9, [\#493](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/493>), under [a rule we fixed before the data](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6920355683>). The test decoder kept the shipped decoder's workers, thread plan and [window](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-01-block-dispatch/index.md>) of blocks in flight, and swapped only the kernel. It decoded four copies of the Wikidata extract at 8, 9, 10, 12 and 20 threads. Each of its ten paired rounds ran the shipped kernel and the three settings of β. At each count, β = 1.5 counts as faster if the 95% interval of its wall-time ratio lies wholly below 1. It counts as slower if the interval lies wholly above.

Stop and walk would replace the lazy kernel, everywhere lazy letters run now, if three things held. β = 1.5 had to be faster at one of those counts or more. It had to be slower at none. And its peak memory had to stay within 10% of the shipped kernel's at every count. Faster at some counts and slower at others is a finding, not an adoption. Stop and walk gets no thread range of its own, and moving the lazy threshold would be a separate decision. Because its verdict could change a default, the rule had one review before the run. The run also recorded two figures without judging them. One is how much slower each setting runs on one thread. The other is how much more processor time it takes at 10 threads than at 1, where a smaller working set should show.

**The verdict: not adopted.** [Our reading of the run](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6922810916>) applied the rule's checker, frozen before the data, to the run's results. β = 1.5 ran slower at 8, 9 and 20 threads. At 10 and 12 we could not tell it from the shipped kernel. Its peak memory stayed within 3% of the shipped kernel's at every count, and the run's guard on a text corpus was inconclusive at every count. Wall time, stop and walk at β = 1.5 over the shipped lazy kernel, on production's plan of one worker a core:

| Threads | Wall time ratio | 95% interval | Reading |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 8 | 1.012 | 1.004 to 1.019 | slower |
| 9 | 1.010 | 1.004 to 1.016 | slower |
| 10 | 0.991 | 0.980 to 1.003 | no difference detected |
| 12 | 0.997 | 0.985 to 1.010 | no difference detected |
| 20 | 1.015 | 1.003 to 1.027 | slower |

**What we learned.** The memory relief is real. Going from 1 thread to 10, the shipped kernel's processor time grows, because the threads compete for the cache. Stop and walk's grows 5% less: its ratio of the two is 0.947 (0.913 to 0.982) of the shipped kernel's. But with one worker a core, that relief did not repay the walk. On one thread stop and walk ran 6.4% slower (1.064, 1.032 to 1.096), because each step of the walk waits for the one before. When we forced two workers onto each core, 12 or 20 of them, stop and walk ran faster: 0.986 of the shipped kernel's time at 12 workers and 0.965 at 20. mibz2's plan never puts two workers on a core of the i9, so that gain is out of reach.

**What comes next.** The cost to remove is the walk's serial wait. The open question is whether the walk can split into independent chains that overlap their waits, or whether the kernel can read the stopped map more cheaply. Until one of those exists, the test variants stay on their branch.

The chain, in short. The full rebuild holds its words to the end because it learns their places only in its last steps. Walking the small map left after an early stop learns the places another way. So the last fifth of the steps never run, and a third of the word bytes never get made. Putting the stop on an existing counter, and copying each word after its first expansion, keep the cost to about 11 or 12 instructions a letter. Since 0.5.1 the lazy kernel runs from 8 threads to 20 on the i9. So a memory cut to it reaches the whole range where threads contend for the cache. The timing said no: with one worker a core, the walk's waits cost more than the memory it saves. With two workers a core the relief showed, so a walk that overlaps its waits could still change the answer. Either way, mibz2 now has a second way to finish an induction, with a proof that it is correct and a kernel that gives the right bytes.

---

# Lazy letters: just-in-time memory for induction

Holding fewer letters at once leaves the cache less crowded, so eight to ten threads decode up to 11% faster despite extra instructions.

16 November 2026 · 11 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-comes-next>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.5.0](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-5-0>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#050---2026-11-16>))

[The width of an induction](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/index.md>) counted how much of a block's rebuild must be held in memory at once, and found it was about a third of what mibz2's Cells kernel actually lays out. This post is about a kernel that keeps only that third, called *lazy letters*, and about what happened when ten threads ran it at once on a 10-core machine.

On a 10-core Intel i9, with each thread decoding a block of its own, lazy letters cut the wall time against mibz2 0.4.0 by 4.2% at 8 threads, 10.8% at 9 and 5.1% at 10. At 10 threads mibz2 0.4.0 runs teams of threads that share a block, so there lazy letters make one block per thread beat the teams. At 4 and 6 threads the extra instructions outweigh the saving, and lazy letters are 3% to 9% slower.

**The recap.** bzip2 compresses text in blocks of up to 900 kB. Each block goes through the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), which reorders its bytes so that equal bytes sit together in runs. Undoing it means following a map from row to row of the sorted block. [Cells](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>), mibz2's kernel for most blocks of the benchmark's Wikidata text, does that on intervals instead of rows. It starts with one interval per run. Each step of the rebuild (the *induction*) shortens the map by letting one interval stand for a longer piece of text. The code calls each interval a *letter* and the text it stands for its *word*. When one letter is left, its word is the whole block. Cells keeps each letter's bookkeeping (its length, where its word is, its neighbours) in a record called a *slot*.

**What width is.** A letter whose word is still one byte long is an untouched piece of an original run: everything about it can be read off the list of runs. Only the letters the rebuild has already changed hold new information. The most of those alive at any one moment is the *width*. On Wikidata it is about 0.32 of the letters, under the order of steps Cells takes. Cells today lays out a slot for every letter before its first step, and keeps them all until the end.

**Why mibz2 cares.** Width is how much state the rebuild keeps in memory. When every thread decodes a block of its own, those states share the processor's cache, and the threads contend for it. Keeping less live state per block eases that.

## What was found

The takeaways, each shown in a section below:

- **Lazy letters keep a third of the slots.** An interval the rebuild hasn't reached yet is kept as a 5-byte entry, and gets a slot only when a step first reaches it. Slots that are finished with go back to a pool. The pool's peak matches the width, 0.318 of the letters, to three digits. The memory the rebuild touches besides its output falls by 38% ([section 1](<#1-what-does-a-block-keep-while-it-is-rebuilt>)).
- **It costs instructions.** The first stage and the induction together take 28% more instructions. Every letter is now visited twice, and the inner loop runs short of registers ([section 2](<#2-what-does-keeping-less-cost>)).
- **At 4 and 6 threads it loses; from 8 it wins.** On a 10-core Intel i9, lazy letters take 3% to 9% more wall time than mibz2 0.4.0 at 4 and 6 threads. From 8 to 10 threads they take 4% to 11% less ([section 3](<#3-what-happened-on-ten-cores>)).
- **At 10 threads it beats the teams.** From ten threads, mibz2 doesn't give each thread a block of its own. It runs teams of threads that share a block, because one block per thread was slower there. Lazy letters reverse that: one block per thread is 5.1% faster than the teams, at 10.6% more processor time.
- **The gain grows with the thread count, as contention for the cache predicts.** Against the current kernel, lazy letters fare better at 10 threads than at 4 in all ten paired rounds ([section 4](<#4-why-would-fewer-bytes-help-only-with-many-threads>)).
- **Since 0.5.0 it is the default from 8 threads.** This is one machine and one text. mibz2 0.5.0 uses lazy letters whenever each thread decodes a block of its own at 8 threads or more, and a confirming run on the i9 is queued ([section 5](<#5-what-comes-next>)).

How much faster mibz2 decodes with lazy letters, by thread count

Lazy letters, one block per thread, against mibz2 0.4.0 on an Intel i9-10900K with 10 cores, decoding an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump, 10 paired rounds per thread count. Below 10 threads mibz2 already gives each thread a block of its own, so only the kernel differs. From 10 threads it runs teams of threads that share a block, so at 10 threads lazy letters makes one block per thread beat the teams. 12 threads uses the cores’ second hardware threads; its interval spans zero. The crossover between 6 and 8 threads is why the production version switches to lazy letters only from 8 threads up.

## 1\. What does a block keep while it is rebuilt?

Cells tracks the letters in two orders. The first is the order of the runs in the block. The second is the same runs sorted by byte value, keeping runs with the same byte in their original order. Each step works at the right-hand end of both orders, at what the code calls the two *fronts*. It compares the two letters there, records a *cell* (one piece of a word, added to a list of rules the writer later expands into text), and moves on. The fronts work backwards from the end, so at any moment most letters are still ahead of them, untouched.

Cells in 0.4.0 gives every letter a slot before the first step. A slot is 20 bytes in the kernel's own buffer, holding the letter's length, its links and where its word is. A second slot, 8 bytes in the output buffer, holds its links in the other order. (The output buffer is free to use until the writer runs, at the very end.) Most of those slots sit unused for most of the rebuild, because most letters are still untouched pieces of runs.

Lazy letters keep an untouched letter as 5 bytes in the output buffer instead. A 4-byte entry in the second order holds its length, its byte and whether the decoder's walk starts there. One more byte, in the first order, repeats its byte. That is all a step needs until a front first reaches the letter. The step itself is unchanged: the same cells, in the same order, written as the same words at the same places.

How lazy letters keep a letter, from untouched to finished

Conceptual. A letter costs 5 bytes until a front reaches it, then holds a pair of slots while it is in play. When it is finished (merged away at a step between two letters of equal length, or closed), its pair goes back on a last-in-first-out free list for the next letter a front reaches.

Two facts, both in [the research journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/caad2bd97e236905a15a970b3a3a945877b4316e/docs/journal/2026-11-15-lazy-letters.md>), mean nothing else needs storing. First, within one byte value, the two orders list the letters in the same order. So a counter for each of the 256 byte values finds a letter's entry in the second order from its byte, with no stored map between the orders (which would cost another 4 bytes a letter). Second, a front reaches a letter first from one order only, and never reads that entry again. So the entry, once used, is overwritten with a tagged pointer to the letter's new slots, for the other front to follow when it gets there.

What the rebuild keeps, eager and lazy

Above: conceptual, ten letters at one moment. Below: counted on one thread over the 196 Wikidata blocks Cells handles (11,090,867 letters), per letter, besides the output buffer. The lazy pool's bytes follow from its peak, the median over blocks.

**The count.** Over Wikidata's 196 blocks, the pool peaks at a median of 0.318 of the letters. No block goes above 0.337. That equals the width the earlier post counted for Cells' right-end order, 0.318, to three digits: the pool holds a pair for each letter the fronts have reached that is still alive. So the memory the kernel holds now follows the width, not the letter count. Per letter:

| Bytes per letter, Wikidata | 0.4.0 | Lazy letters |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Slots in the kernel's buffer | 20.0 | 6.4 |
| Words (the rules and their store) | 15.6 | 15.6 |
| **Total besides the output** | **35.6** | **22.0** |
| Inside the output buffer, before the writer | 8.0 | 7.5 |

The 6.4 bytes are the 20-byte slots of the letters in play at the peak: about 20 × 0.318. Inside the output buffer, lazy letters keep the 5-byte entries. They also keep second-order slots for the letters in play, about 8 × 0.318, or 2.5 bytes a letter. The pools have room for a slot for every letter, so the memory set aside is not smaller; what falls is the memory handed out and touched. Every block decodes to the same bytes as before.

## 2\. What does keeping less cost?

The same count says what it costs. Per letter, on one thread:

| Instructions per letter | 0.4.0 | Lazy letters |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| First stage (laying out the letters) | 81.0 | 71.2 |
| Induction | 115.5 | 181.0 |
| **Both together** | **196.4** | **252.2 (+28%)** |

The first stage gets cheaper, since it writes 5 bytes a letter instead of a slot. The induction gets much dearer, for two reasons. Every letter is now visited twice as each order is read, once untouched and once after it has a slot, and each visit tests which it is. The shipped kernel reads a slot each time with no test. And the lazy loop holds about 30 values at once, against the shipped loop's 19. That is more than the processor has registers for, so some spill to the stack and are reloaded.

These are instruction counts, not times. A first build cost 36% more; a leaner one, which takes slots only in the branches that need them, brought that to 28%. Before any timing, the kernel was set a limit of 10% more instructions, and at +28% it failed it. It was kept as a recorded result, with the open question of whether 38% less memory would outweigh the instructions with ten threads sharing one cache. Only a clock on a 10-core machine could answer that.

## 3\. What happened on ten cores?

The machine is the maintainer's workstation, an Intel i9-10900K. It has 10 cores, each with two hardware threads, and they all share one 20 MiB last-level cache. The run decoded the Wikidata extract at six thread counts from 4 to 12, in 10 paired rounds each. It compared four arms. The first is mibz2 0.4.0. The second gives each thread a block, with the current kernel, and the third does the same with lazy letters. The fourth is described below. All 240 readings produced the same output.

**The rule, set before the data.** [The decision rule](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6902022809>) compared lazy letters with one block per thread on the current kernel, so that only the kernel differed. Memory would count as the cause if lazy letters were faster at 10 threads, with the interval wholly below 1, and level or slower at 4. As a sanity check, the plain one-block-per-thread arm had to match mibz2 0.4.0 at 4 to 9 threads, where they run the same plan. It did: every one of those four intervals spans 1.

**The outcome.** Lazy letters were 8.4% slower at 4 threads, as their extra instructions predict. At 10 threads they were 8.1% faster, with an interval of 6.5% to 9.8%. The rule's case is met. Against mibz2 0.4.0, which is what a user ran then, the figures by thread count are:

| Threads | 4 | 6 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 12 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Wall time, lazy ÷ 0.4.0 | 1.086 | 1.033 | **0.958** | **0.892** | **0.949** | 1.018 |
| 95% interval | 1.070–1.102 | 1.019–1.048 | 0.936–0.980 | 0.875–0.909 | 0.933–0.966 | 0.986–1.051 |
| Processor time, lazy ÷ 0.4.0 | 1.106 | 1.059 | 0.959 | 0.885 | 1.106 | 1.546 |
| What mibz2 0.4.0 runs | a block per thread | a block per thread | a block per thread | a block per thread | 3 teams of 3 | 3 teams of 3 |

At 8 and 9 threads lazy letters are faster and use less processor time as well. At 10 the comparison is with the teams. Teams were chosen there because, on this machine, one block per thread had been 4% slower than the teams at ten threads ([the earlier run](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6900029992>)). With lazy letters, one block per thread is 5.1% faster than the teams instead, at 10.6% more processor time. At 12 threads, two threads share some cores. No change in wall time was detected there, and processor time rose by 55%.

**Memory, measured as the whole process's peak.** One block per thread holds ten blocks' state at once, and teams hold only three. At 10 threads the teams peaked at 73 MB. One block per thread peaked at 191 MB with the current kernel and 186 MB with lazy letters. Lazy letters cut the rebuild's working memory, but a plan that decodes ten blocks at once still uses far more memory than one that decodes three.

**The fourth arm: rules written past the cache.** The induction writes each new word's description, a *rule*, and never reads it back; the writer reads the rules afterwards. Writing them with non-temporal stores, which bypass the cache, saves cache space without changing the amount of memory. At 10 threads no difference was detected (1.011, interval 0.985 to 1.037). At 4 threads it was 2.6% slower. That idea stays closed.

## 4\. Why would fewer bytes help only with many threads?

On one thread, the cache holds a block's working state comfortably, and the processor's time goes on instructions. That is why lazy letters lose at 4 threads: they do more work, and the memory they save was not in short supply.

With a block per thread, each thread's state competes for the one shared cache. A rough calculation shows the scale. A Wikidata block that Cells handles has about 56,600 letters on average. At 35.6 bytes a letter, the rebuild touches about 2.0 MB besides its output. Ten threads together touch about 20 MB, the size of the i9's whole last-level cache. At 22.0 bytes a letter, it is about 1.2 MB a block and 12 MB for ten. This is arithmetic on averages, not a measurement of the cache. The output buffers and the decoder's other stages also use the cache, and not all of a block's state is in use at the same moment.

The measurement that supports contention is the pattern across thread counts. If the extra instructions were the only effect, lazy letters' ratio against the current kernel would be about the same at every count. Instead it falls as threads are added, from 1.084 at 4 threads to 0.919 at 10. The rule asked whether the 10-thread ratio was below the 4-thread ratio round by round. It was in all ten paired rounds (sign test, p = 0.002). At 12 threads, where hardware threads share cores, the ratio against the current kernel falls further, to 0.852. Cache misses were not counted in this run. So this is evidence from timing that memory per core costs time at high thread counts, not a direct observation of the cache. It doesn't say which part of the memory system is the limit: the cache's capacity, the misses themselves, or the bandwidth to main memory. Hardware counters, or runs designed to separate them, would.

## 5\. What comes next?

**Accepting the processor time.** At 10 threads, lazy letters use 10.6% more processor time than the teams. mibz2's release rules send any rise over 10% to the maintainer, and he accepted it. The extra processor time mattered only as a sign of contention for the cache, and the wall time fell.

**In 0.5.0.** mibz2 0.5.0 uses lazy letters for one block per thread [from 8 threads up, and the current kernel below](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/452>), chosen by one constant in the decoder's thread plan. The old kernel stays selectable, so the two can be compared at the same commit. A run at the release, on the i9 from 4 to 20 threads, confirms the switch point under [a rule fixed before it](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6904285481>). It also decides whether one block per thread should replace the teams at more thread counts. A move into counts above the 10 cores, where threads share a core, goes back to the maintainer with the figures.

**A better order of steps.** Lazy letters still take Cells' order, always at the right-hand end, and the pool's peak is that order's width. Other orders build the same rules while finishing letters sooner. The [order census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/437>) found that taking the steps that need no new bookkeeping first, the *free* steps, brings the median width on Wikidata from 0.318 to 0.107 of the runs. Newer simulations, [in review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/446>), choose each step by how much it changes the width. One that still prefers free steps peaks at 0.077 of the runs, and one that puts the change in width first at 0.058. These are counts from a simulator, not a kernel. They also have a cost the counts leave out: lazy letters read the untouched letters as two streams from the right-hand end, and any other order needs letters that neither front has reached yet. [Priced against the kernel's own bytes](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6904481722>), that cost decides it for now. The slots are under a third of what lazy letters touch, and the index any other order needs adds about 8 bytes a letter, so no order cut the kernel's bytes by the quarter the rule asked. Orders that read only near the two streams, which would need no index, are still being counted. The same run will also measure how much slower a block is at 10 threads than at 1, for each kernel, which says how much of the high-thread penalty memory still accounts for.

**What changes in how memory cuts are judged.** Lazy letters failed their own instruction limit and still won where it matters for many threads. Earlier memory cuts were rejected because they cost instructions at 1 to 4 threads. From now on a memory cut is judged by its peak live memory per block and by wall time at 8 to 10 threads.

Since 0.5.0, lazy letters are the default kernel for one block per thread from 8 threads up.

The chain, in short, runs like this. The rebuild needs only a third of the slots Cells lays out. A kernel that keeps only those cuts the working memory by 38%, at 28% more instructions. With few threads that is a loss. With ten threads sharing one cache it is a gain, enough for a block per thread to beat the teams. When threads share a cache, the bytes a block keeps can matter more than the instructions it runs.

---

Its results bundle: [`run-20261115T233002Z.tar.gz`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/ccd052c04b80ac5e2c12dcc3d76ff0042cd8f267/memory-lever/run-20261115T233002Z.tar.gz>), with `summary.txt` (against mibz2 0.4.0), `summary-workers.txt` (against one block per thread) and `lever.txt` (round by round).
- The production plan and the follow-ups: [the team channel, 15 November](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6903395401>) and [again](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6903426694>).
- Background: [the width of an induction](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/index.md>) and [the free closure of an induction](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-free-closure/index.md>).

# The free closure of an induction: where free steps come to rest

The steps that cost mibz2 no bookkeeping can be taken in any order and still meet at one end point, now proved to belong to the block itself.

15 November 2026 · 13 min read · [Research result](<#5-what-is-proved-and-what-is-counted>)

[The width of an induction](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/index.md>), the previous post, looked at mibz2's experimental decoder for bzip2. It found that the decoder can hold about a third as much at its busiest moment if it takes its *free steps* first. A free step is a step of the rebuild that erases one boundary between pieces of the block and creates none. That post also reported that the free steps always reach the same end point, whatever order they run in. This post is about that end point: why the order doesn't matter, how it was proved and checked, and what it allows a decoder to do.

**The recap.** bzip2 sorts the rotations of each block and stores the last byte of each, the *last column*; each sorted rotation is a *row*. To decode, mibz2 follows a map called LF from row to row, reading one byte per move, which spells the block out backwards. A *run* is a stretch of equal bytes in the last column, and LF moves each run's rows together, as one interval. [A new way back from the BWT](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) introduced Cells, the decoder that works on those intervals instead of on rows. Each of its *steps* cuts some rows out of the map, and lets the interval whose rows used to land there jump straight over them. The code calls each interval a *letter*, and the bytes its jump reads, in text order, its *word*. A step happens at a *coincidence*: a boundary where one letter's rows end and another letter's landing place ends too. Every letter starts with a one-byte word, and when the last step is done, a word spells the whole block.

**The width post in brief.** The *width* of a rebuild is the most letters with a word longer than one byte that it holds at once. Cells always steps at the right-hand end of the map. Its width is about 0.32 r at the median on Wikidata, where r is the number of runs in the block. Taking free steps first cuts that to about 0.08–0.11 r. On every block, the peak stayed within the number of letters left once the free steps run out.

**The theorem.** Take free steps in any order until none is left. You always reach the same letters, with the same words, after the same number of steps. The one exception is a cycle of the map that closes completely during the free steps. It takes no further part, and two orders can leave it in different places, with its word rotated. No real block closes its cycle that early.

**Why it matters.** Call the state where the free steps run out the *free closure*. Because the order doesn't matter, it is a property of the block, not of the algorithm that found it. On the 233 large blocks of the Wikidata benchmark it leaves **0.185 r letters** at the median, and takes **0.896 r steps** to reach. Those are counts, and they are now facts about each block: no cleverer order of free steps can change them. The proof is by hand, and a program checked its every case on 10.7 million pairs of steps, with no exception.

**What it allows, and what it doesn't yet.** A decoder may take free steps in whichever order is cheapest to find. Free steps on different letters may go to different threads and still meet at the same state. So one block's rebuild can be split between threads, and it is proved to stay correct. No such decoder has been built or timed.

[Section 1](<#1-what-does-one-step-do>) works one free step on a four-byte block. [Section 2](<#2-does-the-order-matter>) takes its two free steps in both orders. [Section 3](<#3-why-does-it-hold-for-every-block>) gives the proof's shape, and [section 4](<#4-how-was-it-checked>) the machine check. [Section 5](<#5-what-is-proved-and-what-is-counted>) separates what is proved from what is counted. [Section 6](<#6-what-could-a-decoder-do-with-it>) says what a decoder could do with it, and [section 7](<#7-what-is-still-open>) what is open.

## 1\. What does one step do?

Suppose you want to compress the four bytes `abac`. Their four rotations, sorted, are `abac`, `acab`, `baca` and `caba`, so the last column is `cbaa`. It has three runs, `c`, `b` and `aa`, so the rebuild starts with three letters. Call them Y, Z and X:

| Letter | Its rows (top) | LF sends them to (bottom) | Word |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Y, the run `c` | row 0 | row 3 | `c` |
| Z, the run `b` | row 1 | row 2 | `b` |
| X, the run `aa` | rows 2–3 | rows 0–1 | `a` |

The figure draws each letter twice. The top strip shows where its rows sit in the last column. The bottom strip shows where LF sends them, and the shaded band joins the two. The numbers above the strips count boundaries between rows, so boundary 4 is the end of row 3.

One free step on the column of `abac`

Computed by a program that steps the column exactly as the checker in section 4 does; not drawn by hand. Top strip: each letter’s rows. Bottom strip: where LF sends them. Each box shows the letter and its word. Grey boxes are rows the step has cut.

Two things end at boundary 4. In the top strip, X's rows 2–3 end there. In the bottom strip, so does Y's landing place, row 3. That makes boundary 4 a coincidence, and a step can be taken there. Y's one row lands on row 3. Row 3 belongs to X, which sends it on to row 1. So row 3 is only a stopover on Y's way. The step cuts row 3 out, and Y now jumps from row 0 straight to row 1. Its jump reads `c` and then `a`. LF runs backwards through the text, so in text order its word grows at the front: `c` becomes `ac`, which is indeed in `abac`. X loses the row, and keeps row 2, which still goes to row 0.

The step is free because of where Y now lands. Its new landing place starts a boundary at 1 in the bottom strip. The top strip already had a boundary at 1, between Y's row and Z's. So the step erased the boundary at 4 and created none that wasn't already there. A step that is not free, a *paid* step, would put a boundary at a new place, and some later step would have to remove it. A step between two letters of the same length is always free, since one letter simply takes over the other's place.

## 2\. Does the order matter?

The column has a second free step available at the start. At boundary 2, Z's row 1 ends in the top strip. X's landing place, rows 0–1, ends there in the bottom strip. Here Z is the shorter piece, so row 1 is cut. X's row 3 used to land on row 1 and go on with Z to row 2. Now it jumps straight to row 2. That one row splits off from X and becomes Z, with the word `ba`.

Both steps are free, and they share a letter: X. Each one changes X's length, so neither leaves the other's starting point untouched. The figure takes them in both orders.

Two free steps, two orders, one state

Computed, as in the figure above. Green lines mark the free steps available in each state. Taking the step at 4 first and then the one at 2, or the other way round, gives the same letters, places and words: X at row 2 with the word `a`, and Y at row 0, landing on row 2, with the word `bac`.

The left path makes Y's word `ac` first, and then the step at 2 puts `b` in front of it. The right path makes Z's word `ba` first, and then the step at 4 hands Y the whole of `ba` followed by its own `c`. Either way, Y ends with `bac` and X with `a`. In the language of rewriting systems this is a *diamond*, or a *square*. Two steps leave one state, and one step on each side brings them back together.

The tiny block goes on to its end. After the diamond, X and Y form a cycle of two letters, each landing on the other's rows, and one more free step closes it whole. A program tried every one of the twelve orders in which the free steps of `cbaa` can be taken. All twelve take three steps. Each ends with one letter whose word is `abac`, `acab`, `baca` or `caba`: the same cycle, read from different starting points. That is the exception in the theorem. On a four-byte block the whole text closes during the free steps. On the Wikidata blocks, where the free steps stop at about a fifth of the runs, none did. bzip2 stores with every block the row of the original rotation, which says where to start reading in any case.

## 3\. Why does it hold for every block?

Two diamonds on one example prove nothing in general, so the proof goes through a classical result. Newman's lemma, from 1942, says that a system of rewriting steps has a single end point from every start if two things hold.

1. **Termination.** No sequence of steps goes on forever. Each free step erases one boundary and creates none, and a block has only finitely many boundaries, so this holds.
2. **Local confluence.** Whenever two steps are available in the same state, there is some way to continue from each of them so that both reach the same state again.

Termination is what lets the second, local condition decide the global answer. Without it, two paths could keep diverging forever, each step of the way looking reconcilable.

So the proof takes any two free steps available together, at boundaries c₁ and c₂, and shows that they can be brought back together. It rests on two facts. First, a free step touches only its own two letters, and removes no boundary but its own. Second, the place where a free step's shorter letter lands always lies strictly inside the longer letter's interval, so it can never be the other step's coincidence. Then two steps relate in exactly one of four ways:

1. **No letter in common.** Neither step changes anything the other reads, so each stays free after the other, and the two orders give the same state.
2. **One shared letter X**, whose rows end at c₁ and whose landing place ends at c₂. This is the case of `abac`, and the hard one. Each step can be one of three kinds: the letter above wins (it is longer), the letter below wins, or the two are equal. That gives nine combinations of kinds for the pair. The table below shows which can happen.
3. **One shared letter, the other way round.** This is case 2 with the steps' names swapped.
4. **Both letters shared.** The two letters form a cycle of two, and either step closes it. The two results differ only in where the closed letter lies and in which rotation of its word it holds. That is where the theorem's exception comes from.

In case 2, X is the upper letter at c₁, over Y, and the lower letter at c₂, under Z. Rows compare X with Y at c₁, and columns compare X with Z at c₂:

| At c₁ ↓ / at c₂ → | Z longer | X longer | equal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **X longer than Y** | impossible | square; Y and Z equal | impossible |
| **Y longer than X** | square | impossible | square |
| **equal** | square | impossible | square |

The four impossible combinations fail for one reason. For both steps to be free, one of them would have to land strictly inside a letter's interval in the other strip, where no boundary can be. The five squares are each written out in both orders in the proof, and each reaches the same letters, places and words. `abac` is the square in the top row. X has two rows, so it is longer than Y and longer than Z. Y and Z have one row each, as forced.

A last detail settles the step count. Every square closes with one step on each side, and the closing cycles of case 4 need none. So any two complete paths of free steps have the same length, not only the same end point.

## 4\. How was it checked?

The proof was checked against a program that steps every short column exhaustively. It covers every column over 2 letters up to length 14, and likewise over 3, 4 and 5 letters up to lengths 9, 7 and 6. On each column it follows three random complete paths of free steps. At every state along every path, it takes every ordered pair of free steps available, classifies it by case and kinds, and runs both orders. It checks that the two orders reach the same state. In case 4 it checks instead that one step closes a cycle, and that the two agree up to its rotation.

The results, over 10.7 million ordered pairs. *Same state* counts the pairs whose two orders reach the same state, and *closed cycle* the case 4 pairs that agree up to rotation:

| Alphabet, longest | Pairs | Same state | Closed cycle (case 4) | Exceptions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 letters, 14 | 4,322,196 | 4,042,698 | 279,498 | 0 |
| 3 letters, 9 | 3,434,430 | 3,129,050 | 305,380 | 0 |
| 4 letters, 7 | 1,741,700 | 1,531,570 | 210,130 | 0 |
| 5 letters, 6 | 1,164,480 | 991,358 | 173,122 | 0 |

In every alphabet, the combinations of kinds that occur are exactly the ones the proof allows. Case 2 shows its five squares, and case 3 their mirror images. Case 4 shows only the three combinations that close a cycle. None of the four impossible combinations was ever seen. Rerun for this post, the program gives the same counts.

Before the proof, a separate count had run the free steps to the end under different orders and compared the results directly. No two orders ever disagreed, on 404,677 short columns under ten orders each, or on the 233 Wikidata blocks and four blocks of prose. On every real block the results were equal exactly, with no closed cycle to allow for.

## 5\. What is proved and what is counted

The research record labels each statement as proved by hand, or counted (exact for the data it ran on, but no more). For this result:

- **Proved:** free steps in any order reach one end point, up to closed cycles. A program checked every case on 10.7 million pairs of steps.
- **Proved:** every complete path of free steps has the same number of steps.
- **Proved:** after the free closure, no step adds a letter.
- **Counted, on all 233 Wikidata blocks under three orders:** before reaching the closure, free-first orders never held more long words than the closure has letters.
- **Counted, on all 233 Wikidata blocks:** the closure leaves 0.185 r letters and takes 0.896 r steps, at the median.

The two counted figures are now properties of each block, so their spread across blocks is a spread across text, not across algorithms. The Wikidata corpus is an extract of a Wikidata dump. Its blocks here are the 233 with at least 65,536 rows, and each figure is divided by that block's own r.

The free closure of each of the 233 Wikidata blocks

Counted, not timed. Each dot is one block, stacked where values coincide; hover a dot for its block and value. Upper: letters left when no free step remains, as a share of the block’s runs, from 0.075 r to 0.281 r. Lower: the free steps taken to get there, from 0.79 r to 0.99 r. Each block gave the same two numbers under every order tried, as the theorem says it must.

## 6\. What could a decoder do with it?

Everything in this section is a consequence of the theorem, not a measurement.

**Any order is correct.** The cost of a free-first decoder is in finding its free steps. It needs a worklist of ready steps. An earlier count priced that worklist at about 150 instructions a run on one thread, against 115 for Cells' sweep from the right-hand end. The theorem says a decoder may take its free steps in whatever order its worklist yields them: a stack, a sweep, or batches. The end point, the step count and the bound on width hold for all of them. So a worklist can be designed for speed alone.

**Splitting one block between threads.** Two free steps on different letters commute. So free steps can be handed to different threads, and they reach the same state as on one thread. The condition is that each thread's step writes only its own two letters' records. That is a way to split one block's rebuild that is proved correct, which matters for how mibz2 uses many cores. It decodes blocks in parallel either with each thread on a block of its own, or with teams of threads sharing a block. On a 10-core Intel desktop at ten threads, a block per thread took 1.040 times the teams' wall time in the latest run. Its 95% interval is 1.019 to 1.061 ([the run's report](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6900029992>)). The working explanation, not yet measured directly, is that each thread's live state competes for the shared cache. A smaller live state, and a proved way to share one block's free steps, both bear on that.

**A bound fixed by the block.** After the closure, no step adds a letter. So from the closure on, a decoder that takes free steps first never needs more live letters than the closure has. That is about 0.19 r on Wikidata, against the r slots Cells reserves today. Before the closure, the bound held on every block counted.

No free-first decoder has been built. A first decoder that keeps the untouched one-byte letters implicit, and writes a letter only when its word first grows, has been built with Cells' right-end order and is being measured. None of it has been timed yet.

## 7\. What is still open?

**Which steps does the closure leave?** Only equal steps remove letters, and a block's rebuild makes exactly r − 1 of them. So the closure's letter count is 1 plus the number of equal steps that can only become ready after a paid step. Saying which equal steps those are, from the block's runs, would describe the closure without running it. That is the next question.

**One block on many cores, by rounds.** A different route also reaches the end of a rebuild: repeatedly cut the map down to the rows where runs branch, all at once. It collapses a whole Wikidata block to between 2 and 560 letters in 5 to 18 such rounds, and the work within a round is independent. Cells' right-end order, by contrast, has a chain of 93 dependent rounds at the median. As counted, though, each round walks every row it removes, so its work grows with the rows rather than the runs, which is the cost Cells exists to avoid. Whether a round can be computed on letters and their words alone has not been tested.

**Is width a cutwidth?** The width post links width to the *cutwidth* of a graph: line up its vertices, cut between any two, and count the edges that cross. Whether the width of a rebuild is exactly a cutwidth of the block's cycle of rows, bundled by runs, is a conjecture.

The record of the rounds count is [\#440](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/440>).
