# The width of an induction: how much it must hold at once

Taking the steps that cost no bookkeeping first would let mibz2 rebuild a block while keeping about a third as much in memory at its busiest moment.

15 November 2026 · 14 min read · [Research in progress](<#5-what-would-it-mean-for-mibz2>)

[A new way back from the BWT](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) introduced Cells, mibz2's experimental way of undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) that bzip2 applies to every block. Two posts this week cut the memory Cells uses: [hand-me-down slots](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-slot-recycling/index.md>) and [one copy of each interval's details instead of two](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-bottom-slots/index.md>). This post asks a different question about the same memory: how much of it does the mathematics actually need at any one moment?

**The recap.** bzip2 sorts the rotations of a block and stores the last byte of each, the *last column*; each sorted rotation is a *row*. To decode, mibz2 follows a map called LF from row to row, reading one byte per step, which spells out the block backwards. A *run* is a stretch of equal bytes in the last column, and LF moves each run's rows as one shifted interval. Cells works on those intervals instead of on rows. Each step deletes some rows from the map and lets one interval jump straight over them. That interval now stands for more than one byte of text. When one interval is left, it stands for the whole block. The code calls each interval a *letter*, and the text it stands for its *word*. At the start there is one letter per run, and every word is one byte long.

**What width is.** At any moment of the rebuild, some letters still have a one-byte word. Each of those is an untouched piece of an original run. Its length, place and byte can be read off the list of runs, so in principle it needs no record of its own. Only the letters whose word has grown longer than one byte are new information. Call the most of those alive at once the **width** of the induction (the rebuild's sequence of steps), W. It is counted, like everything here, as a share of r, the number of runs in the block. Cells today writes a slot for every one of the r letters before its first step, and keeps r slots throughout.

**What was found.** Width depends on the order in which the steps are taken, by about three times.

- **Cells' order** always takes its step at the right-hand end of the map. At its busiest it holds about **0.32 r** letters with long words. That is the median over the 233 large blocks of the benchmark's Wikidata corpus, an extract of a Wikidata dump.
- **Taking the free steps first** brings that peak down to about **0.08 to 0.12 r**, depending on what is done when no free step is ready. It is **0.11 r** if the rest follows Cells' own order. A *free* step is one whose bookkeeping creates no new boundary between intervals ([section 3](<#3-does-the-order-of-steps-matter>) shows one). The same order also takes about 20% fewer steps: 1.46 r instead of 1.84 r.
- **The free steps have a fixed end point.** Taken in any order until none is left, they always reach the same state, in the same number of steps. That is now proved ([\#438](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/438>)). It follows that a kernel could take free steps in whichever order suits it, or share independent ones among threads. On Wikidata the end state has about 0.19 r letters, and no free-first order's peak exceeded it on any block.

How many letters the rebuild holds, per 100 runs of a Wikidata block

Counted, not timed: medians over the 233 blocks of at least 65,536 rows in the Wikidata corpus. Amber and green are the peaks of letters whose word is longer than one byte, under Cells’ right-end order and under free steps first. Grey is the number of letters, long words or not, left once the free steps run out.

**What is classical and what is new.** The steps are Rauzy–Veech induction, a 1979 construction in the theory of dynamical systems, and the words are the return words that theory has studied since[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#lopez][^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#fick]. Counting the most words alive at once is not part of it. "Width" in this sense is not a standard term of that theory. It is a new measure, and its closest relatives are graph measures such as *cutwidth*[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#layout]: line a graph's vertices up, cut the line between any two, and count the edges that cross. [Section 2](<#2-why-do-only-the-long-words-count>) says where the line between old and new falls.

**What this is not.** These are counts, not timings. They come from one family of text, Wikidata's JSON, with four blocks of prose beside it. Prose gains less: the right end peaks at 0.37 r and free-first orders at 0.21 r. The link to cutwidth is a conjecture. Above all, no decoder that takes free steps first has been built or timed. Finding the free steps needs a worklist, which an earlier count priced at about 150 instructions a run against the right-end sweep's 115. Whether the smaller state pays for that is the next question, not an answer here.

**Why mibz2 cares.** Width is how much state the rebuild keeps in memory. When every thread decodes a block of its own, those states share the processor's cache, and the threads contend for it. Less state per block leaves less for the cache to hold. At ten threads on a 10-core Intel desktop, a block per thread takes 1.040 times the wall time of threads working in teams (95% interval 1.019 to 1.061; [the run's report](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6900029992>)), so the margin is small. [Lazy letters](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-16-lazy-letters/index.md>) tested it: holding only the letters still in play, one block per thread beat the teams by 5% at ten threads, and mibz2 0.5.0 uses it from 8 threads up.

[Section 1](<#1-what-does-the-rebuild-hold-on-a-nine-byte-word>) works a nine-byte word by hand and draws its width. [Section 2](<#2-why-do-only-the-long-words-count>) says why only the long words count, and what is classical. [Section 3](<#3-does-the-order-of-steps-matter>) compares twelve orders of steps, and [section 4](<#4-how-narrow-can-a-free-first-order-be>) gives the bound and the theorem. [Section 5](<#5-what-would-it-mean-for-mibz2>) says what is open, and the [Compendium of Links](<#compendium>) lists the reading.

## 1\. What does the rebuild hold, on a nine-byte word?

Suppose you want to compress the word `possesses`. Its nine rotations, sorted, are its nine rows, and the last byte of each gives the last column `sspssseeo`. LF sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier in the text:

| Row | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Last column | s | s | p | s | s | s | e | e | o |
| LF | 4 | 5 | 3 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 0 | 1 | 2 |

The last column has five runs: `ss`, `p`, `sss`, `ee` and `o`. So the rebuild starts with five letters, each with a one-byte word.

Cells' order removes rows from the right-hand end, so the rows it still keeps are always a prefix, rows 0 to m − 1. Call m the *cut*. Each kept row's letter now jumps from that row along LF, through the removed rows, until it lands on a kept row again. Mathematicians call this the *first return* to the kept rows. The bytes read on the way, taken in text order, are the letter's word.

After four of its seven steps, Cells' order has cut the word at m = 4. The upper panel below draws that moment. Row 0, for example, reads `s` and goes to row 4. Row 4 is removed, so the path goes on, and reads `s` there. It goes on to row 7, also removed, and reads `e`. Then it returns to row 1, which is kept. Read in text order, its word is `ess`. Rows 1 and 3 likewise have the words `oss` and `es`. Row 2 goes straight to row 3, so its word is still the one byte `p`. Three letters out of four have long words, and that is the most this order ever holds on this word: its width is 3.

The same word at the busiest moment of two orders of steps

Worked by hand and checked by a script. Each box is a row with its byte of the last column; dashed boxes are removed rows. Each arc is one LF link, with its arrow at the row it goes to. Under each kept row is its letter’s word: green where it is longer than one byte. Green arcs are the paths that build those words. The removed rows matter only as places a path passes through.

The lower panel takes the free steps first, and section 3 explains what makes a step free. It removes rows 0–2 first, not the right-hand end. It never holds more than two long words at once, so its width is 2. It also finishes in six steps, not seven. The counts after each step, from the start to the single letter at the end, are:

| Order | After each step | Width | Steps |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Right end | 1, 2, 2, **3**, **3**, 2, 1 | 3 | 7 |
| Free steps first | 1, **2**, 2, 2, 2, 1 | 2 | 6 |

Each long word can be checked in `possesses`: `ess`, `oss` and `es` occur in it, and so do `se` and `po`. The steps themselves are animated, on the three-byte word `aab`, in [the post that introduced Cells](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/#1-rebuilding-aab-in-two-steps>).

## 2\. Why do only the long words count?

A letter whose word is one byte is a row, or a few adjacent rows, that LF sends straight to another kept row. It is a piece of an original run, cut shorter. Its first row, its length and the row it goes to all follow from the run it lies in. A decoder could leave it implicit and compute it when needed. A letter with a long word is different: where it jumps, and what it reads on the way, are the result of the steps taken so far.

The long words can be read from the arcs. A kept row has a long word exactly when its LF link crosses into the removed rows. Under Cells' order, the research record proves where each long-word letter begins ([the census entry](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/f03b0fdca71abf45133d0720802ff3d3255a567a/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-15-width.md>)). It begins either at a run's first row whose link crosses the cut, or at the kept row whose path through the removed rows passes a run's first row. So the width counts crossings of the cut, bundled by runs.

Width, stated formally and read on `possesses`

**1\. First return.** Let \\(T\\) be a bijection of a finite set \\(X\\) and \\(D \\subseteq X\\). The first return of \\(T\\) to \\(D\\) is \\(T\_D(x) = T^{\\tau(x)}(x)\\), where \\(\\tau(x) \\ge 1\\) is the least power that lands back in \\(D\\).

Here \\(T\\) is LF on the rows \\(\\{0, \\dots, n-1\\}\\), and \\(D\\) is the set of kept rows: \\(\\{0, 1, 2, 3\\}\\) at the right end’s busiest moment.

**2\. Letters and words.** \\(T\_D\\) is a translation on each of finitely many intervals of \\(D\\). These are the letters \\(\\mathcal{A}\_t\\) after step \\(t\\). The word \\(w\_t(a)\\) of a letter is the sequence of bytes read in its \\(\\tau\\) moves, in text order, and \\(|w\_t(a)| = \\tau\\).

Here Row 0 takes \\(\\tau = 3\\) moves, through rows 4 and 7, and reads `ess`. Row 2 takes one move, to row 3, and reads `p`.

**3\. Width.** Over the steps of one order, \\(W = \\max\_t \\bigl|\\{a \\in \\mathcal{A}\_t : |w\_t(a)| \> 1\\}\\bigr|\\). The number of steps is \\(S\\).

Here Right end: \\(W = 3\\), \\(S = 7\\). Free steps first: \\(W = 2\\), \\(S = 6\\). On Wikidata: \\(W \\approx 0.32\\,r\\) against \\(0.11\\,r\\), and \\(S \\approx 1.84\\,r\\) against \\(1.46\\,r\\).

Definitions 1 and 2 are the classical first-return construction behind Rauzy–Veech induction, for which Viana’s survey (2006) is an introduction, in a finite, discrete form: rows instead of a real interval. Definition 3 is the research record’s, not the literature’s.

**What is classical.** Inducing a map on a smaller set by its first return[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#viana], and shrinking the set step by step, is Rauzy's induction (1979)[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#rauzy]. Veech (1982)[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#veech] developed its dynamical and geometric meaning. Writing the orbit segments as words, so that each step becomes a substitution such as \\(a \\mapsto ab\\), was made explicit by Lopez and Narbel (1999)[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#lopez]. Choosing a different path of steps, instead of always cutting at one end, is the *branching* Rauzy induction of Dolce and Perrin (2017)[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-induction-width/#dolce].

**What is new.** That theory studies orbits, return times, invariant measures and coding. It does not ask how many words a computation must hold at once along a path of steps. Its usual setting also keeps the number of intervals fixed. In mibz2's discrete setting, a step between two letters of equal length deletes one, so the count falls as the rebuild goes on. The closest established ideas come from graph layout. Line up a graph's vertices in some order and cut the line after each prefix. The *cutwidth* of that order is the most edges any cut crosses, and *vertex separation* counts boundary vertices instead of edges. The least vertex separation over all orders equals the graph's *pathwidth* ([Kinnersley 1992](<https://doi.org/10.1016/0020-0190(92)90234-M>)). Width here is the same kind of quantity, with the block's cycle of rows as the graph, its edges bundled into runs, and the kept rows as the prefix. Whether W is exactly a cutwidth is a conjecture. A stand-in for it, the runs crossing the cut upwards, peaks at 0.28 r over the 233 blocks. The exact count on 29 of them peaks at 0.31 r.

**A trap in the terms.** The geometric side of the theory draws each interval as a rectangle, in *zippered rectangles*, and calls the interval's length its rectangle's width. That is λ, a length, not a count of live words, and has nothing to do with W.

## 3\. Does the order of steps matter?

Every step of the rebuild happens where a letter's interval in the map and another letter's landing place end on the same row. The research record calls such a row a *coincidence*. Cells' order always takes the coincidence at the right-hand end. Any other coincidence can be taken instead. Every order rebuilds the block, and the research record proves that the orders counted here build the same rules, the block's Lyndon tree ([the Cells post's §5](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/#5-fewer-steps-by-a-different-order>)). They differ in when each rule is made, and so in how long each letter lives.

A step is *free* when it creates no new boundary: either the two letters have the same length, so one is deleted, or the shorter one's rows land where a boundary already is. In `possesses` at the start, the first free step is at the boundary after row 2. The letter on row 2, `p`, ends there, and so does the place where the letter on row 8, `o`, lands. Both are one row long. The step deletes row 2, and the letter on row 8 now jumps straight to row 3, where `p` went, reading `po`. A step that is not free, a *paid* step, splits an interval somewhere new, and a later step must remove that new boundary. Each free step removes one boundary and adds none.

The census ran twelve orders on every Wikidata block of at least 65,536 rows, and on the four prose blocks. Every final word was checked to be a rotation of its block ([the orders entry](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/f03b0fdca71abf45133d0720802ff3d3255a567a/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-15-width-orders.md>); its [summary](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/f03b0fdca71abf45133d0720802ff3d3255a567a/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-15-width-orders/summary.txt>)). When no free step is ready, a free-first order needs a rule for the paid step: the right end, the largest cell, the smallest, or the leftmost. A *cell* is the stretch of rows a step removes. The orders "told from links" decide whether a step is free from the neighbouring letters alone, as a kernel would have to.

Width under twelve orders of steps, Wikidata and prose

Counted, not timed, from the census’s summary. Each dot is the median width over 233 Wikidata blocks, the line runs from the narrowest block to the widest, and the diamond is the median over 4 prose blocks. Steps are the Wikidata median, per run. Hover a row for its exact figures.

The orders fall into two groups. Every order that takes free steps first has a median width between 0.080 and 0.124 r. Every other order lies between 0.27 and 0.35 r, apart from one that takes only the equal-length free steps first, at 0.171 r. The step count does not decide it. "Free first, else the smallest cell" takes 2.26 r steps, the most of any order, and still has a width of 0.108 r. What sets the width is how soon a letter is closed once it can be.

Per block, the right end's width is 2.04 to 4.84 times that of "free first (told from links), else the right end". The median is 2.98. The right end's exact width here, 0.318 r, is a little above an earlier count of 0.311 r. That count sampled 31 cuts per block on 29 blocks, so it could only miss the peak.

## 4\. How narrow can a free-first order be?

Run free steps until none is left, and call the state reached the *free closure*. On Wikidata it leaves 0.185 r letters at the median (0.075 to 0.281 r), after 0.896 r steps.

**The closure is the same whatever the order (proved).** Free steps taken in any order until none is left always reach the same letters, the same words and the same number of steps. The one exception is a cycle of the map that closes completely within the free steps. Such a cycle takes no further part, and the orders can differ only in which rotation of its word it holds. No real block closes its cycle that early. The proof shows two things. Free steps always stop, since each removes a boundary. And any two free steps available together can be taken in either order and reach the same state again, which it checks case by case. By Newman's lemma, that is enough for a unique end point. A machine check of 10.7 million pairs of steps on short columns found no exception ([\#438](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/438>), [its entry](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/e8c5705082a5908916bd8804d8e11c6bb9cbdbc0/docs/journal/monodromy/2026-11-15-free-closure-confluence.md>) and [log](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/145#issuecomment-6900899853>)). So the closure is a property of the block, like a normal form, and its size is a number the block determines.

**The closure bounds the width (proved after it, counted before it).** After the closure no step adds a letter, so the long words alive can never exceed the closure's letters again. Before the closure, the census found the same on every one of the 233 blocks, under three free-first orders. The width was at most 0.74 of the closure's letters, and 0.45 to 0.57 of them at the median. On a nine-byte word the bound can fail. Every step of `beekeeper` is free, so its closure is one letter, but its width under free steps first is at least 2. On real blocks the bound held without exception.

**What follows for a kernel (a consequence, not a measurement).** A kernel may take free steps in whichever order is cheapest for it, and still reach the same state. Free steps that touch different letters can be given to different threads, and they still reach that state. And a kernel that takes free steps first would need live state no larger than the closure, about 0.19 r letters. On these blocks its peak is nearer 0.11 r.

## 5\. What would it mean for mibz2?

None of this is in the decoder. A kernel that used it would keep letters with one-byte words implicit, reading them from the run list, and write a letter only when its word first grows. Under Cells' order it would hold about 0.32 r letters at most; with free steps first, about 0.11 r. Cells today holds r.

The cost is in finding the steps. Cells sweeps the right-hand end, where the next step is always known, and that sweep is also why its cache misses are only first touches ([\#397](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/397>)). A free-first kernel needs a worklist of ready steps instead. An earlier count priced such a worklist at about 150 instructions a run against the sweep's 115, on one thread. Two things have changed in its favour since. The steps fall from 1.84 r to 1.47 r, and the state to hold falls by about three times. Whether that pays at ten threads sharing one last-level cache is a timing question, and it is the next one for the kernel work.

Three questions remain open:

- **Cutwidth.** Is W exactly a cutwidth of the block's cycle, and can it be bounded from the run lengths alone? This is a conjecture.
- **Speed.** Is any kernel that takes free steps first faster than Cells? Nothing has been timed.
- **The closure without the steps.** An equal-length step says that every row of one letter goes next to the other: a forced adjacency. Genome assemblers join every forced adjacency at once when they compact a graph's unbranched paths, called *unitigs*. That compaction does not depend on any order. The conjecture is that the free closure is exactly that compaction. If so, it could be computed without simulating any step.

The width census and the order census are merged ([\#435](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/435>), [\#437](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/437>)). The confluence proof, [\#438](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/438>), is in review.

# Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

mibz2 tracks each run of equal bytes in two orders, and a run's entry in the second shrinks from 20 bytes to 8 by pointing to the first.

15 November 2026 · 12 min read · [Research result](<#6-how-much-faster-is-the-decoder>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.3.3](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-3-3>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#033---2026-11-15>))

[The last post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-slot-recycling/index.md>) followed Cells, one of mibz2's ways of undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) that bzip2 applies to each block of text. Cells does not decode one position at a time. It works on *intervals*: at the start, each interval is a run of equal bytes in the BWT's output, which the decoding moves as a whole to a new place. In the block `aab`, for example, the BWT's output is `baa`, and its intervals are one `b` and two `a`s. As the decoding goes on, intervals shrink and join.

Cells tracks every interval in two orders at once: where it lies, and where it is moved to. The code calls an interval a *letter*, and keeps a small record for it, a *slot*, in each of the two orders. Until now, both slots held the same two pieces of information: the interval's length, and a reference to the text it stands for. This post shows why the second copy was never needed, and what mibz2 0.3.3 gained by removing it.

## The idea in brief

Cells works through each of its two orders from one end, the order's *front*, so each front reaches every letter once. That gives every letter two visits, one per order.

**A letter's length and text reference are read only at the first of its two visits, and a short proof shows that the top order's slot always holds them at that moment.** Call the two orders top and bottom. If the top front reaches the letter first, the details are read from the top slot, and the bottom slot's copy is never used. If the bottom front reaches it first, the top front has not got there yet, so the top slot has not been touched and still holds the details. Either way, the top slot is enough.

So 0.3.3 keeps the details in the top slot only. The bottom slot shrinks from 20 bytes to 8: it keeps its link to its neighbour, and a pointer to the letter's top slot. Here is what that gives, and what it costs:

- **30% less memory for the slots**, counted on the benchmark's Wikidata corpus, and about a fifth less for the rebuild's whole working area, which also holds the text itself.
- **A faster decoder at four threads on both test machines, and at one and two threads on one of them.** On a 10-core Intel desktop, 0.3.3 took 6.5% less wall time than 0.3.2 at four threads, and about 4% less at one and two. On the project's 2-core CI runner it took 4.2% less at four threads; at one and two threads the change was within noise.
- **The price is an extra memory read.** On 53.7% of slot reads, the processor must read the bottom slot to learn where the top slot is before it can read the details. That could have cost more than it saved; on these measurements it did not.
- **More threads can now usefully decode a block each.** mibz2 switches from giving each thread a block of its own to having threads share blocks at a fixed thread count, the *team threshold*. After 0.3.3, a block per thread was faster up to nine threads on the desktop, and the change moving the threshold to ten threads is released in mibz2 0.3.4. That shift is the work of every improvement to Cells so far, not of this change alone.

[Section 1](<#1-why-does-every-letter-need-two-slots>) builds the two orders from a three-byte example, and shows why each letter needs a slot in both. Sections 2 to 4 show the new layout, why it is safe, and what the extra read costs. Sections 5 to 7 give the measurements: memory, speed, and the team threshold.

## 1\. Why does every letter need two slots?

bzip2 compresses each block of text after rearranging it with the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). The BWT sorts all the rotations of the block and keeps the last byte of each, which tends to put equal bytes next to each other. To decompress, the decoder must undo that rearrangement.

Take the block `aab`. Sorted, its rotations are `aab`, `aba` and `baa`. The BWT's output is their last bytes: `baa`. Sorting the output gives `aab`, the first bytes of the same rotations. Number the sorted rotations 0 to 2 and call them *rows*. The decoder knows which byte of the output goes with which byte of the sorted list, because equal bytes keep their order. The output's first `a` is the sorted list's first `a`, its second `a` is the second, and `b` is `b`. This pairing is called LF, and following it from row to row spells out the block backwards, one byte per step. From row 0, read `b` and go to row 2; read `a` and go to row 1; read `a`. That is the usual way to decode, one position at a time.

LF has a pattern that Cells uses. The output `baa` falls into *runs* of equal bytes: one `b`, then two `a`s. Within a run, consecutive rows go to consecutive rows, so each run moves as a whole. Name the runs B and A. In the output they lie in the order B, A. Where LF sends them, in the sorted list, they lie in the order A, B.

The block `aab`: the same two runs, in two orders

Worked by hand: the BWT’s output `baa` above, the same bytes sorted below. Each band joins a run to the rows LF sends it to. The bands cross because the runs swap places: B, A on top; A, B below.

Each run is one of the intervals, a letter. The code calls the runs as they lie in the output the **top order**, and the same runs where LF sends them the **bottom order**. There are still only two letters, A and B; each has a place in both orders. Each letter has a *length*, the number of rows it covers, and a *word*, the text those rows stand for. At the start, A covers two rows and its word is `a`; B covers one row and its word is `b`.

Cells rebuilds the text by shrinking this picture rather than walking it. Each step compares the letters at the two fronts, the right-hand ends of the orders: here, A on top and B below.

Rebuilding `aab` in two steps

Worked by hand, as in the earlier post on Cells. Each box is a letter, as wide as the rows it covers, with its word inside..

Each word can be checked against the LF walk above. From row 0, B's path reads `b`, then `a`, before it reaches a row that is still kept: that is `ab` read forwards. The full cycle reads `aab`. [The earlier post on Cells](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) works this example through as an animation. On a real block, a letter that covers one row can have a word thousands of bytes long. A step's result is called a *cell*, and it takes the place of the letters it was made from. Long words are not copied: a word made by joining two others is stored as a *rule* that names those two.

To find the letter at each front, and a letter's place in the other order, Cells keeps each order as a chain of slots, one per letter. Before 0.3.3, both of a letter's slots had the same five 4-byte fields:

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Previous slot | the slot before this one in its order |
| Length | how many rows the letter covers |
| Word length and word offset | the letter's text reference: how many bytes of text its word has, and where they, or its rule, are kept |
| Partner | the same letter's slot in the other order |

The letter's length and its word's length are different things: in the example, B's length is one row after step 1, while its word is two bytes long. The previous-slot link and the partner say where a slot sits: next to which slot in its own order, and opposite which slot in the other. The length and the word describe the letter itself, and they were stored in both slots.

## 2\. What changed in 0.3.3?

The top slot stays exactly as it was. The bottom slot keeps only two fields: its previous-slot link, and its partner, which is the letter's top slot. The length and word are no longer stored there; when the bottom front needs them, it reads them from the top slot.

A letter’s two slots, before and after 0.3.3

The layout as `src/cells.rs` documents it, drawn to scale: every field is a 4-byte offset or length, and the word is its length and offset, read together as one 8-byte load. Amber marks the fields the bottom slot used to repeat. After the change, the bottom slot’s second field is the letter’s top slot, and the green arrow is the read that replaces the copy.

Each letter used to cost 40 bytes of slots, 20 in each order. It now costs 28: 20 on top and 8 below. That is 0.700 of the slot memory before, and it matches the count on the Wikidata corpus exactly ([section 5](<#5-how-much-memory-does-it-remove>)).

## 3\. How do we know the top slot still has the details?

Cells reuses slots as it goes: when a letter is used up, its slots are overwritten with the new cell. So a fair worry is that the bottom slot might point at a top slot that has already been overwritten.

The answer is a property of Cells' steps. It is proved in the project's [analysis of which stored bytes are ever read](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/410>), a write-up still under review, which also checked it against every slot read on the Wikidata corpus without a single exception:

**A letter's details are read once, at whichever front reaches it first. Its slot in the other order is then overwritten by the letter's own first cell without being read.**

That leaves two cases.

Whichever front reaches a letter first, its top slot is intact

Conceptual: one letter, X, with a slot in each order. Each order is read from its right-hand end, its front; each step uses up letters at the fronts, so the fronts move leftwards. Green marks where X’s length and word are read. In both cases they are read once, and from the top slot.

In the first case, the top front reaches the letter first. The details are read straight from the top slot. The bottom slot's old copy would never have been read, because the letter's first cell overwrites it.

In the second case, the bottom front reaches the letter first. The top front has not reached the letter yet, so nothing has overwritten its top slot. Cells follows the bottom slot's partner field, reads the length and word from the top slot, and goes on.

So at the one moment the details are read, the top slot holds them in both cases. In the first, it is the slot being read; in the second, the top front has not yet reached it. That is why the copy can always live on the top side, without knowing in advance which front will arrive first. The bottom slot cannot go altogether, though. The bottom order still needs its own chain of links, and each letter still needs a way to its place in the other order. Those two fields are the slot's own state, not copies.

## 4\. What does the saving cost?

Before, reading a bottom slot gave everything at once. Now the processor reads the bottom slot to learn which top slot to go to, and only then can it read the length and word. The second read's address depends on the first read's result. Such a *dependent load* cannot start until the first has finished, which limits how much work the processor can overlap.

The change's own count on the Wikidata corpus found 32.0 million slot reads, of which 17.2 million come from the bottom front. So **53.7% of slot reads gain a dependent load**.

This had gone wrong before. An earlier layout with [16-byte slots](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/398>) added one dependent load per letter read and cost 4.4% more processor time at four threads. Three things make this one cheaper:

1. The bottom slot's link and partner arrive together in one 8-byte read.
2. The top slot it leads to is the one the same step writes the new cell into, so that memory is needed anyway.
3. The decoder already *prefetches*: it asks for a slot several steps before it reaches it, so the slot is in cache by then. It now reads the bottom slot 12 steps ahead and prefetches the top slot it names. Six steps ahead, it prefetches the letter's text too.

The extra read is also off the chain that finds the next slot: the next bottom slot's address comes from the same 8-byte read as the partner. The change was therefore expected to pay mostly when several threads compete for memory, and to break about even on one thread.

## 5\. How much memory does it remove?

The count is from [the change's pull request](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/414>), on the benchmark's Wikidata corpus. Of its 431 blocks, Cells takes 196; the others go to mibz2's ordinary decoder.

The rebuild’s memory, before and after, on the Wikidata corpus

Counted, not timed: \#414’s count over the 196 blocks Cells decodes, at one thread. The working area is the slots, the words’ text and the rules; only the slots shrink.

The slots shrink by exactly the 40-to-28 ratio. The whole working area also holds the words' text and their rules, and those are unchanged. So the working area shrinks by less: it takes 21.6% fewer cache lines, and the median block's goes from 2.90 MiB to 2.27 MiB.

## 6\. How much faster is the decoder?

Two measurements compare 0.3.3 with 0.3.2, decoding the same Wikidata corpus. Both are paired: each round runs both versions in alternation, and the figure is the change in wall time with its 95% interval.

Wall time, 0.3.3 against 0.3.2, decoding the Wikidata corpus

Measured: 10 paired rounds on each machine. The CI runner is an AMD EPYC 9V45 with 4 virtual CPUs on 2 cores; the desktop is an Intel i9-10900K with 10 cores. Each mark is the change in wall time with its 95% interval; green where the interval excludes no change. The desktop’s record gives ratios, 0.3.2 ÷ 0.3.3: 1.043, 1.040 and 1.070 at one, two and four threads; the chart shows each as the share of wall time saved, 1 − 1/ratio.

The desktop's record gives ratios of wall times, which the chart converts to the project's usual form, the share of wall time saved. At four threads the desktop also used about 7% less processor time.

The desktop run also measured 8, 10, 12, 16 and 20 threads, and nothing changed there. 0.3.3 shares blocks between threads from six threads up, so at those counts it did not use Cells at all. As expected, the gain is clearest with several blocks decoding at once. The desktop shows a gain at one and two threads too; the CI runner does not.

## 7\. Why does this move the team threshold?

mibz2 decodes a file's blocks in parallel in one of two ways. With few threads, each thread takes a block of its own and decodes it with Cells; these threads are *workers*. With many threads, threads share blocks in *teams*, which split one block's work between them. Teams cost more coordination, but they keep fewer blocks in memory at once. The thread count where mibz2 switches from workers to teams is the **team threshold**. It was set at six threads on 28 October, and not measured again until after 0.3.3.

Every saving in a worker's memory makes it cheaper to run more workers side by side. So after 0.3.3 the project measured the two directly on the same desktop: a block per thread against the shipped decoder, which used teams from six threads.

A block per thread against teams, on the Intel desktop after 0.3.3

Measured: 10 paired rounds on the i9-10900K, the shipped decoder (teams from six threads; at ten, three teams of three) against a block per thread. Below 1 the workers are faster; green where the 95% interval is wholly below 1. The record gives no interval at ten threads. CPU is the same ratio for processor time; the last column is peak memory, teams → workers.

Workers were faster at every count from six to nine threads, taking 13.9% less wall time at six and 3.6% less at nine. At ten threads the shipped decoder runs three teams of three, so nine threads decode blocks, and it stays ahead: workers took 15.3% longer. Workers also use more memory, since more blocks are in flight: 133 to 188 MB at six to nine threads, against 65 to 81 MB for the teams. At nine threads they used 12.4% more processor time. That is over the project's 10% limit on extra processor time for such a move, so the choice went to the maintainer. He chose workers below ten threads, where each thread has a physical core of its own, and teams from ten. [The change](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/425>) is released in mibz2 0.3.4.

This run measures Cells as it is now, after every improvement since 0.3.0, including [slot recycling](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-15-slot-recycling/index.md>) in 0.3.2 and the smaller bottom slots in 0.3.3. It shows that today's Cells beats the teams up to nine threads on this machine. It does not show how much of the shift is due to the bottom slots alone: no run compared the two layouts at six to nine threads.

## What it teaches

The change began from a question about the algorithm, not the machine: when is each stored value actually read? Once the answer was "exactly once, at the first front to arrive", the layout followed. It is not ordinary deduplication, because the slots are rewritten all the time. What makes it safe is that the one remaining copy is guaranteed to be intact at the one moment it is read.

The same question applies wherever a structure keeps two views of the same item. If only one view's copy is ever read, the other can become a pointer. Whether that pays then depends on the extra read, which here was cheap because the memory it reaches was needed anyway.

---

*The change and its count are in [mibz2 PR \#414](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/414>). The CI and desktop measurements are in the [0.3.3 release notes](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md>), and the desktop run's record is [\#420](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/420>). The team threshold's change is [PR \#425](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/425>).*

# Reduce, reuse, recycle: hand-me-down slots for every fragment of text

Each new text fragment takes over the slot its finished neighbour just vacated, so mibz2 touches 30% fewer slots and needs up to 15% less memory.

15 November 2026 · 13 min read · [Research result](<#7-what-the-benchmarks-tell-us>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.3.2](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-3-2>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#032---2026-11-15>))

One of mibz2's ways of rebuilding a block of bzip2 text works on fragments of it: pieces of the output, each standing for a stretch of the block. It keeps the bookkeeping for every fragment in a small record called a slot, 20 bytes holding the fragment's length, where its text is kept, the slot before it, and its partner slot in a second arrangement of the same fragments. When one fragment is finished, its slot is free just as the next fragment needs one, and mibz2 now hands it over instead of taking fresh memory.

## The idea in a nutshell

**Slot recycling makes mibz2 faster by recognising that, whenever its [Cells algorithm](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-10-rauzy-veech-reconstruction/index.md>) needs somewhere to put a new piece of information, another piece of information has just finished using its space.**

Previously, the algorithm reserved a fresh memory slot for the new piece, leaving the old slot behind. Now, it reuses the old slot immediately.

This is a deceptively simple improvement. The algorithm still performs the same mathematical operations and reconstructs exactly the same bytes. What changes is how much memory it needs to touch while doing so.

On the Wikidata benchmark, slot recycling:

- **Eliminates 29.7% of the slots previously touched** during Cells induction.
- **Reduces peak decoder memory usage by 10–15%.**
- **Makes four-thread decoding 1.7% faster** in the initial paired CI benchmark, without a statistically established speed change at one or two threads.

The important insight is that **we aren't making the mathematics smaller; we're making its physical representation more efficient**. We're taking advantage of something already guaranteed by the mathematics: one slot's useful lifetime ends just as another begins.

And because mibz2's performance is sensitive to memory contention, eliminating unnecessary memory accesses can matter more than shaving a few arithmetic instructions.

## 1\. Why memory matters so much to mibz2

To understand why this is worthwhile, we need to understand what mibz2 spends much of its time doing.

Bzip2 compression uses the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), which rearranges a block's bytes into an order that's easier to compress. Decompression must reverse that rearrangement and recover the original text.

The conventional way to reverse the BWT is to construct a permutation describing where each position leads, then follow that permutation to reconstruct the original sequence.

This is computationally awkward for modern processors.

Each step tells the processor where to look next. The address of the following memory access often cannot be known until the current access completes. If the relevant data isn't in cache, the processor may spend much of its time waiting for memory.

mibz2's original approach was to interleave several independent traversals, allowing the processor to have multiple memory operations in flight.

But the Cells algorithm takes a more radical approach.

**Instead of reconstructing the text by following the permutation one position at a time, Cells exploits the structure of the permutation itself.**

The inverse-BWT permutation has a special organisation: it acts as a translation over intervals corresponding to runs of equal bytes. That allows it to be treated as a finite interval-exchange system.

Using a form of Rauzy–Veech induction, Cells repeatedly simplifies this system. Each simplification combines pieces of the permutation and builds a compact description of the text they represent.

Eventually, the algorithm has enough information to reconstruct the original block.

This can require dramatically fewer algorithmic steps than following every position in the original permutation.

However, those steps have their own cost: Cells must maintain a changing representation of the intervals, their relationships and the words they represent.

That representation is where slot recycling operates.

## 2\. What is a slot?

Imagine that Cells is manipulating a collection of pieces, which we'll call *letters*. Each letter represents an interval together with a word: the sequence of output bytes associated with it.

The induction maintains two orderings of these letters, corresponding to the two sides of the interval exchange.

We can think of them as:

- The **top order**, describing one arrangement of the pieces.
- The **bottom order**, describing the corresponding arrangement on the other side.

These aren't two complete copies of the decompressed text. They're two linked arrangements of the same mathematical pieces.

Each letter has a slot in each order.

Here are both orders for a handful of letters, with each letter's two slots joined:

Two linked orders of the same letters

Conceptual: five slots of each order. Each letter has a slot in both orders, in a different arrangement, so the partner links cross. The induction reads each order from its front, where A and B are, and follows the links to the slots before them.

A slot is a small record in memory. In the implementation shipped before this change, it occupies **20 bytes**, containing the information needed to navigate and manipulate the induction:

| Information | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Previous-slot link | Finds the next piece when advancing through the order |
| Interval length | Describes how many positions the piece covers |
| Word reference and length | Identifies the text represented by the piece |
| Partner-slot reference | Connects its position in one order to the corresponding position in the other |

The slot's five fields, as the code lays them out:

A slot is 20 bytes: five 4-byte fields

The layout as `src/cells.rs` documents it, unchanged by \#408. Every field is a 4-byte offset or length. The table above lists the word’s length and offset as one row, since the induction reads them together. Below, to scale: 64 bytes hold three whole slots and part of a fourth.

The algorithm walks through these two orders, repeatedly taking pieces from their fronts.

As it goes, it transforms letters into *cells*: finished pieces whose words can be represented by literal bytes or by references to previously constructed words.

The slot records are the bookkeeping that makes this transformation possible.

And because there can be many millions of cells, even seemingly small inefficiencies in this bookkeeping accumulate.

## 3\. How an induction step works

At each step, Cells considers two pieces, A and B, one encountered through each order.

Suppose their remaining interval lengths are:

- A has length **7**.
- B has length **3**.

The algorithm takes the smaller length, 3, and constructs a cell representing the corresponding portions of A and B. Its word is constructed by concatenating their associated words.

Now B has been exhausted, while A still has 4 positions remaining.

Conceptually:

One unequal step: B ends, A goes on

Conceptual: the example in the text. Each square is one position. The green squares become the cell; A’s other four stay A’s. B ends, so its slot in the bottom order is free from this step on.

This is a simplification of the mathematical operation, but it captures the essential event.

One letter continues. The other finishes.

If A and B had equal remaining lengths, both would finish together. The interesting case for slot recycling is when their lengths differ, because the surviving letter will eventually produce another cell.

**That next cell needs a place in the other ordering.**

Previously, the algorithm reserved a fresh slot for it.

But notice what has just happened: the other letter, B, has finished. Its position at the front of that ordering is no longer needed.

This is where the opportunity appears.

## 4\. The old approach: make room for a future cell

The original implementation was designed to avoid complicated rearrangements of the linked orders.

When a letter continued after an unequal-length step, Cells *promised* it a slot for its next cell. That slot came from additional space reserved beyond the original letters' slots.

This was straightforward and efficient in an important sense: it avoided having to move existing letters or reorganise the whole structure.

But every promise of a fresh slot extended the set of memory locations the induction would eventually touch.

Across millions of steps, many of these fresh locations occupied cache lines that had not previously been used.

Touching a new cache line may require the processor to bring it into cache, obtain write ownership and eventually evict or write back dirty data. These costs become particularly significant when several workers are competing for limited cache capacity.

Meanwhile, some original slots were already dead.

The algorithm had information about their former contents in registers, yet their memory locations were being left unused.

We had **space becoming available at precisely the moment we were reserving more space elsewhere**.

## 5\. The new approach: recycle the slot that just died

Slot recycling changes how that promised location is chosen.

Returning to our example, B has just finished and A continues.

Previously, the next cell cut from A would receive a fresh slot in the bottom order.

Now it receives **B's former front slot in that same order**.

Here is the bottom order after B ends, before and after the change:

The bottom order after B ends: where A’s next cell goes

Conceptual, after the step in the last figure. Slots are in memory order; the front is the slot the induction reads next, and it moves left as the induction goes on. The promised slot is linked in as the slot before A’s cell, so A’s next cell will be read there. The cell is also written to B’s slot in the top order (not drawn). When A ends instead, the same happens in the top order, with A’s front slot.

This isn't an ordinary memory allocator discovering that a block of memory happens to be free. The algorithm knows, from the structure of its induction, that this specific slot has become available.

The implementation has three crucial facts in its favour.

**First, the finished letter cannot be encountered again through that old front slot.** It was the last remaining piece at the front of its order, and no surviving link leads back to the slot as that letter.

**Second, its corresponding position in the other order has already been replaced by the newly constructed cell.** The pairing and links have been updated to refer to the new structure.

**Third, everything the current operation still needs from the finished letter has already been read into registers.** The old slot's memory contents are no longer required.

Together, these facts establish that the slot can safely take on a new purpose.

Instead of advancing a cursor into fresh storage, the algorithm remembers the location of the slot it just consumed.

In the Rust implementation, two offsets, `fa` and `fb`, track the front slots in the respective orders. When one letter finishes and the other continues, the appropriate front offset becomes the promised location.

The surrounding induction remains essentially unchanged. It creates the same cells, constructs the same words and ultimately produces the same decompressed output.

The difference is that its slots are **reused rather than continually extended**.

That is why the name *slot recycling* is so precise.

## 6\. How much does this save?

The builder, the agent that implemented \#408, [counted](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/408>) what happened across the 196 Wikidata blocks admitted by Cells in the benchmark corpus.

The result was substantial:

| Quantity | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Slots touched | 31,547,362 | 22,181,734 |
| Fresh slots required | 9,365,628 | 0 |
| Reduction in touched slots | — | **29.7%** |

The same counts, drawn to scale:

Slots the induction touches, over the 196 Wikidata blocks

Counted, not timed: \#408’s census of the benchmark’s Wikidata corpus, the 196 of its 431 blocks that Cells admits. The letters’ slots are two per letter, one in each order. Every unequal cell used to take one fresh slot.

Each avoided slot is 20 bytes.

Across those blocks, this corresponds to approximately **187 million bytes of slot storage no longer touched**.

That doesn't mean precisely 187 million fewer bytes travel to DRAM. Cache lines, write allocation, reuse and eviction behaviour determine actual memory traffic.

But it does mean that millions of distinct slot locations are no longer needed.

The allocation can shrink too. The previous implementation reserved room for additional slots based on its cell budget. The new one needs only enough room for the original letters' slots in each order.

And this matters beyond the amount of memory allocated.

### Why fewer slots can mean faster decoding

Modern CPUs don't fetch arbitrary individual bytes directly from main memory for ordinary cached accesses. They work with cache lines, commonly 64 bytes.

A 20-byte slot is small, but enough slots spread over millions of addresses occupy a substantial working set.

When several workers decode different blocks simultaneously, each has its own induction state competing for space in the shared cache.

If their combined working sets are too large, useful data gets displaced, and later accesses may have to retrieve it from slower levels of the memory hierarchy.

Slot recycling attacks that problem directly.

The slot being recycled has only just been read, so its cache line may already be resident. The fresh location it replaces might otherwise require a first touch of a different line.

The immediate benefit isn't fewer mathematical operations. It's **less memory to keep resident and fewer distinct places to access**.

This explains why the change is especially interesting for parallel decoding.

## 7\. What the benchmarks tell us

The initial paired CI benchmark measured the complete decoder, rather than just timing the induction function in isolation.

For Wikidata:

| Threads | Wall-time change | Peak memory change |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | \+0.5% | −9.7% |
| 2 | −0.2% | −12.5% |
| 4 | **−1.7%** | **−14.6%** |

The same run with its intervals, and the memory in megabytes:

The decoder on Wikidata, with and without slot recycling

Measured: \#408’s paired CI bench, 10 rounds on one runner (Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, 4 CPUs on 2 cores), the whole decoder on the Wikidata corpus. Left: the change in median wall time with its 95% interval across the rounds; green where the interval excludes no change. Right: peak resident memory, each a reduction the bench reports as beyond noise. The `records` corpus was 3.4% slower at 4 threads in the same run.

The four-thread wall-time improvement had a reported 95% confidence interval of −3.3% to −0.1%.

That is a modest but positive result on this runner. The one- and two-thread changes were indistinguishable from noise.

The memory reductions are much larger.

This pattern is consistent with the intended mechanism: reducing the working set matters more as concurrency increases.

But we should be precise about what has been established. The CI runner isn't the i9 workstation. It has a different cache hierarchy and different core-sharing conditions. The benchmark demonstrates a benefit on the tested machine, but it doesn't yet establish how much slot recycling helps the i9's known [concurrency plateau](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/index.md>).

[A later paired run on the i9](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6894519106>), a 10-core desktop, shows the gain growing with the number of Cells workers: no change at one or two threads, 4% less CPU at four, and 5% faster wall time at five (interval 4.7% to 6.1%). Peak memory was lower at every thread count from one to five, and nothing changed at six or more threads, where mibz2 uses its team path instead of Cells.

There's also a secondary-workload caveat: the `records` corpus showed a four-thread regression in the same CI run. Correctness was preserved, but the change is not a universal speedup.

The valuable thing is that **the memory reduction is substantial without requiring additional expensive computation**. The extra bookkeeping is minimal, with the front positions already available to the induction.

## 8\. Why this is different from field elision

The terminology initially caused some confusion because two related research ideas both used the word *elision*.

[MONODROMY](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/410>), the team's mathematics agent, investigated whether individual fields inside existing slots could be left unwritten or reconstructed from other information.

It found that approximately 25.5% of the induction's stored bytes were never subsequently read, and that certain mathematical identities could account for an even larger fraction.

That sounds promising, but almost every redundant field shares its 64-byte cache line with live information.

If you stop writing a redundant field while leaving the surrounding record layout unchanged, the processor may still need the same cache line.

So removing those field writes doesn't necessarily make the working set smaller.

**Slot recycling solves a different problem.**

It doesn't selectively remove fields from slots. It removes the need for whole additional slots.

That means entire ranges of memory no longer need to be touched, and the required working set can genuinely shrink.

This distinction is central:

- **Field elision:** store less information in the same locations.
- **Slot recycling:** use fewer locations to store the necessary information.
- **Equal-cell elision:** avoid constructing some cells altogether, replacing those operations with another reconstruction mechanism.

The third idea remains a separate mathematical opportunity. Slot recycling hasn't implemented it or disproved it.

## 9\. Why the change is safe

Reusing memory in an algorithm implemented with unchecked offsets and `unsafe` Rust deserves particular care.

The crucial correctness obligation is not merely that a slot *looks* unused. It must be guaranteed that no later operation still needs its old contents.

The proof comes from the induction's ordering invariant: the consumed front slot has no surviving references as the old letter, and its necessary values have already been captured.

The implementation also narrows the slot regions to the exact number of original letters. Tests check that promised slots stay inside those regions, including cases where there is no spare room beyond them.

The builder compared the new induction against the original on exhaustive small inputs, accounting for the fact that physical slot offsets legitimately differ. The resulting words, rules, state and output agree.

The broader decoder tests, CRC checks and Miri validation passed before the change was merged.

This is important because the optimisation changes where state lives, **not what that state means**.

The resulting decoder remains subject to the same correctness requirements as before.

## 10\. What this teaches us about improving mibz2

Slot recycling is a good example of why sophisticated algorithms still benefit from careful attention to mundane-looking implementation details.

The Cells algorithm is built on substantial mathematics: interval exchanges, Rauzy–Veech induction, permutation structure and compact representations of words.

That mathematics makes it possible to avoid much of the work required by conventional inverse-BWT traversal.

But the mathematical abstraction also introduces a physical representation: linked orders, slots, words and rules.

The performance of the resulting program depends on both levels.

An algorithm can have excellent asymptotic properties and still spend too much time managing its intermediate state.

Conversely, improving that state management can produce worthwhile gains without changing the underlying algorithm at all.

The particularly elegant aspect of slot recycling is that it derives the optimisation from a structural property of Cells itself.

**At every unequal induction step, the continued letter needs a future slot just as the exhausted letter releases one.**

Recognising that relationship removes a whole category of unnecessary memory use.

The successful change therefore sits at the intersection of mathematics and systems programming: a proof about object lifetimes becomes a more efficient memory layout, which becomes a measurable improvement in the complete decoder.

It also points towards the next questions.

MONODROMY has identified a possible asymmetric layout with 20-byte top slots and 8-byte bottom slots. That could mean up to 25% fewer induction lines (an estimate made before recycling), although it introduces an additional dependent load on many accesses. It remains unmeasured, and the earlier [failed 16-byte layout](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/398>) is a warning that compactness isn't automatically speed.

Meanwhile, measuring how memory traffic scales after slot recycling can help determine whether Cells is becoming competitive at higher thread counts.

Those are separate experiments. Slot recycling has already justified itself on its own evidence.

## The essential insight

**Slot recycling makes mibz2 better by exploiting the fact that the useful lifetime of one memory record ends exactly when another needs its space.**

It doesn't eliminate the induction steps. It doesn't change the text reconstruction. It doesn't require a more elaborate parallel algorithm.

It simply stops the program from touching memory it never needed to touch.

That's why a change that is small in code can remove nearly a third of the induction's touched slots — and why understanding the mathematical structure of an algorithm can yield practical improvements well beyond the mathematics itself.

---

*Implementation and evidence: [mibz2 PR \#408](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/408>), [merged on 15 November](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/commit/381fbf1d5f76a7f1689e7546d254b7e2bfd664b6>). For the distinction between slot recycling and field elision, see [MONODROMY's analysis, PR \#410](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/410>).*
