[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/#bijective]: Hideo Bannai, Dominik Köppl and Zsuzsanna Lipták, [*A Survey of the Bijective Burrows–Wheeler Transform*](<https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/01oasics/oasics-vol131-manzinis-festschrift/html/OASIcs.Manzini.2/OASIcs.Manzini.2.html>) drops.dagstuhl.de

    (2025), in the Festschrift for Giovanni Manzini, OASIcs 131. The cyclic BWT and necklace enumeration.

[^/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/#orbit]: Nathaniel K. Brown and Ben Langmead, [Orbit](<https://github.com/drnatebrown/orbit>) github.com

    A library implementing move-structure variants; not a verified drop-in replacement for mibz2's Rust T-vector.

← [The mathematical structure of inverse-BWT navigation](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/index.md>)

# Technical appendix: the mathematics of inverse-BWT navigation

This appendix holds the derivations and side results that [the main post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/index.md>) leaves out to keep its argument moving. It uses the main post's notation, defined in [its section 2](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/#2-why-does-every-run-give-one-shift>): the last column \\(L\\) of length \\(n\\), its \\(\\sigma\\) distinct characters, their frequencies \\(n\_c\\) and starting rows \\(C(c)\\), the first column \\(F\\), rank, select, the next-row map \\(\\Psi\\), and the run count \\(r\\). Equations (1) to (8) are the main post's. This appendix numbers its own (A1) onwards. Its sections can be read in any order. Nothing here has been built or measured in mibz2.

## 1\. Navigation as a select problem

Equation (1) of the main post gives a data-structure reduction:

\\\[ \\boxed{\\text{arbitrary }\\Psi\\text{-query}\\longrightarrow\\text{character-bucket identification}+\\text{select query}.} \\\]

Given a row \\(i\\), determine the unique character \\(c\\) satisfying

\\\[ C(c)\\le i\<C(c)+n\_c. \\\]

Then compute

\\\[ \\Psi(i)=\\operatorname{select}\_c(L,i-C(c)). \\\]

This decomposes the problem into familiar operations on indexed sequences. It means mibz2 can, in principle, represent navigation without storing an explicit successor for every row.

### 1.1 The output character is already known

A T-vector entry conventionally combines the navigation destination and a character. But the character associated with row \\(i\\) is simply \\(F\[i\]\\), which is determined entirely by the histogram:

\\\[ \\boxed{F\[i\]=c\\quad\\text{whenever}\\quad C(c)\\le i\<C(c)+n\_c.}\\tag{A1} \\\]

For a byte alphabet, the character sequence in table order has at most 256 constant intervals and at most 255 changes.

This is an unconditional property of the inverse-BWT table, regardless of whether \\(L\\) is repetitive. **Consequence for mibz2:** the character field does not need to be independently stored in every navigation entry. It may be amortised over groups of rows, or recovered from a bucket directory. This is an important distinction from run-based compression: character sharing remains useful even for highly irregular BWT input.

### 1.2 An exact bound on mixed-character records

Suppose we divide table rows into fixed groups of \\(g\\) consecutive positions. Because \\(F\\) contains only \\(\\sigma\\) character buckets, there are at most \\(\\sigma-1\\) bucket boundaries. Every group containing more than one output character must contain at least one of those boundaries. Thus

\\\[ \\boxed{N\_{\\mathrm{mixed}}\\le \\sigma-1.}\\tag{A2} \\\]

For compact30, \\(g=30\\) and \\(\\sigma\\le256\\), so \\(N\_{\\mathrm{mixed}}\\le255\\). At maximum block size,

\\\[ N\_{\\mathrm{groups}}=\\frac{900{,}000}{30}=30{,}000. \\\]

Hence at most 255 groups can require exceptional handling *solely because their output characters differ*: at most 0.85% of groups, affecting at most 7,650 rows.

This does not limit the number of RAW groups caused by widely separated navigation destinations, but proves that character-bucket crossings are a small, alphabet-bounded issue. **Practical gain:** output-character sharing can be designed around a strict worst-case bound; it does not depend on how repetitive the source text is.

## 2\. Consecutive entries and sparse corrections

### 2.1 The exact count of consecutive navigation entries

Inside any character bucket, define

\\\[ \\Delta(i)=\\Psi(i+1)-\\Psi(i). \\\]

Because the bucket represents increasing occurrence positions, \\(\\Delta(i)\\ge1\\). Moreover, \\(\\Delta(i)=1\\) if and only if the two corresponding occurrences of that character are adjacent in \\(L\\). A run of length \\(m\\) contributes \\(m-1\\) such pairs, giving

\\\[ \\boxed{\\\#\\{i:\\ i,i+1\\text{ lie in the same character bucket},\\ \\Psi(i+1)=\\Psi(i)+1\\}=n-r.}\\tag{A3} \\\]

This is an equality, not an average-case statement. There are \\(n-\\sigma\\) adjacent pairs within buckets, so the exact fraction with consecutive destinations is

\\\[ \\boxed{f\_{\\mathrm{consecutive}}=\\frac{n-r}{n-\\sigma}.}\\tag{A4} \\\]

This gives the BWT run count a precise interpretation as a measure of local navigation irregularity.

Two concepts must not be conflated:

- The number of *descents* of \\(\\Psi\\) (positions where \\(\\Psi(i)\>\\Psi(i+1)\\)) is at most \\(\\sigma-1\\).
- The number of failures of consecutive translation **within buckets** is exactly \\(r-\\sigma\\).

The second quantity is relevant for run-based navigation compression.

### 2.2 A sparse-correction representation

Let the positions of character \\(c\\) in \\(L\\) be

\\\[ x\_{c,0}\<x\_{c,1}\<\\cdots\<x\_{c,n\_c-1}. \\\]

Define excess gaps

\\\[ g\_{c,j}=x\_{c,j}-x\_{c,j-1}-1,\\qquad j\\ge1. \\\]

Then

\\\[ \\boxed{\\Psi(C(c)+k)=x\_{c,0}+k+\\sum\_{j=1}^{k}g\_{c,j}.}\\tag{A5} \\\]

Within runs, excess gaps are zero. A positive excess gap occurs exactly when consecutive occurrences of \\(c\\) belong to different runs. The number of positive gaps is

\\\[ \\boxed{\\sum\_c\\\#\\{j:g\_{c,j}\>0\\}=r-\\sigma.}\\tag{A6} \\\]

Thus the navigation map can be described by one starting destination per character, the positions of \\(r-\\sigma\\) nonzero corrections, their magnitudes, and bucket boundaries.

The query becomes predecessor or prefix-sum over sparse corrections. This is mathematically equivalent to the interval representation, but suggests sparse bitvectors, indexed delta streams, or two-level directories.

**What we have gained:** an exact structural complexity parameter for the map. The important variable is principally \\(r\\), the number of BWT runs, rather than \\(n\\), descents, or Coxeter length (the inversion count, [section 7](<#7-what-does-the-permutree-thesis-contribute>)).

## 3\. Space bounds

### 3.1 Entropy of the stable-sort permutation

Fix the histogram \\((n\_1,\\ldots,n\_\\sigma)\\). The number of possible last-column sequences is

\\\[ M=\\frac{n!}{\\prod\_c n\_c!}. \\\]

There is a bijection between those sequences and permutations increasing within corresponding character buckets. An arbitrary member of the family requires at least

\\\[ \\boxed{B\_{\\min}=\\left\\lceil\\log\_2\\frac{n!}{\\prod\_c n\_c!}\\right\\rceil}\\tag{A7} \\\]

bits in a fixed-length representation. Stirling's approximation gives the leading term

\\\[ \\log\_2 M\\approx nH\_0(L), \\qquad H\_0(L)=-\\sum\_c\\frac{n\_c}{n}\\log\_2\\frac{n\_c}{n}. \\\]

For a byte alphabet \\(H\_0(L)\\le8\\). Thus the stable-sort permutation with fixed histogram contains at most approximately eight bits per row, generally less.

**This bounds representation information, not access latency.** A four-byte T-vector stores redundancy deliberately for cheap successor retrieval.

### 3.2 Elias–Fano gives a constructive representation

Every character bucket contains a strictly increasing sequence of positions. Elias–Fano encoding is designed for such sequences.

For character \\(c\\), a standard Elias–Fano representation uses approximately

\\\[ n\_c\\left\\lceil\\log\_2\\frac{n}{n\_c}\\right\\rceil+2n\_c \\\]

bits before indexing overhead. Summed over all characters,

\\\[ \\boxed{B\_{\\mathrm{EF}}\\lesssim2n+\\sum\_c n\_c\\left\\lceil\\log\_2\\frac{n}{n\_c}\\right\\rceil.}\\tag{A8} \\\]

For an approximately uniform byte distribution this is about \\(10n\\) bits, or approximately 1.125 MB for a 900,000-byte block, versus 3.6 MB for the T-vector.

Elias–Fano supports indexed access to elements without decoding all predecessors; theoretical constant-time access depends on suitable select indexing. It provides a formal alternative even when \\(r\\) is large. It does not exploit long runs as aggressively as a run-based representation, since its general bound depends on symbol frequencies.

### 3.3 A separate information bound from run count

Count length-\\(n\\) words over an alphabet of size \\(\\sigma\\) with exactly \\(r\\) runs. Choose positive run lengths in \\(\\binom{n-1}{r-1}\\) ways, the first character in \\(\\sigma\\) ways, and each subsequent character in \\(\\sigma-1\\) ways:

\\\[ \\boxed{N(n,r,\\sigma)=\\sigma(\\sigma-1)^{r-1}\\binom{n-1}{r-1}.}\\tag{A9} \\\]

The bits required to enumerate this broader family are

\\\[ \\boxed{B\_{\\mathrm{run}}= \\left\\lceil\\log\_2\\sigma+(r-1)\\log\_2(\\sigma-1)+\\log\_2\\binom{n-1}{r-1}\\right\\rceil.}\\tag{A10} \\\]

For \\(r\\ll n\\), this is \\(O(r\\log(n/r)+r\\log\\sigma)\\).

This counts all words with specified run count, not only valid BWT images or fixed-histogram words. It is an achievable representation-size benchmark for the larger family, not a tight bound for bzip2 blocks.

### 3.4 Two independent measures of compressibility

The two measures

\\\[ \\boxed{H\_0(L)}\\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad\\boxed{r} \\\]

answer different questions. Low entropy means concentrated character frequency; low \\(r\\) means few constant BWT runs. A block can have low entropy and many short runs, or high entropy and few long runs.

| Property | Mathematical implication | Relevant structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low \\(H\_0(L)\\) | Fewer stable-sort arrangements | Entropy-based sequence encodings |
| Low \\(r\\) | Few translated navigation intervals | Run descriptors and move structures |
| Small gaps between occurrences | Narrow destination spans | Base-plus-offset records |
| Small \\(\\sigma\\) | Few output-byte bucket boundaries | Shared-character headers |

There need not be one universally optimal compact representation.

## 4\. What the intervals say about compact30

mibz2's compact30 research ([Building a smaller bzip2 decoding table](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-04-compact30-constructor/index.md>)) stores thirty rows per 64-byte record, hence the name, with exceptional RAW records that hold full entries, and attempts to reduce the working set without sacrificing memory-level parallelism.

### 4.1 The ordinary-record condition

compact30 groups thirty consecutive rows into 64-byte records and uses a label transform

\\\[ \\varphi(i)=32\\left\\lfloor\\frac i{30}\\right\\rfloor+(i\\bmod30) \\\]

or

\\\[ \\boxed{\\varphi(i)=i+2\\left\\lfloor\\frac i{30}\\right\\rfloor.}\\tag{A11} \\\]

Two unused labels per group correspond to the record header. For a complete group \\(G=\[a,a+30)\\), ordinary-record conditions are a shared output character and labelled successor offsets fitting in 16 bits. Since \\(\\Psi\\) and \\(\\varphi\\) increase within a bucket, the endpoints suffice.

Ignoring special padding and sentinel cases:

\\\[ \\boxed{F\[a\]=F\[a+29\]} \\\]

and

\\\[ \\boxed{\\varphi(\\Psi(a+29))-\\varphi(\\Psi(a))\\le65{,}533.}\\tag{A12} \\\]

This bounds *encoded successor-label span*, not necessarily raw row-index difference. It captures monotonicity used by the existing builder.

### 4.2 Gap-based interpretation

Suppose the group lies entirely in bucket \\(c\\), with first destination \\(x\\) and last destination \\(y\\). Between the thirty occurrences,

\\\[ y-x=29+\\\#\\{j:x\<j\<y,\\ L\[j\]\\neq c\\}. \\\]

Therefore

\\\[ \\boxed{\\Psi(a+29)-\\Psi(a)=29+h,}\\tag{A13} \\\]

where \\(h\\) is the count of intervening non-\\(c\\) characters. The labelled span is

\\\[ \\begin{aligned} W={}&amp;29+h\\\\ &amp;+2\\left(\\left\\lfloor\\frac y{30}\\right\\rfloor-\\left\\lfloor\\frac x{30}\\right\\rfloor\\right). \\end{aligned}\\tag{A14} \\\]

Apart from bucket crossings, compact30 RAW groups arise from too many intervening characters among thirty occurrences. It is occurrence-gap arrangement, not absolute destination position, that matters.

### 4.3 Guaranteed ordinary groups

If a complete 30-row group lies inside one translation interval,

\\\[ \\Psi(a+t)=p+t,\\qquad0\\le t\<30. \\\]

The raw span is exactly 29, and the labelled span at most 31. The group is guaranteed to fit an ordinary compact30 record. Its offsets form a precomputable pattern, precisely the bulk-emission case in the existing constructor, where the builder writes a whole record from a precomputed pattern because one run of \\(L\\) fills the group.

### 4.4 Exact formula for pure groups

Let translation intervals be \\(I\_t=\[a\_t,b\_t)\\). For group width \\(g\\), the number of complete aligned groups contained in interval \\(I\_t\\) is

\\\[ G\_t=\\max\\left(0,\\left\\lfloor\\frac{b\_t}{g}\\right\\rfloor-\\left\\lceil\\frac{a\_t}{g}\\right\\rceil\\right). \\\]

Therefore

\\\[ \\boxed{G\_{\\mathrm{pure}}=\\sum\_{t=1}^{r}G\_t.}\\tag{A15} \\\]

For compact30,

\\\[ \\boxed{R\_{\\mathrm{pure}}=30G\_{\\mathrm{pure}}.}\\tag{A16} \\\]

This is computable from BWT run boundaries and character ranks without building the entire navigation table.

Every complete group not inside one translation interval crosses a boundary. There are at most \\(r-1\\) such boundaries, each inside at most one aligned group:

\\\[ \\boxed{N\_{\\mathrm{nonpure}}\\le r-1.}\\tag{A17} \\\]

The bound may be loose and non-pure groups can still be ordinary records. But when \\(r\\ll n/g\\), almost all complete groups are guaranteed pure.

### 4.5 Consequence for construction

BWT runs determine destination intervals. Record boundaries can be enumerated in row order, with endpoint spans found by sequential sweeps through run descriptors. Once runs are known, group classification can take

\\\[ \\boxed{O\\left(r+\\frac ng+\\sigma\\right)} \\\]

time without materialising every successor. A scan of \\(L\\) can then scatter final entries into classified records. This gives an \\(O(n+r+n/g)\\)-time construction strategy with appropriate run, record and cursor storage.

It **does not prove** lower instruction count or fewer writes than the fused builder. It proves that record classification need not be interleaved with every per-row scatter: structure permits classification at the interval and group level.

So compact30's exceptions can be bounded and predicted. Character crossings are bounded by 255 groups; pure-run groups can be counted from (A15); ordinary eligibility is expressed by (A12). This enables interval/group-level classification and verification rather than opaque per-row heuristics.

## 5\. Several steps at once

### 5.1 Powers of the navigation permutation

Conventional traversal visits \\(i,\\Psi(i),\\Psi^2(i),\\ldots\\). A multi-step transition computes \\(\\Psi^k(i)\\) while emitting the \\(k\\) intermediate characters:

\\\[ W\_k(i)=F\[i\]F\[\\Psi(i)\]\\cdots F\[\\Psi^{k-1}(i)\]. \\\]

The desired operation is

\\\[ \\boxed{i\\longmapsto\\left(W\_k(i),\\Psi^k(i)\\right).}\\tag{A18} \\\]

For a general permutation this could need \\(n\\) stored entries; an interval-exchange permutation gives a better bound.

### 5.2 Bound on pieces of \\(\\Psi^k\\)

Start with a partition \\(P\\) into \\(r\\) translated intervals, each with constant output byte; there are \\(r-1\\) boundaries. Refine it so that two successive steps follow fixed source intervals. Splits occur at preimages of original boundaries. Since \\(\\Psi\\) is bijective and translates each existing piece, images of the pieces are disjoint intervals partitioning the destination domain. Each original boundary introduces at most one new split across the whole refined partition. Each further step adds at most \\(r-1\\) boundaries. Thus

\\\[ \\boxed{N\_k\\le\\min\\{n,\\ 1+k(r-1)\\}.}\\tag{A19} \\\]

On every refined interval, \\(\\Psi^k\\) is a translation and \\(W\_k\\) is constant.

For two and four steps respectively:

\\\[ \\boxed{N\_2\\le2r-1,\\qquad N\_4\\le4r-3.} \\\]

This bound becomes uninformative when \\(k(r-1)\\) approaches \\(n\\).

### 5.3 Multi-character transition table

Each interval stores its starting row, displacement to \\(\\Psi^k(i)\\), and the emitted \\(k\\)-character word. With interval identifier, output retrieval and destination computation are straightforward. An explicit representation uses

\\\[ \\boxed{O\\left(kr(\\log n+k\\log\\sigma)\\right)}\\tag{A20} \\\]

bits when \\(k(r-1)\\ll n\\). For fixed small \\(k\\), that is \\(O(kr\\log n)\\).

This proves a compact representation for the *function*, not constant-latency arbitrary interval lookup. Multi-character navigation need not inherently require an \\(n\\)-entry jump table.

### 5.4 Implication for mibz2

[Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's 2012 work](<https://researchportal.helsinki.fi/en/publications/slashing-the-time-for-bwt-inversion/>) studied reducing cache misses through multi-character BWT navigation, including two characters per lookup. mibz2 cites it as [prior art](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/concepts/prior-work/index.md>). mibz2 has also built such a table: the pair walk of [PR \#34](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/34>), whose entries hold the row two steps on, was measured and dropped, because each step cost about twice as much and the table took about three times as long to build ([Why 32 couriers beat one](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/concepts/couriers/index.md>)). The interval view suggests representing \\(k\\)-step transitions by run-sensitive translated intervals instead of a complete super-alphabet table.

The number of intervals increases at most linearly with \\(kr\\). For repetitive blocks it can be substantially below \\(n\\), though it may become large for run-rich blocks. Interval identification, segment boundaries and output ordering remain essential. A mathematical \\(k\\)-step operation does not imply one cache miss or CPU instruction.

So the pair \\((\\Psi^k,W\_k)\\) has at most \\(1+k(r-1)\\) translated, constant-output intervals. This establishes a compact *theoretical* representation of multi-character decoding transitions when \\(kr\\ll n\\), without guaranteeing CPU speedup.

## 6\. Cycle structure and necklaces

### 6.1 Cycle count

Let \\(\\operatorname{cycles}(\\Psi\_L)\\) be the number of permutation cycles, and \\(m\_1,\\ldots,m\_r\\) the maximal run lengths in \\(L\\). A characterisation due to Likhomanov and Shur, reported in [a survey of the bijective BWT](<https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/01oasics/oasics-vol131-manzinis-festschrift/html/OASIcs.Manzini.2/OASIcs.Manzini.2.html>), states

\\\[ \\boxed{L\\text{ is a valid cyclic BWT image}\\iff\\operatorname{cycles}(\\Psi\_L)=\\gcd(m\_1,\\ldots,m\_r).}\\tag{A21} \\\]

For primitive input, the permutation is one cycle. Periodic inputs may have several. We must not assume every bzip2 traversal visits all distinct rows in one cycle.

### 6.2 Necklaces and exact enumeration

The BWT identifies cyclic rotations, so its images correspond naturally to *necklaces*. With counts \\(n\_1,\\ldots,n\_\\sigma\\) and \\(g=\\gcd(n\_1,\\ldots,n\_\\sigma)\\), Burnside's lemma gives

\\\[ \\boxed{N\_{\\mathrm{BWT}}=\\frac1n\\sum\_{d\\mid g}\\phi(d)\\frac{(n/d)!}{\\prod\_c(n\_c/d)!}.}\\tag{A22} \\\]

The number of primitive necklaces is

\\\[ \\boxed{N\_{\\mathrm{primitive}}=\\frac1n\\sum\_{d\\mid g}\\mu(d)\\frac{(n/d)!}{\\prod\_c(n\_c/d)!}.}\\tag{A23} \\\]

Here \\(\\phi\\) is Euler's totient and \\(\\mu\\) the Möbius function.

### 6.3 Coprime-frequency simplification

When \\(g=1\\), all source strings with that histogram are primitive:

\\\[ \\boxed{N\_{\\mathrm{BWT}}=\\frac1n\\frac{n!}{\\prod\_c n\_c!}.}\\tag{A24} \\\]

The BWT restriction reduces the stable-sort family by a factor of exactly \\(n\\); the information saving is

\\\[ \\boxed{\\log\_2n\\text{ bits}.}\\tag{A25} \\\]

At \\(n=900{,}000\\), this is approximately 19.78 bits for the entire block. Identifying the original rotation requires a primary index with roughly the same amount of information.

Cycle structure is useful for validity checks, periodicity, testing and traversal assumptions, but it is not a promising independent source of major storage savings. The stable-sort restriction accounts for most of the representational reduction.

## 7\. What does the permutree thesis contribute?

[Tamayo Jiménez](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19732>) studies weak-order lattices, permutree congruences, pattern-avoiding permutations, and related geometry. The inverse-BWT permutation belongs to a classical parabolic quotient of the symmetric group.

Let

\\\[ J=\\{s\_i:\\ i,i+1\\text{ lie in the same character bucket}\\}. \\\]

Then

\\\[ \\boxed{\\Psi\\in W^J}, \\\]

where \\(W^J\\) consists of permutations with no right descents at positions in \\(J\\).

### 7.1 Weak-order inversion statistic

The Coxeter length is

\\\[ \\ell(\\Psi)=\\\#\\{(i,j):i\<j,\\ \\Psi(i)\>\\Psi(j)\\}. \\\]

Stable sorting implies

\\\[ \\boxed{\\ell(\\Psi)=\\\#\\{(i,j):i\<j,\\ L\[i\]\>L\[j\]\\}.}\\tag{A26} \\\]

This gives an exact algebraic rank, but it should not be confused with BWT run count.

### 7.2 Large inversion count can coexist with easy navigation

For \\(L=b^ma^m\\), \\(a\<b\\),

\\\[ \\Psi(i)=\\begin{cases}i+m,&amp;0\\le i\<m,\\\\i-m,&amp;m\\le i\<2m.\\end{cases} \\\]

There are just \\(r=2\\) runs but

\\\[ \\boxed{\\ell(\\Psi)=m^2}. \\\]

Thus quadratic Coxeter length coexists with two translated intervals. This is a valid cyclic BWT image of an alternating periodic word.

Weak-order geometry measures distance from identity under adjacent transpositions; it does not measure cost of successor queries.

### 7.3 Meets and joins

The parabolic-quotient family has weak-order meets and joins, but mibz2 evaluates one fixed permutation rather than optimising over permutations. Meets and joins need not preserve valid BWT images. The permutree thesis does not directly imply a faster decoder; its relevance is the algebraic setting, while useful data structures come from stable sorting, succinct sequences and run-bounded interval permutations.

So weak-order geometry provides context, not the central optimisation. Parabolic quotients explain increasing buckets and inversion structure, but the objects the decoder actually evaluates are

\\\[ \\boxed{\\operatorname{select}\_c(L,k),\\quad\\text{translated intervals},\\quad\\text{move queries},\\quad\\Psi^k.} \\\]

These admit operational data structures and meaningful complexity bounds.

## 8\. Correctness checks and oracles

The mathematical properties support independent invariants:

| Invariant | Exact property | What it checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permutation | \\(\\Psi\\) bijective on \\(\[0,n)\\) | No missing or duplicated destinations |
| Stable-sort identity | Equation (1) of the main post | Correct correspondence with \\(L\\) |
| Bucket monotonicity | \\(\\Psi(i+1)\>\\Psi(i)\\) within buckets | Counting-sort ordering |
| Run structure | Exactly \\(n-r\\) within-bucket adjacent pairs advance by one | Correct run correspondence |
| Interval translation | Equation (2) of the main post, on every run | Correct interval descriptors |
| compact30 classification | Equation (A12) | Ordinary/RAW representation decisions |
| BWT cycle validity | Equation (A21) | Valid cyclic-BWT structure |
| Multi-step navigation | Equation (A18) | Correct jump destinations and emitted words |

These diagnose internal errors more precisely than end-to-end decoded-output comparison.

### 8.1 Independent oracle

Given \\(L\\) and its histogram, construct the reference mapping through equation (1) of the main post. For every row \\(i\\) verify

\\\[ \\Psi\_{\\mathrm{candidate}}(i)=\\operatorname{select}\_{F\[i\]}(L,i-C(F\[i\])). \\\]

This is a complete equivalence check, stronger than traversal from the primary index alone (which need not visit all distinct rows for periodic blocks). For \\(k\\)-step representations verify

\\\[ \\Psi\_{\\mathrm{candidate}}^{(k)}(i)=\\Psi^k(i) \\\]

and

\\\[ W\_{k,\\mathrm{candidate}}(i)=W\_k(i). \\\]

These are development oracles, not obligatory checks in production decoding.

## 9\. The design space and the results

[Section 6 of the main post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/#6-what-would-it-cost-mibz2-and-what-would-settle-it>) keeps three resources apart: navigation storage, construction work and critical-path memory dependencies. mibz2's compact30 work reduced footprint and benefited concurrent traversal, but direct construction remained expensive; the [4 November post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-04-compact30-constructor/index.md>) says bulk emission covered 74.3% of rows on the main Wikidata corpus. The [7 November pipelining work](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-pipelined-teams/index.md>) overlaps a block's construction and traversal with other stages of neighbouring blocks: a team's leader runs the next block's MTF and finishes the previous block while its helpers build and walk the current one.

So mibz2 need not choose only between the complete T-vector and packed per-row T-vectors. Move structures store interval transitions and support repeated navigation. When \\(r\\) is small they offer a theoretical reduction in live navigation storage, with established constructions and query guarantees. The representations the theory offers, with what each costs:

| Representation | Space for navigation | Access complexity | Main consideration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conventional T-vector | \\(32n\\) bits | One direct lookup | High footprint |
| Packed destinations | About \\(20n\\) bits, plus symbols/metadata | Direct addressing | Bit extraction |
| Per-character Elias–Fano | About \\(nH\_0(L)+O(n)\\) bits | Indexed select | More dependencies |
| Simple run descriptors | \\(O(r\\log n)\\) bits | \\(O(\\log r)\\) predecessor | Repeated searches |
| Balanced move structure | \\(O(r)\\) words | \\(O(1)\\) with interval state | Interval transitions |
| Length-capped move structure | \\(O(r)\\) words | Amortised \\(O(1)\\) over distinct full-cycle visits | Coverage assumptions |
| \\(k\\)-step intervals | \\(O(kr(\\log n+k\\log\\sigma))\\) bits | Interval-dependent | Multi-character operation |

The results, in one table:

| Gain | Established mathematical result | Value to mibz2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stable-sort representation | \\(\\Psi\\) is a collection of character-select sequences | Succinct sequence structures |
| Run-bounded representation | \\(\\Psi\\) has at most \\(r\\) translated intervals | Space scaling with \\(r\\) |
| Move structures | \\(O(1)\\) stateful moves in \\(O(r)\\) words | Alternative to full T-vector |
| Linear-time inversion | \\(O(n)\\) time and \\(O(r)\\) additional RLBWT working space under assumptions | End-to-end theoretical feasibility |
| Fixed-record identities | Exact character crossings, spans and pure-group bounds | Formal compact30 analysis |
| Multi-step interval bound | At most \\(1+k(r-1)\\) pieces for \\(k\\)-step navigation | Compact multi-character transitions |

---

**Sources:** as listed in [the main post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-08-inverse-bwt-navigation/#7-the-argument-in-brief>).

# Pipelined teams: how mibz2 0.2.6 decodes 7% faster on ten cores

While a team's helpers invert one block, its leader finishes the last and prepares the next: 7% faster than 0.2.5 on ten cores, for 5% more processor time.

7 November 2026 · 13 min read · [Research result](<#7-where-do-things-stand>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.2.6](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-2-6>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#026---2026-11-07>))

mibz2, our bzip2 decoder written in Rust, decodes a file with small groups of threads that we call teams. A bzip2 file is a series of blocks that can be decoded independently, and each team decodes one block at a time. One thread in the team, the leader, does some of each block's work alone, and the team's other threads, its helpers, wait for it. That waiting is time the decoder could spend decoding. Our new release, 0.2.6, removes much of it.

In 0.2.6, a team works on three blocks at once. While its helpers do the expensive middle part of one block, the leader finishes the block before it and prepares the block after it. On the ten-core machine we test on, with ten threads, this is 7.2% faster than 0.2.5 (95% interval 5.4% to 8.9%), and 6.5–7.0% faster at 11 to 20 threads. It is not cheaper: it uses about 5% more processor time in total, and 7–8 MB more memory at its peak.

That it helps at all is not obvious. In 0.2.5 the leader takes part in the expensive middle part. Pipelining takes it out, so that part runs on one thread fewer and gets slower. The 7% is what is left after paying for that. The first version of the pipeline gained only 4%, for 9% more processor time. Two refinements made it worth shipping: the leader keeps the pipeline full after a small block, and threads that wait go to sleep instead of staying on the processor.

The [previous post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/index.md>) explained why 0.2.5 split ten threads into three teams of three, and proposed this pipeline as the next experiment. This post is its result. [Section 1](<#1-what-does-a-team-do-with-one-block>) shows what a team does with one block, and [section 2](<#2-what-does-pipelining-change>) what pipelining changes and why it might not pay. [Section 3](<#3-what-did-the-first-pipeline-gain-and-why-so-little>) is the first pipeline's measurement, [section 4](<#4-what-did-the-two-refinements-change>) the two refinements, and [section 5](<#5-did-the-new-default-hold-up-against-025>) the run that confirmed the release against 0.2.5. [Section 6](<#6-what-does-it-cost-and-where-does-it-apply>) covers the cost and where it applies.

## 1\. What does a team do with one block?

bzip2 compresses a file in blocks of up to 900 kB each, each compressed with no reference to the others, so each can be decoded on its own. One thread, the scanner, reads the file and undoes the outermost layer of every block, the Huffman coding. The rest of a block's work is done by a team, in three parts:

1. **MTF:** undoing the move-to-front coding, which turns the scanner's symbols back into the block's bytes, though not yet in their original order.
2. **The inverse BWT:** undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform, which bzip2 used to reorder the block's bytes so that similar ones sit together. This puts them back in their original order.
3. **The finish:** RLE1, which expands the runs of repeated bytes that bzip2 shortened first of all, and the CRC, which checks the result against the block's checksum. Then the block's output is handed on, in file order.

The inverse BWT is the expensive part, and the only part a team shares. It has two phases. The **build** fills a table with one 4-byte entry for each byte of the block, saying where the next byte of the original text is. For a full block this table, which we call the T-vector, is 3.6 MB. The **walk** then follows the table from entry to entry, writing out a byte at each step. Each step's address comes from the entry just read, so mibz2 starts many walks at known points through the block, and the team's threads share them. [An earlier post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-02-revisiting-space-time-tradeoff-bwt-inversion/index.md>) works the transform through on a small example.

In 0.2.5, the **leader** does the block's MTF alone, then all three threads build and walk the table, then the leader puts the walk's pieces together and does the finish alone. The two **helpers** take part only in the build and the walk, and wait the rest of the time. In traces of four teams, the time outside the inverse BWT was 29–33% of a block's decode ([the previous post, section 4](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/#4-why-dont-more-threads-on-one-block-help>)). So for roughly a third of each block, a team's helpers had nothing to do.

The test machine is an Intel Core i9-10900K, with 10 cores (20 threads) and a 20 MiB last-level cache shared by all of them. On a machine of that shape, given ten or more threads, 0.2.5 runs three teams of three, nine decoding threads in all, plus the scanner. We write a plan as teams × threads per team, so this one is 3 × 3.

## 2\. What does pipelining change?

**The idea:** have the leader do its lone work while the helpers do the shared part, instead of before and after it. In 0.2.6, while the two helpers build and walk block A, the leader finishes the block before it, Z, and runs MTF on the block after it, B. When it has done both, it joins the helpers in walking A. When A's walk ends, the helpers start building B, whose MTF is already done, and the leader finishes A. The figure shows the two layouts side by side.

A team of three, in 0.2.5 and in 0.2.6

A sketch of the stages and who runs them, from the decoder's code; bar lengths are illustrative, not measured. L is the leader and H a helper. Blue is the leader's lone work, green the shared build and walk, grey a thread waiting. "Finish" is RLE1 and the CRC, and in 0.2.5 also putting the walk's pieces together; in 0.2.6 the last thread out of the walk does that.

We call this **overlap**: a block's MTF or finish runs at the same time as its team's build or walk of another block. It needs a second set of MTF buffers and a second buffer for an assembled block in each team, about 3 MB a team.

**Why it might not pay.** The build and the walk lose a thread. In 0.2.5 three threads build each table. In 0.2.6 two do, and the leader joins only the walk, and only once its own work is done. So the shared part gets slower, and the question is whether the time saved by overlap is larger than the time lost there. The previous post put that in a simple model, and found that if the shared part ran about 1.5 to 1.6 times slower without the leader, the gain would be zero ([section 7](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-07-why-mibz2-stops-scaling/#7-what-will-we-try-next>)). Nothing measured then said how much slower it would run.

## 3\. What did the first pipeline gain, and why so little?

We tested the first version of the pipeline against the plain teams at the same plan, 3 × 3 on ten threads. The test was registered: its comparisons, its possible outcomes and what each would mean were fixed before the run. Each arm decoded a sample of the Wikidata dump, 11.85 MB of bzip2 that decodes to 209.7 MB, 20 times, the arms taking turns in each round. "Speed" here and below is the plain arm's elapsed time over the pipelined arm's, paired round by round, so above 1 means faster. Its 95% interval describes the spread across the 20 rounds of one run, on one machine and one corpus.

The pipeline was faster: 1.042 (1.016–1.068). But it used about 9% more processor time, the time all threads spent running added up (a paired ratio of 0.918, 0.895–0.942). In the model's terms, the result fits a shared part running about 1.4 to 1.55 times slower without the leader, depending on what the hand-offs between threads are assumed to cost. That is a fit, not a measurement, and it is close to the break-even point.

The traces showed why the gain was small. **Only about a third of blocks overlapped:** in 147 of the sample's 431 blocks, the leader's MTF ran during its own team's build or walk of another block. Two features of the first version kept the rest from overlapping.

**Small blocks emptied the pipeline.** A block of fewer than 262,144 bytes (256 KiB) is not worth sharing among three threads, so its team's leader decodes it whole, on one thread. 198 of the sample's 431 blocks are that small. In the first version, the leader took at most one new block while its helpers worked. If that block was small, it decoded it and prepared nothing else. The next block then had to be prepared with the helpers waiting, as in 0.2.5. Each small block cost about one block's overlap.

**Waiting threads never slept.** A thread waiting for the build to end (a helper that had finished its share, or the leader waiting to join the walk) checked a flag 4,096 times, then asked the operating system in a loop to run something else instead (a yield). When nothing else is waiting to run, a yield returns at once, so the waiting thread stays on its core and its wait counts as processor time.

## 4\. What did the two refinements change?

Each refinement was tested on its own against the first pipeline, at 3 × 3 on ten threads and at 3 × 4 on twelve, with its question and outcomes fixed before the run. The figures below are the ten-thread ones; the twelve-thread results agree.

**Small: the leader keeps the pipeline primed.** After a small block, the leader now takes the next queued block too, and runs its MTF in the same stretch. It keeps going until it has prepared a block for its team, or finds none waiting. It never waits for a new block to arrive: a leader that held an unfinished block while waiting for the scanner could leave the two waiting on each other.

A small block in the pipeline, before and after the change

A sketch, not a measurement: bar lengths are illustrative. L is the leader, H the two helpers, and S a small block, which the leader decodes whole. After the change the helpers can wait a little at the end of a run, while the leader finishes B's MTF.

It worked as intended. Overlapped blocks rose from 144 to 236.5 of 431 in this run (medians over six traced rounds; the first run counted 147), and the pipeline got faster: 1.043 (1.020–1.066), with no change detected in processor time, 1.007 (0.987–1.028). It has a cost, which the figure shows: a leader busy with more blocks joins the walk later. Of the 233 blocks large enough for the team to invert together, those whose walk the leader joined late rose from 62 to 113. The registered outcomes had expected a later join to cancel the gain, and had no entry for a later join with a gain. Our reading, not a registered verdict, is that the later join is real and paid for, and that the extra overlap outweighs it, on this machine and corpus.

**Park: waiting threads go to sleep.** A waiting thread still checks its flag 4,096 times, then, instead of yielding, it adds itself to a list and parks: it sleeps until woken, using no processor time. The thread that ends the build wakes every thread on the list. Waking a parked thread takes a few microseconds, which a thread that never slept doesn't pay.

Parking left the elapsed time unchanged, 0.999 (0.981–1.017), and cut processor time by about 5% (a ratio of 1.055, 1.039–1.071). The saving could have come from spinning less before parking, rather than from parking. A control arm that only cut the checks from 4,096 to 2,000, still yielding, changed neither figure: 1.004 for speed and 1.006 for processor time, both intervals holding 1. So the saving is from parking.

Each change against the first pipeline, 3 × 3 on ten threads

Measured, the test machine, 20 paired rounds each, with 95% intervals. Both ratios are the first pipeline's figure over the changed one's, so above 1 is better: faster, or less processor time. Green dots are intervals wholly above 1. The spin control cuts the checks before a yield, and doesn't park.

**Both together** were about as fast as small alone, 1.038 (1.021–1.055), and saved less processor time than parking alone, 1.032 (1.018–1.046) against 1.055. A likely reason is that a busier leader leaves less waiting to sleep through, but that is not established.

**Against the plain teams,** in the same run, the pipeline with both changes was 1.072 (1.053–1.091) as fast as plain 3 × 3, for about 5% more processor time (a paired ratio of 0.951). Its peak memory was 75 MB, against 67 MB for the plain teams of 0.2.5's default. That is the version 0.2.6 ships.

One thing these runs can't do is split the gain into its causes. Some of it may come from the overlap, and some from the way the leader joins the walk as an extra thread once its own work is done. The runs measure the total.

## 5\. Did the new default hold up against 0.2.5?

The 1.072 came from a comparison that was reported, not registered as a decision. So before release we fixed one more test, with its pass rule set before any run: the 0.2.6 build against the 0.2.5 release, each decoding as a caller gets it by default, at 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 16 and 20 threads, 20 paired rounds each. To pass, ten threads had to be at least 1.03 as fast, with its interval above 1. At 11 to 20 threads, each count's interval had to rule out being more than 2% slower. At 8 and 9 threads both builds run four teams of two, unchanged, so those two counts check that nothing else moved. The prediction was 1.07–1.08 at ten threads, about the same above, and no change at 8 and 9.

The run passed. The table gives each thread count's plan in 0.2.6 and its speed against 0.2.5. "CPU" is 0.2.6's processor time over 0.2.5's, and "memory" its peak memory over 0.2.5's, each from the medians of the 20 rounds. 0.2.5 ran the same plans, unpipelined:

| threads | plan | speed (95%) | CPU | memory |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8 | 4 × 2 | 1.002 (0.991–1.013) | 0.99 | 1.00 |
| 9 | 4 × 2 | 1.001 (0.991–1.012) | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 10 | 3 × 3, pipelined | **1.072 (1.054–1.089)** | 1.04 | 1.10 |
| 11 | 3 × 3, pipelined | 1.070 (1.055–1.085) | 1.05 | 1.12 |
| 12 | 3 × 3, pipelined | 1.069 (1.054–1.085) | 1.05 | 1.10 |
| 16 | 3 × 3, pipelined | 1.065 (1.045–1.085) | 1.05 | 1.13 |
| 20 | 3 × 3, pipelined | 1.070 (1.048–1.092) | 1.04 | 1.12 |

0.2.6 against 0.2.5, by the threads asked for

Measured, the test machine, 20 paired rounds a thread count, with 95% intervals. Speed is 0.2.5's elapsed time over 0.2.6's, so above 1 is faster. Green dots are intervals wholly above 1.

From the run's records, at ten threads the median decode of the sample took 0.144 s against 0.156 s, about 1,460 against 1,350 MB/s of output. Processor time rose from 0.98 s to 1.02 s, and peak memory from 69 to 76 MB. The outcome matched the prediction for speed and peak memory (1.10–1.13 against about 1.12), and came in a little under it for processor time (1.04–1.05 against 1.05–1.06). Above ten threads the plan is the same three teams, and the measured gain is about the same. A request for twenty threads still decodes on nine, plus the scanner.

## 6\. What does it cost, and where does it apply?

**The trade-off.** 0.2.6 finishes sooner, but it doesn't do less work: it spends about 4–5% more processor time and 7–8 MB more peak memory than 0.2.5 on this workload. Elapsed time improves because work that used to run while two threads waited now runs beside them. The extra memory is each team's second set of MTF buffers and second assembled block.

**Where it applies.** Only the 3 × 3 plan is pipelined, and the decoder picks that plan only on a machine with 10 physical cores and a 20 MiB last-level cache, given 10 or more threads. Every other plan and every other machine shape decodes exactly as 0.2.5 did. The output is the same bytes in every case: the pipelined path is tested byte for byte against libbzip2, and on corrupt and truncated input, by forcing the plan on any machine. But its speed has been measured on one machine, the test machine, and one corpus, Wikidata. Another processor of the same shape gets the pipeline too, measured or not. The cloud machines that benchmark every change to mibz2 have 4 virtual CPUs on 2 physical cores, so they never take this path. They show only that nothing else moved. Thread counts of 13 to 15, 17 to 19 and above 20 were not measured, though they run the same plan.

**The plain teams are still available.** A caller that prefers lower processor time can ask for 0.2.5's three plain teams directly, with [`BzReader::parallel_planned`](<https://docs.rs/mibz2/0.2.6/mibz2/struct.BzReader.html#method.parallel_planned>) and the plan [`Plan::Teams`](<https://docs.rs/mibz2/0.2.6/mibz2/parallel/enum.Plan.html>):

```rust
use mibz2::{parallel::Plan, BzReader, Kernels};

// three plain teams of three, as in 0.2.5
let reader = BzReader::parallel_planned(
    file,
    Plan::Teams { teams: 3, k: 3 },
    12, // blocks in flight: the default's window at this plan
    Kernels::detect(),
);
```

## 7\. Where do things stand?

The argument runs like this. In 0.2.5, a team's two helpers waited through about a third of each block, while the leader did MTF and the finish alone. 0.2.6 has the leader do that work while the helpers build and walk another block. That takes the leader out of the build, which slows it, so the first version gained only 4%, for 9% more processor time. Two changes made it pay: preparing the next block after a small one raised overlap from about a third of blocks to about half, and putting waiting threads to sleep took back about half of the extra processor time. A registered run of the release against 0.2.5 confirmed 7.2% at ten threads, and 6.5–7.0% at 11 to 20.

0.2.5's three teams were 8.8–8.9% faster than 0.2.4's four teams of two at ten threads, and 0.2.6 is 7.2% faster than 0.2.5. Multiplied together, the two would put 0.2.6 about 17% ahead of 0.2.4 there. That is a projection from two separate runs, not a measurement: a direct comparison of the releases has not yet run.

What remains open is in two places. The previous post's question, why each extra block in progress slows the others, is unchanged by this release. And the pipeline still leaves the leader's serial work inside each team. The next question is whether moving that work onto threads of its own, outside the teams, would do better on the same number of cores ([pull request 251](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/251>)). Nothing about it has been measured yet.

The general lesson: when part of a job can't be shared, it can still run beside the part that is. Whether that pays depends on what the shared part loses to make room, and here the answer was found only by measuring.

# Why mibz2 stops scaling at eight threads, and why three teams help

Each block decoded at once slows the others, and more threads per block barely help, so three teams of three beat four of two by 9%. Why blocks interfere is open.

7 November 2026 · 15 min read · [Research in progress](<#8-where-do-things-stand>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.2.5](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-2-5>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#025---2026-11-06>))

On a ten-core desktop processor, mibz2, our bzip2 decoder written in Rust, got faster as we gave it more threads, from one to eight. Past eight it stopped. Twelve, sixteen or twenty threads decoded no faster than eight. A decoder that can't use the cores it is given leaves time on the table for anyone decompressing large files, and the reason it stops says where the next gain has to come from.

The reason is not the number of threads. It is how many pieces of the file the decoder works on at the same time. A bzip2 file is a series of blocks that can be decoded independently, and mibz2 decodes several at once, each with a small group of threads. We measured two things. Every extra block in progress slows down every other block. And extra threads on the same block barely speed it up. Together they mean that fewer blocks, each with more threads, beat more blocks with fewer threads. Our latest release, 0.2.5, decodes three blocks at once with three threads each, where 0.2.4 decoded four with two each. In two runs at ten threads, it was 8.8% and 8.9% faster, used 11–12% less processor time and 18–19% less peak memory.

What we have not measured is *why* the blocks slow each other down. The leading explanation is that each block needs a large table, and the tables compete for the processor's shared cache. The evidence for that comes from a simpler test program, not from the decoder itself, and a careful review of an earlier draft of this analysis made us withdraw part of it. So this post keeps three things apart: what was measured, what is inferred, and what we will test next.

[Section 1](<#1-how-does-mibz2-decode-with-several-threads>) explains how mibz2 splits a file among its threads. [Section 2](<#2-what-happens-when-we-change-the-number-of-blocks-and-the-threads-on-each>) gives the measurements behind the two findings, and sections [3](<#3-why-would-more-blocks-at-once-slow-each-block-down>) and [4](<#4-why-dont-more-threads-on-one-block-help>) look at each one in turn. [Section 5](<#5-what-did-three-teams-of-three-gain>) is the release's own measurement, [section 6](<#6-what-did-the-review-change>) what the review changed, and [section 7](<#7-what-will-we-try-next>) the next experiments.

## 1\. How does mibz2 decode with several threads?

bzip2 compresses a file in blocks of up to 900 kB each (at its default level, 9). Each block is compressed on its own, with no reference to the others, so each can be decoded on its own too. That is what makes a parallel decoder possible: different threads can work on different blocks at the same time, and the decoder puts their outputs back in order at the end.

Decoding one block undoes bzip2's steps in reverse. One thread, which mibz2 calls the scanner, reads the compressed file and undoes its outermost layer, the Huffman coding, for every block ([an earlier post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-05-huffman-bit-buffer/index.md>) covers that stage). The rest of a block's work happens on the threads that decode it, in three parts:

1. **MTF:** undoing the move-to-front coding, which turns the scanner's symbols back into the block's bytes, though not yet in their original order.
2. **The inverse BWT:** undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform, which bzip2 used to reorder the bytes so that similar ones sit together. This puts them back in their original order.
3. **RLE1 and the CRC:** expanding the runs of repeated bytes that bzip2 shortened first of all, and checking the result against the block's checksum.

The inverse BWT is the most expensive of the three. It works in two phases. The **build** makes a table with one 4-byte entry for each byte of the block, saying where the next byte of the original text is to be found. For a full block that table, which mibz2 calls the T-vector, is 3.6 MB. The **walk** then follows the table from entry to entry, writing out a byte at each step. Each step's address comes from the entry just read, so the steps form a chain through the table, jumping to an unpredictable place each time. A jump that finds its entry in a nearby cache is quick. One that has to go to main memory waits hundreds of cycles. [Revisiting the space–time tradeoff in BWT inversion](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-02-revisiting-space-time-tradeoff-bwt-inversion/index.md>) shows the transform and its table worked through on a small example.

A chain of dependent jumps can't be split between threads directly, since each step needs the one before. mibz2 gets around this by starting many chains at known points through the block, so several threads can share one block's build and walk. We call the threads that share a block a **team**. One of them, the **leader**, also does the block's MTF, RLE1 and CRC alone, and puts the walk's pieces together at the end (the **assembly**). The others are its **helpers**: they join in only for the build and the walk. A team decodes one block at a time, with one table, and then takes the next.

So a thread count is really two numbers: how many teams, which is the number of blocks and tables in progress at once, and how many threads each team has. We write a plan as teams × threads per team: 4 × 2 is four teams of two.

The machine these measurements come from is an Intel Core i9-10900K. It has 10 cores, each able to run two threads at once (20 in all), and a 20 MiB last-level cache, the L3, which all ten cores share. Until 0.2.5, mibz2's rule was teams of two, and as many teams as keep their tables within about 0.7 of the L3. On the test machine that is four teams. Asked for 8, 10, 12, 16 or 20 threads, the decoder ran the same four teams of two, plus the scanner. That is why it stopped at eight: past eight it declined the extra threads. Under that rule, 0.2.4 levelled off at about 1.27–1.31 GB/s of output from 8 threads up.

The two plans on the test machine's ten cores

A sketch of the plans, not a measurement of what is in the cache. L is a team's leader, H a helper. Each team's table is 3.6 MB for a full block; each team also has other buffers, not drawn.

## 2\. What happens when we change the number of blocks, and the threads on each?

To see what four teams of two were missing, we ran a grid of plans that varied the two numbers separately: 2 to 8 teams, of 2, 3 or 4 threads each. Each plan decoded the same sample of the Wikidata dump, 11.85 MB of bzip2 that decodes to 209.7 MB, 20 times, in rotating order, with threads placed by the operating system as users run it. The figure below groups the plans by their number of teams. That is the most tables the plan can have in progress at once, not a measured count of how many were in progress at each moment.

Throughput by the number of teams, all thread counts per team together

Measured, the test machine, 20 rounds a plan (the [team-size grid](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/d95ca1ea/docs/journal/2026-11-06-team-size.md>)). A vertical bar spans the plans with that many teams but different threads per team. The rate is megabytes of decoded output a second.

Two things stand out. **Each team gets slower as teams are added**, and steeply: from 558–583 MB/s each with two teams, to 461–466 with three, about 320 with four and 110 with eight. Adding a fourth team adds a fourth block in progress, but makes every block slow enough that all four together are slower than three. Total throughput peaks at three teams, 1,382–1,399 MB/s.

And **at a fixed number of teams, the threads per team hardly matter.** With four teams, each team decoded 319, 325 and 320 MB/s with two, three and four threads. The extra threads cost processor time without buying speed. The table below gives the four-team plans against the old default, with the best three-team plans for comparison. "Against 4 × 2" is the ratio of throughputs, paired round by round, with its 95% interval across the 20 rounds; "CPU" is total processor time over 4 × 2's.

| plan | threads | MB/s | against 4 × 2 | CPU | peak memory, MB |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 × 2 (the old default) | 8 | 1,276 | 1 | 1 | 82 |
| 4 × 3 | 12 | 1,300 | 1.017 (1.008–1.026) | 1.26 | 82 |
| 4 × 4 | 16 | 1,279 | 1.003 (0.993–1.014) | 1.52 | 82 |
| 3 × 3 | 9 | 1,382 | 1.075 (1.058–1.093) | 0.89 | 67 |
| 3 × 4 | 12 | 1,399 | 1.097 (1.083–1.111) | 1.04 | 68 |

The four-team rows were the experiment's registered tests: their pass rule, a gain of at least 3%, was fixed before any run. Neither passed. The three-team rows were exploratory: picked out after the fact, so they proved nothing on their own. They were then confirmed in runs registered for them, and the release's plan in two more ([section 5](<#5-what-did-three-teams-of-three-gain>)). Peak memory, meanwhile, rose by about 15 MB with each team: 52 MB at two teams, 67 at three, 82 at four and 138 at eight.

That leaves two questions. Why does each extra block slow the others? And why doesn't a block go faster with more threads?

## 3\. Why would more blocks at once slow each block down?

**This part is inferred, not measured in the decoder.** The leading explanation is about the shared cache. Each team's walk jumps unpredictably through its own 3.6 MB table, and is fast only while the entries it needs are in the L3. All teams share that one cache, so each extra table takes room the others were using. As an intuition: several people each searching their own large reference book, all spread out on one desk. With two books, most pages stay open. With eight, pages keep being put away to make room, and fetching them back is slow.

The evidence comes from a test program that runs only the inverse BWT, the build and the walk, with each block's thread fixed to a core of its own, and no teams. In October we ran it on the test machine with hardware counters, which count events inside the processor. One of them is the **L3 hit share**: of the memory requests that miss the cores' own small caches, the share the L3 answers rather than main memory. Plotted against the table bytes in use at once, it stays near 1 while the tables are small, then falls once they approach the cache's size.

L3 hit share against the table bytes in use at once (inversion only)

Measured, the test machine, in a program that runs only the build and walk, one block a core ([footprint journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/42794eba51a651238ce9dd3165fe546970a020a8/docs/journal/2026-10-29-libsais-knee.md>)). bzip2's compression level sets its block size: at level 3 blocks are 300 kB, so their tables are a third the size of level 9's. Not a measurement of the decoder.

Four other observations from that program point the same way:

- **Requests wait longer.** A request that misses the cores' own caches waited on average 67 cycles with four tables, 137 with six and 361 with eight.
- **Main memory saturates.** From six tables on, traffic to main memory levels off at 28–29 GB/s.
- **A control isolates the table's size.** A variant that changes the walk's code but keeps a 4-byte table got the same hit share as the standard one at six tables (0.814 against 0.793).
- **A smaller table moves the drop.** A 3-byte table (2.7 MB a block) moved the program's best number of blocks from four to six, where it ran 1.100 (1.093–1.108) times as fast as the standard table's best.

That is good evidence that the size of the tables matters, *in that program*. It doesn't settle the question for the decoder, for three reasons.

First, the program isn't the decoder. It has no teams, no MTF, RLE1 or CRC, no scanner, and none of the decoder's other buffers. Second, table bytes don't explain everything even there. With the smaller level-3 blocks, ten tables kept a hit share of 0.940 and yet ran slower than eight, mostly in the build, with requests waiting longer at nearly the same hit share. So a limit on how many requests the cores can have outstanding, or on the number of cores loading the cache at once, is not ruled out. Third, the decoder's own counters were never read: the operating system's settings on the test machine didn't allow it during the team-size run.

There is also a simpler puzzle. Four full tables are 14.4 MB, below the cache's 20 MiB. Each team has other buffers besides its table, such as space for the walk's pieces and for the block's output: several megabytes of reserved capacity each. But capacity is not what is being read at any moment, and how much of those buffers sits in the cache at once is not measured. An earlier draft of this analysis added those capacities up to a 20 MiB "hot set" that filled the cache. The review showed that a sum of capacities and peaks can't establish that, and the claim was withdrawn ([section 6](<#6-what-did-the-review-change>)).

Two other explanations also fit the measurements. The teams' waits for each other could be what makes blocks slow, rather than memory. And three teams of three use nine threads on ten cores, so one core is free, which changes how the operating system schedules everything else. No measurement of the decoder yet tells these apart.

## 4\. Why don't more threads on one block help?

**Measured:** with four teams, a third thread per team bought 1.7% (0.8–2.6%) for 26% more processor time, and a fourth bought nothing detectable, 0.3% (−0.7% to 1.4%), for 52% more. A trace of each block's decode, which records when each block starts and finishes, shows the same thing from inside: with four teams, a block took on average 1.394, 1.380 and 1.403 ms with two, three and four threads.

Part of the reason is plain arithmetic: not all of a block's work is shared. Only the build and the walk are, and only inside the call that does the inverse BWT. The leader does the MTF before that call, and RLE1 and the CRC after it, alone.

One block's work in a team

The stages and who runs them, from the decoder's code. The shares are measured, in traces of four teams on the test machine: medians of six runs each at two, three and four threads a team. Inside the call the team also waits for its slowest member; those waits are not timed separately.

The traces give the time inside and outside the inversion call for each block:

| plan | a block's decode, ms | inside the inversion call, ms | outside it, ms | outside share |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 × 2 | 1.394 | 0.993 | 0.400 | 28.75% |
| 4 × 3 | 1.380 | 0.935 | 0.441 | 32.14% |
| 4 × 4 | 1.404 | 0.946 | 0.462 | 32.64% |

These are averages over the sample's 431 blocks, some of them small, so they are not the time for one full 900 kB block. On one of the cloud machines that benchmark every change to mibz2 (CI), with one thread, the stages cost, per output byte: 0.41 ns for MTF, 0.04 for assembly, 0.05 for RLE1 and 0.07 for the CRC, which the leader does alone, against 0.48 for the build and 1.09 for the walk, which a team shares.

So about 29–33% of a block's time is outside the shared part, and more threads can't shorten it. But that share is not the whole of the work that can't be shared. The inversion call also includes work the leader does alone (setting up, and assembling the pieces), and time the team spends waiting for its slowest member. The time outside the call also includes scheduling and the tracing itself. The traces can't separate these, so the true unshared share isn't known.

**What the measurements don't separate** is why the shared part itself doesn't speed up with a third or fourth thread. The candidates, each visible in the code, are:

- the cost of waking helpers and of waiting for the last one to finish;
- the setup and assembly the leader does alone, inside the call;
- the build's checks that each thread writes only its own part of the table;
- the number of pieces a block is split into, which grows with the threads per team;
- two threads sharing one core, once there are more threads than cores;
- memory, as in section 3.

Waiting isn't free either: a helper with nothing to do checks for work up to 2,000 times before it sleeps, which costs processor time.

One more measurement bears on core sharing. With four teams pinned to particular processors, giving the threads one core each ("spread") against pairing them on cores ("packed") made the biggest difference at two threads a team: packed was 23% slower (1,055 against 1,369 MB/s in the median round). With three threads a team it was 8% slower, and with four, 1%. But the packed arm also had fewer cores to use (4 against 8 for eight threads), so this compares how many cores were available, not which threads shared them.

## 5\. What did three teams of three gain?

The grid's three-team plans were chosen after the fact, so before changing the decoder we registered a test of the change itself, with its pass rule fixed before any run: 0.2.5's plan against 0.2.4's, at 8 to 20 threads, 20 rounds each, and a second run to confirm it. Both runs passed. At ten threads:

| run | speed against 0.2.4 | processor time | peak memory |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| first | 1.089 (1.075–1.103) | 0.88 | 0.82 |
| confirmation | 1.088 (1.076–1.101) | 0.89 | 0.81 |

The intervals are 95% intervals across the 20 paired rounds of one run. Neither run detected harm at 11, 12, 16 or 20 threads, the registered check there. A separate comparison of the two releases found 0.2.4 taking 11.9% longer than 0.2.5 at ten threads, and 8.1–8.7% longer at 12 to 20.

At ten threads or more on a machine of this shape (ten cores, a 20 MiB L3), 0.2.5 runs three teams of three. A request for twenty threads still decodes on nine. The result covers this processor and this workload. It shows that three teams are faster. It doesn't show why, which is section 3's open question.

## 6\. What did the review change?

The first version of this analysis was reviewed adversarially by another member of the project, who recomputed its numbers from the archived traces. All seven objections were accepted, and the version this post is based on takes them in. Four changes matter for the argument.

The first draft claimed that the decoder's buffers formed a 20 MiB working set that filled the cache. That was a sum of reserved capacities and peaks, not a measurement of what is read at the same time, and it was withdrawn. The first draft also read the flat block times in section 4 as memory saturation. The review pointed out that they can't separate memory from waiting, unshared work or core sharing, and that claim was withdrawn too. The outside share in section 4 was also recomputed: the first draft divided by the wrong total, and called the whole inversion call "build and walk", when it includes setup, assembly and waits. And the first draft's 1.10–1.30× estimate for the next experiment was replaced by the model in section 7, which shows that no such floor follows from the measurements.

## 7\. What will we try next?

**First: let the leader work on other blocks while its helpers build and walk.** Today a team's helpers wait while the leader runs MTF before a block and RLE1 and the CRC after it. In the proposed pipeline, the leader runs the next block's MTF and the previous block's RLE1 and CRC while the other threads build and walk the current one. It needs one more buffer for the next block's bytes, about 1 MB a team. A prototype is being built.

A team's timeline, today and as proposed

The proposal, not a measurement: bar lengths are illustrative. Whether it pays depends on how much slower the build and walk run with one thread fewer, and on what the hand-offs cost.

Whether it pays is not obvious, because the shared part loses a thread: in a team of three, the build and walk would run on two. A simple model, from the review, puts numbers on that. Let \\(S\\) be the leader's work outside the shared part, \\(P\_0\\) the shared part today, \\(\\alpha\\) how much slower the shared part runs with a thread fewer and more blocks in progress, and \\(H\\) the cost of hand-offs that can't overlap. Then the time a team spends per block, today and pipelined, and the speed-up, are

\\\[C\_0 = S + P\_0, \\qquad C\_1 = \\max(S,\\ \\alpha P\_0) + H,\\\]

\\\[\\text{speed-up} = C\_0 / C\_1.\\\]

For three teams of three, the grid's throughput gives \\(C\_0\\) = 1.056 ms a block per team: three teams, 209.7 MB in 431 blocks, at 1,382 MB/s. That figure includes start-up and the end of the run, so it is an approximation, not a measured service time. Taking \\(S\\) = 0.40 ms, the time outside the inversion call in section 4, leaves \\(P\_0\\) = 0.656 ms. The model's speed-up then depends almost entirely on \\(\\alpha\\):

Modelled speed-up of the pipeline, against α

Modelled, not measured. The break-even points are where the curves cross 1, at α of about 1.61 and 1.53. The measurements don't bound α.

If the shared part ran no slower, the pipeline would be 1.61× as fast, or 1.50× with 0.05 ms of hand-off cost per block. If it ran 40% slower, 1.15× or 1.09×. At 1.6× slower the gain is gone. If the shared part slowed to what it takes under four teams of two, 0.94–0.99 ms, the gain would be 1.07–1.12×, or 1.02–1.07× with the hand-off cost. Nothing measured so far says which \\(\\alpha\\) to expect, so no gain and a loss are both possible outcomes, and will be registered as such.

The test will compare like with like. To isolate the pipeline, pipelined against not pipelined at the same plan and thread count: three teams of four against three teams of four, and three of three against three of three. Separately, pipelined three of four against today's default at ten threads, which is the comparison a user would care about. Each will report processor time and peak memory alongside the elapsed time. The prototype must also record when each thread starts and finishes each stage of each block, so that the trace shows blocks really overlapping. Without that, a result says nothing about the mechanism.

**Second: placement, as a control.** Pinned against unpinned threads, recording which thread ran on which processor, for today's plan and for three teams of four. It makes no prediction of its own. It is needed to read the pipeline's result, since that plan uses more threads than there are cores.

**Third: a smaller table under teams.** The inversion-only program's 3-byte table moved the fall in hit share to more blocks, so the table's size is a real factor. But that table's 1.10× gain was against the same program's standard table, not against the decoder: against the decoder's own team code (four teams of two), in the same tests, it ran at 0.687 (0.680–0.695) of the speed, on six cores against eight. A different compact table, which packs 30 entries into each 64-byte record, ran 4.8% and 7.7% slower than the standard one at four threads on CI. And no smaller table has been measured under teams. So it comes after the first two.

**Last: shrinking the other buffers.** There is no measurement of how much cache they take, so nothing yet says this would help.

## 8\. Where do things stand?

The chain of the argument runs like this. A thread count is really two numbers, blocks in progress and threads per block. Each extra block slows every other block, enough that three blocks beat four. Extra threads on one block barely help, partly because about a third of a block's time is work its leader does alone. So three teams of three beat four teams of two, as two registered runs confirmed. Why extra blocks hurt is not settled: competition for the shared cache is the leading explanation, with good evidence from a simpler program and none yet from the decoder.

The pipeline prototype, its registration and the placement control are in progress. Nothing in this post changes the decoder.

The general lesson: more threads help only if the work they add runs alongside the slowest step. Here the slowest step has two parts, the blocks competing with each other, and each block's work that one thread does alone.
