# Huffman decoding in mibz2: keeping the bit buffer in a register

The Huffman decoder wrote its bit buffer to memory and read it back at every lookup. Kept in a register, the stage ran 13% faster on Intel and 5% on AMD.

5 November 2026 · 16 min read · [Research result](<#9-what-the-benchmark-measured>)

Shipped in mibz2 [0.2.2](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/#release-0-2-2>) ([changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#022---2026-11-05>))

A decoder reads a compressed file one byte at a time, but the codes inside a bzip2 file aren't whole bytes. They are Huffman codes: each is a run of bits of its own length, one bit for a very common symbol and a dozen or more for a rare one, packed end to end with nothing between them. So a decoder keeps a bit buffer, a small holding area for bits it has read from the file but not yet decoded. In mibz2, our bzip2 decoder written in Rust, the buffer is a single 64-bit integer. The decoder reads each code off its top end, shifts the rest up behind it, and tops it up with more bytes from the file when it runs low.

This post is about where that integer was kept. It held the same bits and the decoder did the same work, but the compiled code wrote the buffer to memory after every code and read it back before the next. Even from the processor's nearest cache, a read of a value just written waits several cycles for the write, and every code waited that long. Rearranged so the compiler could keep the buffer in a register, the thread that reads the codes, which mibz2 calls the scanner, ran 12.9% faster on an Intel Xeon 8370C CI runner and 5.0% faster on an AMD EPYC 9V74.

The benchmark decodes a fixed sample of the Wikidata dump: 12 slices of it, 210 MB once decoded. On the Intel runner a one-thread decode of that sample ran 2.7% faster. The scanner is about a tenth of the decode, so its own saving accounts for about half of that figure; the rest is within the noise of the other stages. On the AMD runner no change in the whole decode was detected. Some AMD cores can serve a read of an address just written without the usual wait, which leaves less to remove there. On Intel the cut fell short of the 15–25% predicted for it.

[Section 1](<#1-what-a-bit-buffer-is>) shows a bit buffer at work on a small example and as mibz2's code. [Section 2](<#2-reading-a-code-with-a-lookup-table>) is how the decoder reads a code with a lookup table, and why each code waits for the last. [Section 3](<#3-where-this-sits-in-bzip2-and-in-mibz2>) places this in bzip2's format and in mibz2's decoder. Sections [4](<#4-what-the-census-found>) to [6](<#6-the-change-the-state-as-a-value>) are how the stored buffer was found, why the compiler put it there, and the change. Sections [7](<#7-what-was-predicted-before-any-timing>) to [9](<#9-what-the-benchmark-measured>) give the prediction, the correctness checks and what the benchmark measured, run by run.

## 1\. What a bit buffer is

Huffman coding gives each symbol a code of its own length: short for common symbols, long for rare ones. The codes are chosen so that no code is the beginning of another, which is what lets them be packed end to end with no separators. Reading from the start, the bits seen so far can only ever be the beginning of one code.

Reading a toy Huffman code

A made-up code, not one of bzip2's. The ten bits 0110100111 hold five symbols. Their boundaries are found only by reading the codes in order.

Take a made-up alphabet of four symbols, A to D, where A is the most common: A gets `0`, B `10`, C `110` and D `111`. The ten bits `0110100111` then read as A, C, B, A, D. Notice what the reader had to do. It could only tell that C began at the second bit once it had read A, and only tell where B began once it had read C. Where a code starts depends on the lengths of all the codes before it.

A computer, though, reads the file in bytes, eight bits at a time, and these codes don't line up with bytes. The bit buffer bridges the two. mibz2 loads the file's next bytes into a 64-bit integer, `buf`, with the first unread bit at the top (the left end, written in binary). Two more numbers go with it, and together they are the reader's whole state, [`Bits`](<https://docs.rs/mibz2/0.2.2/mibz2/bits/struct.Bits.html>):

| Field | Type | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pos` | `usize` | the next byte of input to load |
| `buf` | `u64` | the stream's next bits, the first of them in the most significant bit |
| `live` | `u32` | how many of `buf`'s top bits are valid |

Three operations act on it, each a line or two of Rust:

- **Peek** at the next \\(n\\) bits without consuming them: `buf >> (64 - n)`. For the next three bits that is `buf >> 61`, which moves the top three bits to the bottom of the number.
- **Skip** \\(n\\) bits once a code of that length has been read: `buf <<= n; live -= n;`. The code's bits fall off the top, and the next code moves up to take their place.
- **Refill** when the buffer runs low: load the eight bytes at `pos`, OR them into `buf` just below the bits still live, and advance `pos` by as many whole bytes as fitted. That leaves at least 56 bits live.

The figure below runs the toy bits through a ten-bit buffer. Each press of its button is one peek and one skip: it says which code the bits at the front begin with, and then shifts that code out, so the next one moves to the front.

Try it: decode the toy bits one code at a time

The code: A = `0` B = `10` C = `110` D = `111`

1. 0
2. 1
3. 1
4. 0
5. 1
6. 0
7. 0
8. 1
9. 1
10. 1

The buffer, its next unread bit on the left. In green: the bits of the code at the front, and that code in the key above. Dotted: room left by bits already shifted out.

**Decoded so far**

none yet

**Unread bits (`live`)**

10

**The last shift, in Rust**

`nothing shifted yet`

Read the next code →Reset

Read in order: the buffer starts `0`, which is A. Shifting A's one bit out brings `110` to the front, which is C. Then `10` is B, `0` is A and `111` is D. Each shift moves the buffer left by the length of the code just read.

In mibz2 the buffer is 64 bits wide, not ten, and a refill tops it up long before it runs out.

So the buffer is just an integer and a few shifts. It isn't an array or a special piece of hardware, and the whole state is three numbers: `pos`, `buf` and `live`.

## 2\. Reading a code with a lookup table

In the figure, each symbol was found by matching the front of the buffer against the four codes. A simple decoder makes that match a bit at a time. It looks at the first bit: if it is 0, the symbol is A. If not, it looks at the second bit: if that is 0, the symbol is B. If not, it looks at the third. Each bit of a code costs a step, so the toy's ten bits take ten.

Fast Huffman decoders, mibz2 among them, replace those steps with a single lookup in a table made before decoding starts. The toy's longest code is three bits, so peek at the next three bits, whatever they are: `buf >> 61`, the peek from section 1. No code is longer than three bits, so the first code is always inside them. A shorter code leaves bits over, and those belong to the codes after it. Three bits have only eight possible values, and for each one we can work out in advance which codes it begins with:

| Next three bits | They begin with | Bits to skip |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| `000` | A, then A | 2 |
| `001` | A, then A | 2 |
| `010` | A, then B | 3 |
| `011` | A | 1 |
| `100` | B, then A | 3 |
| `101` | B | 2 |
| `110` | C | 3 |
| `111` | D | 3 |

The three bits, read as a number from 0 to 7, pick the row. Many rows hold more than one code: `010` is A's code `0` followed by B's code `10`. So a row can name two symbols, and one lookup then decodes both. The bits to skip are the lengths of the codes the row names, added up: A and B are 1 + 2 = 3 bits. When the bits after the first code don't make a whole code, the row names just the one symbol. `011` is an example: its `11` is only the start of C or D, so the row says A and skips one bit, and the next lookup sees the rest.

With this table the toy bits `0110100111` take four lookups instead of ten steps:

| Lookup | Next three bits | The row says | Bits to skip | Decoded so far |
| ---: | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| 1 | `011` | A | 1 | A |
| 2 | `110` | C | 3 | A C |
| 3 | `100` | B, then A | 3 | A C B A |
| 4 | `111` | D | 3 | A C B A D |

mibz2's table works the same way, at a larger size. A bzip2 code can be up to 20 bits long, and a table with a row for every 20-bit value would have about a million rows, 4 MB of them: far too large for the processor's nearest cache, which holds tens of kilobytes. So mibz2 peeks at ten bits instead. Its [table has 1,024 entries](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/src/block.rs#L45-L72>) of 32 bits each, 4 KB in all. Ten bits is a balance: with fewer, more codes would be too long for the table; with more, the table would outgrow the cache. Most of bzip2's codes are shorter than ten bits, so most entries are like the toy table's rows: one or two symbols, and how many bits to skip.

Ten bits can't settle every case, and two other kinds of entry cover the rest. A code longer than ten bits only begins in those ten bits. Its entry says so, and the decoder reads that code a bit at a time on a slower path, as libbzip2 (the reference bzip2 library) does. Long codes belong to the rarest symbols, so this path is seldom taken. And if no code at all begins with the ten bits, the file can't be valid bzip2, so that entry marks the block as corrupt.

The bit buffer, and one table lookup

Conceptual, drawn just after a refill. The divisions in the bar are bytes. A refill leaves 56 to 63 bits live; four lookups use at most 40 of them.

On the Wikidata sample, about 83% of lookups decode two symbols at once ([our counts](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-binding-census/serial-stages.md>)). A refill leaves at least 56 bits live, and four lookups use at most 40, so the fast loop refills, makes four lookups, then refills again.

One lookup is four steps:

1. take the top ten bits of `buf`;
2. load the table entry they index;
3. take the code's length from the entry;
4. shift `buf` left by that length.

Step 1 of the next lookup needs the result of step 4 of this one. However many instructions the processor could run at once, it can't start a lookup before the last one has finished its shift. So the time a lookup takes is the latency of this chain: the time each step waits for the one before it. Any step added to the chain adds its latency to every lookup.

## 3\. Where this sits in bzip2 and in mibz2

The bit buffer is the first thing a bzip2 decoder touches, because Huffman coding is the last of bzip2's four compression steps, and a decoder undoes them in reverse. bzip2 splits its input into blocks of up to 900 kB and compresses each block on its own:

How bzip2 compresses a block, and how a decoder undoes it

The four steps of bzip2's compression of one block. Each is undone in the opposite order, so a decoder starts with the Huffman codes.

The first step shortens any run of four or more identical bytes to four bytes and a count: bzip2's first run-length coding, RLE1. The second, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), reorders the block's bytes so that bytes which occur in similar contexts end up next to one another. [An earlier post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-02-revisiting-space-time-tradeoff-bwt-inversion/index.md>) works through it with the word `banana`. The reordered block is full of repeats, and the third step, move-to-front coding (MTF), turns repeats into small numbers. It keeps a list of byte values ordered by how recently each was seen, and replaces each byte by its position in that list: a byte that just appeared becomes 0, one seen a little earlier 1, and so on. Runs of zeros are then written compactly with two special symbols, RUNA and RUNB: the second run-length coding, RLE2.

What comes out is a sequence of symbols from a small alphabet: RUNA, RUNB, one symbol for each list position other than 0, and an end-of-block symbol. A block that uses 100 distinct byte values has an alphabet of 102 symbols. The block is mostly runs and small positions, so a few symbols are very common and most are rare. That imbalance is what the fourth step, Huffman coding, turns into fewer bits.

A bzip2 block uses not one code but several. The encoder builds between two and six code tables, each suited to a different mix of symbols. It switches between them every 50 symbols, picking for each group of 50 the table that codes it in the fewest bits. So the block begins with a header that tells the decoder how to follow along. It says which byte values occur in the block, which fixes the alphabet. It holds each code table, stored as the length of every symbol's code: the codes themselves follow from their lengths by a fixed rule, so the lengths are all that need storing. And it holds a selector for each group of 50 symbols, naming the table that group was coded with. bzip2's codes are at most 20 bits long.

A bzip2 block: the header, then its symbols in groups of 50

Simplified: the header also holds the block's checksum and where the inverse BWT starts. The selectors are themselves compactly coded. The table numbers shown are an example.

So reading a block's symbols means reading its header, then, for each group of 50, taking the table its selector names and reading codes with it one after another, until the end-of-block symbol. mibz2 builds a lookup table like section 2's for each of the block's code tables. Within a group of 50, its fast loop runs while at least eight of the group's symbols remain, since four lookups can decode eight; the group's last few symbols go through a slower loop.

mibz2 splits a decode between two kinds of thread, as the [post on block dispatch](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-01-block-dispatch/index.md>) describes. One thread, the scanner, reads the stream from the start. For each block it reads the header and decodes all the block's symbols. This can only be one thread working in order: a block's end is found only by reading up to its end-of-block symbol, and the next block begins straight after it. The scanner then hands each block's symbols to a worker, and several workers run at once. A worker does the rest. It undoes the move-to-front coding and RLE2 together, inverts the Burrows–Wheeler transform in two parts (it builds a table, then walks it), then expands RLE1 and checks the block's CRC, a checksum stored in its header.

Where Huffman decoding sits in mibz2

Measured: the base build's one-thread stage costs on the Intel Xeon 8370C runner, in cycles per byte of output at the runner's reported clock, 11.28 c/B in all (the second benchmark run of section 9). At one thread the stages run one after another on one CPU; at four, the scanner's thread runs beside the workers.

At one thread every stage runs on the same CPU, one after another, so the scanner's share of the time is its share of the decode: on the Intel runner, 1.19 of 11.28 cycles per output byte, about 10.5%. At four threads the scanner runs alongside the workers. All four of the runner's CPUs are then busy, so the scanner's CPU time still costs wall time, at about a quarter of its own rate. These shares come from [a census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-binding-census.md>) we took of what limits the decoder's speed on CI's runners, stage by stage. Its journal entry calls it the binding census, after the resource that binds each stage: the one whose limit it runs into first, whether that is the processor's instructions, memory, or waiting on another thread.

## 4\. What the census found

The [census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-binding-census.md>) asked what limits today's decoder on CI's runners. One of its lines of inquiry took the stages that run in sequence, and read the scanner's machine code. In the four-lookup loop, each lookup ended by storing `buf` to memory, and the next began by loading it back.

A store followed by a load from the same address costs few instructions, and it doesn't wait for the cache: the processor hands the stored value straight to the load. That hand-over is called store-to-load forwarding. It still takes time, about 4–5 cycles on Intel's Ice Lake cores such as the 8370C's, and here it was part of the lookup chain. The census estimated a lookup at about 13–15 cycles with the reload, against about 8–9 with `buf` in a register. These figures are estimates, from the listing, the instruction counts and the measured cycles, not counts of events: CI's runners expose no hardware performance counters.

One lookup's chain, before and after

Estimated, not measured: the census's reading of the listing for Ice Lake. The measured saving is in section 9.

Across the four runner models the census measured, the scanner took 6.9–10.3% of the four-thread wall time (7–10% in its summary) and 11–14% of the one-thread time. It estimated that removing the forward would recover 0.5–4.1% of the four-thread wall, and 1.7–5.6% at one thread, and called it "The cheapest and most certain mechanism on this front."

## 5\. Why the compiler kept the buffer in memory

Nothing in the Rust asked for a store. The loop calls the reader's methods, which are small and marked `#[inline(always)]`, so their bodies are compiled into the loop. Two calls are not inlined: the slow path for codes longer than ten bits, and the slow refill near the end of the input. Both are marked `#[cold]`, and on master before the change both took the reader by reference, as `&mut Bits` ([`decode_entry_slow(e, br)`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/66a9dedd/src/block.rs#L343>), [`refill_slow(&mut self)`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/66a9dedd/src/bits.rs#L49-L50>)).

Passing a reference to a function that isn't inlined lets the reader's address escape. As far as the compiler (LLVM) can tell, that function might read or change the reader, so the reader's fields have to be in memory, at that address, whenever such a call can happen. The calls are rare, but one can happen at any lookup. A second constraint follows from the first. The loop writes each decoded symbol through a pointer into the output, `out[n]`, and once the reader's address has escaped, LLVM must assume such a write might change it too. So it loads `buf` again after the writes ([registration](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-huffman-register.md>)).

This is one of the four steps, from master before the change, as the [archived listing](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-huffman-register/asm-excerpt.txt>) gives it (the bench binary, rustc 1.99.0, in Intel syntax: destination first). `r15` holds the reader's address:

```text
ab240  mov    rsi,QWORD PTR [r15+0x18]                              bits.rs:74
ab244  mov    rax,rsi                                               bits.rs:74
ab247  shr    rax,0x36                                              bits.rs:74
ab24b  mov    edx,DWORD PTR [r9+rax*4]                              block.rs:326
ab24f  mov    eax,edx                                               block.rs:331
ab251  shr    eax,0xb                                               block.rs:331
ab254  and    eax,0x3                                               block.rs:331
ab257  je     ab450 <mibz2::block::read_item+0x12c0>                block.rs:331
ab25d  mov    ecx,edx                                               block.rs:332
ab25f  and    ecx,0x1f                                              block.rs:332
ab262  shl    rsi,cl                                                bits.rs:81
ab265  mov    QWORD PTR [r15+0x18],rsi                              bits.rs:81
ab269  sub    DWORD PTR [r15+0x20],ecx                              bits.rs:82
```

| Instructions | What they do |
| --- | --- |
| `mov rsi,QWORD PTR [r15+0x18]` | load `buf` back from the reader in memory: the forward |
| `mov`, `shr rax,0x36` | its top ten bits (a shift right by 54), the index |
| `mov edx,DWORD PTR [r9+rax*4]` | load the table entry |
| `mov`, `shr`, `and`, `je` | the entry's symbol count: none means the slow path |
| `mov`, `and ecx,0x1f` | the bits to consume, the entry's low five bits |
| `shl rsi,cl` | consume them |
| `mov QWORD PTR [r15+0x18],rsi` | store `buf` back to the reader |
| `sub DWORD PTR [r15+0x20],ecx` | take them from `live`, in memory |

Over a four-lookup iteration the registration counts five stores and three reloads of `buf`, and four read-modify-writes of `live` in memory: about one forward on the chain per lookup.

## 6\. The change: the state as a value

The change, [\#204](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/204>), moves the three fields into a small struct that can be copied, `Reg`, and has the loop hold one in a local variable ([`src/bits.rs`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/src/bits.rs#L6-L24>)):

```rust
pub struct Bits<'a> {
    data: &'a [u8],
    r: Reg,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
pub(crate) struct Reg {
    pos: usize,
    buf: u64,
    live: u32,
}
```

- **The logic moves unchanged.** Refill, peek and skip become methods of `Reg`.
- **The cold paths take the state by value** and return the state after: `decode_entry_slow(&self, e: u32, r: Reg, data: &[u8]) -> (Result<u16, ErrorKind>, Reg)`, and `refill_slow(mut self, data: &[u8]) -> Reg`. No call receives the state's address, so the compiler can keep its fields in registers, and pass them into a cold call and back like any other arguments.
- **The loop works on a copy.** [`read_item`](<https://docs.rs/mibz2/0.2.2/mibz2/block/fn.read_item.html>) takes the state out of the reader before the symbol loop, with `let (data, mut r) = br.parts();`, and writes it back once, with `br.set(r)`, on every way out of the loop.
- **The loop is rotated.** The refill moves from the top of the four-lookup loop to its foot. With the refill at the top, the state was carried from one pass of the loop to the next in memory, which cost a store and a reload every refill. The refills happen at the same points as before:

```rust
if left >= 2 * STEPS {
    r.refill(data);
    loop {
        for _ in 0..STEPS {
            step!(true);
        }
        if left < 2 * STEPS {
            break;
        }
        r.refill(data);
    }
}
```

`Bits`'s public methods keep their signatures, and the block header is parsed as before. This is the same step in the new build, from the same listing:

```text
ab582  shr    rcx,0x36                                              bits.rs:71
ab586  mov    rdx,QWORD PTR [rsp+0x28]                              bits.rs:71
ab58b  mov    edx,DWORD PTR [rdx+rcx*4]                             block.rs:335
ab58e  mov    r9d,edx                                               block.rs:340
ab591  shr    r9d,0xb                                               block.rs:340
ab595  and    r9d,0x3                                               block.rs:340
ab599  je     ab853 <mibz2::block::read_item+0x1643>                block.rs:340
ab59f  mov    ecx,edx                                               block.rs:341
ab5a1  and    ecx,0x1f                                              block.rs:341
ab5a4  shl    rdi,cl                                                bits.rs:78
```

`buf` is in `rdi`, and the step ends at `shl rdi,cl`, with no store. The loop's only stores now are the symbol writes. It still loads values that don't change during the loop from the stack, such as the table's address (`[rsp+0x28]`). Nothing in the loop stores to them, so those loads wait on no forward, and their addresses don't depend on the chain.

## 7\. What was predicted, before any timing

Before any CI timing, the change was registered: its mechanism, the measurements that need no timing, a prediction and a decision rule, committed before any CI timing of the branch ([registration](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-huffman-register.md>)).

Instruction counts from callgrind, which counts every instruction a program executes, on the bench corpus:

| Instructions | Before | After | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Per four-lookup iteration | 153.8 | 144.8 | −5.9% |
| The whole scanner | 746.2 million | 727.4 million | −2.5% |
| Per byte of output | 3.56 | 3.47 | −2.5% |

The forwards also leave the lookup chain: four in each iteration, about 0.94 a lookup on average. The registration then estimated the saving at about \\(F\\) cycles a lookup, where \\(F\\) is the store-to-load forwarding latency on the runner, plus the 2.5% of the scanner's instructions:

| Figure | Predicted |
| --- | --- |
| Scanner stage, one thread, Intel Ice Lake (8370C), \\(F\\) about 4–5 | 15–25% faster |
| Scanner stage, one thread, AMD and Intel Golden Cove (8573C) | 0–25% faster |
| Wikidata wall, one thread, Intel | 1.5–3.5% faster |
| Wikidata wall, four threads | 0.5–2.5% faster |
| MTF, table build, walk, RLE1, CRC | unchanged: their code is untouched |

The AMD range is wide because some cores can rename a store and a later load of the same address: they recognise the pair and hand the value over without the forward's latency. Whether CI's AMD runners do that for this code wasn't known.

The decision rule had four parts:

- **Correctness, required:** CI green, and the same bytes on every corpus in every bench run.
- **Benefit, required:** in at least one run, the Wikidata one-thread wall or CPU faster beyond noise, or the one-thread scanner stage faster beyond noise with the whole decoder's one-thread point estimate not slower; and the same figure not slower in the other run.
- **Refutation:** a scanner cut under 10% on an Intel runner, or any other stage moving beyond noise, would refute the mechanism.
- **No harm, required:** a wall figure flagged slower is settled by one more run on the same head. Flagged again, the rule fails. At most three runs, with each run's CPU named.

## 8\. Is it still the same decoder?

The change has to give exactly the same symbols, and fail in exactly the same way on corrupt input. Before timing:

- **A differential** ran master's `bits.rs` and `block.rs` against the new ones, outside the repository, on 52 files and 164,076 cases of intact and mutated blocks. It compared 9.15 billion symbols, every case was identical, and all 11 error kinds that can be reached were exercised.
- **A scanner-only driver** gives the same 24,979,299 symbols, with the same hash.
- **New tests:**

  - the reader's state stepped as the loop steps it, compared with the input's bits;
  - 4,000 fully written blocks, with real or corrupt codes up to 20 bits, bit flips and cuts. Each is compared with a reference that decodes one lookup at a time: the symbols, the error, the end bit and whether it read past the input;
  - 300 corrupted level-1 streams, compared with libbzip2.

In both benchmark runs, every corpus decoded to the same bytes with both builds, and CI passed.

## 9\. What the benchmark measured

The CI benchmark decodes every corpus with the base build and the PR's build in alternating order, ten paired rounds a run. It runs on a GitHub-hosted runner with four virtual CPUs: two physical cores, each running two hardware threads (SMT siblings). The CPU model varies from run to run. It ran twice on \#204's final head, 53cc38db: once on an AMD EPYC 9V74 (Zen 4) and once on an Intel Xeon 8370C (Ice Lake). Each change below is the PR's build over the base: the geometric mean of the rounds' paired ratios, with its 95% interval in percent beneath it. Negative is faster. "Wall" is the elapsed time to decode the Wikidata sample.

| Figure | Predicted | Intel 8370C | AMD 9V74 |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Scanner, one thread | Intel: −15% to −25%<br>AMD: 0 to −25% | −12.9%<br>(−13.9, −11.9) | −5.0%<br>(−6.3, −3.6) |
| Scanner, cycles a byte |  | 1.19 → 1.04 | 1.18 → 1.12 |
| Wall, one thread | Intel: −1.5% to −3.5% | −2.7%<br>(−4.3, −1.1) | \+1.0%<br>(−0.7, +2.6) |
| Wall, two threads | none | −2.5%<br>(−4.6, −0.3) | −1.3%<br>(−4.0, +1.5) |
| Wall, four threads | −0.5% to −2.5% | −1.3%<br>(−5.6, +3.3) | −0.3%<br>(−3.2, +2.6) |
| Other stages | no change | none moved | none moved |

**On Intel, the stage cut missed its prediction.** It was 12.9%, against 15–25%. That is above the 10% the rule set as the refutation, so a saving of the predicted kind was there, but smaller than the model estimated. By our arithmetic, which is derived rather than measured, the stage saved 0.15 cycles per output byte at the runner's reported clock. At the census's 0.0646 lookups per byte, that is about 2.3 cycles a lookup, against the 4–5 the model estimated. With no hardware counters on CI, the benchmark can't say which part of the model was wrong.

**On AMD, the cut was smaller still, as the mechanism allowed.** It was 5.0%, about 0.9 cycles a lookup by the same arithmetic, and inside the 0–25% registered for a core that may rename the forward. That fits renaming, but no counter shows it.

**One-thread decoding got faster on Intel, and no change was detected on AMD.** On Intel the whole one-thread decode was 2.7% faster, inside the predicted 1.5–3.5%. The scanner's own saving explains about half of that point estimate: 0.15 of 11.28 cycles per byte, 1.3%. The rest is within the noise of the other stages, none of which moved beyond noise. On AMD the one-thread decode was +1.0% (−0.7%, +2.6%), with no change detected either way.

**One run's interval understates how much a figure moves between runs.** Each interval above describes the spread between one run's ten rounds. A/A controls, benchmark runs on merges that left the decoder alone, show the one-thread figure also moving by about 0.7% from run to run. With that spread added, the Intel one-thread result is −2.7% (−4.8%, −0.6%): still faster.

**At four threads, no change was detected on either runner.** The prediction, 0.5–2.5%, is smaller than the benchmark can resolve at four threads, where the intervals here are 6–9 points wide. At four threads the scanner thread's CPU time fell from 0.15 to 0.12 seconds on Intel and from 0.09 to 0.08 on AMD, out of about 1.6 and 1.1 seconds in all. No figure was flagged slower in either run.

Under its rule, the change passed. Correctness held. The Intel run showed the benefit, with the one-thread wall and CPU both faster beyond noise, and the AMD run's same figure was not slower. The Intel stage cut was above the refutation threshold, no other stage moved, and nothing was flagged as a harm.

PR \#204 met its registered decision rule and was merged on 5 November 2026, as 264ae5bb.

## 10\. What it shows

The Huffman codes, the tables and the bits consumed are the same as before, and the scanner runs only 2.5% fewer instructions. What changed is the chain each lookup waits on. On Intel, 2.5% fewer instructions gave a 12.9% shorter stage, because what was removed, the forward, was part of that chain. Elsewhere in mibz2 the opposite has happened: in the [post on memory-level parallelism](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-02-memory-level-parallelism/#4-cutting-instructions-helped-the-walk-but-not-four-worker-throughput>), removing a third of the walk's instructions made no difference to four workers. An instruction count predicts time where the instructions sit on the critical path.

The pattern is easy to recreate. A loop carries a value from one iteration to the next, and also passes a reference to it to a function that isn't inlined, such as a cold path that takes `&mut self`. The value's address escapes, so it lives in memory, and every iteration costs a store and a reload. Passing the state by value and taking it back keeps it in registers. The census found two other store-to-load chains, in MTF's list and in the table build's byte cursors. Those are different: there the data lives in memory because the algorithm keeps it there. The bit buffer had no reason to be in memory, only a reference that let it escape.

A decode that takes more symbols a lookup is being prototyped separately, and would combine with this change. The census estimated that a wider table, now, would take at most about another 10% off the scanner, which is under 1% of the four-thread wall.

- the listings: [`asm-excerpt.txt`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-huffman-register/asm-excerpt.txt>), and the instruction counts per address in [`cg/`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/264ae5bb/docs/journal/2026-11-05-huffman-register/cg>);

# Call on mibz2: cutting instructions from bzip2 decoding with an autonomous swarm

Each of four agents does one part of the research. A GitHub doorbell lets them hand work to each other directly, without me acting as their message bus.

4 November 2026, revised 5 November · 20 min read · [Meta](<#10-where-it-stands>)

[The last post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/2026-11-04-compact30-constructor/index.md>) was about compact30, my effort to give the decoder's navigation table a smaller representation. Four agents did the research behind it, but until today they could only work together if I copied each one's messages to the next by hand.

This post is about how they now pass work between themselves through the repository: who does what, how a message gets from one agent to another, and what I learnt from running it: an afternoon, a first full cycle, and then a first night with nobody watching. That night produced real gains, and one ordinary mistake that taught me the most: a message can be sent, and recorded as sent, without ever being delivered.

## 1\. A tale of four agents

The Coordinator is Claude Code. It writes the code for each change in the plan, compiles it, runs the tests and keeps the results. When a result is ready it posts a checkpoint: a comment saying what was built and which commit holds the evidence.

The Guardian and the Researcher both read every checkpoint, looking for different things. The Guardian checks the result against the research charter: which gates it passes, what work can follow, and what has to come to me. The Researcher looks at the reasoning: whether the argument holds, whether something else explains the numbers, whether there's a better direction, and whether the Guardian has got it right.

The Optimiser works on the instruction counts themselves. It reads the source, the compiled listings and the execution counts, works out transformations that remove instructions, and keeps the ledger of what each one saves. Its proposals are what the Coordinator builds next.

The Guardian, the Researcher and the Optimiser all run Astra, a model I use through ChatGPT, each as a ChatGPT Work task with its own reasoning-effort setting. What separates them is what they're responsible for, not the model. The roles, and the branch each one owns, are written down in [ROLES.md](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/09e4ef6cb7c845781b0a2cb0d2c1a4fe6f33fe47/docs/journal/compact30-channel/ROLES.md>). To reproduce the setup, these are the settings:

| Role | Runs as | Model | Reasoning effort | Started by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinator | Claude Code session | Claude, as configured for the session | High | a subscription to the shared channel, \#145, and the PRs it follows |
| Guardian | ChatGPT Work task, *Compact30 (W) Guardian* | Astra | Extra High | a new comment in its inbox, \#161 |
| Optimiser | ChatGPT Work task, *Compact30 (W) Optimiser* | Astra | Ultra | a new comment in its inbox, \#160 |
| Researcher | ChatGPT Work task, *Compact30 (W) Researcher* | Astra | Extra High | a new comment in its inbox, \#162 |

Each Astra agent's instructions live in the repository as its **agent spec**, beside ROLES.md. [SPEC.md](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/5fbdd2c9c09f753282d9c5608ef236657837efa9/docs/journal/compact30-channel/SPEC.md>) holds what the three have in common: how a run goes, from the inbox comment to the receipt, the work and the review, and the reasoning behind that design. `SPEC.OPTIMIZER.md`, `SPEC.GUARDIAN.md` and `SPEC.RESEARCHER.md` each say only what that agent's work is. A task's prompt in ChatGPT is a single sentence pointing at its two files at one pinned commit. So an agent's behaviour changes only by a commit to its spec and a new pin, both of which stay in the record. SPEC.md also holds the one command that loads a new pin into all three tasks.

The team: three Astra agents and Claude Code, joined by one repository

Claude Code builds each change and posts a checkpoint. The Guardian checks it against the rules and the Researcher checks the reasoning, while the Optimiser hunts for more instructions to cut. All four work through the same repository.

## 2\. Every result is a commit

A checkpoint points at a commit, never at a branch, because a branch keeps moving. The commit holds the source and its baseline, the compiled listings, the toolchain, the test records, the execution counts and the arithmetic that ties them together. Reports and scripts go in files, and the comment links to them.

That lets a reader check a claim rather than take it on trust. If the Optimiser predicts that a change will remove a load from the inner loop, the checkpoint shows whether the compiled code actually lost it, whether setup got more expensive, whether a caller picked up a spill, and how often each path runs.

Each agent writes only to its own branch: the Coordinator to the implementation branches, the others to their reports, decision logs and ledgers. Every file has one author, and a review never edits the code it reviews. Each agent also keeps its working state on its branch, which is why a fresh run can pick up exactly where the last one stopped.

## 3\. Comments as messages, events as the clock

The agents talk in comments on pull requests. Each comment starts with a short header:

```
FROM: coordinator
TO: guardian
RE: prototype 2 @ 29dd071f8787a28560a7a081fd7ac0ef13991466
TYPE: CHECKPOINT
```

`FROM:` names the sender, since every agent posts from the same account. `TO:` records who it's for, `RE:` pins the commit, and `TYPE:` says what kind of message it is. The [protocol](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/09e4ef6cb7c845781b0a2cb0d2c1a4fe6f33fe47/docs/journal/compact30-channel/PROTOCOL.md>) has six types:

| Type | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `CHECKPOINT` | a result at a pinned commit, ready to assess |
| `REVIEW` | an assessment, with its evidence on the sender's branch |
| `PROPOSAL` | an idea to consider; not permission to build it |
| `DECISION` | a decision the sender is allowed to make |
| `ACK` | what was received, and what happens next |
| `ESCALATION` | something only I can decide |

The messages travel through draft PRs that are never merged. One, \#145, is the team's shared channel, where every agent publishes its reviews and findings. Each Astra agent also has a quiet inbox of its own, where it receives work: [\#160](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/160>) for the Optimiser, [\#161](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/161>) for the Guardian and [\#162](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/162>) for the Researcher. Each experiment has a PR of its own too.

Here is what that looks like on GitHub. Every comment comes from my account, `lmmx`, and the small badge on the avatar shows which app posted it: Claude's mark for the Coordinator, ChatGPT's for the Astra agents. The header is the only thing that says which agent wrote it.

Three agents, one account: a checkpoint from the Coordinator, the Guardian's review of it, and the independent reviewer's report, all on \#145.

**Read the whole exchange**

The originals: [the checkpoint](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6632963394>), [the Guardian's review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6633274082>) and [the independent review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6634356048>).

A new comment is also what wakes the agents up. Each Astra agent is a Work task subscribed to new comments on its own inbox and nothing else, so the filtering happens before a run starts. The inbox is the address: every comment in it is for its agent. The Coordinator posts each checkpoint to the inbox of every agent that should act on it, so a checkpoint for the Guardian and the Researcher is two comments, one in each inbox. Each run fetches its comment, reads from the header who sent it and what kind of message it is, and does the work. It commits a receipt to its own branch first, then its progress as it goes, and publishes its `REVIEW` on \#145. The Coordinator subscribes to \#145, so a reply reaches it within seconds.

This keeps each agent's attention on its own work. An inbox carries only messages meant for its agent, so the other agents' reviews, CI results and pull requests never start a run there. An investigation that takes a quarter of an hour runs to the end undisturbed, and everything it finds still comes back to one place.

One cycle: a checkpoint to two inboxes, two reviews, the next step

Each arrow is a pull-request comment. A checkpoint goes to the inbox of each agent that should act on it, and each review comes back on the shared channel, \#145, where it wakes the Coordinator. No Astra agent polls, and nothing goes through me.

## 4\. A receipt for every message

Before doing any work, a run checks its cursor: a file on its branch listing the comments it has already handled. Then it loads what it needs, does the work, posts its result, and adds the comment to the cursor. If several comments arrive at once, each is checked separately. For technical reviews the key also includes the PR, the candidate's commit and a hash of the evidence, so a repeated request can't be mistaken for a revised candidate.

The cursor answers "have I already done this?" for the next run, and it lets me trace every message to what came of it. Two cases it doesn't cover on its own: a run that posts its result but stops before saving the cursor, and two runs of the same agent at once. Recording the result's commit and comment ID makes the first recoverable. I haven't tested either case yet.

A review queue in the repository lists what is waiting on whom. Work that depends on a pending review waits for it, and everything else goes ahead.

## 5\. What a message can authorise

The [research charter](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/09e4ef6cb7c845781b0a2cb0d2c1a4fe6f33fe47/docs/journal/2026-11-04-compact30-research-charter.md>) sets out what is authorised: the representation, the reference builder, the baselines, and for each prototype a registered design, acceptance criteria and a fixed number of attempts. Inside that, the Coordinator implements and tests without asking me, and the Guardian makes the decisions delegated to it. Anything that widens the work, such as a new prototype, new unsafe code or integration into production, needs me.

So the rule is: **a message in the repository can narrow what's allowed, but only I can widen it, and only in the Coordinator's session.** A finding can put a prototype on hold. A proposal can suggest something new, but nobody acts on it unless it's already authorised or I say so. Charter amendments are approved the same way, and every review cites the charter revision it applied.

This matters because every agent posts through my GitHub account, as the screenshots in section 3 show, so `FROM: guardian` names a role without proving who wrote it. The repository also limits who can comment, and the channel PRs are locked. Before the Guardian went live it was tested on exactly this: it was sent forged requests for things only I can approve, and turned both of them down.

## 6\. Reproducible, independent review

The main figure for compact30 counts the instructions executed by the whole table builder and everything it calls, weighted by how often each path runs on the corpus. Setup, fallbacks, callers, callees and extra memory operations all count, and a saving that only moves work elsewhere is charged where the work lands. Correctness needs its own evidence: byte-identical output against the reference builder, safety arguments for release builds, Miri checks for undefined behaviour, and mutation tests that break an invariant on purpose to show the tests notice.

Reviewers treat the implementer's write-up as a set of claims to check, and work the figures out again from the source, listings, counters and test records. Before prototypes are combined, the charter also asks for one review by an agent that has seen none of the discussion. The ongoing Researcher can't do that: it has followed the work, and it suggested some of the tests. So it started a fresh helper whose only input was a pinned brief, and recorded exactly what that helper was given. A fresh run on its own wouldn't have been enough: the point is that the reviewer never saw the discussion.

## 7\. What running it looks like

The first afternoon taught me what to expect. Mostly it comes down to patience, and knowing where to look.

Runs are long and quiet. A Work task can spend anything from a minute to a quarter of an hour on one message: the Researcher's revision of this post took about sixteen minutes, most of it reading the record and testing drafts on simulated readers. Between runs, a task's page just shows that it has worked. That means it is waiting for its next comment, not that it has stalled.

Each run has room to finish. Its inbox receives nothing else while it works, and the Coordinator sends an agent its next brief only after the last one has been published. A run commits a receipt first and its progress as it goes, so if one ever stops part-way, a short resume in its inbox picks it up from its last commit.

Watch the repository, not the task pages. Every message ends in a receipt: a cursor commit on the agent's own branch, then a `REVIEW` on \#145 that cites it. A message with a receipt but no review is in progress. One with neither, while the agent's branch is still, gets a resume, once.

When an agent starts a helper of its own, I ask it to keep its run open until the helper has published, and to record both the launch and the result. The independent reviewer was set up this way, with its settings and inputs written to the repository before it began.

Keeping things moving is the Coordinator's job. When the record goes quiet, it checks the receipts, works out who has the next step, and posts the checkpoint that starts it. No Astra agent runs on a timer. On the first night the Coordinator's session had one, waking it every quarter of an hour to re-read its mode note; otherwise it too wakes on events. Nothing sits waiting for me.

## 8\. What a shared message board got wrong

The design above is the second one. The first put every message on one PR, \#145, and let every agent read the whole board. It looked simple, and over the evening of 4 November it went wrong in five ways.

**Every event woke every agent.** Each Work task started on any comment in the repository, fetched it, and decided for itself whether it was addressed. A review from one agent, a CI result, a preview bot's comment or a merged PR started a run in all three, and nearly all of those runs ended straight away with "not for me".

**A new run displaced the one in progress, and nothing caught the loss.** The automation keeps one current run per task. When an event arrived while a long run was still working, the new run took its place, and the earlier one stopped without an error, a partial result or any record of what it had read. There was no dead-letter queue to catch it. That evening six briefs to the Optimiser went this way. Each run started and began reading, and each was overtaken within two or three minutes: by the other agents' reviews of the same checkpoint, by a bot, or by a merge. None of them committed anything. From outside, it simply looked as if the Optimiser had gone quiet.

**A dead-letter queue** is the post office's room for letters that can be neither delivered nor returned. A message system keeps one so that a failed message is set aside where someone can find it. The first design had none, so a displaced run left no trace.

**Routing by header was brittle.** Each agent decided from `TO:` and `TYPE:` lines whether a comment was meant for it, sometimes by exact string. A checkpoint naming two agents had to be worded exactly right for both, and a message that failed the test was dropped without trace.

**Noise spent the wakes.** Every one of those runs counts against a task's use of the automation, and on a busy board most of them went on comments the agent then ignored.

**The connector added friction.** The Astra agents reach GitHub through ChatGPT's GitHub connector, not a shell with `git` as the Coordinator has. Their runs hit errors such as a call missing its repository argument, or "no usable execution environment". Each was recoverable, but each one lengthened a run, and a longer run was more likely to be overtaken. The task settings also can't show their subscriptions back, so the only way to confirm where an agent listens is to watch where it wakes.

The inboxes fix all five. An agent's subscription now covers its own inbox and nothing else, so the only events it sees are its own work, and there's nothing to filter by header. With nothing else arriving, a long run finishes. A receipt is committed first, so a stopped run leaves a trace that a one-line resume can pick up. The wake budget goes on work. And each agent's instructions are an agent spec at a pinned commit, so what each one does can be read in the repository, not inferred from a task page.

They also bring a failure of their own: when the address is the mechanism, a message sent to the wrong address fails without a sound.

## 9\. Trust, but verify

In the inbox design a comment in \#160 wakes the Optimiser, and the same comment on \#145 wakes nobody but the Coordinator. That is what keeps each agent's attention on its own work.

**A checkpoint that looked dispatched.** On the night of 4–5 November the Coordinator ran the research with nobody watching. At 06:03 UTC it sent the Optimiser a brief in [\#160](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/160#issuecomment-6651023083>), and the review came back at 06:12. At 07:38 it posted the next brief, reporting that the fused post-walk pass (\#183) had been rejected, to [\#145](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6652503445>) instead, and at 08:21 an addendum to the [same place](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6653242752>). Both had the right header and the right `TO:`, the first pinned its commit, and GitHub accepted both. Then the Coordinator waited for a review that couldn't come.

I found it at my morning check, by looking at what had happened rather than at what had been reported:

- the two comments were on \#145;
- the Optimiser's inbox had received nothing since 06:03;
- its task's run history showed no run since 06:12.

The Coordinator had intended to dispatch an assignment, and GitHub had confirmed that a comment was posted. Neither fact established that the Optimiser had received the work. Correctness of intent and correctness of record both held. Correctness of effect didn't.

**The recovery didn't need me as a message bus.** I pointed out the discrepancy. The Coordinator re-sent both messages as one checkpoint in the [right inbox](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/160#issuecomment-6653416078>) at 08:31, said so in that message, and [logged the mistake](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/commit/10a8af6e>) in the channel log. The Optimiser's run started from that comment, its cursor marked the brief finished, and its [review](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6653724458>) came back at 08:48, proposing the next build. The work had sat at the wrong address for 53 minutes. Once the error was visible, the system recovered by its own means: a corrected checkpoint in the right inbox, and a review back on \#145.

**A guard that guarded nothing.** At 08:26 the Coordinator squash-merged [\#185](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/185>), naming the commit it expected as the PR's head, so that the merge would be refused if anything had been pushed after CI tested it. It passed `c32ba5db3b0f…`: the first eight characters of the real head, `c32ba5db9df8…`, padded out to forty with characters it made up. The merge went through anyway. The right commit merged, since nothing had been pushed after it. But the check the Coordinator relied on to merge only the commit CI had tested had checked nothing. A short prefix had been refused on an earlier merge, which was why the check seemed to work. The Coordinator noticed when it read the head back, fourteen seconds after merging.

Both mistakes have the same shape: an agent's report of its own action is a claim, like any other claim in this project, and it needs an observable effect behind it. The research already works that way, since every result pins a commit that a reviewer can check. The coordination didn't. The answer isn't for me to watch more closely. It's small, deterministic checks on the few actions whose effects matter, so that a route is computed rather than remembered, and a posted message or a merge is read back rather than assumed. The Coordinator still runs them on itself, so they narrow this failure rather than remove it.

| Check | What it compares | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `route` | an assignment's destination: the role's inbox, or, while it is busy, staged on \#145 as `TYPE: QUEUED` | required before each assignment; none posted since it landed |
| `verify` | the posted comment, read back by ID: its PR, its header, the only assignment in flight | required after each; replayed, it fails the 07:38 misroute and passes the 08:31 dispatch |
| `head-sha` | a merge's expected head against the PR's exact 40-character head, before the merge and, with `--merged`, after it | before: since \#186; after: since \#190; rejects \#185's SHA |
| `audit` | every message on \#145 and the inboxes since the inbox cutover | in use at each session start and wake-up; in its tests, the 120 comments up to 08:49 give exactly the two misroutes |
| the tripwire | each new comment on \#145 or an inbox, checked by a GitHub Actions workflow that runs independently of the Coordinator | in use as a record: a failing check on \#145's head until the next commit there; no event for the Coordinator |

The first four are one stdlib script, [`coord.py`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/b773431366def44a1214a0c42a6b0fe0b606d870/.github/coordination/coord.py>), added in [\#186](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/186>), and the repository's `CLAUDE.md` says when the Coordinator runs each one. The script only reads: it never posts, edits or deletes. The tripwire can't stop a misroute, only report it. It never edits, moves or re-posts a comment, and never dispatches anything itself, so it can't create work of its own.

**QUEUED** marks work that must wait its turn. While a role is busy, its next brief is set down on \#145, and the Coordinator carries it to the role's inbox once the role is free.

The tripwire needed the same treatment as everything else. A workflow started by a comment runs only from master, so each version could be tested only after it merged. The Coordinator tested each one with a deliberate, labelled misroute on \#145, and each test found something that the code and its unit tests hadn't.

**A check run** is one line in a pull request's list of checks. GitHub gathers a workflow's runs into a suite, and the Coordinator hears only when a whole suite finishes.

- **The first** was classified correctly, and then its warning couldn't be posted: \#145 is locked, and the Actions bot can't comment on a locked conversation.
- **The second** raised a failing check run on \#145 instead. The check showed red, but nothing woke the Coordinator.
- **The third** made its check run start in progress and then fail, to reopen the suite. The suite stayed green and sent no event: a GitHub Actions suite follows its workflow run, not check runs added to it.

One of these tests refuted a claim that had already merged: \#188 went in saying its check run would wake the Coordinator, and its test showed within a minute that it didn't.

So the tripwire is a record, not an alarm. It leaves a failing check on \#145's head commit, independently of the Coordinator, and the check shows on \#145 until the next commit to the channel branch. The Coordinator finds the misroute itself, by running `audit` at the start of each session and every time it wakes.

The merge guard needed the same treatment, and got it only while this post was being checked. A reviewing agent pointed out that GitHub refuses a mismatched head, and it does: a merge of [\#139](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/139>) was refused with a 409 on 2 November. The guess had never reached GitHub. The merge tool takes the expected head as `expectedHeadSha`, and the Coordinator had been passing it as `sha`, a name the tool doesn't have and drops without a word. The prefix refused earlier had met the tool's own format check, under the right name. Read back, eight merges between 02:12 and 09:36 had passed the head that way, among them an earlier guess on [\#167](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/167>) and four merges made after `head-sha` existed. Each merged its PR's final head, so nothing wrong landed, but none was checked. `head-sha` had checked the value; nothing had checked that the value reached the merge. [\#190](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/190>) adds the missing step: the SHA goes in `expectedHeadSha`, and `head-sha --merged` reads the merge back and passes only if the PR merged at exactly that head.

Three gaps remain. The checks are run by the Coordinator on itself: `CLAUDE.md` says when, but nothing outside its session makes it run them, and the tripwire, the one check outside it, can only leave a mark. The Coordinator can't see the Astra tasks' run history; it infers a run from receipts in the cursors, which `route` reads. And a brief that was delivered but never started, one with no receipt half an hour after it was posted, is still caught only by the Coordinator noticing a quiet record (section 7). A mechanical check for it would close the loop from sent to started. It isn't built.

## 10\. Where it stands

The [channel log](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/abc14cc284bb971142cf5347bf8072014bc5a37a/docs/journal/compact30-channel/log.md>) records each step. The trigger was first tested on the Guardian: a comment started its run, it published an assessment, and its review woke the Coordinator. The first real cycle followed on [a checkpoint](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6632963394>) covering two prototypes. The Guardian's run started nine seconds after it was posted, checked both prototypes against the gates, and [asked](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/145#issuecomment-6633274082>) for the independent review.

That review came back while this post was being finished. The Researcher launched the isolated reviewer, and its [report](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/153>) arrived as a comment on the channel. Both prototypes pass on correctness and safety, and so does v3's finaliser. Two things need fixing before anything is combined: some changed paths still need their own execution counters, and both prototypes remove the same instruction, so their savings overlap. That is the next checkpoint.

On 5 November the redesigned setup ran its first full round:

- **The Optimiser** ranked the whole decoder's candidates from its inbox. It put P87, a production-shaped change that writes the walk's output over a buffer it has already consumed, first.
- **The Coordinator** built P87 and registered a decision rule before measuring it.
- **The Guardian and the Researcher** reviewed that rule from their inboxes before the benchmark finished. The Guardian's review changed it.
- **The change** made the four-worker Wikidata decode 2.2% faster in one run, and favourable but inconclusive in a second, with 6.8% less memory and no slower row. It [merged](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/164>).

Then all three agents took their next assignment under the new specs:

- each woke only on its own inbox;
- each committed a receipt within a minute or two, and published its review on \#145;
- the Guardian also moved itself onto its current operating spec.

The first reviews under the new design corrected the Coordinator's write-up before it was published.

The rest of that night was the first long test. At 02:52 UTC, at my instruction, the Coordinator's [mode note](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/e8b136fed714b54d79b7fa9914b70f815d2a4d8a/docs/journal/compact30-channel/MODE.md>) was amended to tell it to fan out hard on the hard research, and to do tests, CI and documentation itself rather than spend agents on them. From then until my morning check it ran with nobody watching. Only the Optimiser was in the loop: the Guardian and the Researcher received no work after 00:36.

The Coordinator's Claude Code workflows put several agents on one question at once. In one, three agents mined an old CI sweep, modelled each runner's per-core miss resources and built a walk keyed on SMT co-residency, and three sceptics each refuted part of that work. Another reviewed the fused post-walk change through three lenses, one of them a differential of about 14,600 valid and corrupt inputs against master, which [found no divergence](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/160#issuecomment-6653416078>). The workflows' own records stay in the Coordinator's session; the journal keeps what they found. Every decoder change that reached a pull request still went through the CI benchmark, under a decision rule registered before its first run, without review by the Guardian or the Researcher.

Five decoder changes merged. Two trimmed the move-to-front stage ([\#170](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/170>), [\#172](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/172>)). [\#171](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/171>) staged the walk's output through one tile, for a four-thread wall 5% to 14% faster over five runs. [\#180](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/180>) widened the window of blocks in flight, for 8% to 10% in three runs, at a cost of 4% to 6% more CPU and 8 MB more memory. The Coordinator weighed that in the journal and accepted it, noting that the extra CPU still has to be measured in wikidata-pq's pipeline, where the decoder shares its cores. [\#181](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/181>) removed the deferred flags that \#171 had carried with it: the decoder ran about 4% more instructions and still got faster. That fits the reading that the walk is bound by memory requests in flight rather than by instructions, though no hardware counter has shown it. The [benchmark history](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/history/index.md>), which chains each merge's own paired run, now puts the four-thread Wikidata wall at 0.75× its value at \#69 (95% band 0.69–0.82), against 0.85× before \#180. The chain assumes that a change measured on one runner holds on another.

As much again was tested and rejected. The 32 KiB tile, 1024 offsets a lane, filled the whole of Zen 4's L1D and ran 23.5% slower even at one thread (\#177, \#178). The fused post-walk pass ([\#183](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/183>)) halved the simulated cache misses after the walk, but the four-thread wall wasn't shown to follow: neither PR run was faster there beyond noise, though the fusion alone was, by 1.5%. October's four-copy win for a walk keyed on SMT co-residency reversed on today's staged walk. Split condition variables were rejected on a count of wasted wakes before anything was built.

Each is written up in the journal with its runs. The walk round had already redirected the work: since the 06:03 checkpoint the Optimiser has ranked candidates by the memory traffic of four workers on two SMT cores, not by instruction counts, and the fused pass and split condition variables were its first and third picks. Their failures narrowed the search to the walk's random reads and its table's footprint. The next build the Optimiser proposed is a retest of compact30's smaller table under today's staged walk, though its own prior on it is weak.

So the work moves without me relaying it. When a message went to the wrong address, the record showed it, and the Coordinator corrected it without my carrying anything across, though it took me to notice. Now the Coordinator reads each message and each merge back rather than assume they landed, and a misroute leaves a failing check on \#145 that the Coordinator didn't write. Whether all of this makes the research faster will keep showing in the benchmark history.

If you want to set up something similar:

- give each agent its own inbox, and one shared place to publish;
- have each run commit a receipt before it works, and its progress as it goes;
- point every message at an exact commit;
- wake agents with events rather than timers, and keep those events few;
- keep every agent's instructions in the repository at a pinned commit;
- write down what a message is allowed to authorise;
- decide what an independent reviewer gets to see;
- check effects, not reports: read every message back where it should have landed, and every merge back after it lands.

My own part is choosing the scope and making the decisions the charter keeps for me.
