# 32 lanes, 8.6 chains: where the inverse BWT walk spends its cycles

The decoder's 32-lane walk runs 8.6 times faster than one chain. That figure may not mean what it seems: the walk may already hide memory latency, and spend too many instructions on each byte.

31 October 2026 · 7 min read · [Open question](<#6-what-would-count-as-a-breakthrough>)

This post asks how much parallel work the CPU actually does inside mibz2's inverse-BWT decoder, and whether hardware capacity is lost to the way Rust compiles the loop.

The interesting part is that the suspected problem may not be too little parallelism at all. The figures could instead mean that the CPU already hides memory latency well, but spends too many instructions on each decoded byte.

## 1\. Why does the BWT decoder have 32 lanes?

The inverse BWT repeatedly looks up the next position in a table. Simplifying the actual code:

```rust
let q = t[row];
row = q >> 8;
output.push(q as u8);
```

The next lookup depends on the result of the previous one: r<sub>i+1</sub> = Ψ(r<sub>i</sub>).

The CPU cannot know where to look next until the current lookup completes. This is called pointer chasing, and along one chain it is inherently serial.

mibz2's answer is to divide the inverse-BWT traversal into 512 segments and walk up to 32 independent segments at once. Each lane has its own row position, destination and segment state.

Independent traversal chains

Four of the 32 lanes. Within a lane, each lookup waits for the one before it; across lanes, the CPU can overlap the lookups.

The source calls this walk `room_segments::<32, PF_L1>`. The `PF_L1` part enables a prefetch hint for the next T-vector entry. The "room" algorithm batches output writes to avoid a buffer-capacity check on every byte, but it still performs one dependent lookup for every decoded byte.

## 2\. Where does "8.6 effective chains" come from?

Two measured figures:

| Measurement | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| One dependent chain | 38.55 cycles/byte |
| The 32-lane room walk | 4.49 cycles/byte |

Their ratio is 38.55 ÷ 4.49 = **8.59**.

So the walk achieves about 8.6 times the byte rate of the serial chain, provided the two measurements are comparable. It does **not** mean that only 8.6 of the 32 lanes are working.

That distinction decides whether the next optimisation should look for more parallelism, or for less work per byte.

## 3\. Why 32 lanes might yield only an 8.6× speed-up

Imagine a processor that takes 39 cycles to complete a dependent table lookup. If one lookup starts every 4.49 cycles, the average number in progress is about 39 ÷ 4.49 ≈ 8.7.

That is Little's law: concurrency equals request rate multiplied by latency. Computer architecture distinguishes this achieved memory-level parallelism from the number of independent chains a program makes available.

But consider what that means for mibz2. A full round of the walk, one step for each of the 32 lanes, takes 32 × 4.49 ≈ 144 cycles.

One round of the room walk, against one lookup's latency

Illustrative, from the two measured figures above. About 8.6 lookups overlap at any moment, yet every lane's lookup returns long before that lane's next turn.

If a lookup takes roughly 39 cycles, the CPU has ample time to finish a lane's lookup before it comes back to that lane in the next round. So all 32 lanes can be making progress without 32 loads ever being in flight at once.

That would place the bottleneck somewhere else.

There is another caveat. The room walk explicitly prefetches future entries, so its actual demand-load latency may be much lower than the 38.55 cycles of the single chain. The two figures also need the same CPU, revision and cache conditions. So 8.6 is best read as an illustrative latency-hiding factor, not a measured count of outstanding memory requests.

## 4\. What to look for in the machine code

Here is one iteration of the hot loop, simplified:

```rust
for lane in lanes.iter_mut() {
    let q = t[lane.row];                   // dependent load
    if q & START != 0 { /* handoff */ }    // branch
    lane.row = q >> 8;                     // next link
    prefetch(t, lane.row);                 // future memory request
    *base[lane_index].add(off) = q as u8;  // output store
}
```

Several explanations compete:

| Suspected limit | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Register pressure | Too few architectural registers to hold all 32 lanes' row and output state, so the generated loop keeps reloading and storing bookkeeping |
| Instruction-window pressure | Too many instructions separate successive independent T-vector loads, which limits what the CPU can have in flight |
| Execution throughput | Address generation, branches, prefetches and stores use enough execution resources to set a floor in cycles per byte |
| Memory-system saturation | The core already overlaps enough lookups, and exposing more chains won't help |

A Zen 3 core, for example, has a 256-entry reorder window and a finite number of load and miss-tracking resources: substantial, but not unlimited.

Reading the disassembly, not just the Rust, shows which dependencies LLVM actually creates. One promising possibility is that the CPU spends too much time maintaining `lane.row`, `lane.seg`, `lane.p` and `lane.end` relative to the useful BWT lookup.

The segment-start branch, by contrast, is rarely taken: about 512 boundaries per 900,000 bytes, or 0.057% of steps. Even a 20-cycle misprediction at every boundary costs only about 0.011 cycles per byte, so boundary mispredictions alone can't explain an opportunity of more than 1 cycle per byte. The throughput of the per-byte branch and bookkeeping could still matter.

## 5\. What does "four groups of eight" mean?

This is scalar batching, not necessarily SIMD. The idea is to arrange the 32 logical lanes as four groups of eight, so that each group's working state is easier for the compiler to keep in registers.

But there's a trap.

Batching the 32 lanes as four groups of eight

Green lanes have a lookup the CPU can overlap. Batching helps only if every group still has lookups in flight within the processor's instruction window.

If an implementation runs several rounds of group 0 before touching groups 1 to 3, it may expose only eight independent chains to the CPU at once. Under the idealised 38.55-cycle latency, eight chains have a latency floor of 38.55 ÷ 8 = **4.82 cycles per byte**, already slower than today's 4.49.

That doesn't prove batching fails: real latency changes with prefetching and caching. But it shows how saving register operations can lose to reduced overlap.

The better transformation reduces lane bookkeeping while still exposing independent loads from all four groups within the processor's instruction window.

## 6\. What would count as a breakthrough?

The question is which of two fundamentally different paths applies.

Two diagnoses, two different optimisations

Path B is an inference from the lane-count curve flattening near 24 lanes and from the 32-lane walk already tolerating one chain's latency. It is not yet a verified machine-code finding.

**Path A, insufficient overlap:** show that the generated code serialises independent loads unnecessarily, then remove those dependencies without giving up register locality or adding costly memory traffic.

**Path B, too much work per byte:** show that overlap is already sufficient and that the core is limited by its instruction stream, then reduce row-state reloads, address calculations or output bookkeeping while keeping all 32 chains.

The current hypothesis leans towards Path B, given that the measured lane-count curve flattens near 24 lanes, and that the 32-lane scheme already tolerates one chain's latency. That is an inference, not a verified finding.

So the question to settle is:

> Are the 32 chains insufficiently exposed, or are they already exposed well enough, while the processor wastes cycles advancing each one?

The two answers call for completely different optimisations, which is why a careful, disassembly-level investigation is worth doing.

A way to save roughly 1.2 cycles per walked byte, on the later decoder baseline of 10.78 cycles per byte, would be worth about 11% of total decoder time, before any gain from the MTF stage. That is why this direction has much greater breakthrough potential than further polishing the MTF selector.

[mibz2 · Research blog](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/blog/index.md>)

# Compact navigation tables for the inverse BWT: early findings

Most of the inverse BWT's navigation table follows simple patterns: what a census of real blocks found, and what comes next.

29 October 2026 · 10 min read · [Work in progress](<#what-comes-next>)

This research began with a simple question:

> Can succinct data structures make my bzip2 decoder faster?

The answer so far is that the large table the decoder uses to reconstruct text stores more than it needs to, and much of what it stores follows simple patterns.

This is no longer only theory: a census of the benchmark corpus's actual data shows those patterns.

What follows starts from the beginning and assumes no background in compressed indexes.

## 1\. The decoder follows a chain of pointers

When bzip2 compresses some text, it performs the Burrows–Wheeler Transform (BWT).

The BWT rearranges the characters in a way that helps compression. But recovering the original text requires following a particular sequence of positions.

Imagine an enormous collection of numbered cards.

Each card tells you which card to visit next.

A miniature pointer chain

1. Card 03→
2. Card 15→
3. Card 20→
4. Card 36→
5. Card 41→
6. Card 52→
7. Card 64→

Currently at card **0**1 of 7 visited

Follow pointer →Reset

Path: 0 → 3 → 6 → 4 → 1 → 5 → 2

Each card contains the number of the next card. The highlighted card is the current position: follow the pointers from card 0 until every card has been visited.

mibz2's decoder uses a table called the T-vector, which is essentially a much larger, more sophisticated collection of such cards.

For each position, it stores:

- Where to go next.
- The character associated with that position.
- A marker used by mibz2's cooperative traversal algorithm.

At maximum bzip2 block size, this table occupies approximately 3.6 MB.

mibz2's 32-lane implementation already tackles one major cost: instead of following one chain and repeatedly waiting for memory, it follows many independent chains at once.

That's memory-level parallelism (MLP).

So far, so good.

But then we asked a different question.

> Why do we need four bytes for every card?

## 2\. The cards aren't arbitrary

Take these two sequences of destinations:

Two groups of eight pointers

For Group A, storing eight values individually is reasonable.

But Group B?

You only need to remember:

> Start at 427 and add the position within the group.

One starting number replaces eight separate numbers.

The permutation mibz2's inverse BWT decoder follows, called Ψ (psi), isn't a completely arbitrary permutation.

Because of how the BWT is constructed, it consists of increasing sequences of positions.

That means consecutive entries within a particular character group always point to increasing positions.

They won't necessarily be consecutive like Group B—but they're at least sorted.

And that gives us opportunities to compress them.

This is where succinct data structures entered the picture.

## 3\. Succinct structures are about storing the pattern, not the individual facts

In ordinary programming, we tend to store arrays of values directly.

A succinct representation asks:

> Can I describe the arrangement of these values more economically and reconstruct any particular value when needed?

For example, rather than storing:

```text
1000, 1002, 1005, 1008, 1010
```

you might store:

```text
base = 1000
```

and:

```text
offsets = 0, 2, 5, 8, 10
```

The offsets are much smaller than the absolute values, so they may require fewer bits.

This is called frame-of-reference encoding, or FOR.

Another technique, Elias–Fano, is especially suited to sorted integer sequences. It separates the higher and lower parts of each number and compresses the high parts using the sequence's monotonicity.

Neither is magic; you save memory at the cost of some work to recover an individual value.

And that creates our main tension:

> A more compact table is useful only if reconstructing its pointers doesn't make the decoder slower than before.

## 4\. What the census found

Initially, we had no idea how well these representations would fit real BWT data.

Perhaps the values were increasing but widely scattered, making compression awkward.

So we wrote a census program to inspect them.

It found more structure than the theory alone guarantees.

What our census found in the benchmark corpus

These two percentages overlap: they aren't two separate populations.

The important observation is that more than three-quarters of the measured rows may be represented using a simple arithmetic rule.

That is much better than we could have assumed from the mathematics alone.

It's the difference between saying:

> This encoding should work in principle.

And:

> We've examined the actual pointers, and most of them exhibit precisely the structure this encoding is designed to exploit.

It does not yet mean the decoder will be faster. But it establishes that there is something real to exploit.

## 5\. Why the CPU's cache lines became central

Now we reach the hardware connection.

Modern CPUs don't fetch arbitrary isolated bytes from main memory one at a time. They work with cache lines, commonly 64 bytes.

Imagine a cache line as a little tray of data.

If the next pointer lives in that tray, the processor can fetch the tray and extract what it needs.

The first design asks:

> What if we could store 32 pointers in exactly one 64-byte cache line?

The fixed-cache-line proposal

mibz2's current representation uses four bytes per pointer.

So the new design could halve the navigation table's storage, before exception overhead.

And crucially, the record can be found immediately from the current row number.

No searching for where the record was stored.

This is very important because mibz2's greatest strength is how quickly it can issue independent memory requests.

A compact representation that introduces multiple dependent searches could destroy that advantage.

The fixed-size record tries to avoid precisely that.

## 6\. A second design: a two-tier layout

If 77.6% of rows belong to simple consecutive groups, why devote an entire 64-byte record to each of those groups?

Most of the record would contain information we don't actually need.

So we proposed a two-tier layout.

Two-tier Ψ navigation

It is a compromise.

For the common case, the small directory entry already gives us the next pointer.

For the less common case, we fetch extra information.

Because the directory is tiny compared with the current T-vector, it may fit much more comfortably in cache.

And because we don't allocate a full 64-byte record for the simple groups, the storage could become much smaller.

Our initial calculation suggested something in the neighbourhood of 5.6 bits per row, before additional exceptions and bookkeeping.

That's not a measured final footprint. It's an optimistic model built from the reported distribution.

The attraction is real, but so is the risk: whenever we need the second record, we introduce another memory dependency.

## 7\. Why a smaller table could make mibz2 faster

Suppose mibz2 is decoding one full-sized bzip2 block.

Its T-vector for that block is 3.6 MB.

But mibz2 can work on multiple blocks concurrently.

With several full-size blocks in flight, their tables compete for space in the CPU's shared cache.

Eight simultaneous full-block tables

Illustrative table storage for eight full 900 KB blocks. The two-tier estimate (dashed) excludes additional exception and alignment overhead.

Earlier measurements on a 10-core workstation already show evidence of a shared-cache residency threshold.

When the live tables become too large, the processor must fetch more data from slower parts of the memory hierarchy.

Smaller tables would let more of them stay resident in the same cache capacity.

We might see fewer expensive memory misses.

Even if each individual pointer is slightly more expensive to decode, the overall decoder could become faster.

This is the same kind of trade-off Julian Seward studied in 2001.

But mibz2 adds modern multicore concurrency and 32-lane traversal.

The goal is not to have the smallest possible table. It's to make the whole machine finish decoding sooner.

## 8\. Open questions

There are three substantial unanswered questions.

**First, how much does decoding a compressed pointer cost?** With the current T-vector, the CPU loads a 32-bit value and extracts the next row. With a compressed record, it may need shifts, masks, a format test and sometimes an additional memory access. Even a small amount of extra work matters when repeated millions of times.

**Second, how expensive is construction?** The compressed table must be built from the BWT before it can be traversed. A representation that makes traversal faster but takes twice as long to build might lose overall.

**Third, does the 77.6% translation property hold broadly?** We know it appears in our benchmark corpus. We don't yet know how stable it is across different types of compressed data, and it's not a universal mathematical guarantee.

We have enough evidence to investigate these questions seriously, but not enough to claim a faster decoder.

## 9\. What is known and what is not

| Finding | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Ψ has increasing sequences that can be compressed | Mathematically established |
| Actual benchmark data contains abundant consecutive-position groups | Measured by our census |
| Fixed 64-byte records can represent the overwhelming majority of measured groups | Strongly supported by the census; complete encoding still needs validation |
| A two-tier directory could shrink storage further | New design hypothesis |
| Reduced working sets can improve cache residency | Supported by mibz2's existing performance measurements |
| Either compressed design will beat the current decoder | Unknown |

And the most important distinction of all:

> We've found evidence that the data is compressible in a form suited to fast navigation. We haven't yet proved that navigating the compressed representation is faster.

These are separate claims.

## 10\. The underlying idea

The underlying point is that the T-vector—the enormous table of navigation pointers—isn't fundamentally necessary in its current form.

It's a convenient way to store answers to questions.

The BWT already contains the information from which those answers can be derived.

Succinct data structures teach us to exploit that fact.

But our work adds an interesting twist:

> Rather than pursuing the absolutely smallest possible encoding, we're looking for a carefully chosen amount of redundancy that allows the CPU to recover answers quickly.

In other words, sometimes storing a little unnecessary information makes the whole algorithm faster.

That's what makes the problem so subtle.

A theoretician might ask:

> How close can we get to the minimum number of bits?

A systems programmer might ask:

> How few instructions can we execute per pointer?

Our research asks:

> How should we arrange the information so that the CPU can follow millions of pointers with as little waiting as possible?

That brings information theory, succinct data structures, cache architecture and instruction scheduling together in one problem.

## Where we've arrived

Our research journey

## What comes next

The census shows there is structure to exploit. It says nothing yet about speed, and the next steps are the measurements that will. They run in order, one controlled comparison at a time.

The roadmap, in order

Each step's prediction and pass and fail thresholds are written down before it runs. Status on 29 October 2026, after the workstation run of \#81.

The first of them has now run. Building the table in one pass, rather than copying first and scattering after, made the cooperative build 1.31× faster on the 10-core workstation. That raises the bar for every compact design: each must now beat the fused 32-bit build and its walk, not the old two-pass one.

It also sharpens the question. The most interesting version of a compact table is not one made by compressing a finished T-vector, but one built straight from the BWT, record by record, so the full 32-bit table is never written at all. Writing fewer bytes need not mean doing less work, so that too will be measured before anything is built on it.

Three table designs are kept as candidates. None is built yet, and they will compete on measured construction and navigation cost, not on size alone:

- **24-bit direct links:** the simple reference, a quarter smaller than today's table.
- **Fixed 64-byte records:** 32 pointers to a cache line, 16.16 bits a row on the corpus.
- **Two-tier descriptors:** 5.70 bits a row on the corpus, but 12–36% of steps need a second, dependent load, and on less regular inputs the design loses its advantage.

This post will be updated as the results come in. The work is tracked on [\#81](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/81>) and [\#79](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/79>).

## The bottom line

We've moved from:

> "Maybe succinct data structures could save us some memory."

To:

> "We have evidence that most of the permutation can be represented by simple rules, and we have several concrete ways of exploiting those rules while protecting the memory-level parallelism that makes mibz2 fast."

We now have a real engineering question to settle: whether those smaller representations can make the CPU finish its work faster.

The working hypothesis, in one line:

> A decoder may get faster not by following its pointers more efficiently, but by not storing most of them individually.

---

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Since this was written**
>
> The census has since been refined and the designs' sizes counted exactly. On the corpus's 233 full blocks:
>
> - 77.39% of rows are in groups that are one run, ranging from 63.7% to 88.0% per block;
> - the fixed 64-byte records come to 16.16 bits a row;
> - the two-tier design comes to 5.70 bits a row, where 12–36% of steps need its second lookup.
>
> On other inputs, such as random or already-compressed data, runs are rare. There the two-tier design is larger than the fixed records, while the fixed records still fit at about 16.3 bits a row. The details, sources and the full discussion are in the research journal (`docs/journal/2026-10-29-succinct-review.md`, [\#94](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/94>)) and on [\#79](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/79>).

# History

- **In wikidata-pq.** mibz2 was written in [lmmx/wikidata-pq](<https://github.com/lmmx/wikidata-pq>), whose split decodes the Wikidata JSON dump. A profile there found the bz2 decode about half of the split's CPU, bound by the inverse BWT's chain of dependent loads, and a prototype walked it as interleaved chains (lmmx/wikidata-pq\#194). The production decoder followed behind a flag (`WIKIDATA_BZ2_DECODER=native`, lmmx/wikidata-pq\#197): on CI, the split's CPU fell 20.6% and its wall 16.6% against lbzip2.
- **The bake-off.** Before going further, it was timed against pbz2, fbz, the `lbzip2` crate, indexed\_bzip2, lbzip2 and libbzip2 on the dump's blocks. pbz2 0.2.0 tied it; the others were 1.5–1.9× slower at 4 threads (lmmx/wikidata-pq\#199).
- **Its own repository.** The decoder's history moved to [lmmx/mibz2](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2>) by `git filter-repo`, its paths renamed and each `#N` in its commit messages rewritten to `lmmx/wikidata-pq#N`, with its journals. It was published as 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 on crates.io and PyPI, the crate and the Python package at one version.

The [journals](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/background/journals/index.md>) record each step, and [Status](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/background/status/index.md>) says where the research stands now.

# Status

*As of 29 October 2026.* This page is a snapshot of where the research stands. The evidence is in the [journals](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/background/journals/index.md>) and the pull requests linked below.

**In short:**

- A faster way to run the inverse BWT on a many-core machine has been found, confirmed and explained.
- **It is not in the released decoder yet.** mibz2 0.1.5 decodes as it did, and every figure here is the inversion stage alone, not whole decompression.

## The starting point: a knee at four workers

- mibz2's decoder gives each worker its own block. The inverse BWT then walks that block's table: about 3.6 MB for a full 900 kB block, one random load per output byte.
- On a 10-core i9-10900K, with a 20 MB shared L3, throughput peaks at **4 workers** and falls beyond them. Eight tables don't fit in the L3, and the walk's loads go to DRAM.

## The finding: cooperative inversion

Several cores share one block's table: the table is built together and walked together, each core taking segments of the walk from a shared counter. An arm is written *N*x*k*: *N* blocks in flight, *k* cores on each. Production's independent workers are *p4*, *p8* and so on.

Measured on the i9 in the research harness ([PR \#73](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/73>)):

| arm | what runs | inversion MB/s | against p4 (paired, 95% interval) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| p4 | production, 4 independent workers | 1,465 | 1 |
| p8 | production, 8 independent workers | 662 | 0.47 |
| 4x2 | 4 blocks, 2 cores each | 1,808 | **1.230** (1.217–1.243) |
| 3x3 | 3 blocks, 3 cores each (9 cores) | 1,942 | **1.323** (1.312–1.335) |
| s3x3 | libsais 2.12.1, 3 blocks on 3 threads each | 2,355 | 1.59 |

- **The confirmation was registered before the runs.**

  - 4x2 and 3x3 were each run alone against p4, 20 paired rounds each.
  - Each beat p4 in all 20 rounds, and every block's output was checked.
  - 4x2 reproduced its discovery figure within 0.3%.
  - 3x3 came in 2.3% under its discovery figure, as picking the best of 19 arms would predict.
- **[libsais](<https://github.com/IlyaGrebnov/libsais>)'s inverse BWT is still about 20% ahead** at 3x3 (1.195× ours, paired). It gains from cooperation by the same factor as ours, about 1.5×. The gap between them is the kernel.

## Why it works: two mechanisms, measured

A hardware-counter study on the same machine ran each arm alone under `perf stat`, with counters that include the walk's software prefetches. It was 588 runs, none multiplexed ([PR \#84](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/84>)).

| arm | L3 hit share of data reads past L2 | reads in flight, machine-wide | wait per read |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| p4 | 94.5% | 28.1 | 67 cycles |
| p8 | 65.7% | 70.0 | 366 cycles |
| 4x2 | 94.9% | 38.8 | 64 cycles |
| 3x3 | 96.7% | 41.9 | 66 cycles |

- **Residency.**

  - With eight cores either way, four shared tables (4x2) stay in the L3 where eight independent ones (p8) don't. The hit share rises from 66% to 95%, and each read waits 64 cycles instead of 366.
- **Overlap.**

  - With four tables either way, the second core on each (4x2 against p4) leaves the hit share and the wait unchanged.
  - It puts 1.38× as many reads in flight.
- **3x3 has both:** a higher hit share than p4, a third fewer reads missing the L3 per byte, and 1.49× the reads in flight.
- **The counters account for the timings.** Little's law on them (reads in flight over the wait, against reads per byte) reproduces each arm's measured throughput to within 0–11%.

## What it points at

The cooperative kernel retires more instructions per output byte than production's or libsais's:

| kernel | instructions per output byte |
| --- | ---: |
| production (p4) | 23.8 |
| cooperative, one core a block (4x1) | 31.8 |
| cooperative, 3x3 | 35.3 |
| libsais, one core a block (s4x1) | 21.4 |
| libsais, 3x3 | 23.2 |

- **Its 4x1 penalty is instructions, not memory.**

  - The cooperative kernel on one core a block (4x1) runs at 0.87× production.
  - Its reads and waits are within 10% of production's; it executes a third more instructions.
- **libsais's lead is fewer reads.**

  - It makes 0.86–0.89 reads past L2 per byte, against our 1.40–1.55. That is one dependent load for two output bytes.
  - It does so within about 23 instructions a byte.
  - mibz2's own two-byte walk (\#6) wins only past the knee. At its best it reaches 0.86× the one-byte walk's best.

## What's next

| order | work | what it is for |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 1 | [\#77](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/77>): the cooperative kernel's instructions, attributed to code by `perf annotate` ([PR \#85](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/85>)) before any change | production's instructions a byte, and production's speed at one core a block |
| 2 | [\#78](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/78>), [\#81](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/81>): the build's recount and extra pass | a cheaper shared build: 43% of 3x3's time |
| 3 | [\#79](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/79>): a smaller table | more teams resident at once (a scheduling gain, not one for 3x3 itself) |
| later | a two-byte walk within production's instruction budget | libsais's fewer reads a byte |

**Still open in the counter record:**

- 3 short checks of the raw L3 event's accounting, with their criteria fixed in advance. It counts a steady 23–39% more requests than `offcore_requests.all_data_rd`, and the likely cause is prefetches into L3.
- The study's conclusions rest on the arm-to-arm directions, which a second, independent pair of counters reproduces.

**Before any of this reaches a release:**

- the cooperative build and walk must pass the decoder's correctness checks: the segment oracle, fuzzing and Miri on the shared table;
- the whole decoder must be A/B'd at 4–10 cores, where an inversion-stage gain counts only as far as it survives;
- other CPUs must be measured too. CI's 4-core runners can't show a gain that only exists past four workers, so the workstation measures it.

# Behind the scenes

Reading the account from [observatory/intention](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/observatory/intention>). It can also be read there, starting from `current/account.md`.

## About this page

Most of the team that works on mibz2 is agents. During the coordinator era, one role — the Observer — did none of the code work; it watched the others and wrote down what they were doing, and why, for someone who hadn't been following. Since 26 November 2026 the team works through [`frontier/`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/master/frontier>), and this page continues to render the Observer's historical record from `observatory/intention`.

What it writes is kept on a branch of its own, [`observatory/intention`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/observatory/intention>), which shares no history with the code. Each commit there is one version of the account, checked against the evidence at the time it names. A later version corrects an earlier one and leaves it standing.

The page stays as it is when the account changes. Your browser reads the branch when the page opens, and everything shown comes from the same version. The page looks again every five minutes while it is open. GitHub allows sixty unauthenticated requests an hour from one address. If it turns the page away, the page shows nothing rather than risk mixing two versions, and links to the account on GitHub instead.

# Development

## Layout

| path | contents |
| --- | --- |
| `src/` | the crate: the bit reader, block parsing, MTF, the inverse BWT, RLE1, the CRC, streams, the parallel decoder, `BzReader`, and `python.rs` (the extension module, feature `python`) |
| `tests/` | the Rust tests against libbzip2 (`decode.rs`, `corpus.rs`), their corpora in `tests/common/` |
| `examples/` | `ab` (the A/B harness), `bzcat`, `fuzz` (a mutation fuzz loop), `windows` (real dump windows checked) |
| `benches/` | `cargo bench` |
| `bench/` | the CI benchmark's scripts and its pinned Wikidata windows |
| `python/mibz2/` | the Python package, and `_mibz2.pyi`, the stub of the compiled module |
| `python/tests/` | the Python tests |
| `docs/site/` | this site; `docs/journal/` the development journals |

## Building and testing

The tools: a Rust toolchain, [uv](<https://docs.astral.sh/uv/>), [just](<https://just.systems/>), and for the lints taplo, whitespace-format and cargo-machete.

```sh
just py         # maturin develop, then pytest
just test-ci    # cargo test and the doc tests
just clippy     # clippy on every target and feature, warnings as errors
just pc         # formatting and lints (as pre-commit runs them)
cargo test --release                                   # against libbzip2
cargo run --release --example fuzz -- 600 1            # a mutation fuzz loop, libbzip2 the oracle
cargo run --release --example bzcat -- 4 < f.bz2 > f   # the parallel decoder as a command
```

On aarch64: `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `apt install qemu-user gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu`, then `cargo test --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu --config .cargo/aarch64-qemu.toml`.

### The toolchain

The Rust toolchain is pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` (1.99.1), and rustup uses it for every build in the checkout: CI, the benchmark, the release wheels and the workstation recipes. The compiler moves the decoder's figures more than many of the effects being gated. Lazy Cells' induction, for one, took 219 instructions a letter under 1.97 and 176 under 1.99.1 in one research binary, where a candidate against it swung from 37.6 instructions a letter fewer to 22.6 more. In the benchmark binary the same candidate moved far less (+6.2 under 1.98.0, −7.1 under 1.99.1): codegen differs by binary as well as by compiler. So gates are counted on the benchmark's own arms, built with the pinned compiler. A comparison between toolchains is not a comparison of the code.

- **The workflows name the same version** (`dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.99.1`, maturin-action's `rust-toolchain`). test.yml checks that they agree with the file. A deliberate exception says why on its line: Miri runs on nightly, and a registration's dispatch uses the toolchain it froze.
- **Every workstation bundle records the toolchain** (`toolchain.txt`, written by `bench/bundle.sh`).
- **Bumping the toolchain is its own pull request,** with nothing else in it. The benchmark builds each arm with its own commit's toolchain, so that pull request measures the new compiler against the old one.
- **The published crate and sdist leave the file out:** a downstream build uses its own toolchain, from `rust-version` (1.80) up.

The segmented walks' unsafe code also runs under [Miri](<https://github.com/rust-lang/miri>), on blocks small enough to interpret: `cargo +nightly miri test --lib -- miri_` (about a minute; CI runs it on changes to `src/bwt.rs`). Those tests assert they reached the transitions the walks' handoffs guard (a buffer growing, a pass ending with a buffer full, a lane coming into the tail full, and so on), so a walk change that stops them reaching one fails rather than passing having checked less.

## Benchmarking

Performance is measured on CI (`.github/workflows/bench.yml`, the [benchmark](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/index.md>)): a pull request that touches the decoder gets a comment with its head against its base. Locally, the same harness:

```sh
cargo build --release --example ab
target/release/examples/ab gen corpora 4
target/release/examples/ab run runs.jsonl --arms mibz2,pbz2,lbzip2 --threads 1,4 --rounds 5 corpora/*.bz2
target/release/examples/ab summary runs.jsonl
```

Where the parallel decoder's time goes as its thread count grows (\#39) is measured by the occupancy instrument (`examples/occupancy.rs`, feature `trace`), run on the pinned Wikidata corpus by one recipe on any machine, as CI's Occupancy workflow does:

```sh
just bench-occupancy                             # 1, 2, 4, ... up to the CPUs allowed
just bench-occupancy --threads 1,2,4,8,12,16,20
```

It needs cargo, python3, git and lbzip2, and writes `occupancy-<UTC time>.json`: the machine as the process sees it, each thread count's throughput and the cost of tracing, and the decoder's own timeline (workers decoding or idle and why, the scanner, the reader, and per block its CPU time and run-queue wait). It is a diagnostic: the benchmark's paired A/B decides what is faster.

The benchmark has a version of its own (`BENCH` in `bench/report.py`), with its history in [`bench/CHANGELOG.md`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/bench/CHANGELOG.md>):

- **A pull request that changes the benchmark** (`bench/`, `examples/ab.rs`, `examples/phases.rs`, `.github/workflows/bench.yml`) either adds a changelog entry with its new version, or says in its description why no version is needed.
- **A major version that redefines a family of figures** adds itself to that family in `MEANING` (`bench/report.py`), so the site's history splits that family there and joins the others across it.
- **`python3 bench/test_report.py`** checks that `BENCH` and the newest entry agree, and that the history joins versions but never runner models, core counts, corpora or a corpus's different contents.

## Commits

Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](<https://www.conventionalcommits.org/>) (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `ci:` ...); the `conventional-pre-commit` hook checks them. `release-plz.toml` groups the changelog by these prefixes.

# Documentation

The site is built with [Zensical](<https://zensical.org/>) from `docs/site/` and `zensical.toml`. The Python API reference is generated by mkdocstrings from the package's docstrings and the compiled module's stub (`python/mibz2/_mibz2.pyi`).

```sh
just docs-serve   # build, serve and rebuild on change
just docs-check   # strict build, site checks, and the pages' examples as tests
```

- `docs/scripts/check_site.py` checks that every page is in the nav, that internal links and anchors resolve, that every page has a description matching its llms.txt entry, and that every public name is in the API reference.
- `docs/scripts/check_render.py` finds Markdown that rendered as something else (a list run into a paragraph, a stray heading, a flattened nested list), and `docs/scripts/look_pages.py` opens the changed pages in Chromium and screenshots them (`just docs-look`). Before a page is published, its render is read: see the `publish-page` skill in `.claude/skills/`.
- `docs/conftest.py` runs each page's Python examples with pytest (`pytest docs/site`); a `pycon` block's output must match.
- `docs/scripts/bench_history.py` turns the `bench-results` branch into the benchmark pages' data (`docs/site/assets/bench-history.json`) and tables (`docs/generated/`) before each build. Without a checkout of the branch (`--store`), it reads `origin/bench-results`, or writes empty ones.
- `docs/site/assets/data/lane-sweeps.json` holds the measured walk timings by lane count that [Why 32 couriers beat one](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/concepts/couriers/#lane-counts>) draws (`assets/javascripts/couriers.js`). It is written by hand, from the record: one panel a sweep, each with its own axes, its points (`x`, `y`, and optionally `lo` and `hi` for an interval) and its source. A new sweep is a new panel; the page draws every panel. Only measured points go in it.
- `docs/site/assets/data/frontier.json` holds the measured series that the [Throughput–memory frontier](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/benchmarks/frontier/index.md>) page draws (`assets/javascripts/frontier.js`): throughput against measured peak RSS, and against computed live table memory. It is written by hand, from the record, under the rules in its `about` field. The page's tables give the same values, and stand in for the charts if the script does not run.

## Publishing

`.github/workflows/site.yml` builds the site on every push to master, and after each Benchmark run on master, and publishes it to the `gh-pages` branch, served at [https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/>). A pull request from this repository gets a preview under `pr-preview/pr-<number>/`, linked from a comment on the pull request and removed when it closes. Previews start once the repository's Pages source is set to the `gh-pages` branch.

Each deploy writes only its own path: production the root, a preview its own directory. Pages rebuilds the branch on every push, and a push that lands mid-build cancels that build, so the next build publishes both. A preview's check therefore waits for the outcome, not for one build: it passes once the preview serves the files of its own run, whose assets carry `?v=<commit>`.

# Releasing

The crate and the Python package are released at one version, from one commit.

## Deploy Release

Run the **Deploy Release** workflow (`deploy.yml`) with a bump (patch, minor or major). It runs `just release`, which:

1. bumps the version in `pyproject.toml` (`uv version --bump`) and sets the crate's in `Cargo.toml` to match;
2. writes the crate's changelog with release-plz;
3. commits `chore(release): bump 🐍 -> vX.Y.Z` and tags `py-X.Y.Z`;
4. pushes the commit and the tag, then starts **CI** on the tag (a tag pushed with the workflow's token starts no workflow by itself).

CI on a `py-*` tag builds the wheels and the sdist and publishes them to PyPI, and publishes the crate to crates.io with release-plz (which tags `mibz2-vX.Y.Z` and makes the GitHub release). Both use Trusted Publishing, in the `pypi` and `crates-io` environments.

## Out-of-band cases

- **Tag Release** (`tag.yml`): tags an existing commit `py-<version>` at the version its `pyproject.toml` and `Cargo.toml` already hold (no bump), and starts CI on the tag. Each registry is skipped where it already has the version.
- **Release Notes** (`release-notes.yml`): makes a version's GitHub release (`v<version>`) at a given commit if it does not exist, or updates its notes, from that version's section of `CHANGELOG.md`.
- **A wheel job that never got a runner** (0.1.6: both macOS jobs were cancelled after 15 minutes waiting, so Release was skipped and PyPI had nothing while crates.io had the crate): re-run the failed jobs on the tag's own CI run. Release then uploads with `--skip-existing`. Don't bump, re-tag or republish. CI reports a runner that never came the same way as a failed build ("cancelled"/"failure"), so check whether the job's steps ran at all before treating it as a build failure.

## Release notes: the evidence

Every version's section of `CHANGELOG.md` is the GitHub release's notes, so it carries the release's evidence. release-plz writes a one-line entry per commit (and only for commits that touch the crate's files). After the release, rewrite the section by hand:

1. **Dispatch the tag-to-tag bench.** Run **Benchmark** (`bench.yml`) from the Actions tab with *Use workflow from* the new tag and `base` the previous tag:

   ```sh
   gh workflow run bench.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f base=vX.Y.W
   ```

   It is a paired A/B like a pull request's (the base's own harness binary as the arm `mibz2@base/ab`, the order alternating round to round), on one runner. Its figures are the run's summary and its artifact (`bench-pr-<sha>`: `result.json`, `comment.md`, `runs.jsonl`, `stages.jsonl`); nothing is recorded. The base needs `examples/ab.rs`, and the stage table needs `examples/phases.rs` (v0.1.2 on); v0.1.3 and v0.1.4 have run as bases this way. The comment's "the merge base with master" means the base given.
2. **Write the entry** to the template below, from that run alone, in a pull request. Never add up or chain the pull requests' figures: they were measured against other bases, often on other runner CPUs. A section holds no line starting `## [` (Release Notes ends the section there), so its headings are `###` and below.
3. **Re-run Release Notes** (`release-notes.yml`) once the pull request is merged, with the version and its release commit, so the GitHub release takes the section from master.

### The template

```markdown
## [X.Y.Z](https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/compare/vX.Y.W...vX.Y.Z) - YYYY-MM-DD

One or two sentences: what changed for a user, and the release's own Wikidata figure at
1 thread and at the runner's cores, from the tag-to-tag run.

### Measured: vX.Y.Z against vX.Y.W

| corpus | threads | wall, vX.Y.W → vX.Y.Z (median) | wall change (95% interval) | peak RSS | same bytes |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|

Peak RSS, same bytes, and the stage table's rows for any stage a change moved (with the
total), as bullets.

<details><summary>Reproducing this run</summary>

The rerun command and the artifact's name; both tags' full SHAs; the runner's CPU, cores,
clock, kernel and image; rustc; the bench version, rounds and threads; the corpora's bytes
and full SHA-256s (`result.json`'s `corpora`).

</details>

### <!-- 3 -->Performance (one heading per group: Features, Bug Fixes, ...)

- **The change, in a few words** ([#N](https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/N))
  - *Mechanism:* one or two sentences.
  - *Measured, in its pull request:* its own paired figures, with the runner CPU.
  - *Trade-offs:* what got slower or bigger, and why it was kept.
  - *Evidence:* the bench comment, its runs, the journal entry.

### Downstream: wikidata-pq (if it exists; marked measured or modelled)
```

- **Decoder figures and downstream figures stay apart.** wikidata-pq's figures go under their own heading, each marked *measured* (a run, linked) or *modelled* (what the model assumes).
- **Measurement-only and docs-only changes** get one line each: what they add, and that the decoder's figures did not change.
- **Rejected experiments** go in the journal (`docs/journal/`), not the changelog.

# mibz2

mibz2: a fast bzip2 decoder, block-parallel and multi-chain within each block.

- `decompress`: a whole .bz2 in memory, decoded.
- `open`: a .bz2 file (a path or a binary file object) read as a buffered binary file, decoded as it is read.

Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned, and each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. Bytes read from a stream before its end come from blocks whose own CRCs matched, but the stream as a whole is verified only when a read reaches its end: until then, treat what has been read as provisional (see `BZ2Reader.verified`).

## DecodeError

Bases: `ValueError`

The input is not valid bzip2 data.

## decompress

```python
decompress(data: bytes | bytearray, threads: int | None = None) -> bytes
```

Decode a whole .bz2 (its streams one after another), every CRC checked.

It runs on every CPU this process may use, or on `threads`, as the Rust crate's `Plan::for_threads` spends them: a block a worker (past the physical cores on 8 to 10 of them, one a core; on the i9-10900K, one a core but one), or teams of 2 sharing each block (from 11 threads on 11 or more cores, or past the cores on 6 or 7).

Raises:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `DecodeError` | When the input is not valid bzip2 data. |

## BZ2Reader

```python
BZ2Reader(source: Source, threads: int | None = None)
```

Bases: `RawIOBase`

A .bz2 file's decoded bytes, read in order (an unbuffered binary file).

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `source` | `Source` | A path, or a binary file object open for reading (its `read` is called). | *required* |
| `threads` | `int \| None` | Decoding threads: `1` decodes on the reading thread; more decode blocks at once, as the Rust crate's `Plan::for_threads` spends them: worker threads, a block each (past the physical cores on 8 to 10 of them, one a core; on the i9-10900K, one a core but one), or teams of 2 sharing each block (from 11 threads on 11 or more cores, or past the cores on 6 or 7). `None` (the default) asks for every CPU this process may use. | `None` |

Raises:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `DecodeError` | From a read, when the input is not valid bzip2 data: a block whose CRC does not match (none of its bytes are returned), a stream whose combined CRC does not match (raised by the read that reaches the stream's end), or a malformed or truncated stream. The error says which block and bit it was found at, which is where decoding failed and need not be where the input was damaged. |

### readable

```python
readable() -> bool
```

True: a reader is readable.

### readinto

```python
readinto(b: Any) -> int
```

Read up to `len(b)` decoded bytes into `b`; 0 at the end (when verified).

### readall

```python
readall() -> bytes
```

Read and return all remaining decoded bytes until EOF.

### read

```python
read(size: int | None = -1) -> bytes
```

Read up to `size` bytes, or all remaining bytes if `size` is negative or `None`.

### readline

```python
readline(size: int | None = -1) -> bytes
```

Read and return one line, or up to `size` bytes if `size >= 0`.

### readlines

```python
readlines(hint: int = -1) -> list[bytes]
```

Read and return a list of lines; stop after `hint` bytes if `hint > 0`.

### verified

```python
verified: bool
```

True once a read has reached the end and every block's and stream's CRC matched.

Until then, the bytes read so far have each passed their block's CRC, but the stream's combined CRC has not yet been checked.

### close

```python
close() -> None
```

Stop decoding (its worker threads stop) and close the reader.

## open

```python
open(
    source: Source, threads: int | None = None, buffer_size: int = 1 << 20
) -> BufferedReader[BZ2Reader]
```

Open a .bz2 file for reading, decoded as it is read.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `source` | `Source` | A path, or a binary file object open for reading. | *required* |
| `threads` | `int \| None` | Decoding threads, as for `BZ2Reader`. | `None` |
| `buffer_size` | `int` | The buffered reader's buffer, in bytes. | `1 << 20` |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `BufferedReader` | A buffered binary file over a `BZ2Reader` (its `raw`), whose `raw.verified` says whether the whole input has been read and verified. |

Examples:

```pycon
>>> import bz2, mibz2, tempfile, os
>>> path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.bz2")
>>> with bz2.open(path, "wb") as f:
...     _ = f.write(b"line one\nline two\n")
>>> with mibz2.open(path) as f:
...     lines = f.readlines()
...     verified = f.raw.verified
>>> lines, verified
([b'line one\n', b'line two\n'], True)
```

# mibz2 (Rust)

The crate's API documentation is on [docs.rs](<https://docs.rs/mibz2>).

| API | what |
| --- | --- |
| `decode`, `decode_parallel(data, threads)` | a whole .bz2 in memory |
| `BzReader::new(r)`, `BzReader::parallel(r, threads)`, `parallel_with(r, threads, slots, kernels)` | a `Read` adaptor; a bad stream is an `io::Error` (`InvalidData`) wrapping `mibz2::Error` |
| `StreamDecoder::new(threads, slots, kernels)` | the push form: `write` compressed chunks from one thread, `read` decoded bytes from another, `close`, `cancel`; at most `slots` blocks in flight |
| `scan(data)` → `BlockSpan { index, start_bit, end_bit, crc, stream, level }` | block boundaries, without decoding |
| `decode_blocks(data, start_bit, end_bit, level, kernels, out)` → `Range` | a range of whole blocks, each CRC checked |
| `Error { kind: ErrorKind, block, bit }` | what is wrong with the input, and where |
| `Kernels::detect()`, `Kernels::scalar()` | the SIMD kernels, or the portable ones |
| `bwt::InverseBwt` (`Segmented`, the default; `Plain`), `decode_with::<I>`, `StreamDecoder::with_inverse::<I>` | the inverse-BWT kernel, swappable and timeable as part of the whole decoder |

```rust
// the block boundaries (each block's header and Huffman symbols read, nothing decoded),
// then any range of whole blocks decoded on its own, on any thread
let data = std::fs::read("file.bz2")?;
for span in mibz2::scan(&data) {
    let span = span?;
    let mut part = Vec::new();
    let range = mibz2::decode_blocks(&data, span.start_bit, span.end_bit, span.level,
                                      mibz2::Kernels::detect(), &mut part)?;
    // range.blocks: each block's (start bit, end bit, CRC); mibz2::combine(...) gives a
    // stream's combined CRC from its blocks'
}
```

# mibz2

A bzip2 decoder built for memory-level parallelism.

mibz2 decodes bzip2. It is block-parallel, as lbzip2 is. Within a block, its inverse BWT is walked as 32 interleaved chains, so a core keeps many of the walk's cache-missing loads in flight instead of one.

Think of a courier who learns each address only on arriving at the last one: the bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next. That is the ordinary inverse BWT. mibz2 runs 32 such delivery chains through one dispatch centre, so while one waits for its next address, the others move. None of them travels faster; the waits overlap. [Why 32 couriers beat one](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/concepts/couriers/index.md>) explains the idea, where it stops paying, and what has been measured.

- Its output is byte for byte libbzip2's, and every block CRC and stream CRC is checked.
- It runs on any x86-64 or aarch64 CPU. Its SIMD kernels (AVX2, PCLMULQDQ) are chosen at run time, and each has a portable scalar twin.
- The library depends on std only.

```pycon
>>> import mibz2
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(open("file.bz2", "rb").read())
>>> data[:18]
b'line one\nline two\n'
>>> with mibz2.open("file.bz2") as f:
...     lines = f.readlines()
...     verified = f.raw.verified
>>> len(lines), verified
(2000, True)
```

Its name is for "multi-chain inversion of bzip2". It was written in [wikidata-pq](<https://github.com/lmmx/wikidata-pq>), to decode the Wikidata dump, and knows nothing of Wikidata ([history](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/background/history/index.md>)).
